title: Improve version.py generation
description:
I've been working on my own version.py generation for STScI's packages--it works pretty similarly, but with a couple differences:  
- I also started out making it an extension of the build_py command, but I ended up changing it to regenerate the file on every setup.py run--this ensures that an updated version.py file is created for commands such as 'develop' and 'sdist'.  It doesn't seem to add any noticeable time to running setup.py.
- The version.py uses the SVN revision info getter to automatically update its SVN info on import _if_ the package is installed in develop mode.  That way, when installed in develop mode the revision is always up to date.  I would want the same for git.  It doesn't do this if the package is not installed in develop mode, so it doesn't hurt import time otherwise.  The code for doing that is just part of the version.py template.

I'm open to other ideas for exactly how to implement this, but I would want to add these capabilities.

title: sdist doesn't include wcs header files and scripts directory.
description:
Hello,

I tried Python 2.6 and Python 2.7.   Running `python setup.py install` in the `astropy` repo, doesn't create any problems since all the files are accessible. But this is a problem when trying to install this from a `sdist`, for example by automated testing software like `tox`. 

Bug in setuptools/distutils?

Using `recursive-include astropy/wcs/src *.h` in `MANIFEST.in` works.

If `MANIFEST.in` is specified then only the files mentioned in it gets copied; setuptools/distutils does not use its default file finding algorithm in this case. 

Additional comments (with what I think are the reasons):

The `scripts` directory doesn't get copied, since `setup.py` removes the only file `README.rst` in this directory. 

The contents of  `AstroPy.egg-info/` doesn't get cleared/updated between two runs of `setup.py`. For example, say we run `setup.py sdist` using the `MANIFEST.in` mentioned above. Now remove the line from MANIFEST.in, ad run `setup.py` again. This time the header files will get included, even though they are not specified in MANIFEST.in. I guess that this is because the header files get listed in `AstroPy.egg-info/SOURCES.txt` the first time, and the list gets reused. This leads to major confusion: I just lost 1.5 hours. Deleting `AstroPy.egg-info` leads to the previous behaviour.

If `AstroPy.egg-info` is deleted, without deleting `version.py` AND `version.pyc`, then the `import astropy` line in `setup.py` complains that `AstroPy` distribution doesn't exist. The `astropy/__init__.py` tried to run `version.py` which uses `AstroPy`, causing error.

Prasanth

title: Support overriding config options via environment variables
description:
I first wrote this as a comment in #35, but I'm creating a separate issue for this so it doesn't get forgotten. I will volunteer to implement it. This is slightly higher priority now that I'm getting somewhere with PyFITS implementation, and I would like to hook it into the eventual config system. It would be good to have the ability to override any config options via environment variables. These environment variables would follow some standard naming convention like `ASTROPY_SUB_PACKAGE_OPTION`. There could also be some way to register shorter aliases for commonly used options, but I don't have any thoughts yet on the specifics of that.

In order to support these environment variables transparently, the easiest approach I see (which I usually end up doing anyways) is to provide a simple wrapper around `ConfigObj` objects. I like to use something simple like `Configuration`. This is a much simpler object than the `ConfigObj` so that fewer details of reading/writing the configuration are exposed to subpackage/affiliated package authors. It would still provide a dictionary-like interface and many of the methods of `ConfigObj`. Though rather than `write()` it has a `save()` method which I think is a little more obvious. If a user wants to update the configuration they simply call `config.save()`. This method would prevent saving any values that were overridden by environment variables.

Using a wrapper can have other eventual benefits, since it allows us to provide some abstractions around the configuration object that aren't specific to any one backend implementation (not that I would suggest we move away from `ConfigObj` or anything--it's just nice to have additional flexibility).

- astropy.config.configs (maybe?)

title: Issue when multiple conftest.py files are in the tree
description:
I'm running into some issues with running tests in a specific environment (Jenkins + virtualenv) and I've finally figured out to how reproduce it:

```
git clone git://github.com/astropy/astropy.git
cd astropy/
mkdir directory
cd directory/
git clone git://github.com/astropy/astropy.git
cd astropy/
python setup.py test
```

which fails with the following error:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):

    return pytest.main(args=all_args, plugins=plugins)

    self.add_option(option)
  File "/opt/local/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/lib/python2.7/optparse.py", line 1020, in add_option

  File "/opt/local/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/lib/python2.7/optparse.py", line 995, in _check_conflict

```

This is because py.test imports the plugins twice because it finds them in `astropy/conftest.py` _and_ `astropy/directory/astropy/conftest.py`. This is precisely what happens in Jenkins - there is a checkout of astropy inside another checkout of astropy. So is there a way to make sure that py.test stops e.g. at the first `conftest.py`? >>> import astropy.io.fits

title: Implement affiliated package registry
description:
The Astropy vision states that _Affiliated packages will be listed in a central location (in addition to PyPI) that will allow an easy installation of all the affiliated packages, for example with a script that will seamlessly download and install all the affiliated packages. The core package will also include mechanisms to facilitate this installation process._

An easy way to do this would be to simply have a file in the astropy.github.com repository containing a list of affiliated packages with names, URLs, etc., as a JSON file. This file can then be accessed by an affiliated package installer. This also means that affiliated packages are added to the JSON file through proper commits to the astropy.github.com repository, which prevents anyone from registering a package. I can take a stab at this, unless anyone has a better idea for how to implement this?

title: When to install compatibility packages
description:
I'm confused by the Astropy behavior with compatibility packages. At the moment, if I have the genuine pyfits installed, and no astropy installation, astropy installs the legacy shim. If the legacy shim is already installed, it doesn't install it. This seems to be contradictory with the warning message:

```
------------------------------------------------------------
The legacy package 'vo' was found.
To install astropy's compatibility layer instead, uninstall
'vo' and then reinstall astropy.
------------------------------------------------------------
```

which suggests to me that the correct behavior is that if the _real_ PyFITS is installed ('legacy package'), then the shim should _not_ be installed, and that if people want the shim, they should uninstall the real package. However, if the installed `pyfits` is the legacy shim, then it should be re-installed in case it has been updated. Is that not the intended behavior? If so, the following code has the wrong logic:

```
found_legacy_module = False
try:
    location = imp.find_module(old_package)
except ImportError:
    pass
else:
    # We want ImportError to raise here, because that means it was
    # found, but something else went wrong.

    # We could import the module here to determine if its "real"
    # or just a legacy alias.  However, importing the legacy alias
    # may cause importing of code within the astropy source tree,
    # which may require 2to3 to have been run.  It's safer to just
    # open the file and search for a string.
    filename = os.path.join(location[1], '__init__.py')
    if os.path.exists(filename):
        with open(filename, 'U') as fd:
            if '_is_astropy_legacy_alias' in fd.read():
                found_legacy_module = True

shim_dir = os.path.join(get_legacy_alias_dir(), old_package)

if found_legacy_module:
    warn('-' * 60)
    warn("The legacy package '{0}' was found.".format(old_package))
    warn("To install astropy's compatibility layer instead, uninstall")
    warn("'{0}' and then reinstall astropy.".format(old_package))
    warn('-' * 60)

    if os.path.isdir(shim_dir):
        shutil.rmtree(shim_dir)
    return (None, None)
```

I think it should be:

```
if '_is_astropy_legacy_alias' not in fd.read():
```

title: io.fits should return table data as Astropy Tables
description:
This issue here as a reminder that this work needs to be done at some point (there's also a ticket for this in PyFITS' tracker).  Currently PyFITS/astropy.io.fits has its own custom array class for representing FITS table data.  Since FITS tables do have a few "special" features it will probably still be necessary to have a special class specifically for FITS tables, though for the sake of consistency it should at least be based on the Astropy Table class (which is a lot cleaner and more usable than what PyFITS currently has anyways).

This won't be doable for the first release--it's a big change and will be very difficult, if not impossible, to implement in a backwards compatible manner.  For the first release it's probably better that astropy.io.fits (not to mention the pyfits legacy shim) work as a drop-in replacement for PyFITS.

This work will also have to be backported to PyFITS, so I'll want to tie it to an eventual PyFITS release.

title: Should fitscheck be renamed
description:
Dear developers,

Both astropy and python-pyfits provide a 'fistscheck' program which could lead to a conflict when both are installed.  If the two programs do the same job, we can keep the same name and it's up to the distribution packagers to decide which one to use.
But if astropy's fitscheck is significantly different, maybe it's a good idea to use a different name so that both versions can co-exist (and because packagers could choose different name to avoid the conflict in their distributions).

Yannick

title: Provide a way to define named hyperlinks in autogenerated docs
description:
The docstrings in `io.vo` have a number of links into the VOTable standard.

It is much nicer to write:

```
A class to represent the top-level VOTABLE_ element.
```

and put

```
.. _VOTABLE: http://www.ivoa.net/Documents/PR/VOTable/VOTable-20040322.html#ToC9
```

elsewhere at the top of the `rst` file, than it is to put

```
A class to represent the top-level `VOTABLE <http://www.ivoa.net/Documents/PR/VOTable/VOTable-20040322.html#ToC9>`_ element.
```

directly in the docstring.  Aside from being harder to write, they make using the docstring in a tool like IPython (at the console) much clumsier.

In the current iteration of the `io.vo` docs, there is a `references.txt` file and each file has an `.. include::` directive at the top to include this file.  I wonder whether it's possible to include this from each generated documentation page, or achieve a similar result by some other means...

title: Implement writing to .fits.gz files
description:

```
IOError: Writing to gzipped fits files is not currently supported
```

Given that the `gzip` module is in the standard library in Python, is there any reason why this can't be done?

title: Combining Table objects
description:
This is a feature request for various ways to combine `Table` objects. Specifically, it would be useful to have the option to:
- append two tables (similar to `append` in ATpy, but more robust to slight differences in types). This would be useful for two tables that have the same columns, and where one table should be appended after the other.
- joining two tables either via inner or outer joins (see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Join_(SQL)). I already started working on something like that for ATpy, but it never quite made it, see https://gist.github.com/877990 (however, that code does seem to be pretty generic and fast, so it might be recyclable).

cc @taldcroft

title: Improve Table slice behavior for string-type input
description:
From the discussion for PR #264.

Indexing a table with something like `t[['a', 'b', 'c']]` might succeed or might throw a cryptic exception.  Even in the success case the returned object is probably broken.  The docs are clear on this but it would be better if the code doesn't allow such badness.

The code thinks that it is getting a "slice" which could be an actual slice object or an np fancy index slice.  So it makes a new table with the same column definitions and then applies the "slice" to the `ndarray` data object.  That explains the misordering because an `ndarray` can also accept a list of column names, but the new Table gets defined with the original column names.

``` python

    def _new_from_slice(self, slice_):
        """Create a new table as a referenced slice from self."""

        table = Table()
        table.meta = deepcopy(self.meta)
        cols = self.columns.values()
        names = [col.name for col in cols]
        data = self._data[slice_]

        self._update_table_from_cols(table, data, cols, names)

        return table
```

I think it could be a little more clever and if `_slice` is not an actual `slice` object, then try `_slice = np.asarray(_slice)`.  That will use numpy to efficiently determine the types of everything in `_slice` and fail if they are not homogeneous.  It also allows detecting at that point if `_slice` consists of all strings in which case the tuple path of `__getitem__` could be taken.  I think this strategy would be reasonably efficient since `np.asarray` will just pass back anything this is already an ndarray, and I bet numpy does this anyway on a list input to `ndarray.__getItem__`.

title: Issues for next release
description:
Below is a list of issues/items to consider changing regarding the release process, based on my experience doing the 0.1 release.
1. I added an instruction about this, but it's sort of in a strange order right now: I think it's good to have whoever is doing the release do a `python setup.py sdist` and then _test_ that it can be unpacked, built, and have the tests succeed.  Right now that comes _after_ the tag is committed, so you'd have to reset the repo to go back and fix problems that it might reveal.  So a better ordering would be to have the releaser first make the changes to the version number, then do an `sdist`, then unpack, build, and test the sdist, and only if that succeeds does it actually commit the release tag.
2. `python setup.py install` is necessary right now (along with the virtualenv), but only because the `zest.releaser` hooks need to be installed.  It seems strange to require an install to do a source release, so if `zest.releaser` is not used in the next round, the install and virtualenv could be eliminated.  In this case, however, it's important to make sure a build happens, because otherwise Cython won't compile the .pyx files to .c (and the .c files are necessary for release).
3. It's confusing that we use `zest.releaser`, but then don't actually use its upload feature.  So it might be good to either put in a hook to have it not try to upload, or dispense with `zest.releaser`
4. Right now, the PyPI entry is registered with my account - it's probably not important right now, but it should probably be changed at some point to be based on the astropy.team e-mail account (I _think_ PyPI lets you designate people as having rights to edit an entry, so we could do that).
5. Items 1-3 above would probably require some major hacking in `zest.releaser`, so it might be easier to write our own self-contained script, and just pull parts of `zest.releaser` where convenient (particularly the PyPI interaction and the version file changes, which we're still using mostly unmodified).
6. We should also add a file in the docs to store public keys for checking releases, and this needs to be added to the release procedures.

@iguananaut - should I assign this to you, or would you prefer not to deal with it?

title: Unify section header characters
description:
This is a placeholder if someone has the desire to unify the section header characters throughout the astropy docs to use the same ordering, which is now standardized as `* = - ^ " + : ~`.

I wrote a quick script to determine all unique sets of character orders used in the RST section headers.  I _think_ it works, but this was fast without too much test.  It's here in this gist: https://gist.github.com/3208992.

Upshot: for astropy RST files in docs/ the sets we use are:

```
  % find . -name "*.rst" | xargs ./header_chars.py
  ...  # bunch of files and their section orderings
  #*=
  *=-"
  *=-^"
  -^".
  -^">
  =-^"
  =-`
```

You can find which files correspond to a particular set with (e.g.):

```
  % find . -name "*.rst" | xargs ./header_chars.py | grep '=-`'
  ./wcs/history.rst =-`
  =-`
```

It's probably not much work to take this script and extend to actually do the fixing.

title: io.ascii doesn't know about table column formats
description:
If I make an `astropy.table.Table` and do `table['somecolumn'].format = '%.2f'`, the various table printing methods work as expected: the column prints as a 2 sigfig floating point number.  However, if I then do `astropy.io.ascii.write(table,'somefile.dat')`, the resulting ascii file does _not_ respect the format specifier for the column.

I'm not actually sure if it's better to have it do so or not, but it's ambiguous whether it's supposed to or not, so this issue can be viewed as either a request to implement this (respecting `format` when using `astropy.io.ascii.write` on a table), or clarifying in the docs that this will _not_ work the way one might expect.

RuntimeError: maximum recursion depth exceeded while calling a Python object
```

After further investigation, it looks like an upstream issue with numpy. See: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/385
This could be circumvented by modifying the `__repr__` method of `astropy.table.Row`

```
def __repr__(self):
    return "<Row {0} of table\n values={1}\n dtype={2}>".format(
        self.index, self.data, self.dtype)
```

by

```
def __repr__(self):
    return "<Row {0} of table\n values={1!r}\n dtype={2}>".format(
        self.index, self.data, self.dtype)
```

Note: `self.data` is the one with type `numpy.void` and causing the problem

title: Allow for multi-dimensional input values to Time
description: Currently Time accepts only scalar or 1-d values.  It should be easy enough to allow multi-dimensional inputs, but this requires tests and doc changes.  This issue is a placeholder to implement this improvement.

title: Improve scale validation infrastructure in Time
description:
The current `Time` code correctly does validation of the input scale in all cases (AFAIK).  But it is done in a somewhat fragile way that should be improved.  

The issue is that in some cases (mostly string formats) the validation needs to be deferred until after the format class has determined whether or not the input values are appropriate.  This is to allow for auto-format detection.  In other formats the scale validation is done in `set_jds()`.  If a new TimeFormat subclass is created the coder needs to know where to do the validation.  So it's not very clean at this point, though as said all existing code does work.

title: Leap second handling in Time (future-proofing)
description: Time currently uses a SOFA routine that only knows about leap seconds through July 2012.  This may need to be updated in a few years.

title: Use table interpolation to provide default UT1 to UTC offset
description: Tables published by the Internation Earth Rotation and Reference System Service (IERS) provide the UT1 to UTC offset over some range.  Get a good version of such a table and use it to provide default UT1 to UTC offsets if the user doesn't supply them.

title: Allow users choice of providing UT1-TT or UT1-TAI in Time
description:
From @fgrollier on astropy-dev:

In the current implementation of Time, there is only one way to go from one timescale to UT1, which is to provide `dut1 = UT1-UTC`. This is problematic because it allows to compute UT1 only in the time span where UTC is defined. I think the user should have the choice of providing (UT1-TT or UT1-TAI), these values being the only ones available for very broad validity range.

title: Transparently support uint16 and uint32 in astropy.io.fits (for tables)
description:
It would be great if PyFITS could transparently support unsigned 16- and 32-bit integers in Tables. Even though the FITS standard does not directly support this, a 16-bit unsigned integer can be written as a 16-bit signed integer with BSCALE=1 and BZERO= 32768. Similarly, a 32-bit unsigned integer can be written as a 32-bit signed integer with BSCALE=1 and BZERO= 2147483648. This could work for both input and output - i.e. if a 16-bit unsigned integer is written, then BZERO and BSCALE are set appropriately, and if BSCALE=1 and BZERO=32768 and the column is a 16-bit signed integer, it is converted to a 16-bit unsigned integer upon reading.

For info, cfitsio already does this: http://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/fitsio/c/c_user/node23.html

[Note: This functionality already works in PyFITS using uint=True when opening the file. However it only works for images, not tables.]

title: Consider moving `astropy.io.vo` to `astropy.vo`
description:
Since the Astropy `vo` sub-package may end up implementing more than just a file format, I wonder whether it would make more sense to move it to `astropy.vo`. For example, if in future we supported a VO cross-matching service, this is not really I/O. I'm bringing this up before 0.2 as it''d be good to decide on this before the first public release, since it represents a big change in API. I guess that I worry that sub-packages could end up being buried deeply:

```
astropy.io.vo.table
astropy.io.vo.samp
astropy.io.vo.cone_search
```

etc. I don't feel _strongly_ about it, but it's been nagging me for a while. One _could_ consider getting rid of `io` alltogether and moving `fits` to the top-level and `ascii` to `astropy.table.ascii` (since it's specifically table I/O). Anyway, just an idea, but wanted to see what other people thought about this.

cc: @mdboom @taldcroft @iguananaut @eteq

title: Issue with operations on ``astropy.table.Column``
description:

In [5]: t['a']
Out[5]: 
<Column name='a' units=None format=None description=None>
array([1, 2, 3])

In [6]: t['a'].mean()
Out[6]: 
<Column name='a' units=None format=None description=None>
array(2.0)
```

Maybe this is a feature and not a bug, but I just wanted to check whether we should consider this intended behavior? Should operations that return a scalar just return the scalar, not in a Column object?

title: Fractional powers in the Units subpackage
description:
Right now, units can only have integer or integer + 0.5 powers. I can see how this would make the internals easier, but it does lead to some unexpected behavior (from a user-perspective). For example, let's say I have a volume `Quantity` -- I can't take the cubed root of that object because units don't know how to handle

```
(u.m**3)**(1./3)
```

Another example is in polytropic stellar structure equations, where there may be something like

```
density^(4/3) / mass^(1/3)
```

We know that the units reduce to something like `kg / m^4`, but this isn't supported.

I'm not sure there is an easy way to implement this -- in fact, I can only think of fairly convoluted solutions -- but I at least wanted to get some discussion going on this.

title: Increase default precision in output ASCII files
description:
If I read the following file:

http://www.mpia.de/~robitaille/astropy/aj285677t2_votable.xml

and output it to an ASCII table:

```
from astropy.io.votable import parse

f = parse('aj285677t2_votable.xml')

t = f.get_first_table().to_table()

t.write('aj285677t2_votable.txt', format='ascii')
```

the precision on the floating point values is too low:

```
col1 col2 col3 col4 col5 col6 col7 col8 col9 col10 col11 col12 col13 col14 col15 col16 col17
"SSTGLMC G000.0000+00.1611" 0 0.1611 266.2 -28.85 nan nan nan 9.8 9.2 8.6 8.1 9.1 8.2 nan nan AA
"SSTGLMC G000.0000-00.4342" 0 -0.4342 266.8 -29.16 nan nan 12 8.3 6.7 5.4 4.3 6.9 4.3 nan 0.89 IA
"SSTGLMC G000.0031-00.5072" 0.0031 -0.5072 266.9 -29.2 nan nan nan 13 10 7.6 5.7 10 5.7 nan 1.4 IA
```

I feel like by default the ASCII output should match the precision of the floating point values, i.e. ~8 significant digits for float32, and ~14-15 for float64. In ATpy, we used the approach that the values should round trip (to within floating point precision) when writing/reading to e.g. IPAC tables.

@taldcroft - what do you think?

title: Improve numeric Table / io.ascii output precision
description:
In `Table` column output  there is some loss of precision possible because when no column format is specified then the output defaults to `str`, which doesn't round-trip for full precision doubles.   This affects `io.ascii.write` because that uses the `Table` formatting machinery.   See #526 which was the genesis of this issue.

From Python 2.7, `repr` is a good choice for numbers because it makes the output the smallest possible that is consistent with a binary value.  But for previous python versions I believe `repr` will generate a lot of `0.9999999999234232` where users would expect `1.0`.   @astrofrog has data indicating most astropy users are on Python 2.7 or later.

``` python
In [44]: t = Table([[1.000000000000056789]], names=['a'])

In [45]: print t
 a 

---
1.0

In [46]: t
Out[46]: 
<Table rows=1 names=('a')>
array([(1.0000000000000568,)], 
      dtype=[('a', '<f8')])

In [47]: from astropy.io import ascii

In [48]: ascii.write(t)
a
1.0
```

title: Add feature: rotate spherical coordinate
description:
Once #471 gets merged I want to add code to rotate a given point on the sphere around a given center by a given angle.

Should this be implemented as an independent function

```
def rotate(point, center, angle)
```

or a `SphericalCoordinatesBase` method?

```
SphericalCoordinatesBase.rotate(center, angle)
```

I think it's very easy to implement with numpy:
- Transform `center` to `point` system
- Convert `center` and `point` 3D cartesian vectors
- Compute rotated `point` vector using Rodrigues formula ( http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigues%27_rotation_formula )
- Convert rotated `point` vector back to spherical coordinates.

@eteq Is this a welcome addition?

title: Copying astropy objects
description:
Being able to make an independent copy of a given object is generally useful for almost all objects.

The use case I have in mind is this: I often write functions that take an input object (a Time, Coordinate, Table, HDU, WCS, ...) and I want to change some attributes without having to know or care about all other attributes, and return a modified version, leaving the input object unchanged.

One example is #542, where I wanted to copy and modify a Coordinate but didn't know how to do it ...

Python programmers are usually familiar with the `copy(x)` and `deepcopy(x)` functions from the Python standard library [copy module](http://docs.python.org/3/library/copy.html).

This would be one option for astropy, we would have to add `__copy__()` and `__deepcopy__()` for classes where the default Python behaviour wouldn't work (I haven't tried calling `copy` and `deepcopy` for many astropy objects, so who knows, maybe this already works very well everywhere?) but in any case we should test and document it for end-users if this is the standard way to work in astropy.

The alternative is to add `.copy(self)` and / or `.deepcopy(self)` or `copy(self, deep=True)` methods to most classes. Some `astropy` classes like `astropy.units.quantity.Quantity` or `astropy.wcs.wcs.Wcs` do this already:
http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/search.html?q=copy

Many others, like e.g.  `astropy.table.Table` or `astropy.coordinates.GalacticCoordinate`  don't have a `copy(self)` method.

There is one class, `astropy.time.Time`, which calls `deepcopy` [replicate](http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/_generated/astropy.time.core.Time.html?#astropy.time.core.Time.replicate).

What do we want for `astropy`?

If others think this is an important topic we could try to hash out a proposal here and then put it on `astropy-dev` mailing list or as an `astropy-api` pull request?

The most important point I think would be to hash out the semantics of `copy` and `deepcopy` for each case and how to write unit tests in a generic way so that the effort of adding this to all astropy objects remains small.

title: Add concurrent.futures to astropy.utils.compat
description:
Pun not intended in the milestone.

Python 3.2 adds a nice interface for async execution of background tasks: http://docs.python.org/dev/library/concurrent.futures.html

There's already a need for this kind of functionality in #552 (which is currently fulfilled by a simple thread-based approach), and I suspect there will be others.  A backport of this module exists and is based on the original reference implementation for the PEP that described this feature: http://pypi.python.org/pypi/futures

It's a small and simple library, and we should consider including it with our other batteries.

title: Add format keyword to io.ascii read and write, deprecate Reader and Writer

Use the same string values as in `Table`.  The `Reader` and `Writer` keywords to provide a Reader/Writer class will be deprecated in 0.3 and eventually removed.

title: IPython notebooks for astropy tutorials
description:
It would be nice to have IPython notebooks for astropy tutorial.

This has been mentioned [here](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/357#issuecomment-11384929), but should be discussed independently of that ticket.

Ideally there would be a simple workflow where the rendered notebooks are converted to `rst` and rendered in the `astropy` theme.

This is pretty new territory, but here are some references where this or something similar has been discussed / tried:
- http://jakevdp.github.com/mpl_tutorial/#
- https://github.com/ipython/nbconvert/pull/35
- https://github.com/ipython/nbconvert/issues/54
- http://statsmodels.sourceforge.net/devel/examples/index.html

Besides from the technical issue, there's the question of where to put the notebooks and how to integrate it with the existing astropy website or sphinx docs.
Here my suggestion would be to let anyone make astropy notebooks, put them in their own github repos or gists, render them with nbviewer and collect links with one-line descriptions at
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/wiki/notebooks

If that sounds OK I can add that wiki page and make a short astropy intro notebook that demonstrates a few lines of code from each astropy sub-package, probably simply copy & pasting the first example from the sphinx docs of each astropy sub-package. This could be a nice way for people to start exploring astropy.

title: Decompose cgs units to other cgs units
description:
This is something I noticed with looking into #572:

```
In [1]: from astropy.constants.cgs import e

In [2]: e.unit.decompose()
Out[2]: Unit("3.162278e-05 kg(1/2) m(3/2) / (s)")
```

This is correct, but I still would have expected:

```
Out[2]: Unit("g(1/2) cm(3/2) / (s)")
```

Since the scale on what I get instead is not 1, it seems like this could lead to trouble if one is not careful.  I'm not sure how easy this is to fix though.

title: Add support for PC001001 style keywords in astropy.wcs
description:
It would be nice if astropy.wcs could support the PC001001 syntax (for what should be PC1_1 according to the WCS papers).

As pointed out by @iguananaut:

http://tdc-www.harvard.edu/wcstools/wcstools.wcs.PC00

> The 1996 proposed FITS WCS standard used PC001001, PC001002, PC002001, and PC002002 to represent the rotation matrix but retained CDELT1 and CDELT2 for the scale. It is also read by this software, but should not be used for new WCS's.

I've come across modern files that use this convention, and such files don't cause astropy.wcs to crash - it just returns the wrong result, which is dangerous.

distribute-setup.py has a DEFAULT_VERSION set to 0.6.28, while the versions are:

  - testing (upcoming Wheezy): 0.6.24
- in Ubuntu

  - Quantal (12.10) 0.6.28 (resp. 0.6.28dev-r0)

title: Add On / off Poisson stats methods
description:
I would like to add on / off Poisson stats methods to `astropy.stats` but wanted to discuss the methods and API before making a pull request.

In X-ray and gamma-ray astronomy it is common to count the number of events in an `on` region that (potentially) contains signal and background and an `off` region that should only contain background. Typically the background exposure ratio
`alpha = on_exposure / off_exposure`
is known for the instrument and one then goes on to estimate
`background = alpha x off`
for the on region and
`excess = on - background`.
It is known that the `on` and `off` counts are Poisson distributed and the goal is to estimate the signal strength and significance.

The formulas to compute the significance of the observed excess are (at least in gamma-ray astronomy) computed with the Li&Ma formula (see https://gist.github.com/4478124#file-on_off-py-L67 ). The inverse problem of computing the sensitivity (required excess given some background level and desired significance) has to be computed using an iterative numerical method (see https://gist.github.com/4478124#file-on_off-py-L197 ), so does the excess error.

A very common special case that should be implemented directly is that the background level for the on region (where the source is) is know without statistical error:

```
def significance(x, mu):
    """Li & Ma formula for alpha -> 0.
    @param x: measured on count
    @param mu: known background level in on region"""
    return sign(x - mu) * sqrt(2) * sqrt(x * log(x / mu) - x + mu)
```

Other useful Poisson count stats related functions are [cash](http://cxc.cfa.harvard.edu/sherpa/statistics/#cash) and [cstat](http://cxc.cfa.harvard.edu/sherpa/statistics/#cstat), which are already implemented in [sherpa.stats](https://github.com/taldcroft/sherpa/blob/master/stats/__init__.py)

Other common methods in gamma-ray astronomy and high-energy physics are[Rolke](http://root.cern.ch/root/html/TRolke.html) and [Feldman-Cousins](http://root.cern.ch/root/html/TFeldmanCousins.html).

There's many more useful Poisson count data related methods (approximations, ways to include systematic errors, ...)

My suggestion would be to implement the methods mentioned above (and more as needed by others) in a separate module `astropy.stats.poisson`, or make that a package with a few sub-modules.
Some iterative methods like Feldman-Cousins will have to be implemented in C or C++ or Cython.

One big question is whether we should use functions or classes, e.g.

```
def lima_significance(on, off, alpha):
    return ...
```

or

```
class OnOffMeasurement:
    def __init__(on, off, alpha):
        ...
```

with significance, ... as members.

---

@taldcroft and others, please comment:
- What methods do we want in `astropy.stats`? (I've mentioned what I want / need above)
- What API do we want? (I have a slight preference for functions at the moment)
- How should we implement this? (write everything from scratch using `numpy` and `scipy.stats` and `scipy.optimize` and iterative methods in Cython? or write everything in C and wrap with Cython?)

title: Add lookup and fill methods to NDData or Histogram
description:
Would it make sense to add lookup and fill methods to NDData or to create a `Histogram` sub-class?

The use cases I have in mind are:
- Given an image and a list of float pixel coordinates (e.g. source positions from SExtractor), `look up` the values of the pixels corresponding to those pixel coordinates. This is nontrivial to get right without a 0.5 or 1 pixel shift.
- Given an image and a list of world coordinates, `look up` the corresponding pixel values. This would probably be implemented by converting to pixel coordinates and then calling lookup on these, but it would be be convenient for the user to simply give world coordinates and not have to think about the pixel coordinate definition (where is `(0,0), (0.5,0.5), (1,1)`).
- Given an image with coordinates `RA, DEC` or spectrum with coordinate `Energy` or cube with coordinates `GLON, GLAT, Energy` and a list of coordinates, `fill` the image/spectrum/cube with these events.
- As for `lookup`, it would be nice if `fill` would either accept pixel or world coordinates.

Some background: in high-energy physics or X-ray and gamma-ray astronomy data typically either consists of event lists (e.g. each photon has a reconstructed position and energy). It is common to have millions or billions of events and to run binned analyses by histogramming the events first, which is what `fill` does, so this should be as fast as possible.
It might actually make sense to think about creating a separate `NDHistogram` class as an `NDData` subclass, with functionality similar to what the high-energy physicists use
http://root.cern.ch/download/doc/3Histograms.pdf
but aware of FITS pixel coordinate binning convention and world coordinates.

title: Support updating astropy config defaults when updating versions
description:
The astropy configuration system was adjusted in #498 so that it generates a default configuration file at `python setup.py install`, but waits until astropy is imported to place that file in the users' astropy configuration directory.  This works fine once, but if the configuration options are changed in later versions, the file is not updated unless the user deletes it.  

As discussed on the mailing list, a good solution to this is to essentially diff the users' configuration file against the default, and add any lines that the user hasn't changed, but astropy's defaults _have_ changed.  We should try to implement this for v0.3.0, or possibly v0.2.1

(@mdboom and @iguananaut were involved heavily in these discussions, so if either of you want to take it on, feel free.  Otherwise I will try to at some point)

title: python setup.py install in clean repo bypasses custom build
description:
If we run:

```
python setup.py build
python setup.py install
```

then the custom build command is used for the build, and the custom install command for install. However, if in a clean repository, we do:

```
python setup.py install
```

the custom build command never gets executed (instead, `build_py` and `build_ext` are called). This means that when doing

```
python setup.py install
```

in a clean repository, the config file will never get generated, which causes `import astropy` to not work _anywhere_ because there is no default config file (since this gets generated in the custom build command). See #651 where I ran into this issue.

EDIT: just to clarify, for anyone not familiar with the code - this is because the config file gets generated inside the custom AstropyBuild.run method, which does not get called if running only `install`.

@eteq @iguananaut - any ideas?

title: Support Quantity, Time, and Coordinates in Table objects
description:
This idea resulted from a discussion with @hamogu today - it would be nice to have the concept of columns in tables intelligently dealing with e.g. Quantity, Time, or Coordinate (once they support arrays) columns. For example, it would be nice to be able to do:

```
>>> t = Table()
>>> t.add_column(Column('obsdate', Time(np.array([1.,2.,3.]), scale='utc')))
```

and then `t['obsdate]` would seamlessly return a `Time` object. This could also work for coordinates (once they support arrays). Maybe this is too much magic, but I was trying to think of how one would actually store coordinates and times in tables in practice, and this seemed like it would make it very easy for users. Along the same lines, one could just store any arbitrary `Quantity` object:

```
>>> t.add_column(Column('d', np.array([1,2,3]) * u.m))
>>> t['d']
<Quantity [1 2 3] m>
```

with the unit being separated from the array and stored in the `Column` unit attribute until the data is accessed again. Of course, this raises the issue of whether in general, accessing a column or a cell should return the value, or a `Quantity` if units are present.

title: suggest_backports.py issues
description:
I'm working now on backporting a lot of the merged PRs for v0.2.x.  It's mostly going smoothly but I need to document a few issues that have cropped up:
1. There was apparently a manual merge of #629, though the script still picked that up as a merged PR. However, it failed to return the correct merge commit for that PR. Instead it returned the SHA for the last commit before the merge.  I'm not sure why that is but I suspect it could have something to do with how github handles the events on manually merged PRs.
2. If one runs the script multiple times between tags it still lists commits that have already been cherry-picked and backported. It's not clever enough to filter out all PRs that have already been backported. In particular, this can happen when commit message comparison fails, because sometimes when cherry-picking there will be a merge conflict, which causes the autogenerated commit message to append a list of files that conflicted.  This part of the commit messages needs to be ignored.
3. Turns out walking commits is even more subtle than I thought; I naively assumed GitHub's API would just automatically list commits in the order that they're shown in GitHub's GUI. But alas we have to write our own code to handle DAG walking.

title: Simplify boilerplate code for subclassing SphericalCoordinatesBase
description:

When subclassing SphericalCoordinatesBase, one has to use a private function to auto-generate the appropriate attributes, and a lengthy and confusing template to overwrite the docstrong for any particular latitude/longitude-like coordinate system.  It would be better if this was less complicated.  

This could either be implemented as an all-in-one sort of private function, using a metaclass, or possibly even just suitably altering `SphericalCoordinatesBase.__init__`.

title: Angle.format doesn't pad for neative angles
description:
I noticed incorrect behavior in an oddly particular case:

```
>>> a = coords.Angle(-1.36546543,'deg')
>>> a.format(u.degree,sep=':',pad=True,precision=2,alwayssign=True)
'-1:21:55.68'
```

The problem is that there should be a '0' between the '-' and the '1'. Note that this is specific to negative angles - the 0 goes in correctly for positive angles:

```
>>> a = coords.Angle(1.36546543,'deg')
>>> a.format(u.degree,sep=':',pad=True,precision=2,alwayssign=True)
'+01:21:55.68'
```

title: Developer documentation: write "HOW TO" about package data in affiliated packages.
description:
Affiliated packages for various subfields of astronomy are likely to include package data specific to the subfield. It would be nice to have a step-by-step "HOW TO" (with an example) in the developer documentation on the proper way to include such data.

There are currently guidelines on package data and configuration [here](http://astropy.readthedocs.org/en/latest/development/codeguide.html#data-and-configuration). The process is fairly obvious for small data (<100kb), but it is not exactly clear how to extend the outlined process to a third-party server for the affiliated package. One might be able to figure it out by reading the docs for `astropy.config` and `astropy.utils.data`, but it would be nice to have a simple example that shows the following:
1. Adding a default configuration file for the affiliated package (wherein the `dataurl` for the affiliated package is set)
2. How to appropriately name your data files on the server side.
3. A simple class or function in the affiliated package that uses the data.

The documentation might also address some related questions that came up for me regarding data file sizes:

**Related question 1:** How big is too big? (for even the externally hosted data scheme) Specifically, I'm thinking here of the SFD dust maps, which are ~200MB.

**Related question 2:** Is/should/could there be a way to install or cache files somewhere other than the user's home directory? (1) For a system-wide install used by multiple users, you might want to only have one copy of the package data. (2) Also, on some systems, disk quotas in home directories are quite small and data is meant to reside elsewhere (or should the user just set `XDG_CACHE_HOME` accordingly in this case?)

title: Add "extragalactic" and "galactic" unit systems
description:
#579 added the `to_system` functionality to `units`.  This provides an easy way to convert units between `cgs` and `si`.  A nice addition would be to also support `galactic` and `extragalactic` unit systems.  These systems would be like `cgs`, but with the natural length scale in `kpc` or possibly `Mpc` for `extragalactic` and `pc` for `galactic`, and with `km/s` the natural velocity scale.

This _may_ require more work, because `km/s` is not an irreducible unit.  But I haven't looked closely enough to know how one might do this with the `to_system` logic.

cc @mdboom

title: Name resolve test failures
description:
I've been getting some semi-random test failures in `astropy.coordinates.tests.test_name_resolve` due to HTTP timeouts and the like.

These tests really ought not be making actual HTTP requests.  They should use some pre-canned "correct" responses from the sesame server and use mock HTTP requests to get them.

title: Exception logging tests failing in ipython
description:
On both Astropy master and on the v0.2.x branch, when I run `astropy.test()` from an IPython prompt I get failures in the `test_exception_logging` and `test_exception_logging_origin` tests.

Based on what I can tell from the debugging I've done so far, upon first import the exception logging hook _does_ get installed properly through the IPython exception handling mechanisms.  But somewhere in the course of the tests (and this happens even when just testing the 'tests' package) `sys.excepthook` is being reset to the original built in hook.

title: LDFLAGS not used
description:
The Debian packaging system uses a special set of LDFLAGS (and CFLAGS, CPPFLAGS as well) to enhance the security of libraries and executables, see http://wiki.debian.org/HardeningWalkthrough

The current release (0.2b2) does not obey if LDFLAGS are set. Instead, is always uses its own set of flags. It would be nice if LDFLAGS would be used in the 0.2 release. Otherwise, could I get some advice on how to use them?

title: Allow Table.add_column to use kwargs to create a new column
description:
(this was partially inspired by discussion in #726) 

Right now, to create a new Column in a table, you have to do:

```
tab.add_column(Column(...))
```

that is, you have to explicitly create a Column object, even if that's the only thing you pass into `add_column`.  I propose to enhance this to allow the following usage:

```
tab.add_column(name='a',data=somearray)
```

which would be the same as

```
tab.add_column(Column(name='a',data=somearray))
```

This would be fully backwards-compatible.  The only catch is that the `index` and `col` keywords have to be available to `add_column`, so they can't be passed on to `Column`.  This doesn't seem too much of a problem, though, because `Column` doesn't currently have  either keyword (and I can't think of any reason why it would in the future).

I'm happy to implement this myself, but if @taldcroft or @astrofrog think it's a bad idea, I don't want to spend the time to do so.

title: Tool to get SFD dustmap values
description:
(This is based in part on the discussion in #700) 

We should add a function/class that retrieves the Schlegel, Finkbeiner, and Davis 1998 dustmaps, caches them, and uses that to get E(B-V) at arbitrary locations (specified by objects from `astropy.coordinates`).  We probably also should include the R_X coefficients from the SFD paper, so people can get out extinctions directly in their preferred bandpass.

We might also include the improved [Schlafly & Finkbeiner 2011](http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...737..103S) calibrations, although that might not be "standard" enough yet.

Note that there's already a python/numpy [implementation of the interpolation scheme in astropysics.](https://github.com/eteq/astropysics/blob/master/astropysics/obstools.py#L2272) So most of the work is already done between that and the astropy data/caching framework.

title: `download_file` does not do anything about encodings
description:
This is prompted by #491, where it was discovered that our `--remote-data` tests were not working because Travis gets http://www.google.com somewhere that uses `iso-8859-1` encoding (and the ü character). `astropy.utils.data.download_file` had no way of knowing this, so it assumed ascii and failed to decode the page.  #734 will solve this particular problem by switching us to a web page that will always have consistent encoding.

However, the underlying problem (?) remains: `download_file` doesn't look into the html headers.  The "content-type" header carries the character set information on google's page, so when the download is finished and the url request discarded, that information is lost.  To make things even more annoying, there are actually a bunch of different ways a file can specify it's encoding - 3 different syntaxes that are actually in the HTML (for regular HTML, HTML5, and XHTML) in addition to the "content-type"...which some servers use and some don't.

I can imagine a few solutions: we could add keywords to `download_file` that one could use to decode the downloaded file (unless 'b' is in the mode).  Or we could try to automatically decide when this needs to happen (based on reading "content-type" add perhaps the content itself).  Or we can just leave it alone and say its up to the user to know what the encoding is. (Which I imagine will almost always be true in typical astronomy data cases.)

P.S. there is now a file at http://www.astropy.org/_static/test_encoding.html that's encoded in iso-8859-1 with ü in it.  That can be used to create tests if we actually do anything about this.

title: Include units in Table column descriptions
description:
This was discussed briefly in #683 - it would be nice if the basic 'ascii' output from Table also included units information, when present.  E.g., writing a table with  `t.write('filename', format='ascii')` where the columns have units should give something like:

```
#distance time
#meter second
1.2 3.4
5.6 7.8
```

title: Add direct method for getting pretty-formatted strings from coordinate objects
description:
Prompted by @pllim's question on the astropy-dev list, it occured to me that it would be useful to have a `format()` method on coordinates.  That is, the following ought to work:

```
>>> c = ICRSCoordinates(187.70592, 12.39112, unit=(u.degree, u.degree))
>>> c.format()
'12h30m49.4208s +12d23m28.0320s'
>>> str(c) == c.format()
```

`format` would have some options to control formatting, and would be all syntactic sugar over the existing `Angle.format()` options.  The main point would be to use sensible defaults - i.e. equatorial-like coordinates would output "xxhyymzz.zs +dxxmyyszz.z" style and the like.

title: Quantity is mutable but defines a __hash__ method
description:
The `astropy.units.Quantity` class is mutable because its `value` and `unit` properties both have setters, but it also declares a `__hash__` method. Usually, only immutable objects should be hashable.

Here are two distinct Quantities:

```
>>> from astropy import units as u
>>> a = 5 * u.second
>>> b = 6 * u.second
```

And here they are as keys of a dictionary:

```
>>> c = {a: 'foo', b: 'bar'}
>>> c
{<Quantity 5 s>: 'foo', <Quantity 6 s>: 'bar'}
```

Since the two Quantities are mutable, we can change the properties of one of them to make them equal and render one of the dictionary values inaccessible:

```
>>> a.value = 6
>>> c
{<Quantity 6 s>: 'foo', <Quantity 6 s>: 'bar'}
>>> c[a]
'bar'
>>> c[b]
'bar'
```

title: Confusing error message for failed table assignment
description:
When `Table.__setitem__` fails the error message can be misleading:

```
>>> t = Table([[1, 2]])
>>> t[1] = 1, 2  # provided too many values for setting a row
   1168             self._data[item] = value
   1169         except (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError):
-> 1170             raise KeyError("Column {0} does not exist".format(item))
   1171         except:
   1172             raise

KeyError: 'Column 1 does not exist'
```

Need to be more careful about the cause of the exception.

description:

The categories I have in mind:
- geometric transforms & WCS transforms (astropy + skimage?)
- stellar photometry (photutils, python wrapper of daophot?)

- graphical interaction (pyds9)
- GUI fitting of generic models (pymodelfit?)

description:
It appears that the numpy 1.4.1 tests in travis are now all failing due to a segfault.  It's a little hard to tell exactly when this appeared, but the first commit that I can find showing it is the same as the failure that #782 fixes appeared in.  This might be coincidence, though, because there are several PRs in between that and the previous "good" one.

I also can't reproduce this locally on OS X, but I'm not sure I would, because the compiler and c stdlib might be different. I think Travis is on Ubuntu, so that's probably the place to look.

It may well be this is a numpy 1.4.1 bug, in which case we probably just want to skip the test in that case and let the rest run.  But it's currently causing the tests to fail, so we want to at least determine the cause.

title: Develop uncertainties framework for NDData
description:
As has been discussed in a variety of settings, we should decide on a framework for representing uncertainties in `NDData`.  Currently the only thing in there is std/var, and we should develop a framework that allows specifying more complex error distributions if desired. (and this _will_ be needed for #448).

This framework also should include a reasonably generic way of specifying how to propogate errors when `NDData` objects are combined or otherwise operated on.  This was one of the major reasons for having `NDData` in the first place, after all.

description:

Currently it is looking for 'comment' instead of 'writer_comment' prior to Writer instantiation and throws an exception when writer_comment is passed as an argument since it gets passed into the object instead of being handled below.

This is correct, need to fix bug and add appropriate tests.

title: Add wheel distribution(s) of Astropy
description:
PEP-427 defining the Wheel format has finally been accepted after months of deliberation. This is finally the first ever documented and blessed binary distribution format for Python (it's a little like the .egg format but should not be confused with it--it's for distribution _only_ and is not designed so that packages can be directly imported from .whl files).

A reference implementation is here: https://bitbucket.org/dholth/wheel

Plans are afoot to add support to pip now that the PEP has been accepted.

Eventually there will be some stdlib support for wheel as well, possibly as part of the ongoing distilb project.

So it would be worth embracing the future at some point providing Wheel distributions for all the platforms we support (including Linux).

title: Coordinates uses different unit error from units
description:
While looking at some of the code in `coordinates` today, I noticed this: `from .errors import UnitsError`, which reminded me: `coordinates` has an exception class that is called `UnitsError`.  This was written before `units` was finished, and was intended as a stand-in for an appropriate exception in `units` that should be used to mean "You tried to use something that's a non-sensical unit in this context."  E.g., giving a velocity as the unit for a `Distance` object.

In `units` there is a `UnitsException` class, but it's not clear to me that this means quite the same thing - I think it's the base for all `units` subpackage errors, rather than meaning "you used the wrong unit."

We certainly should at least change the naming scheme here so they aren't so similar sounding... and I think it might be better to just add a class in `units` like `IncorrectUnitsError`.  The we can change all the `coordinates` errors to point to that instead of the class inside `coordinates.errors`.  @mdboom or @adrn, what do you think?

title: Table.meta can be overwritten without warning/exception
description:
At the moment, `meta` can be accidentally replaced by a non-dict-like object:

```
In [10]: t = Table()

In [11]: t.meta = 'not dict-like'

# no exception
```

In my opinion, meta itself should be a read-only property (which of course would be editable) to avoid accidentally overwriting it with a non-dict-like object (which would cause bugs elsewhere for any code assuming `meta` is dict-like).

@taldcroft - what do you think?

title: Can we make astropy.io.fits (and other) function/method names PEP8-compliant?
description:
PEP8 recommends that:

_Function names should be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary to improve readability_

We've tried to stick to this in many parts of Astropy, but some of the code that was incorporated from other packages, such as `astropy.io.fits`, do not necessarily follow this::

```
fits.getdata
fits.getheader
fits.writeto
```

I would personally be in favor of changing these to the PEP8-compliant names (`get_data`, `get_header`, `write_to`etc.) and adding aliases for backward compatibility. Is there any reason why this couldn't be done? Given how much code is out there that uses PyFITS, I don't think we would necessarily need to deprecate the old names, but all the docs could be updated to reflect the new names, so that over time, people would switch to the PEP8-compliant names.

@iguananaut - is there any reason that we can't do this?

What do others think?

title: WCS should accept / return coordinates objects
description:
It might be nice to build in support so that conversions _from_ world coordinates accept any Astropy coordinates object and conversions _to_ world coordinates return a coordinates object as well (once `Angle` and other coordinate object accept arrays) . For example:

```
>>> worldcoords = coord.ICRSCoordinates([[151.1241, 11.134], [12.4123, -41.1231]], unit=(u.deg, u.deg))
>>> wcs.wcs_world2pix(worldcoords)
...
```

I also hate the function names in `wcs` but I'm not sure there's anything we can do about that..

title: wcs method names are confusing
description:
As @adrn pointed out in #812, the method names on the `WCS` object are less than ideal, though I should point out they are a significant improvement over the `wcslib` names, e.g. `p2s`, `s2p` etc.

I think the best solution is to probably have `pix_to_world` and `world_to_pix` with keyword args to control which of the transformations are performed (defaulting to all) and then we would deprecate the existing methods.

title: WCS objects should have a naxis3 attribute if appropriate
description: WCS objects currently have an naxis1 and naxis2 attribute. However, there is no naxis3 attribute for WCS objects describing cubes

title: Don't require ``.bases`` for ``decompose()``
description:
Currently, `decompose` requires a list of base units to be specified:

```
In [4]: u.pc.decompose(u.cgs.bases)
Out[4]: Unit("3.085678e+18 cm")
```

However, I don't see any reason why we can't allow

```
In [4]: u.pc.decompose(u.cgs)
Out[4]: Unit("3.085678e+18 cm")
```

to work, i.e. if the object passed is a module, the `bases` attribute is checked. This makes a lot more sense in terms of readability (of course, `u.cgs.bases` should still work, just proposing to also have `u.cgs` work).

@mdboom - what do you think?

title: Feature Request: ipython extension
description:
Inspired by http://www.southampton.ac.uk/~fangohr/blog/physical-quantities-numerical-value-with-units-in-python.html in particular, it would be great to have astropy-ipython integration via an extension.

Some discussion on astropy-dev:
https://groups.google.com/d/topic/astropy-dev/7d7TnT-fQLA/discussion

As @eteq points out, the simple unit syntax introduced in the `PhysicalQuantity` extension isn't particularly beneficial because astropy already supports a very short syntax (though I'd argue the `u.m` example looks too much like `um` for micron... maybe an argument against using the extension's approach).  

However, there may be other ways in which an ipython extension could improve astropy usability.  This issue or the astropy discussion list would be a good place to mention those.

title: Write a transition guide for asciitable => io.ascii migration
description:
Provide guidance for people migrating their analysis and code from `asciitable` to `io.ascii`.  The biggest difference is between `Table` and `recarray`.

Kelle writes:

"from the bottom of my heart, I request that you post some useful operations like the one below to help people switch between the two datatypes in the transition phase. there's no way i would have been able to figure that out on my own."

Referring to:
BTW, if you really want an asciitable-like recarray (e.g. for legacy code), you can do:

```
>>> dat = io.ascii.read(...)
>>> dat_recarray = np.array(dat).view(np.recarray)
```

Basically that lets you access columns like dat_recarray.my_column instead of dat['my_column'].  But you lose a lot of Table goodies in that translation process.

title: Automated detection of scripts in setup.py doesn't work as advertised.
description:
In setup.py the files to install in the scripts directory are detected so:

``` python
scripts = [fname for fname in glob.glob(os.path.join('scripts', '*'))
           if fname != 'README.rst']
```

However, fname will always be of the form 'scripts/script', _e.g._, 'scripts/README.rst'.  So if there is a README.rst file in scripts, it will not be eliminated from the list.  One solution is to do:

``` python
scripts = [fname for fname in glob.glob(os.path.join('scripts', '*'))
           if os.path.basename(fname) != 'README.rst']
```

This same problem exists in package-template/setup.py and probably exists elsewhere in astropy-related packages.

title: Filetype identification can fail for some URLs
description:
File this bug under "theoretical" -- but we'll probably want to address it at some point.

As an example, the `is_latex` identifier is:

```
def is_latex(origin, args, kwargs):
    return isinstance(args[0], basestring) and args[0].endswith('.tex')
```

This will fail if the file comes from a remote URL with parameters, such as:

```
http://astropy.org/texserver.tex?foo=bar
```

Rather than using `endswith`, we should probably write a utility function to check the extension of a file that uses some combination of `os.path.splitext` and `urlparse.urlparse().path`.

Even then, we're still in trouble, because:

1) `download_file` doesn't read the mimetype in the HTTP header.  If it did so, it could use the `mimetypes` module to make a reasonable guess about a file extension to use.

2) Once it did that, the cache system would have to be updated to store the mimetype either in the cache database or in the file extension of the file things are cached in.

So the real solution is to move all of the file identifiers to do content-based checks whenever humanly possible and avoid all of this...

title: units: operations on dimensionless units
description:
Hi,

in further playing with units, I tried something simple:

```
def doppler(v): return 1.+v/si.c
doppler(10. * u.km/u.s)
```

But this gives
`TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'Quantity'`

Of course, this can be resolved with

```
def doppler(v): return 1+(v/si.c).to(u.dimensionless_unscaled).value
doppler(10. * u.km/u.s)
```

Which gives
`1.0000333564095198`

But this seems needlessly inelegant. My suggestion would that if a Quantity can be made dimensionless, no complaint is made for addition, raising to non-half powers, etc.  Similarly, for conversion to a numpy array, I would again suggest that if it is possible to convert to dimensionless units, this is done silently, reserving the warning for the case it is well-deserved (actually, if it were up to me, I'd raise an exception, as I think it is better to force the user to make an explicit choice). A specific advantage might be for, say, model atmosphere fitting.  Currently:

```
g = (si.G*u.solMass/u.solRad**2)
np.log10((g/(u.cm/u.s**2)))
```

gives
`WARNING: Converting Quantity object in units 'm3 solMass / (cm kg solRad2)' to a Numpy array [astropy.units.quantity]
-10.175624209420819`

Instead it would be nice if it would do the same as:

```
np.log10((g/(u.cm/u.s**2)).to(u.dimensionless_unscaled))
```

`4.4384281484130499`

(I realise `np.log10(g.cgs)` also gives the right answer, even if with the warning)

Thanks!

Marten

title: Table / ascii: if header_start is specified, data_start should default to header_start+1
description:
Not sure if this has been discussed in other issues, but I'm thinking that if the user specifies the `header_start` keyword, `data_start` should be automatically set to `header_start+1`. Here's an example that might illustrate...

Let's say I have a CSV file like this:

```
Some random, uncommented text, blah blah blah
name,ra,dec
"object_a",15.6346,21.5128
"object_b",11.10422,-11.4123
```

If I use `ascii.read()` and specify _just_ `header_start`, it thinks all the columns are typed `string`:

```
>>> data = ascii.read("filename.csv", header_start=1)
>>> data.dtype
dtype=[('name', 'S8'),('ra', 'S8'), ('dec', 'S9')]
```

Whereas if I specify `data_start`:

```
>>> data = ascii.read("filename.csv", header_start=1, data_start=2)
>>> data.dtype
dtype=[('name', 'S8'), ('ra', '<f8'), ('dec', '<f8')]
```

title: creating a Time with multiple Time(format=datetime) objects gives an error
description:
I've noticed some unexpected behavior with the `datetime` support in `time` recently added by @taldcroft in #860.  It may not actually be related to that (that is, it might be true for all formats), but I first noticed it after the #860 merge, so it _might_ be connected.

When I do `Time([dt1,dt2],scale='utc')` (`dt1` and `dt2` are `datetime.datetime` objects), I get exactly what I expect: A `Time` object that contains an array with two elements.  Similarly, when I do `Time(t1)` (where `t1` is a time object) I get out the natural expectation: a copy of `t1`.  However, if I do this:

```
t1 = Time(dt1, scale='utc')
t2 = Time(dt2, scale='utc')
tarr = Time([t1, t2])
```

I get an error about it being an invalid format.  I would have instead expected to get back a new `Time` object with a two-element array that looks just like `Time([dt1,dt2],scale='utc')`

title: Make astropy.utils.release usable by affiliated packages
description:
At the moment, `astropy.utils.release` contains several instances of:

```
    if data['name'] != 'astropy':
        return
```

which makes it usable only by the Astropy core package. Removing these checks and adding

```
# Set up release hooks for package
entry_points = {}
for hook in [('prereleaser', 'middle'), ('releaser', 'middle'),
             ('postreleaser', 'before'), ('postreleaser', 'middle')]:
    hook_ep = 'zest.releaser.' + '.'.join(hook)
    hook_name = 'packagename.release.' + '.'.join(hook)
    hook_func = 'astropy.utils.release:' + '_'.join(hook)
    entry_points[hook_ep] = ['%s = %s' % (hook_name, hook_func)]
```

(and adding `entry_points` to the call to `setup()`) seems to work, so I was wondering if there is a way to write `astropy.utils.release` that doesn't require checking the package name? Is the risk that if we get rid of the check, _any_ package's release will call Astropy?

title: Make a pretty printer for OrderedDict
description:
`OrderedDict` is used in many places within astropy, but printing an OrderedDict object gives an ugly and difficult-to-read output.  `pprint` is no better.  Some quick googling led to some stackoverflow answers but nothing really helpful.

Having a readable representation of these objects would be useful.  One idea is to customize `pprint.pformat` to work with OrderedDict, then use that as `__repr__` or `__str__` in astropy the OrderDict class.

If someone is bored maybe this would be a good little project...

title: WCS.calcFootprint uses corner pixel centers -> should use corner pixel corners?
description:
[`WCS.calcFootprint`](ttp://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.wcs.WCS.html#astropy.wcs.WCS.calcFootprint) claims this in the docstring:

> A footprint is defined as the positions of the corners of the image on the sky after all available distortions have been applied.

But the footprint returned is not really for the corners of the image, but for the positions of the corner pixel centers. IMO the corners of the image should be the corners of the pixel corners.

E.g. at the moment one coordinate returned is the world coordinate corresponding to pixel coordinate `(1, 1)`, but the corner of the image really corresponds to pixel coordinate `(0.5, 0.5)`.

Does this make sense?
How do you want to handle this?

title: Enable doctests in Sphinx docs
description:

But stagnation of examples in the documentation prose in rst files is also a problem (see for example #910).  It is also possible to run the doctests in these files, but this will require a bit more tweaking of the test framework so I've made it a separate issue from #746.

This way we can ensure that most of our examples are kept actually working.

title: astropy.io.ascii.write does funky stuff with quotes in format specifiers
description:
I am trying to output a string enclosed in double quotes, like this `"some value"` or `"1.23"`

So, this is the baseline table:

```
>>> tab = astropy.table.Table({'a':[1]})
>>> astropy.io.ascii.write(tab, sys.stdout, formats={'a':'{0}'})
a
1
```

Now, let me try to add double quotes to the format specifier:

```
>>> astropy.io.ascii.write(tab, sys.stdout, formats={'a':'"{0}"'})
a
"""1"""
>>> astropy.io.ascii.write(tab, sys.stdout, formats={'a':'{0}"'})
a
"1"""
```

Escaping with `\` does not help either

```
>>> astropy.io.ascii.write(tab, sys.stdout, formats={'a':'{0}\"'})
a
"1"""
```

title: Make convolve and convolve_fft more consistent
description:
At the moment, convolve and convolve_fft have slightly different behaviors - for instance:

- convolve_fft treats Inf values as NaNs, but convolve does not

There may be other differences too. We should try and make the behavior more consistent.

title: Remove scipy tests from Travis
description:
The requirement to have SciPy available for the tests in Travis has, in my opinion, made the Travis tests almost unusable.  For one, it has inflated the build time for them immensely--I used to get results for pull requests pretty quickly.

Part of that may be due to growth in use of Travis by other projects and thus increased demand for its build servers.  But the fact that we have to build all of SciPy as part of every single Astropy build has to be a major source of the slowness.  Plus it has made the logs difficult to get to--it is necessary to download the log--it is not viewable directly on the Travis website.  And even then it's huge and is just too much to scroll through.

I honestly don't see how it's worth the trouble.  Can we not just let the Jenkins builds do the "all batteries included" tests and go back to using Travis as quick, if not imperfect feedback on most pull requests?

title: Better integrate ``astropy.coordinates`` with ``astropy.vo``
description:
Currently (as of #552) the `astropy.vo` code requires the user to separate out the components of coordinates to do a cone search:

```
>>> from astropy import coordinates as coord
>>> c = coord.ICRSCoordinates.from_name('M31')
>>> c.ra, c.dec
(<RA 10.68471 deg>, <Dec 41.26875 deg>)
>>> result = conesearch.conesearch(
...     c.ra.degrees, c.dec.degrees, 0.1, catalog_db=my_catname)
```

I think it would be nice if users could also do:

```
>>> from astropy import coordinates as coord
>>> c = coord.ICRSCoordinates.from_name('M31')
>>> result = conesearch.conesearch(c, 0.1, catalog_db=my_catname)
```

i.e. we should make it so `conesearch` can also take a coordinate object instead of two separate coordinates in degrees.

This somewhat came out of the discussion about vaopy and also out of the discussion in #945 (#945 talks about using coordinates as `input` to a conesearch -- if we're going to do that, we should also provide an interface to get coordinates as `output` of a conesearch).

title: Add unit-checking math functions
description:
I don't yet know if this is a good idea, or I'm inadvertently writing a belated April Fools' joke, but...

It might be handy to have a set of math functions that do unit checking and take and return `Quantities` (or `Angles` -- but those are soon be more-or-less the same thing).

For example:

```
    >>> q = 90 * u.degree
    >>> astropy.units.math.sin(q)
    1.0
    >>> astropy.units.math.arcsin(1.0)
    <Quantity 1.57079632679 rad>
    >>> _.degree
    90.0
```

I think that these should be strict about requiring quantities and not raw unadorned Numpy arrays, otherwise users will just try to bypass the type-checking by putting `.value` everywhere and we'll have gained nothing.  These functions already exist without unit checking in Numpy, so if that's what the user wants, they should use those.

        if self.delimiter is None:
            delimiter = ' '
        else:
            delimiter = self.delimiter

        if self.csv_writer is None:
            self.csv_writer = csv.writer(self.csv_writer_out,
                                         delimiter = self.delimiter,
                                         doublequote = self.doublequote,
                                         escapechar = self.escapechar,
                                         quotechar = self.quotechar,
                                         quoting = self.quoting,
                                         lineterminator = '',
```

title: VO Cone Search should handle error response properly
description:
From Ray Plante (2013-04-17)

> Error Handling:
> 
> VO Data access services can have three classes of failure modes:
> 1.  the HTTP response fails (and you don't get back any XML)
> 2.  the service returns illegal/non-compliant XML
> 3.  the service returns a legal response but encodes an error 
>       successfully caught and reported within the VOTable response. 
>       (e.g. incorrect parameter syntax was used).
> 
> The module (mostly) handles the first two cases (1 raises 
> urllib2.URLError and 2 raises VOSError); however, I do not see 
> support for 3.  Before extracting the results table, the module 
> should check the status of the INFO element to determine if a caught 
> error occurred and raise an exception accordingly.
> 
> Note that the encoding of errors in the VOTable is slightly different 
> between Conesearch and the later DAL protocols.  
> 
> VAOpy provides exception classes that differentiate between these 
> errors and in particular pulls out errors reported within the VOTable 
> and throws an exception accordingly for consistant error handling.

He was referring to Section 2.3 in http://www.ivoa.net/documents/REC/DAL/ConeSearch-20080222.html

> The service must respond with a stubbed version of the VOTable in the case of error.
> This must happen if the three required parameters (RA, DEC, SR) are not all present,
> or if their values cannot be parsed to floating-point numbers, or if the numbers are out
> of range (DEC=91.0, for example). The service may also make an error return if the
> search radius (give by the SR parameter) is larger than the MaxSR parameter of the
> Resource Profile (see Section 3).
> 
> In the case of error, the service MUST respond with a VOTable that contains a single
> PARAM element or a single INFO element with name="Error", where the
> corresponding value attribute should contain some explanation of the nature of the
> error. If an INFO element is used, it must appear as a direct child of one of the
> following elements:
> - the root VOTABLE element (which is preferred by this document), or
> - the RESOURCE element
> 
> If a PARAM element is used, it must appear as a direct child of one of following
> elements:
> - the RESOURCE element, or
> - a DEFINITION element below the root VOTABLE element (which is discouraged by this document).

Example XMLs from the document above as follow.
1. Error INFO as child of VOTABLE (preferred)

```
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE VOTABLE SYSTEM "http://us-vo.org/xml/VOTable.dtd">
<VOTABLE version="1.0">
  <DESCRIPTION>MAST Simple Cone Search Service</DESCRIPTION>
  <INFO ID="Error" name="Error" value="Error in input RA value: as3f"/>
</VOTABLE>
```

title: Add option to project `separation` onto an ellipse
description:
Right now separation only gives the angle between two points.  Another common "separation" in astronomy is the distance _projected_ along a particular axis (e.g. the major axis of a galaxy).  This would be particularly useful because of the rather sordid history of various people confusing which way a PA goes ("degrees east of north" I think is the most common convention).

Also useful (at least in galaxy contexts) might be an "elliptical" distance  (where the separation along the major and minor axes is weighted by the ellipticity).

This should probably await until some of the significant coordinate internal changes are done, so I'm not targeting a particular milestone.

However, if -at some point in the future- quantities would be derived from np.ndarray, then there are more ufuncs that should be supported (np.square, np.power [with the same restrictions as `__pow__`], all the comparison operartors).

title: UTC <=> TAI does not round trip for dates 1960 to 1972
description:
As initially discussed in #1030, between 1960 and 1972 the UTC scale had a variable rate, so the length of a second changed slightly.  During this time period you cannot round trip between UTC and other scales like TAI.

```
In [30]: t1 = Time('1965-01-01 00:00:00', scale='utc')

In [31]: t1.tai.utc  # to TAI and back to UTC doesn't give same value
Out[31]: <Time object: scale='utc' format='iso' vals=1964-12-31 23:59:59.997>
```

This is a direct consequence of the underlying SOFA routines not round-tripping for times in this time regime.

```
In [32]: from astropy.time.sofa_time import tai_utc, utc_tai
In [33]: jd1 = np.array([2440587.5], dtype=np.double)
In [34]: jd2 = np.array([0], dtype=np.double)
In [35]: jd1_tai, jd2_tai = utc_tai(jd1, jd2)
In [36]: jd1_tai_utc, jd2_tai_utc = tai_utc(jd1_tai, jd2_tai)
In [37]: jd1 - jd1_tai_utc
Out[37]: array([ 0.])

In [38]: jd2 - jd2_tai_utc
Out[38]: array([  6.00000000e-08])

In [39]: jd2 - jd2_tai_utc * 86400.0  # Off by 5.184 millisec
Out[39]: array([ 0.005184])
```

This needs to be brought up to the SOFA developers to understand if this is a bug or expected feature of a non-uniform time scale.
