title: Improve subclassing of models
description:
Subclassing a model with parameters is currently no easy task.  Subclassing an _abstract_ model with no parameters or `evaluate` defined is easy.  For example we provide `Fittable1DModel` and `Fittable2DModel` as base classes for many models, but these do little more than provide default `inputs` and `outputs` as well as other class attributes like `fittable = True` as a convenience.

But subclassing a model with parameters is currently quite fraught with difficulties.  In particular, if you subclass a model but have different parameters in the subclass than those in the base class.  I hoped that #3679 would improve matters here, and it does, but not enough.  With #3679, when you subclass a model by default you don't inherit _any_ of that model's parameters.  If you want your subclass to have some of the same parameters you include them manually in the class definition.  However, it also makes it possible to inherit parameters by including `_inherit_descriptors_ = (Parameter,)`.

Overriding or inheriting parameters partially works.  The resulting subclass will have the correct set of `Parameter` descriptors.  However, much of the difficulty comes in the `__init__`.  The default `__init__` method that gets generated in this case is terribly broken, because by default it calls `super(cls).__init__(...)` and passes down _all_ arguments to the super class's `__init__`, which may not take all the same parameters.  So I really need to come up with a better default `__init__` implementation that allows only the relevant arguments to be picked off by base class `__init__`s, but still assembles all the arguments properly when it gets down to `Model.__init__`.  

This can also be worked around by hand-writing an `__init__` in the subclass.  It can work if it passes in all arguments as keyword arguments, but that's tedious and ugly.  A more careful default `__init__` implementation should enable this to be handled better.

What's even trickier though is you subclass a model and don't inherit any of its Parameters.  The effect is that you can still access the subclass's `Parameter` descriptors due to the normal attribute access rules of Python.  But because the parameter initialization code is working only on the subclass it ignores the base class's parameters and doesn't set values for them.  One thought might be to override `OrderedDescriptorContainer.__getattribute__` so that it doesn't allow Parameter lookups from base classes when parameters aren't inherited.  Another option would be to just always require Parameters to be inherited when subclassing, which would simplify matters.

`__call__` has some of the same problems as `__init__` for Models, especially if the subclass changes the number of inputs or outputs.  This is something that we might choose to disallow altogether, though one might be able to come up with a use case for it (when going reducing the number of inputs, anyways, there needs to be a way to provide defaults for any inputs that are factored out).

title: Bug copying HDUs with scaled data from one file to another
description:
This is yet another example of how broken the current data model is for FITS data.

When copying an HDU from one file to another, for example like:

``` python
source = fits.open('path/to/source.fits', do_not_scale_image_data=True)
with fits.open('path/to/dest.fits', mode='append') as dest:
    dest.append(source['SCI'])
```

if `source['SCI']` has non-trivial BSCALE/BZERO the scaling info is dropped from the appended HDU (while the original integer values for the data are still written).  Without `do_not_scale_image_data` the scaled physical values are written, and the integer values are lost.  Since the data in `source['SCI']` wasn't touched, it should just keep the raw data intact.

The problem is that when performing operations like this the state about the data scaling is dropped.  This is because that state lives in attributes on the HDU object itself (when really it should belong to the data array itself).  An ideal solution would be a special class for FITS data that maintains its scaling state.  But an interim solution to the bug would be to make sure the scaling state is copied from the source HDU to the new HDU on the destination file.

title: Always convert to native byte order with FITS Table.read()
description:
Having non-native byte order in tables causes a number of problems which have been documented in #4034 and #1156.  I just ran into another weird issue writing HDF5 files using PyTables.

In #1156 there was general consensus that always converting to native byte order when using `Table.read()` for FITS files would be a good thing.  The direct `astropy.io.fits` interface would be available if that behavior was not desired.

@embray provided a small code snippet that should do the job:

```
sys_byteorder = ('>', '<')[sys.byteorder == 'little']
if col.dtype.byteorder not in ('=', sys_byteorder):
    col = col.byteswap().newbyteorder(sys_byteorder)
    # Do something with col array...
```

This issue is to formally decide to go forward with this plan and then do it!

title: Table.read and io.ascii dtype and treatment of very large/small numbers
description:
When checking for correct parsing of very long exponents  in PR [#3655](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/3655#issuecomment-130096672) I came upon a general inconsistency in the treatment of numbers outside the range of `float64` referenced above.
In short, the standard Python reader reads these as `inf` and `0.e0`, respectively, while `fast_reader=True` results in reading the respective column as a `str` array.
1. Obviously the behaviour between the Python and C readers should be consistent.
2. Reading such values as strings might make sense to at least preserve what information is there; on the other hand this can result in a few out-of-range entries converting the entire column to a possibly not very useful `str` array instead of a `float64` array with a finite number of invalid data. `inf` and `0.0` are also the results of the plain Python `float('1.1e666')` etc. conversions.
3. Whichever is chosen as the common default, the user should probably have the option of choosing the format that is useful for them, but apparently the ascii reader provides no means to enforce a `dtype` on input data the way e.g. `np.genfromtxt` does:

```
In[104]: tab = Table(names='A B C'.split(), dtype=('S', 'S', 'f8'))
In [105]: tab.read('1000.1e906 2.0e-302 3\n0.42e+000 0.5 .42e-500', format='ascii.no_header', guess=False)
Out[105]: 
<Table length=2>
   col1      col2    col3  
  str10    float64   str8  
---------- ------- --------
1000.1e906  2e-302        3
 0.42e+000     0.5 .42e-500
In [106]: tab.read('1000.1e906 2.0e-302 3\n0.42e+000 0.5 .42e-500', format='ascii.no_header', guess=False, fast_reader=False)
Out[106]: 
<Table length=2>
  col1    col2    col3 
float64 float64 float64
------- ------- -------
    inf  2e-302     3.0
   0.42     0.5     0.0
```

since the initialisation of the table is completely ignored upon `read()`. Is there any other way to prescribe a table's `dtype` beforehand (apart from the obvious workaround of first reading it into an `np.array` with one of the `npyio` routines?

title: Add generic binary tree class
description:
Over in [this comment](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/3915#discussion_r36866623) I noted that the `BST` class added for table indexing, and the `ExpressionTree` class used in compound model evaluation share many similarities.

It would probably be good to have a generic binary tree type somewhere (utils? astropy.datastructures?  I dunno...) that has methods like pre/post/in-order traversal (iterative and recursive versions?) and various other tree manipulation routines,   BST and ExpressionTree can subclass it for their particular purposes.

I also like the `BST` class's separation of the `Node` class from the tree itself, and would like to figure how to best integrate that into the `ExpressionTree` implementation.  Not entirely sure how that works with the optional `bintrees` support though...

title: Provide a way to say if two WCS have the same world coordinate system
description:
For WCSAxes, I need a way to know whether two WCS objects have the same world coordinate system, though not necessarily the same projection. In form of code, the question is whether:

``` python
xp1, yp1 = 10, 10
xw, yw = wcs1.all_pix2world(xp,1 yp1, 0)
xp2, yp2 = wcs2.all_world2pix(xw, yw, 0)
```

is a valid operation or not. The projections could be different but as long as the actual world coordinate system is the same, this is valid. I've written a simple function that basically checks whether the following are the same:

```
wcs.naxis
wcs.wcs.ctype
wcs.wcs.axis_types
wcs.wcs.specsys
wcs.wcs.radesys
wcs.wcs.equinox
wcs.wcs.restfrq
wcs.wcs.restwav
```

Is this sufficient to guarantee that the world coordinates are the same in both systems? If not, what needs to be added? Are any of the above redundant?

Can we include a function in `astropy.wcs.utils` that does this check?

cc @mdboom @nden

title: ndarray-like base class
description:
Although I don't recall exactly what the reasons were, I believe for good reasons the `Time` class does _not_ subclass `numpy.ndarray`.  Nevertheless, array-like `Time` objects behave a lot like `ndarray` in that indexing works as one would expect with an `ndarray`, and it implements all of the `ndarray` methods.

The `SkyCoord` class also does not subclass `ndarray` for good reasons, but supports similar indexing operations for arrays of coordinates.  Unlike `Time`, it does _not_ support `ndarray`-like methods.  But I feel like it would be good if, so long as we're offering array-like special objects, we should strive to emulate the `ndarray` interface as consistently as possible with those objects (as we also do with `Quantity`, which of course _is_ an `ndarray` subclass).  I think not all such methods and attributes are always applicable, but I think this should be a general goal at least.  It would be consistent and represent the least astonishment to users.

That's why I'm suggesting a base class that provides stubs for many applicable `ndarray` attributes and methods.  `Time` and `SkyCoord` (and any other applicable classes--I'm thinking `Model` as well) can use this class as a mixin and implement only those interfaces that make sense for the class.  To an extent this can be made pretty automatic too--`Time` has a generic method that knows how to represent a `Time` as a couple of bare `ndarrays`, apply the `ndarray` methods directly, and then reconstitute the result as a `Time`.  So most `ndarray` methods can be implemented just by implementing a general method(s) for to-from `ndarray`.

One thing `Time` is currently missing, which we should also have, is some equivalent of `np.concatenate` that works with non-ndarrays.  Not sure yet exactly how I see that working--maybe as a classmethod.

title: Getting further array-like operations working for astropy.modeling model sets
description:
Model sets in astropy are a great addition, which allows to have a set of models (defined by the same function) within one astropy structure. Hence we can do: ModelSet = MyModel(par1=[a1,a2,a3],par2=[b1,b2,b3]). However, it is not yet (easily) possible to then slice the ModelSet to:
- do a simple slicing: ModelSubSet = ModelSet[0,2] or ModelSubSet=ModelSet[-1]
- or easily add a new one NewModelset = ModelSet  + MyModel(par1=[a4,a5],par2=[b4,b5])

Having such options would be a fantastic addition I think. This would make a model set a very flexible tool to manipulate N times the same MyModel and associated subsets.

title: io.fits.getdata() lower and upper keywords broken
description:
astropy 1.0.2 broke the functionality of the `lower` and `upper` arguments to astropy.io.fits.getdata when reading binary fits tables.  Prior to 1.0.2, the returned FITS_rec object properly handled case insensitive column names, while allowing the lower/upper keywords to specify what should be used if those objects were cast to normal numpy.array objects or written back out.  Starting with astropy 1.0.2, this broke; using the `lower` or `upper` arguments resulted in _neither_ case working.  The code below demonstrates the problem:

```
import astropy
print astropy.__version__

from astropy.table import Table
t = Table([np.zeros(5), np.ones(5), np.arange(5)], names=['a', 'b', 'c'])
t.write('lower.fits')
t = Table([np.zeros(5), np.ones(5), np.arange(5)], names=['A', 'B', 'C'])
t.write('upper.fits')

#- Without the lower/upper keywords, columns can be accessed with either
#- upper- or lower-case names; the .dtype.names reflects whatever was in
#- the source fits file
from astropy.io import fits
lower = fits.getdata('lower.fits', 1)
upper = fits.getdata('upper.fits', 1)

print lower.dtype.names
print upper.dtype.names

np.all(lower['a'] == lower['A'])    #- Works
np.all(upper['a'] == upper['A'])    #- Works

#- Prior to astropy 1.0.2, the upper/lower keywords affected the case of
#- .dtype.names and how they are cast to normal numpy.array objects, while
#- still supporting case-insensitive column names.  This broke with
#- astropy 1.0.2, where neither upper- nor lower-case works after using
#- the upper/lower keywords.
lowup = fits.getdata('lower.fits', 1, upper=True)
lowup.dtype.names
lowup['A']              #- KeyError
lowup['a']              #- KeyError
lowup.A                 #- Works
np.array(lowup)['A']    #- Works

uplow = fits.getdata('upper.fits', 1, lower=True)
uplow.dtype.names
uplow['A']              #- KeyError
uplow['a']              #- KeyError
uplow.a                 #- Works
np.array(uplow)['a']    #- Works
```

title: Add a .raw_data attribute to FITS HDUs
description:
As @leejjoon suggested way back in #993, it might be nice to have a convenient way to get at the raw, unscaled data of FITS arrays that have scale factors.

I always intended that to be a feature in some kind of FITS data class (that would also be used for columns of tables, so that individual columns can be accessed as scaled or raw).  

But in the meantime I think it would be fairly straightforward to add a `.raw_data` attribute to all HDU classes.  I think for the most part this could be implemented simply by wrapping the same code used by `.data`, but with `self._do_not_scale_image_data = True` set temporarily.  I just set "Effort-medium" because there may be some subtleties I haven't thought of yet, and there may also need to be some refactoring to avoid code duplication.

title: Timezone convenience method for astropy.time.Time
description:
Right now, if you want to get a localized datetime from an astropy time, you have to type a long string of calls to `pytz` like this: 

``` python
>>> import pytz
>>> from astropy.time import Time
>>> t = Time.now()
>>> pytz.utc.localize(t.datetime).astimezone(pytz.timezone('US/Hawaii'))
datetime.datetime(2015, 9, 2, 9, 15, 26, 284400, tzinfo=<DstTzInfo 'US/Hawaii' HST-1 day, 14:00:00 STD>)
```

(localize the naive datetime as a UTC time, convert to another timezone with `pytz`). I’ve been thinking about how to make timezone manipulations more convenient in [astroplan](https://github.com/astropy/astroplan) and it seemed like this would be a convenient way to solve the problem also for other users outside of astroplan. 

Are there good reasons not to make a method on `astropy.time.Time` objects called `astimezone` that does what that last line does – accepting one argument that goes into the `datetime.astimezone` method and returning the result? For example, the above code would become: 

``` python
>>> t = Time.now()
>>> timezone = pytz.timezone("US/hawaii")
>>> t.astimezone(timezone)
```

I tried to implement this, but the mysterious workings of `TimeFormat` prevented me. If this isn't a dumb idea, I'd love some advice on how to implement it.

title: fitsdiff doesn't properly report values with different type by same str()
description:
I've seen variations of this come up a few times before.  The problem is that [`report_diff_values`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/io/fits/diff.py#L1214) converts numeric values to strings before displaying the diff.  So if you have one card that contains the string value `'1.0'`, and one with the float `1.0`, although the cards will be reported as different the report doesn't show a useful diff since both values look the same as strings.

A simple workaround would be to have `report_diff_values` also explicitly report type differences (it should also show the value and/or the diffs of the values, but make explicit when there's a type difference).

description: ``` --> from astropy.nddata import NDDataArray, StdDevUncertainty --> n = NDDataArray([1,4,9], uncertainty=StdDevUncertainty([1,2,3])) --> o = NDDataArray(n) Traceback (innermost last): File "", line 1, in File "/home/jturner/Ureka/variants/nddata/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy-1.1.dev13355-py2.7-linux-x86_64.egg/astropy/nddata/compat.py", line 89, in __init__ super(NDDataArray, self).__init__(*arg, **kwd) File "/home/jturner/Ureka/variants/nddata/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy-1.1.dev13355-py2.7-linux-x86_64.egg/astropy/nddata/nddata.py", line 89, in __init__ self.uncertainty = data.uncertainty File "/home/jturner/Ureka/variants/nddata/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy-1.1.dev13355-py2.7-linux-x86_64.egg/astropy/nddata/compat.py", line 114, in uncertainty if self.unit and value._unit: File "/home/jturner/Ureka/variants/nddata/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy-1.1.dev13355-py2.7-linux-x86_64.egg/astropy/nddata/compat.py", line 138, in unit return self._unit AttributeError: 'NDDataArray' object has no attribute '_unit' --> ``` This happens because L89 of compat.py calls `NDData.__init__()`, which calls NDDataArray's uncertainty setter, which calls the unit getter when an NDUncertainty is defined, which accesses `self._unit`, which isn't set until L93 of nddata.py (just a few lines lower down), nor in `NDDataArray.__init__()`. Also... when instantiating NDDataArray from another instance, the `flags` attribute does not get copied as expected from the input data. The class only copies flags if passed directly as a parameter by the user. This attribute should get copied by NDDataArray separately from the `super().__init__()`, since its parent NDData doesn't have flags. Thanks! James.

title: Instantiating NDData subclass from parent object doesn't copy attributes
description: In `NDData.__init__()`, attributes get copied from an existing instance only if it has the same `__class__` as the object being instantiated. Shouldn't this instead do `isinstance(data, NDData)` explicitly? Requiring the same `__class__` prevents instantiating NDDataArray properly from an NDData instance (or a subclass from an NDDataArray etc.), eg.: ``` --> a=NDData([1,4,9], uncertainty=StdDevUncertainty([1,2,3])) --> print a.uncertainty --> b=NDDataArray(a) --> print b.uncertainty None ``` I'd have thought it would be fair game for NDData's own `__init__` to accept _any_ NDData instance and not just whatever sub-class you happen to be creating at the time ;-). Otherwise, it's difficult for sub-classes to delegate their own `__init__` to their parents if they want to be "upwards-compatible" (not sure whether I'm overlooking some other consideration though). If you agree, this would also imply changing my pull request #4130 to use `NDDataArray` instead of `__class__`. I won't do that before you comment though. Thanks! James.

description:
Hi,

I've been trying to fit Voigt line profiles in Astropy. The LevMarLSQFitter was unable to return reasonable fits to the amplitude or the centroid. I checked into the Voigt1D model source code and noticed that it seems like two of the derivatives are switched in the RETURN call: x0 and amplitude.

Joel Leja

title: NDArithmeticMixin uncertainty propagation for multiplication/division
description:
I used the arithmeticMixin sometime now but only recently I realized that in some circumstances it makes the wrong "decisions". When multiplying something with an uncertainty with something that has no uncertainty it does not even want to propagate the uncertainty (why?)

For example

```
import numpy as np
from astropy.nddata import NDData, NDArithmeticMixin, StdDevUncertainty
class Test(NDArithmeticMixin,NDData):
    pass
uncert = StdDevUncertainty([1,1,1])
a = Test([1,2,3], uncertainty=uncert)
b = Test([1,2,3])
a.multiply(b).uncertainty.array
#Output: array([1, 1, 1])
#but it should be array([1,2,3]) since the uncertainty for 
#a constant times an uncertain value is just the constant times the uncertainty
```

The problem is in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/nddata/mixins/ndarithmetic.py#L149 . There it decides that the uncertainty should not be propagated if only self or operand has an uncertainty. Same problem also arises for division. 

This is not easily fixed since for example the StdDevUncertainty (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/nddata/nduncertainty.py#L329) also raises an Error if the other data has no uncertainty. (also there is a lot of duplicate code in each propagate_\* method)

title: VO Cone Search validator noncritical warnings to depend on VO Table schema version
description:
According to http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/io/votable/api_exceptions.html , some VO Table warnings only apply if VO Table schema version is such-and-such. To accommodate more accurate validation reporting, `astropy.vo.validator.validate.noncrit_warnings` configuration item needs to be changed to account for VO Table schema version (1.0, 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3).

**Proposed Solution**

Since using `dict` in configuration item is not an option, we can replace `noncrit_warnings` with `noncrit_warnings_[ver]` (e.g., `noncrit_warnings_v1d1`, `noncrit_warnings_v1d2`, and so forth). Each will have a list of noncritical warnings that is customized for that version. For example, VO Table schema version 1.1 will use `noncrit_warnings_v1d1`.

**Work Description**
- The configuration changes go into `vo/__init__.py`
- `ConfigAlias` items and validation logic in `vo/validator/validate.py` need to be updated accordingly
- Documentation and change log definitely needs updating
- Tests should work as-is, but some results might change
- Update tutorial

**Backward Compatibility**

Not backward compatible. I do not see a need for it. If users update `astropy` with this new configuration setting, they will not need the old one.

title: Misleading IOError when passing a urlopen object in to fits.open()
description:
Per this SO question: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/32643206/how-do-i-open-a-fits-file-from-a-url-in-astropy

As noted in the answers, one can already pass a URL as a string in to `fits.open()` and that will work fine.  A `urlopen` object has never been supported (intentionally) in the first place.  But it could be supported easily so long as the file is opened in readonly (or denywrite) mode.  It just needs to be handled explicitly.  In any case the error message one gets is also misleading:

```
ERROR: IOError: File-like object does not have a 'write' method, required for mode 'ostream'. [astropy.io.fits.file]
```

This happens despite not explicitly requesting 'ostream' mode.

title: astropy.io.fits.HDUList.writeto creates invalid output with uint input
description:
The following produces an invalid fits file when started from a fresh python session:

```
from astropy.io import fits
import numpy as np

#- Verification fails after first write
hx = fits.HDUList()
hx.append( fits.PrimaryHDU(np.zeros(10)) )
hx.append( fits.CompImageHDU(np.zeros(10).astype(np.uint16), uint=True) )
hx.writeto('blat.fits', clobber=True)
```

This can be checked by re-opening and verifying:

```
fx = fits.open('blat.fits')
fx.verify()

WARNING: VerifyWarning: Verification reported errors: [astropy.io.fits.verify]
WARNING: VerifyWarning: HDU 1: [astropy.io.fits.verify]
WARNING: VerifyWarning:     'TFIELDS' card at the wrong place (card 9). [astropy.io.fits.verify]
WARNING: VerifyWarning: Note: PyFITS uses zero-based indexing.
 [astropy.io.fits.verify]
```

Oddly enough, if you write two files in a row using the same I/O code, the first one is bogus while the second one is valid:

```
from astropy.io import fits
import numpy as np

def write_and_verify(filename):
    hx = fits.HDUList()
    hx.append( fits.PrimaryHDU(np.zeros(10)) )
    hx.append( fits.CompImageHDU(np.zeros(10).astype(np.uint16), uint=True) )
    hx.writeto(filename, clobber=True)
    fx = fits.open(filename)
    fx.verify()
    fx.close()

write_and_verify('blat.fits')  #- fails verification
write_and_verify('foo.fits')   #- succeeds
```

i.e. be careful when debugging this: you have to keep re-starting your ipython session to be able to reproduce the bug, or otherwise it magically starts to "work".

non-uint input seems to work fine.  I haven't found any combination of uint=X and/or verify=Y that produces a valid fits file on the first write when the input data are unsigned.

Using astropy 1.0.4, numpy 1.9, and python 2.7.10 a built by Anaconda for a Mac.

title: astropy.io.fits.append ignores header keyword
description:
astropy.io.fits.append ignores the header keyword:

```
from astropy.io import fits
import numpy as np

outfile = 'blat.fits'
data = np.arange(10)
fits.writeto(outfile, data, clobber=True)
hdr = fits.Header()
hdr['EXTNAME'] = 'BLAT'
hdr['BLAT'] = 'FOO'
fits.append(outfile, data, header=hdr)

fx = fits.open(outfile)
fx.info()
fx[1].header  #- missing EXTNAME and BLAT
```

Creating an HDUList ahead of time and writing out everything at once does work:

```
from astropy.io import fits
import numpy as np

outfile = 'blat.fits'
data = np.arange(10)

hx = fits.HDUList()
hx.append(fits.PrimaryHDU(data))
hdr = fits.Header()
hdr['EXTNAME'] = 'BLAT'
hdr['BLAT'] = 'FOO'
hx.append(fits.ImageHDU(data, header=hdr))

hx.writeto(outfile, clobber=True)
fx = fits.open(outfile)
fx.info()
fx[1].header
```

However, I don't always have all my HDUs ready at once and it is indeed convenient to just be able to append a new HDU to a pre-existing file with a single command.

title: astropy.io.fits defaults to memmap=True ?
description:
Hi,   I am working with fits files that contain a few thousand extensions (spectra) each.    Looping over each extension causes my computer to run out of file handles and my code crashes with a "Too many open files" error.  I think this is related to the memmap error in the warning box on the astropy.io.fits documentation:

"When opening a file with memmap=True, because of how mmap works this means that when the  HDU data is accessed (i.e. hdul[0].data) another handle to the FITS file is opened by mmap. This  means that even after calling hdul.close() the mmap still holds an open handle to the data so that it  can still be accessed by unwary programs that were built with the assumption that the .data attribute  has all the data in-memory."  

I get the crash without setting memmap, and with setting memmap = True.  It goes away with memmap=True and del hdu[ext].data  or just setting memmap =  False.  It looks to me like I'm defaulting to memmap = True.    Is that the correct behavior?  If so, it should probably be noted  more clearly in the documentation.

title: Provide a way to restore transform graph to previous version
description:
While debugging the failures in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/3757, I realized that one of the issues was that tests that add e.g. representation classes, frames, and transformations make permanent changes to e.g. the transform graph and other global variables in astropy.coordinates. We should provide a way to save the version prior to the tests and restore afterwards. For representation classes, the solution is simply to copy the `REPRESENTATION_CLASSES` dictionary and restore it after, but for the transform graph this is a bit more complicated. Having a way to export and restore a state (e.g. via some kind of dictionary) would be very useful.

We should also go though and make sure none of the other coordinate tests are having side effects. We don't want users to be running `astropy.test()` in a session then getting different results afterwards.

title: Fix bug in GCRS<->ICRS conversion for near-earth objects
description:
As has been discussed a fair amount in the astroplan project, as well as on the mailing list (the thread starting with https://mail.scipy.org/pipermail/astropy/2015-August/003907.html), there's a significant bug with the GCRS<->ICRS transformation for coordinates that are close to the earth (seems to be within <~1 AU).  For a regression test demonstrating the problem, see the first few commits in https://github.com/eteq/astropy/tree/fix-gcrs-trans 

I'm pretty sure I understand the source of this (basically, it's due to an incomplete workaround to some of ERFA's limitations), and hence am assigning it to myself.  Making this issue mainly so that we can try to get it fixed before a final v1.1 release.  

An item to consider, though: once fixed, should this be included in the 1.0.x branch?  While it is a bug in that the transforms aren't right, it is _technically_ an API change in case someone worked around it already... (@astrofrog and/or @embray)?

title: Bayesian blocks gamma_prior() called incorrectly?
description:
`gamma_prior` is defined as:

```
def gamma_prior(self, N, Ntot):
    """
    Basic prior, parametrized by slope gamma.
    See eq. 3 in Scargle (2012)
    """
    if self.gamma == 1:
        return 0
    else:
        return (np.log(1 - self.gamma)
                - np.log(1 - self.gamma ** (Ntot + 1))
                + N * np.log(self.gamma))
```

and it is called in `fit()` in the following context:

```
def fit(self, t, x=None, sigma=None):
...
    N = len(t)
    ...
    for R in range(N):
        ...
        A_R = fit_vec - self.prior(R + 1, N)
```

If you look at Scargle's definition (eq. 4, Scargle 2012), astropy `Ntot` ~ Scargle's "N" and astropy `N` ~ Scargle's N_blocks.

The values being passed into `N` and `Ntot` are "the number of data points _currently_ in the fit" and "the _total_ number of data points to be fit".

Looking at Scargle's definitions of these variables, I believe that `N` and `Ntot` should be "the number of **blocks** currently in this realization of the fit" and "the number of data points _currently_ in the fit".

I hope I have explained this correctly. It makes sense to me in that as you add more blocks, the prior probability is decreased, thus incurring a higher penalty as you add more change points. This is tweaked by adjusting gamma.

title: Inherit docstrings for bounding_box on subclasses
description:
As noted in #4264, when a `Model` subclass defined the `bounding_box` property or method, if it has its own docstring that docstring ends up being lost--this is because of how the metaclass swallows the `bounding_box` member of the subclass and replaces it with the base `Model.bounding_box` property.
See for example `Gaussian2D`.

This actually has two negative effects:
1. `Gaussian2D.bounding_box.__doc__` displays the docstring for `Model.bounding_box`, not
    the docstring for `Gaussian2D.bounding_box`.
2. It is impossible to reference `Gaussian2D.bounding_box` in Sphinx.  It results in a missing reference.
    For example [this line](https://github.com/embray/astropy/blame/6bf60b3308217cedae00acaa84c4e781e409f36d/docs/modeling/bounding-boxes.rst#L33) was originally a direct reference, but it didn't work.  That should be fixed.

This is just a documentation issue, but is worth fixing.  I think it can be fixed by slightly going back on some of my changes in #4236 and make it so that each subclass _does_ get its own `property` object in its `__dict__` for `bounding_box`, rather than just referring directly to `Model.property`.  It's slightly wasteful, but only slightly.

title: fits.BinTableHDU error with uint8 data
description:
Using astropy 1.0.6 and numpy 1.10.1, this fails:

```
import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits

#- Fails
dtype = [('x', '>f4'), ('y', 'uint8')]
data = np.zeros(10, dtype=dtype)
hdu = fits.BinTableHDU(data)

#- Fails
dtype = [('x', '>f4'), ('y', 'uint8')]
data = np.zeros(10, dtype=dtype)
hdu = fits.BinTableHDU(data, uint=True)
```

Both fail with:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/sbailey/anaconda/envs/fitsbug/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/table.py", line 327, in __init__
    new_data[k] = data[k] - bzeros[dtype.itemsize]
KeyError: 1
```

The problem is from the uint8 type in the numpy structured array; using int8 works:

```
#- Works

data = np.zeros(10, dtype=dtype)
hdu = fits.BinTableHDU(data)
```

Surprisingly this also works:

```
dtype = [('x', '>f4'), ('y', 'uint8', (3,4))]

hdu = fits.BinTableHDU(data, uint=True)
```

I tripped across this from reading a fits file that had uint8 data and then not being able to write the data back out into a new file so simply avoiding uint8 is not an option.

title: Review of coordinate transformations (esp. #4254)
description:
This is coming out of the discussion in #4254 .  Basically, that got merged without a thorough review of the actual transformation methodology (there was code review, but not necessarily a methodology/mathematical correctness review).  So, when possible, someone should review that code for the details of how the transformations are implemented. (In particular for #4254, there's a specific question at https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/4254#discussion-diff-42795137 that probably requires someone who's willing to go in and wrap their head around the geometry of the situation.)

More generally, this issue encapsulates my concern that quite a bit of the  transformation code in `coordinates` has not been "conceptually" reviewed.  That is, all of the code has been reviewed from a coding style/interface perspective, but not necessarily a review of the mathematical/scientific content.

I realize this is a pretty big ask because the transform code is quite complex and involves a lot of overlapping frames and concepts... But specifically _because_ of that, I think it's quite important that we make use of the hive mind on these topics.  

Hopefully someone is willing to volunteer for this - I shouldn't do so because I _am_ the original author of the majority of this stuff.  I'm milestoning this for v1.2 mainly just as a way to give whoever might volunteer a deadline: as we all know, deadlines are the best way to get things done!

cc @adrn @mhvk @astrofrog @taldcroft @bmorris3

title: Determine why the Moon's AltAz coordinates vary across codes
description:
This comes out of the discussion in #4254, as well as some offline discussion about  [astroplan](https://github.com/astropy/astroplan) development.

If you execute the gist at https://gist.github.com/eteq/08dba433082e57b7f2af (with astropy master, [pyephem](http://rhodesmill.org/pyephem/), and [skyfield](http://rhodesmill.org/skyfield/) installed), you see this:

```
PyEphem (Alt, Az, Dist): (55.4920153458 deg, 239.031895666 deg, 356424.848107 km)
Skyfield (Alt, Az, Dist): (55.32651159 deg, 239.298837015 deg, 356413.96585 km)
Skyfield(de430) (Alt, Az, Dist): (55.3265117716 deg, 239.298837058 deg, 356413.965628 km)
jplephem/Astropy (Alt, Az, Dist): (56.0578669005 deg, 239.043478848 deg, 356423.493806 km)
jplephem/Astropy(ICRS) (Alt, Az, Dist): (56.0596259457 deg, 239.03677597 deg, 356421.587215 km)
```

That demonstrates that there are disagreements about the as-observed location of the moon at the ~0.5-1 degree level (and ~10 km distance), but between astropy and the other two, as well as between skyfield and pyephem.  

It's quite possible this level of difference is driven by subtle differences in how the various frames are defined rather than any sort of implementation bug... But we should try to get to the bottom of the differences, if possible.

And once we've figured it out, even if there are no bugs to be fixed, hopefully this investigation can provide a thorough battery of tests to be added to the testing suite.

cc @mhvk @bmorris3 @brandon-rhodes

title: Add Heliocentric and Barycentric frames to coordinates
description:
With reference to #2244. Specifically addressing @mhvk's point 1 in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/2244#issuecomment-153469821. It would be very useful if we could add the above frames to the coordinates package.  I don't think this should be too hard - I've included a first stab below.

The transformation framework allows you to calculate the location of the observatory in GCRS coordinates (see below). @eteq's transformation agrees with the code I posted in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/2244#issuecomment-64900470 to within 70m, so that's a tiny part of #4268 ticked off. 

```
from astropy.coordinates import sites
import astropy.coordinates as coord
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy import units
site_list = sites.get_builtin_sites()
WHT = site_list['lapalma']
now  = Time.now()
itrs = coord.ITRS(WHT.itrs.cartesian,obstime=now)
gcrs = itrs.transform_to(coord.GCRS(obstime=now))
```

The position and velocity of the heliocenter and barycenter can be found using `erfa.epv00`, which is is consistent with the JPL ephemeris within 11.2 km = 4micro-sec and 5 mm/s, so the addition of a Heliocentric and Barycentric frame to the coordinates package doesn't look hard, e.g

```
def gcrs_to_bcrs(gcrs_loc):
    tdb = gcrs_loc.obstime.tdb
    #returns BCRS position and velocity of Earth in AU and AU/d
    h_pv,b_pv = erfa.epv00(tdb.jd1,tdb.jd2)    
    # assume scalar obstime! and unpack position array
    b_pos = b_pv[0,:] * units.AU
    new_rep = CartesianRepresentation(gcrs.cartesian.xyz + b_pos)
    return BCRS(new_rep,obstime=gcrs_loc.obstime)
```

One snag with the example above is that it assumes the obstime of the frame is a scalar.

title: transformation of frames doesn't always work for frames with multiple obstimes
description:
The code below works exactly as I'd expect:

```
from astropy import time, coordinates as coord
now = time.Time.now()

WHT  = coord.EarthLocation(lat=28.76063889,lon=-17.88163889,height=2332.)
itrs = coord.itrs(WHT.itrs,obstime=now)
gcrs = itrs.transform_to(coord.GCRS(obstime=now))
```

but the code below doesn't work at all

```
times = time.Time([57329.906211306305,57329.92],format='mjd',scale='utc')
itrs = coord.itrs(WHT.itrs,obstime=times)
gcrs = itrs.transform_to(coord.GCRS(obstime=times))
```

In general I guess this transform could be ambiguous, but where the two times arrays are identical, or the same size this ought to be able to do something sensible I think. Fixing this would make implementation of #2244 much easier.

While trying to read in a Latex table I copied-and-pasted from an arXiv paper, I learned an oddity: the Latex reader fails with an obscure error if you just put in the contents of a latex table (see stack trace at the end.  I see no reason why it shouldn't be possible to have it parse Latex style tables _without_ the `\begin{table}`/`\begin{tabular}{ccccccccccc}` and corresponding `\end` commands. title: Doppler shift a spectrum with a given radial velocity
description:
Hi all,

I have for a long time missed this functionality in `astropy`: to shift a spectrum with a given radial velocity (RV).
The procedure is quite easy:
1. Multiply the wavelength with `(1+rv/c)`.
2. Interpolate the flux to the new wavelength vector.

As for now, I always use [`PyAstronomy`](http://www.hs.uni-hamburg.de/DE/Ins/Per/Czesla/PyA/PyA/index.html) for this. This [function](http://www.hs.uni-hamburg.de/DE/Ins/Per/Czesla/PyA/PyA/pyaslDoc/aslDoc/dopplerShift.html) does the RV shift. I would like to write this function for `astropy` (if it does not exists), but were should it be? I am familiar with pull requests and the github workflow.

Cheers,
Daniel

title: Improve efficiency of getattr(tm, scale), particularly access to jd1/jd2
description:
When accessing an arbitrary time scale for a `Time` object, the internal object is always replicated.  This came up in #4302.

```
    def __getattr__(self, attr):
        """
        Get dynamic attributes to output format or do timescale conversion.
        """
        if attr in self.SCALES and self.scale is not None:
            tm = self.replicate()
            tm._set_scale(attr)
            return tm
```

What about:
- Return `self` if `attr == self.scale`?
- Cache other scales so getting both `jd1` and `jd2` after transforming will be efficient?
  Roughly:

```
    def __getattr__(self, attr):
        """
        Get dynamic attributes to output format or do timescale conversion.
        """
        if attr in self.SCALES and self.scale is not None:
            if attr == self.scale:
                tm = self
            elif attr in self._scale_cache:
                tm = self._scale_cache[attr]
            else:
                tm = self.replicate()
                tm._set_scale(attr)
                self._scale_cache[attr] = tm
            return tm
```

title: Ideas for modifications and extensions of the Bayesian Block algorithm
description:
I think I was asked to open an issue as a reminder for future work on this.  (I am very new to github, so please bear with me if I am messing up here … )

The context is modifying the way the prior on the number of blocks is implemented.  
I am not sure that a general user-defined prior can be made consistent with the need for block additivity of the total fitness function.  … but you guys are clever can perhaps this can work.

Here is some brainstorming of possible extensions:
Maybe the algorithm/prior can be modified to constrain the number of blocks in various ways:  
- maximum value
- miminum value
- specified range (or even a list) of values
- other constraints … even number, odd number, …

I think the most interesting area lies in higher dimensions.  It was a great surprise to me when the modification valid for arbitrary dimension (with one caveat, but a reasonable one) was proved by the San Jose State math people I work with.

title: Create AstrometricFrame
description:
This issue is the second part of #4209, along side #4338 : this issue is about creating a new frame (tentatively called `AstrometricFrame`) that is a rotation of some other frame to be centered at a specific point.

From one my comments in #4209 proposing this:

> Also implement a new frame  - lets call it `AstrometricFrame`?  This would be a frame with one frame attribute: the "origin" coordinate.  This would along the lines of what @mhvk and @smaret are proposing, although it has to be a full rotation (rather than just `cos(dec)` flattening) to account for positions that might be farther away than the small angle approximation allows. Note that the code to do this is _already_ in the `GalactocentricFrame` transformation - that's actually even _more_ complicated than this because it allows an additional "roll" angle (whereas here we're saying the new y-axis has to point in the same direction as the old y-axis at the astrometric point).  We could also add a `SkyCoord` convenience method to get the astrometric frame of a coordinate, allowing use like `coord1.transform_to(coord2.astrometric_frame())`, which would then trivially give us the angles we'd need for `spherical_offsets`.

Perhaps @mhvk, @smaret, or @taldcroft would be interested in implementing this (based on the #4209 conversation)?  Although certainly other volunteers are welcome...

title: "ReferenceError: weakly-referenced object no longer exists" with FITS columns
description:
This issue was revealed by a StackOverflow question:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/33850641/how-to-merge-two-table-with-pyfits

I feel that in principle what the user was doing here should have worked.  The "Delayed" data mechanism being used here for the columns is a hold-over from much older versions of PyFITS, and needs to be reworked.

This would actually be addressed by the plan I've long had for refactoring FITS I/O so that the I/O details for reading an individual array (where that could also be a single column in a table) are fully separated from the HDU object itself, which is somewhat more ephemeral.

The way this would work is that all the details of the data structure for a FITS file would be determined from the header(s) when the file is first read, and cached in a data structure that associates the info with that file (along with a timestamp) or file-like object.  When using mmap this might also hold an existing mmap to the file, though I'm less sure of how I feel about that.  Anyways, point being, a "delayed read" of an array would work by looking into this cache for the physical details about where to find the array data, and then return it, without going through the HDU object itself.  This would also speed up the "convenience" functions, since they can access cached details about a file without having to re-read all the file's headers each time the same file is accessed.

This has been my plan for a long time but it hasn't been high priority.

title: Units error in icrs_to_helioecliptic (in icrs_to_helioecliptic)

In [line 76 of ecliptic_transfprms.py](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/v1.1.x/astropy/coordinates/builtin_frames/ecliptic_transforms.py#L76) there appears to be a bug:

units.au is multiplied with a result and then added to a scalar; I believe there are simply missing parentheses here.  This then creates/reveals a dimensions issue (at least when used with via calling `transform_to` on an array.)   What worked for me was adding two changes.  Replacing the current line 76 with:

`heliocart = ((from_coo.cartesian.xyz).T + delta_bary_to_helio) * u.au`

and then updating line 82 to be:

`newrepr = cartrepr_from_matmul(rmat, ICRS(CartesianRepresentation(heliocart.T)))`

I did some spot checking of this on a transformed array of coordinates and the handful I checked appear correct.

title: Context manager for CGS E&M units?
description:
(This is a follow-up of #4355, combining comments by @eteq and myself; EDIT (2021): this also is meant to replace #1687, #5879 - calculate magnetic energy density, etc.; #4086 - coulomb-statcoulomb equivalency)

There are multiple versions of the E&M system in cgs [1] which are mutually incompatible. As a result, many cgs E&M unit conversions in astropy are not normally possible. It might be possible to devise a context manager within which conversion is allowed, i.e., one would do something like

```
with u.set_em_system(u.cgs.emu):
    ...
```

and one could then happily convert charge per second into the relevant current, or calculate a force from just `charge1 * charge2 / distance**2` in the cgs ESU system.

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centimetre%E2%80%93gram%E2%80%93second_system_of_units#Derivation_of_CGS_units_in_electromagnetism

title: FITS: improve support for column-oriented binary tables
description:
Column-oriented FITS tables (take a look [here](http://www.star.bris.ac.uk/~mbt/topcat/sun253/outColfits.html)) can be read and written with the current astropy FITS I/O library, however each field in the resulting python table has an extraneous dimension of size 1. See the example below.

Such kind of file can be generated easily with IDL and mwrfits:

``` idl
table = {id:[0,1,2], str:['foo','bar','anotherstring'], f2d:[[0.2,0.3,0.5], [1.5,4.8,-1.5]]}
mwrfits, /create, table, 'table.fits'
```

Reading this table in python:

``` python
from astropy.io import fits

table = fits.getdata('table.fits', 1)
table['id'].shape  # (1, 3)    should be (3,)
table['str'].shape # (1, 3)    should be (3,)
table['f2d'].shape # (1, 2, 3) should be (2, 3)
```

PS: I am not as skilled in python as I would like to be, so if you know of a user-friendly way to do the same thing as the IDL code above, but in python, I would be very grateful!

title: Unit.to_string contains whitespace for vounit format
description:
according to the documentation the "vounit" format should be the VO 1.0 format but when using this in the `to_string` method one does not get a compliant VO representation of the unit which uses dot as a product and not whitespace:

```
import astropy.units
vo = astropy.units.format.VOUnit()
u = vo.parse("m s") # technically not VO syntax but leniency on input is ok
print(u.to_string("vounit"))
```

--> `m s`
This is not correct it should be `m.s`. The VO reference unity library does not accept this as VO format.
Its probably not a big deal as most unit standards accept space as product, but it is usually wise to be strict on what one produces even if one is lenient in what on accepts.
using astropy 1.1rc2

title: Release final v1.2
description:
[edited by @astrofrog @taldcroft]

There was a list of issues in this issue that had been copied over from the 1.1 issue (#3519) but which also diverged from what we did for 1.2 in the end, so I've moved that to the wiki: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/wiki/Old-to-do-list-for-1.1

Instead, here are some feature pull requests that we might want to exceptionally consider backporting to the 1.2.x branch before the release (these should be considered by the coordination committee):
- [x] Refinements/API changes for `AstrometricFrame` - #4941
- [x] Example Gallery improvements - #4924
- [x] Support for choosing different sources for planet positions - https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/4920 - @mhvk @StuartLittlefair @eteq
- [x] #4952 - this is a bug fix (there are other bug fixes _not_ in this list because they are included by default), but is noted here because it is important for #4920 to actually get the right answers for some items.  Note that #4979 needs to be backported _first_ before #4952 (it was originally one issue, but it turns out the changes in #4979 need to go to 1.0.x too, while the changes merged in #4952 are 1.2.x, so it was split into two issues)
- [x] Auto-downloading of IERS-A data - https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/4436 - @taldcroft @mhvk @eteq

Other to-dos for the release:
- [x] Release and update astropy-helpers in astropy and package-template if needed
- [x] Write 'what's new in 1.2'
- [x] Do a v1.0.x release
- [x] Clean up changelog - @astrofrog
- [x] Update IERS B file (#4994)
- [x] Backport any PRs milestoned as v1.2.0 merged after the feature freeze (mostly bug and documentation fixes, and maybe a couple of feature PRs from the list above)
- [x] Update list of contributors
- [x] Update stats on contributions in 'What's new'
- [ ] Update release tooling/instructions for latest procedures

One question is, do we actually bother doing another bugfix release in the v1.1.x branch, or do we just move those changelog entries to v1.2.0?

title: Time.get_delta_ut1_utc() is not consisent with Time.ut1.value-Time.utc.value during leap seconds
description:
If I instantiate an astropy.time.Time instance in the middle of a day in which a leap second occurs and then calculate dut1 using get_delta_ut1_utc(), I get different (often by a minus sign) values than if I calculate the dut1 using ut1.value-utc.value.

The script below demonstrates what I mean.

utc_list is a list of JD's selected from the list of leap seconds published at

http://maia.usno.navy.mil/ser7/tai-utc.dat

I first loop over them, calculating dut1 using both methods described above and printing the results.  They agree.

If I take utc_list, subtract 0.2 (so that utc_list is in the middle of the day on which the leap second is applied), and perform the same analysis, the two methods for calculating dut1 give wildly different results.

If I take utc_list, subtract 1.2, and perform the same analysis, the two methods for calculating dut1 again agree.

This is using version 1.1 of astropy.

```
import numpy as np
from astropy.time import Time

if __name__ == "__main__":

    utc_list = np.array([2445516.5, 2446247.5, 2447161.5, 2447892.5,
                2448257.5, 2448804.5, 2449169.5, 2449534.5,
                2450083.5, 2450630.5, 2451179.5, 2453736.5])

    print '\ncompare get_delta_ut_utc with ut1-utc at exact moment of leap second'
    print '#'
    print '# get_delta_ut1_utc().value, 86401.0*(ut1.value-utc.value)'
    for utc in utc_list:
        jd = Time(utc, scale='utc', format='jd')
        print jd.get_delta_ut1_utc().value, 86401.0*(jd.ut1.value-jd.utc.value)

    print '\n'
    print 'displace by 0.2 days so that we are considering a moment during'
    print 'the day of the leap second'
    print '#'
    print '# get_delta_ut1_utc().value, 86401.0*(ut1.value-utc.value)'
    for utc in utc_list:
        jd = Time(utc-0.2, scale='utc', format='jd')
        print jd.get_delta_ut1_utc().value, 86401.0*(jd.ut1.value-jd.utc.value)

    print '\n'
    print 'displace by 1.2 days so that we are outside of the leap second day'
    print '#'
    print '# get_delta_ut1_utc().value, 86400.0*(ut1.value-utc.value)'
    for utc in utc_list:
        jd = Time(utc-1.2, scale='utc', format='jd')
        print jd.get_delta_ut1_utc().value, 86400.0*(jd.ut1.value-jd.utc.value)
```

title: Improve "building from source" documentation for Linux
description:
I've had at least a few people trying to install Astropy on Linux not realizing that a missing "Python.h" means they need to install the python development package for their system.  The current documentation simply reads 

> You will need a compiler suite and the development headers for Python and Numpy in order to build Astropy. On Linux, using the package manager for your distribution will usually be the easiest route

and then goes on to give lots of OSX-specific instructions.  It does not give any more information for Linux.  In the past I've been hesitant to pile on too much information for Linux because 1) An implicit assumption (often incorrect) that Linux users can be expected to "know what they're dong" and 2) It's hard to give comprehensive instructions for different Linux distros.

However, the existing text is horribly vague even under that rubric.  It should at least mention that most distros have a separate Python development package called either "python-dev" or "python-devel".  It also couldn't hurt to supply examples with apt-get and yum at a minimum.

While we're at it I think that section should also be reorganized.  It should open with some general text, and then be broken into subsections specific to OSX, Linux, and ~~Windows~~.  This will make the section less cluttered, and easier to navigate to the information a specific user needs for their platform.  This will at least address a small part of #1807.

**Update:** As I noted in #4420 there are not any existing build instructions specific to Windows, so implementing this task should not include that, as it's a non-trivial undertaking.  Instead this task should include just:
- [x] Reorganize the existing text so that OS-specific instructions are corralled into OS-specific subsections, and
- [x] For the Linux specific section add the aforementioned requirement of installing the OS's Python-dev package.

title: Path objects not supported in low-level I/O packages
description:
In at least `io.ascii` and `io.fits` (and perhaps `io.votable`) one gets unexpected exceptions if a Python 3 `Path` object is passed as the file name.  This was first noted in #4405, where a partial fix was put in place in the I/O registry layer to translate a `Path` object to a string.

In general a `Path` object should be accepted anywhere a file object is accepted.  At least that would be the theory, with no idea of the difficulty and implications.

title: Compound model expressions not displayed when printing compound model instances
description:
Currently, if you create a compound model class and then print it out, the display of the class shows the expression that was used to create it:

```
<class '__main__.CompoundModel1'>
Name: CompoundModel1
Inputs: ('x',)
Outputs: ('y',)
Fittable parameters: ('amplitude_0', 'mean_0', 'stddev_0', 'amplitude_1', 'mean_1', 'stddev_1')
Expression: [0] + [1]
Components: 
    [0]: <class 'astropy.modeling.functional_models.Gaussian1D'>
    Name: Gaussian1D
    Inputs: ('x',)
    Outputs: ('y',)
    Fittable parameters: ('amplitude', 'mean', 'stddev')

    [1]: <class 'astropy.modeling.functional_models.Gaussian1D'>
    Name: Gaussian1D
    Inputs: ('x',)
    Outputs: ('y',)
    Fittable parameters: ('amplitude', 'mean', 'stddev')
```

Here the expression is shown as `[0] + [1]`, where the numeric indices are used for terseness.  One can then look at the list of components to see what each component of the expression is.  I've long held that this display could be improved, but I don't have a great idea for how, yet.  Please suggest something! 

But anyways the point of this bug is that while the _class_ shows the components properly, if you print a compound model instance it doesn't give any useful information about the components:

```
In [23]: TwoGaussians = Gaussian1D + Gaussian1D

In [24]: gg = TwoGaussians(1, 0, 0.1, 1, 0.5, 0.3)

In [25]: print(gg)
Model: CompoundModel2
Inputs: ('x',)
Outputs: ('y',)
Model set size: 1
Parameters:
    amplitude_0 mean_0 stddev_0 amplitude_1 mean_1 stddev_1
    ----------- ------ -------- ----------- ------ --------
            1.0    0.0      0.1         1.0    0.5      0.3
```

One can certainly print the class of the model like: `print(type(gg))`, but that's rather obtuse.  The model instance should show all the components just as the model class does.

I think this should be easy enough for a novice to fix, with a bit of effort.

title: clear_download_cache() does not work in Python 2.7
description:
In Python 2.7, clearing the download cache runs into two problems, related to #4426.  First:

```
In [1]: astro
1.1

In [2]: from astropy.utils import data

In [3]: !rm -rf /Users/aldcroft/.astropy/cache

In [4]: f = data.download_file('http://google.com', cache=True)
Downloading http://google.com [Done]

In [5]: data.clear_download_cache()

In [6]: f = data.download_file('http://google.com', cache=True)

In [7]: import os

In [8]: os.path.exists(f)
Out[8]: False
```

This is because the shelve file name _without_ the `.db` extension is removed if it exists (which it doesn't, but that is not caught in the code).  This relates to a fundamental issue with shelve on Python 2, which is that you don't know (and cannot determine in general) the name of the backing database file(s).  This could be fixed by putting them into a sub-directory with a known name and then clobbering that.

title: Change release documentation to use twine instead of setup.py upload
description:
It seems that at least part of the "right" solution to [my post-release woes](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/4406#issuecomment-166372262) is to prefer using [twine](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/twine) to upload distributions to PyPI, rather than using `setup.py upload`.

Twine can and should also be used to register distributions (as an alternative to `setup.py register`) though the documentation doesn't make this obvious currently.

This doesn't solve all the issues I ran into, but we should update our documentation to prefer it, and I will work on post-release procedures that use it as well.  I've known about twine for some time, but never used it just because I was using Python versions that use HTTPS by default, as I suspect are @eteq and @astrofrog who are so far the only other people who have made Astropy releases.  But for affiliated package authors as well we should probably switch to recommending twine.

title: io.ascii CDS reader requires at least 2 description characters
description:
In the ReadMe, the Explanations column must have at least two characters to get properly recognized by the regex.  A column descriptor with no characters at all after the name is skipped entirely.  The example below will not read correctly:

```
================================================================================
Byte-by-byte Description of file: *
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   Bytes Format Units  Label  Explanations
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1-   2   I2    ---     year         To get true calendar year, add 1900 for 
                                      MJD<=51543 or add 2000 for MJD>=51544)
  3-   4   I2    ---     month
```

Here is the regex:

```
        re_col_def = re.compile(r"""\s*
                                    (?P<start> \d+ \s* -)? \s*
                                    (?P<end>   \d+)        \s+
                                    (?P<format> [\w.]+)     \s+
                                    (?P<units> \S+)        \s+
                                    (?P<name>  \S+)        \s+  # the \s+ means spaces are *required*
                                    (?P<descr> \S.+)""",  # \S.+ means at least two chars are needed
                                re.VERBOSE)
```

It isn't clear if this explanation column is required, but we should make it optional just in case.

title: Sometimes creating compound models doesn't preserve parameter.fixed
description:
Look what I found. This one is ok:

```
>>> from astropy.modeling import models
>>> a = models.Gaussian1D(mean=10.)
>>> a.mean.fixed = True
>>> b = models.Const1D(2.) + a
>>> b[1].mean.fixed
True
```

This one is not:

```
>>> a = models.Gaussian1D(mean=5.) + models.Gaussian1D(mean=10.)
>>> for x in a: x.mean.fixed = True
>>> a[1].mean.fixed
True
>>> a.mean_1.fixed
True
>>> b = models.Const1D(2.) + a
>>> b[2].mean.fixed
False
>>> b.mean_2.fixed
False
```

Since it works in the first case, the intent is to have the constraints be preserved, correct? My guess is that there's something about making a compound model out of another compound model that loses the fixed attribute setting...

title: Deprecate and eventually remove Python 2 support
description:
Python 2 is legacy.  Python 3 is the present and future of Python.  I don't need to repeat the arguments here.

I'm not currently suggesting a timeline for this.  Just that we need to continue doing what we can to push the community away from Python 2 through documentation, tutorials, articles, and social pressure (and technical pressure in less critical areas, such as offering Python-3-only features).

Of course, before we even deprecate Python 2 support there should be an Extra-Long-Term-Support release that guarantees critical bug fixes as needed for institutional users stuck on Python 2.

lazyproperty: Documentation misleading
description:
I tried the `lazyproperty` from the utils.decorators today and it is works as expected but one thing is very strange. The documentation states that

If a setter for this property is defined, it will still be possible to manually update the value of the property, if that capability is desired.

Well but at least with python 3.5 the setter/deleter are always created. To stay with the example in the docstring of the decorator

class LazyTest(object):

        print('Computing the value for complicated_property...')
        return 42
lt = LazyTest()
lt.complicated_property
#Computing the value for complicated_property...

#42
# New
lt.complicated_property = 10
lt.complicated_property
#10
del lt.complicated_property
lt.complicated_property
#Computing the value for complicated_property...
#42
```

I didn't expected this behaviour from the docstring and was searching for some time now where my code went wrong. If this is intentional I would suggest altering the docstring or if it wasn't intentional maybe there is a way to alter it. I haven't checked but maybe this may also be something that was different in an older python version. Or am I misunderstanding the documentation?

title: Move sphinx build to python3 and latest numpy
description: As we're moving to python3, the sphinx build should also be on python3 and some care should be taken to ensure that all the references actually go to the python3 documentation. As of this writing, just using an intersphinx link to `docs.python.org/3/objects.inv` has problems. See https://github.com/astropy/astropy-helpers/pull/214

title: Write better documentation for PR screwups
description:
I've written comments [like this](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/4483#issuecomment-171358998) more times than I can count now.

We should find places to better emphasize (both in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) and in the developer docs) that short of deleting your fork, almost all git mistakes can be fixed.  And more to the point, if you have opened a PR, that PR can be fixed by fixing the issues locally and then doing a `git push --force` of your fixed branch to the existing remote branch of the same name.

We can't provide documentation for how to fix every mistake in git.  We do already link to the [git choose-your-own-adventure](http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/development/workflow/development_workflow.html#if-something-goes-wrong) but we might make that more prominent.  

More importantly though we need to emphasize that the contents of your remote branch (i.e. the branch on your GitHub fork) is ephemeral, and can be completely replaced, after the PR has been opened, with the appropriate `git push` command, after any mistakes have been fixed.

It is not unlikely that this is a problem of our build machines (I already experienced some flakiness there); so the bug report is more for completeness -- and if others observe similar.

title: QTable not always converting to Quantity?
description:
I've noticed some odd behavior with QTable that seems counter-intuitive, but I'm not sure whether it's a bug or a feature.  Consider the following snippet:

```
tab = QTable.read(...)
tab['X'].unit = u.Mpc

top2 = []
for k,v in elvii_pairs.items():
    top2.append(v['X'][:2])
top2 = u.Quantity(top2).flatten()
```

I would have thought that top2 would then be a Quantity with units Mpc, but instead it ends up as a _dimensionless_ Quantity.

Similary, I would have thought this would also do the same:

```
top2 = []
for k,v in elvii_pairs.items():
    top2.extend(v['X'][:2])
top2 = u.Quantity(top2)
```

But this also yields a dimensionless result.  The cause of this at least I understand, given this snippet:

```
qornot = top2['X'][0]
assert hasattr(qornot, 'unit')  # AssertionError!
```

That is, indexing a single element of a column yields a python number, _not_ a Quantity.  But that seems very unexpected behavior given that `QTable` is supposed to yield Quantities.

@taldcroft @mhvk, are any/all of these bugs, or intended behavior?

title: wcs.WCS.slice() does not modify NAXISj values

title: NDArithmeticMixin arithmetic fails when wcs.WCS present even if identical
description:
The `wcs.WCS` class does not implement the equivalence test functions `__eq__()` and `__ne__()`. Consequently an attempt to test the equivalence of two `WCS` instances reduces to checking identity.  Example:

```
In [19]: w = ccd.wcs

In [20]: w2 = copy.deepcopy(w)

In [21]: w == w
Out[21]: True

In [22]: w == w2
Out[22]: False
```

This causes issues with, for example, `nddata.NDArithmeticMixin._arithmetic` which attempts to check that `nddata.NDData` objects have the same WCS before performing arithmetic on them and raises an exception if the check fails.  This effectively prevents any arithmetic on `nddata.NDData` objects that have WCS as this check will always fail unless the two `wcs.WCS` are references to the same instance.  

astropy/ccdproc#204
astropy/ccdproc#283

title: Simplify access to FITS regular axes
description:
FITS files often contain something like this:

```
CTYPE6  = 'RA      '                     /Axis name                             
CRPIX6  =      1.0000000000000           /Reference pixel                       
CRVAL6  =      54.125448370833           /Reference value in right ascens. (deg)
CDELT6  =      1.0000000000000           /Pixel increment                       
CROTA6  =      0.0000000000000           /Axis rotation                         
```

in the primary HDU header. The way get the RA value now is (assuming it always should be the 6th axis)

```
assert hdu.header['CTYPE6'] == 'RA'
ra = hdu.header['CRVAL6']
```

Or else one has to loop over the axes to find which is named 'RA'.

Wouldn't it be better if we could just use `hdu.header['RA'].value` or something? Same applies to `CRPIX`, `CDELT`, `CROTA`.

title: Get scaled data from FITS GroupData
description:
After reading a data table (`GroupData`) from a FITS file there is no straightforward way to convert it to a plain `numpy` array with scaling applied. Currently I use code like this everywhere:

```

```

where `data` is the `GroupData` object.

I think something simple like a property implemented similar to the above would be nice. If that's OK, I can implement it.

ascii.write([rest_wav_mum, fl_jy, obs_wav_mum, source],
            fileout,
            names=['RestWav (micron)', 'Fl (Jy)', 'ObsWav (micron)', 'Source'],
            delimiter='\t',
            formats={'rest_wav_mum': '%.4f','fl_jy': '%.4e','obs_wav_mum': '%.4f','source':'%d'})
```

The source of the confusion is that the keys in the `formats` dictionary need to match the names in `names`. The docstring is not specific about the form that the dictionary needs to have, and I think this is a mistake that might be easy enough to make. The problem is that unmatched format specifiers pass silently, without any exception or error. I would like to suggest raising an exception or warning for `formats` keys that don't match any of the columns.

(The above code should have been

```
ascii.write([rest_wav_mum, fl_jy, obs_wav_mum, source],
            fileout,
            names=['RestWav (micron)', 'Fl (Jy)', 'ObsWav (micron)', 'Source'],
            delimiter='\t',
            formats={'RestWav (micron)': '%.4f','Fl (Jy)': '%.4e','ObsWav (micron)': '%.4f','Source':'%d'})
```

which, indeed, works.)

title: Ordering of covariance matrix with tied parameters
description:
I am trying to use the modeling/fitting framework with astropy v1.1. I have a compound model (constant + 2 2D Moffat functions), where I am tying the shape parameters for the 2 moffat functions to be the same. The resulting fit works and looks good, but I am having trouble figuring out the ordering on the covariance matrix returned in the 'fit_info' dictionary. The documentation says that it has the same order as `model.param_names`, but with tied parameters there is a shape mismatch:
- `len(model.param_names)`: 13
- `fitter.fit_info['param_cov'].shape`: (10,10)

There are three tied parameters so that makes sense, but now what is the correct correspondence between parameters and covariance matrix row/column?

Here is the code that does the fitting:

``` python
@models.custom_model
def Moffat2D(x, y, amplitude=1.0, x_0=512.0, y_0=512.0, x_gamma=6.0, y_gamma=6.0,
             alpha=1.0):
    """Two dimensional Moffat function with different scale parameters for both axes"""
    rr_gg = (x - x_0) ** 2 / x_gamma**2 + (y - y_0) ** 2 / y_gamma ** 2
    return amplitude * (1 + rr_gg) ** (-alpha)

def fit_moffat_psf(data, x_mean=512, y_mean=512, x_fwhm=6, y_fwhm=6):
    """
    Fit a moffat function to the PSF. A moffat function is given by

    $I_r = I_0 [1+(r/\gamma)^2]^{-\alpha} $

    Where $I_0$ is the intensity at the center of the PSF, $\gamma$ is the
    half-width at half maximum in the absense of atmospheric scattering, and
    $\alpha$ is the atmospheric scattering coefficient.

    Parameters:
    ===========
    - data:      np.ndarray with shape(nx, ny)
                 The data to be fit.

    - x_mean:    np.ndarray with shape (N_sources)
                 The initial guesses for the x-position of all of the sources to fit

    - y_mean:    np.ndarray with shape (N_sources)
                 The initial guesses for the y-position of all of the sources to fit

    - x_fwhm:    np.ndarray with shape (N_sources)
                 The initial guesses for the width of all of the sources in the x-direction

    - y_fwhm:    np.ndarray with shape (N_sources)
                 The initial guesses for the width of all of the sources in the y-direction
    """
    # Make sure we have numpy arrays
    x_mean = np.atleast_1d(x_mean)
    y_mean = np.atleast_1d(y_mean)
    x_fwhm = np.atleast_1d(x_fwhm)
    y_fwhm = np.atleast_1d(y_fwhm)

    YY, XX = np.indices(data.shape)

    # Generate the model to fit
    p_init = models.Const2D(amplitude=0)
    for xi, yi, xwi, ywi in zip(x_mean, y_mean, x_fwhm, y_fwhm):
        p_init += Moffat2D(amplitude=data[np.round(yi).astype(int), np.round(xi).astype(int)],
                           x_0=xi, y_0=yi,
                           x_gamma=xwi, y_gamma=ywi,
                           alpha=1.0)

    # Tie the first two shape parameters together
    p_init.x_gamma_1.tied = lambda mod: mod.x_gamma_2
    p_init.y_gamma_1.tied = lambda mod: mod.y_gamma_2
    p_init.alpha_1.tied = lambda mod: mod.alpha_2

    # Fit the data
    fitter = fitting.LevMarLSQFitter()
    moffat = fitter(p_init, XX, YY, data, maxiter=1000)

    return moffat, fitter
```

title: astropy not future proof( Python 4 )
description:
While having a look at the pytest_plugins i noticed several occassions where

```
if six.PY2:
    <code>
elif six.PY3:
    <code>
```

was used.
For future proof applications that won't need a complete code review(like what happened when python3 was released), checking for `six.PY3` should be avoided. Instead write `if six.PY2` and put the python3 code into `else` instead of `elif six.PY3`. By treating python2 as the special case python3 and python3+ will behave the same which is desirable since the python dev team announced they won't do major changes to the code like what they did when going from python2 to python3

I know this won't be an issue for the near future. But since i think this awesome project will witness python4, I just wanted to let you know this Issue so new additions to the code can be made with this knowledge.

title: writeto() method produces invalid CHECKSUM with CompImageHDU
description:
I am looking into how to mimic the operation of the CFITSIO "fpack" utility with astropy.io.fits and am worried about invalid checksum values written to the compressed files. Specifically, I want to do lossless Rice compression on unsigned short images (BITPIX=16).

For reference, I see the same behavior in astropy 1.0.3 and 1.1.1 (both with anaconda from Continuum Analytics). The Python version is 2.7.11 and numpy is 1.10.2 with MKL acceleration. The OS is CentOS 6.

I am able to essentially mimic the operation of fpack (i.e., compress a BITPIX 16 FITS image) like so:

```
idata, ihdr = pf.getdata("image.fits", header=True, uint=True, do_not_scale_image_data=True)
compressed_HDU = pf.CompImageHDU(data=idata, header=ihdr, uint=True)
compressed_HDU.writeto("image.fits.fz", clobber=True, checksum=True)
```

The code above produces the correct data content (I can read the data back and pixels are identical to the original) but fitsverify identifies a problem with the checksums. For reference, I have fitsverify 4.16 built against CFITSIO version 3.270. For comparison, I have attached the fitsverify output from both the fpack-created image (no problems) and the astropy-created image (bogus checksums).

I have also attached complete header listings of the astropy and fpack file variants for examination. Both files correctly have DATASUM=0 for the empty primary header (the CHECKSUMs differ because of comment differences, which is expected).

The astropy.io.fits checksum for the _uncompressed_ data (ZDATASUM) appears to be correct. To double-check this, I ran a copy of the original image through fpack, funpack, and then fpack again (see the "fff" header listing attached) and confirmed that ZDATASUM values match what astropy puts in. Long story short, the writeto() method seems to correctly write a compressed image HDU when given the appropriate options, but the checksum and datasum for the compressed image are bogus.

title: io.fits add ability to efficiently load single extension header
description:
Currently io.fits/pyfits always loads all extension headers regardless whether one wants them all or not.
At least the obvious api function `getheader` has this behaviour.

This slows down simple tasks like just checking the primary extension headers keys considerably when the number of extensions is large as it needs to seek through the full file.
Obviously seeking the file is required to load the later extensions but it should only try to read as much as it must to satisfy the users request.
