title: Initializer signature/docstring for astropy.wcs.WCS omits mention of filename-based initialization
description:
I was recently demonstrating the use of `astropy.wcs.WCS` in a class where I asked people to consult the docstring to figure out how to initialize the WCS from a file. It was only then that I realized the concise form of initializing a WCS (the one I actually use all the time) is totally non-obvious from the docs!

On the [main WCS module page](http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/wcs/index.html), there's an example that goes

```
>>> from astropy.wcs import WCS
>>> w = WCS('image.fits')
>>> lon, lat = w.all_pix2world(30, 40, 0)
>>> print(lon, lat)
```

If you were to look at [the WCS class docs](http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.wcs.WCS.html#astropy.wcs.WCS) you could be forgiven for being somewhat confused as to how the first argument to the initializer is interpreted in that example. The relevant text:

> `class astropy.wcs.WCS(header=None, fobj=None, key=u' ', minerr=0.0, relax=True, naxis=None, keysel=None, colsel=None, fix=True, translate_units=u'', _do_set=True)`
> 
> `header` : astropy.io.fits header object, Primary HDU, Image HDU, string, dict-like, or None, optional
> If header is not provided or None, the object will be initialized to default values.

I can probably make a PR for this if people agree the docstring should be improved. If there's canned text used in other places where Astropy takes filenames as strings in addition to the more explicit passing of the right kind of object, I can use that. (Just point me to an example!)

title: Make keyword argument names follow documented conventions
description:
I noticed that the new [LombScargle](http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.stats.LombScargle.html#astropy.stats.LombScargle) class accepts a kwarg `nterms` (number of terms), but [this function](http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.stats.akaike_info_criterion_lsq.html#astropy.stats.akaike_info_criterion_lsq) wants `n_params` and `n_samples`. 

Similarly, [match_coordinates_sky](http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.coordinates.match_coordinates_sky.html#astropy.coordinates.match_coordinates_sky) takes `matchcoord` and `catalogcoord`, but [get_constellation](http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.coordinates.get_constellation.html#astropy.coordinates.get_constellation) takes `short_name`. 

I'd find it useful if we picked some conventions to follow for naming function arguments across the whole astropy package and document this by adding a section to the [Coding Guidelines](http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/development/codeguide.html#coding-style-conventions). But,  I recognize that it might be annoying to deprecate a bunch of keyword arguments across the package. What do you think?

title: io.registry doesn't handle inherited formats correctly
description:
[discovered on v1.2, tested against build of `master/HEAD` on OSX]

The `io.registry` currently doesn't handle inherited format registration well; if a class doesn't have a format registered but one of its ancestors does, whichever `(format, class)` pair was registered first will be used.

It seems to me that the match should come from whichever object is closest to the target in the MRO.

Consider the following example:

``` python
from astropy.io import registry
from astropy.units import Quantity

# set up .read() for grandparent
Quantity.read = classmethod(registry.read)

# define parent
class SubClass1(Quantity):
    pass

# define child
class SubClass2(SubClass1):
    pass
```

Now we can define a `read` method for the grandparent (`Quantity`):

``` python
# define reader for grandparent
def read_grandparent(f):
    return Quantity([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], unit='m')
registry.register_reader('simple', Quantity, read_grandparent)
```

and if we try and match the reader for the grandchild (`SubClass2`) it should return `read_grandparent`, and it does:

``` python
>>> print(registry.get_reader('simple', SubClass2))
<function read_grandparent at 0x11099dcf8>
```

Now if we define a `read` method for the parent (`SubClass1`):

``` python
# define reader for parent
def read_parent(f):
    return SubClass1([6, 7, 8, 9, 10], unit='s')
registry.register_reader('simple', SubClass1, read_parent)
```

because `read_grandparent` was registered first, it still matches as the 'best' match:

``` python
>>> print(registry.get_reader('simple', SubClass2))
<function read_grandparent at 0x11099dcf8>
```

If this is a bug, the following patch to `astropy/io/registry.py` seems to fix it for me, by searching up the `__mro__` and returning the first match:

``` diff
diff --git a/astropy/io/registry.py b/astropy/io/registry.py
index d00f0c2..e6caf0f 100644
--- a/astropy/io/registry.py
+++ b/astropy/io/registry.py
@@ -415,6 +415,13 @@ def _is_best_match(class1, class2, format_classes):
         In this case the subclass will use the parent reader/writer.
     """
     classes = [cls for fmt, cls in format_classes]
+    # search inheritance of class1
+    for cls in class1.__mro__:
+        if class2 is cls:  # class1 will inherit from class2
+            return True
+        if cls in classes:  # class1 will not inherit from class2
+            return False
+    # keep old logic, just in case
     is_best_match = ((class1 is class2) or (issubclass(class1, class2)
                                             and class1 not in classes))
     return is_best_match
```

title: Incorrect order of corners in calc_footprint?
description:
@OlgaVorokh and I noticed a possible bug in the order of the corners in calc_footprint:
http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/_modules/astropy/wcs/wcs.html#WCS.calc_footprint

The docstring says:

> The order is counter-clockwise starting with the bottom left corner.
> which implies this order:
> "bottom left", "bottom right", "top right", "top left"

The code contains this:

```
corners = np.array([[1, 1],
                                [1, naxis2],
                                [naxis1, naxis2],
                                [naxis1, 1]], dtype = np.float64)
```

which we think corresponds to:
"bottom left", "top left", "top right", "bottom right"
because naxis1 is connected to left and right, and naxis2 is connected to top and bottom.

At least that's how it appears when opening the image in ds9.

PS: We're adding a similar method to the `gammapy.image.SkyImage` class, that's when we noticed this issue.  https://github.com/gammapy/gammapy/pull/642

cc @nden

title: Table.__init__ with Mapping
description:
Would it be possible to lower the restrictions of `Table.__init__` (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/table/table.py#L320) to `collections.Mapping` instead of `dict`?

That would allow customized mappings to be used, especially if one subclasses `Mapping` or `UserDict` instead of `dict`. Both of them do not evaluate to `True` currently:

```
>>> isinstance(collections.UserDict(), dict)
False
```

while they are considered as instance of `collections.Mapping`:

```
>>> isinstance(collections.UserDict(), collections.Mapping)
True
```

title: remote_data does not apply in the example gallery
description:
This came up in discussion of #5210, although it's not really directly related.  The basic question is: should we have  the remote data machinery apply to the sphinx examples, and if so, how?  Right now it effectively applies to the whole documentation because the doctests run, and they will catch any situation where the internet is accessed without the `remote_data` flag being used.  But the sphinx example gallery bypasses this because it isn't recognized as part of the doctests.  

My preference I think is to leave it as-is.  The argument for that restricting remote_data would render some of the examples non-functional.  For example, the coordinates example uses `SkyCoord.from_name` as a critical element.  So with `remote_data` off the whole example would have to be skipped.  And the sphinx build is _not_ generally assumed to be non-internet - the intersphinx machinery requires the internet, and we let that run on e.g. travis without complaint.

cc @astrofrog @adrn @bsipocz

title: Support binary SI prefixes, units
description:
Astropy provides support for information units such as bit, byte, kilobit, kilobyte, but does not support the SI-approved prefixes for binary (i.e., 1024-based, instead of 1000-based) notation, such as:
- kibibyte (KiB = 1024 B)
- mebibyte (MiB = 1024^2 B)
- gigibyte (GiB = 1024^3 B)
- tebibyte (TiB = 1024^4 B)
- pebibyte (PiB = 1024^5 B)
- exbibyte (EiB = 1024^6 B)
- zebibyte (ZiB = 1024^7 B)
- yobibyte (YiB = 1024^8 B)

And corresponding units for bits.

I'm preparing a Pull request, in case the community thinks this is valuable.

title: indexing of astropy coordinate object is 25 times slower than indexing the cartesian representation
description:
Basic issue:  I have skycoord objects containing arrays of coordinates and need to extract the Cartesian coordinates for a subset of these objects.  It turns out that indexing the skycoord object and then converting to Cartesian coordinates takes at least 25 times longer than converting the entire array of coordinates to Cartesian representation and then indexing.

Sample code to reproduce:

```
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy import units as u
import numpy as np

c = SkyCoord(ra=np.random.uniform(size=100)*u.rad, dec=np.random.uniform(size=100)*u.rad,distance=np.random.uniform(size=100)*u.pc)

ind = 50

%timeit res = c[ind].cartesian.xyz
%timeit res = c.cartesian[ind].xyz
%timeit res = c.cartesian.xyz[:,ind]
```

On Mac OS 10.10.5, python 2.7.12, ipython 5.0.0, astropy v1.2, results are:

> I think we should do the switch to Python 3 on RTD **after** the release so that we can deal with things step by step. Note that RTD will not stop serving existing docs, so once we make the switch on RTD to Python 3, only new docs will need to be build-able. This suggests to me the following timeline:
- [X] Merge #4556 and keep Travis on Python 2.7
- [X] Go ahead with the 1.2 and 1.0.10 releases
- [X] Switch default travis build to python 3, but not yet the docs [#5155]
- [X] Switch Travis and RTD to build the docs with Python 3. At this point, new `latest` builds will start building with Python 3, and future 1.2.x builds will also be fine since the 1.2.x branch includes the changes here. [#5135]
- [ ] Backport any required changes for the docs to build to astropy-helpers 1.0.x, and release a new version of the helpers
- [ ] Update the 1.0.x branch of astropy core to the latest astropy-helpers and do whatever fixes are needed to get it building without errors on Python 3
- [ ] Carry out a new 1.0.x release, which will now build correctly on RTD

title: Observatory: EarthLocation with more site-related information
description:
Hi there,

If one wants to access the sites database in astropy (which I understand are observatories), one uses a class called `SiteRegistry` (`coordinates/sites.py`), which returns 1) a list of names and 2) a list of objects `EarthLocation` (`coordinates/earth.py`), through the use of a mapping dictionary `_lowercase_names_to_locations`.

Now that's not cool if the database of observatories gathers not only `latitude`, `longitude` and `elevation`, but also the timezone, the average pressure, the average temperature, and any other relevant information (source, aliases, website, humidity, wind, etc).

I dirty fix is to access `EarthLocation._get_site_registry()._loaded_jsondb` which stores the raw content of the database, however that's not really satisfactory for many reasons.

The idea would be to implement a new class "Observatory" (or whatever better name), which gathers all observatory information. It would most probably inherit from `EarthLocation`.
There could be another new class "ObservatoryRegistry", that mimics `SiteRegistry` unless it is replaced to output a list of "Observatory" instead of a list of `EarthLocation`.

What do you think?

CC astroplan @cdeil, @bmorris3, @bsipocz

Cheers

title: Formatting Quantity and other mixin columns
description:
The current mixin formalism provides only a way to specify a default column format via the `info` attribute.  For instance:

```
class QuantityInfo(ParentDtypeInfo):
    """
    Container for meta information like name, description, format.  This is
    required when the object is used as a mixin column within a table, but can
    be used as a general way to store meta information.
    """
    attrs_from_parent = set(['dtype', 'unit'])  # dtype and unit taken from parent
    _supports_indexing = True

    @staticmethod
    def default_format(val):
        return '{0.value:}'.format(val)
```

But as noted in #5263 this does not provide the ability to set the `info.format` attribute in a way that should work, e.g. `dat['a'].info.format = '%f'`.  This ends up failing here (in `table/pprint.py`) because `'%f' % quantity` fails:

```
def _possible_string_format_functions(format_):
    """Iterate through possible string-derived format functions.

    A string can either be a format specifier for the format built-in,
    a new-style format string, or an old-style format string.
    """
    yield lambda format_, val: format(val, format_)
    yield lambda format_, val: format_.format(val)
    yield lambda format_, val: format_ % val
```

In the particular case of `Quantity`, everything would work just dandy if `val` were actually `val.value`.  That suggests one potential generalization of allowing for a method in `info` that transforms from the actual object being formatted to `val`.  Another idea to handle this is providing overrides for each of the above three string format functions.  This is probably more general and powerful, but comes with a performance penalty that might be non-trivial.  Maybe we could make two versions of `_possible_string_format_functions`, one which gets called if there are info overrides and the other (equivalent to the current version) if there are no info overrides.

Thoughts @mhvk?

title: io.fits fails roundtrip for numpy arrays with strings
description:
With astropy 1.2.1 and python 3.5, A numpy array with strings (dtype 'S'fails a roundtrip test to the fits format:

``` python
from __future__ import print_function
import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits

a = np.zeros(10, dtype=[('X', 'S5'), ('Y', 'f8')])
fits.writeto('test.fits', a, clobber=True)
b = fits.getdata('test.fits')

print(a == b)
print(a['X'] == b['X'])  #- scalar False in py3.5; vector of True in py2.7 !
print(a['Y'] == b['Y'])
```

this appears to be because `b['X']` is changing the dtype from 'S5' to '<U5' on the fly:

``` python
print("b.dtype is", b.dtype)
print("b['X'].dtype is", b['X'].dtype)
print("a['X'].dtype is", a['X'].dtype)
```

results in

```
b.dtype is (numpy.record, [('X', 'S5'), ('Y', '>f8')])
b['X'].dtype is <U5
a['X'].dtype is |S5
```

It does happen to work with I cast `b` back to a vanilla numpy ndarray:

``` python
c = np.asarray(b)
print(a == c)
print(a['X'] == c['X'])
print(a['Y'] == c['Y'])
```

results in

```
[ True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True]
[ True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True]
[ True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True  True]
```

The tests that fail are:

This works when writing the same data converted to a Table object, and also works when creating the BinTableHDU from columns by hand.  This test is a demonstration of the failure reported in #5268 .
- writing then reading a numpy structured array containing a 2D column of strings using `astropy.io.fits.writeto` and reading back in with `astropy.io.fits.getdata`: the dtype seems to have mixed up the number of unicode bytes vs. the number of characters to write.

title: Optimizing Cosmology.comoving_distance
description:
Lots of cosmological calculations (ones depending on `comoving_distance` at least) are fairly slow on large arrays.  [It looks like this is because the integration is performed repeatedly for every redshift value (I think?)](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/cosmology/core.py#L1217-L1218) --- which is wasteful.  For example, if I'm looking for the comoving distances at redshifts `z = [0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0]` then the results of all but `max(z)` (in this case `1.0`) are going to be (implicitly) recalculated in the calculation of `max(z)`.   Shouldn't there be a fairly easy way to calculate the results for all input values of `z`, something like:

```
# sort redshifts
inds = np.argsort(z)
sz = z[inds]
dc = np.zeros_like(sz)
integrand = 0.0
z1 = 0.0
# Iterate over all redshifts in order
for ii, z2 in enumerate(sz):
    # Integrate from previous redshift to `z2`
    integrand += integrate_func(z1, z2)
    dc[ii] = integrand_to_com_dist(integrand)

# *un*sort to match input array
return dc[np.argsort(inds)]
```

---

Edit: Perhaps if `len(z) > NUM` (for some appropriately chosen `NUM`) the code can switch between the current way it's working (e.g. `len(z) < 10`) or performing a single integral, dumping intermediate steps as needed (e.g. `len(z) >= 10`, for example)

title: How do ASCII columns get written with the correct width in FITS binary tables?
description:
FITS binary tables that contain unicode columns get written row-by-row, and unicode columns are converted item-by-item using `numpy.char.encode(item, 'ascii')`.  This returns a byte array, but with a size that differs from the width of the original array.

Here is a highly simplified example:

``` python
>>> foo = ['ELG']*5 + ['BLAT']*5
>>> bar = np.array(foo)
>>> bar
array(['ELG', 'ELG', 'ELG', 'ELG', 'ELG', 'BLAT', 'BLAT', 'BLAT', 'BLAT',
       'BLAT'], 
      dtype='<U4')
>>> np.char.encode(bar[0], 'ascii')
array(b'ELG', 
      dtype='|S3')
>>> with open('foo.dat', 'wb') as f:
...     np.char.encode(bar[0], 'ascii').tofile(f)
... 
```

This writes 3 bytes, not 4, which is the correct width of the column.

title: fits.PrimaryHDU ignores BITPIX when called with a header
description:
When constructing a PrimaryHDU that contains no data, the default value for `BITPIX` is set to 8. This is true even when PrimaryHDU is passed a header with an existing BITPIX keyword.

Once this value is set, it's impossible to change without directly editing the `hdu._bitpix` attribute (setting `hdu.header['BITPIX'] = 16` has no effect, for example). Whenever the header is verified or updated, the value is reset to the stored `hdu._bitpix` value, and since there's never any data associated with the header, there's no reason for the HDU to think otherwise.

This wouldn't be a problem (there's no data for the FITS header to argue with, after all), except that some pipelines will crash with the wrong BITPIX. Since there's no FITS standard value for BITPIX when no data is associated with a header, there's never any warning or error, and the BITPIX value is changed silently.

At the very least, some kind of warning or information is essential. A better way to set the BITPIX value for an HDU with no data is probably important, especially when the HDU is passed an existing header.

title: AltAz cartesian system is left handed!!!
description:
The majority of the community uses a right handed system for cartesian coordinates.
Given that Az is measure N to E the Cartesian components of a right handed system should be:
x=cos(alt)sin(az)
y=cos(alt)cos(az)
z=sin(alt)

The only solution is that You are measuring Az from E to N (and forgot this when implementing the rotation), or you are using a left handed system. Please, please use a right handed system and fix this. Maybe it only happens after transform_to.
To see run:

```
import numpy as np
from astropy.coordinates import *
from astropy.units import *
from astropy.time import *

s = SkyCoord(ra=45*deg,dec=45*deg)
eloc = EarthLocation(0*m,0*m,6356752*m)
aa = AltAz(obstime=Time(1234,format='gps'),location=eloc)
strans = s.transform_to(aa) #bring to altaz frame
x = np.cos(strans.alt.rad)*np.sin(strans.az.rad)#points to E
y = np.cos(strans.alt.rad)*np.cos(strans.az.rad)#points to N
z = np.sin(strans.alt.rad)#points to zenith
print x,y,z
print strans.cartesian.xyz
print "x and y are swapped!"
```

title: Wonky conditional in astropy.io.ascii.core
description:
Chanced across some very unusual code in astropy.io.ascii.core. I don't think it's responsible for my colleague's issue, but I believe it should be looked at as it almost certainly does not work as intended.

In #910, this code was added to `core.py` starting at [line 745](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/io/ascii/core.py#L745-L749):

``` python
            # when we write tables the columns may be astropy.table.Columns
            # which don't carry a fill_values by default
            for col in cols:
                if ~hasattr(col, 'fill_values'):
                    col.fill_values = {}
```

If you were curious like me, this is _not_ a TypeError. In fact...

``` python
In [1]: ~True
Out[1]: -2

In [2]: ~False
Out[2]: -1

In [3]: if ~True: print("ok")
ok

In [4]: if ~False: print("ok")
ok
```

So, that branch of code will always run, whether or not the column has a `fill_values` attribute.

title: Equivalencies and log-scale units
description:
Equivalencies seem to work only into one direction with log-scale units:

``` python
from astropy import units as apu
from math import log10, sqrt

# Note, engineers define the dB(uV/m) to operate on |E|^2 (to make dB-scale equivalent to power)
dB_uV_m = apu.dB(apu.uV ** 2 / apu.m ** 2)

a = 10 * apu.uV / apu.m
b = 20 * dB_uV_m

# Without equivalencies, the following cannot work (of course)
a.to(dB_uV_m)
b.to(apu.uV / apu.m)
# both raise:
# UnitConversionError: 'uV2 / m2' and 'uV / m' (electrical field strength)
# are not convertible

E_field_equivalency = [(
    apu.uV / apu.m,
    dB_uV_m,
    lambda x: 10. * log10(x ** 2),
    lambda x: sqrt(10 ** (x / 10.))
    )]

# Now, the following works:
a.to(dB_uV_m, equivalencies=E_field_equivalency)
# <Decibel 20.0 dB(uV2 / m2)>

# But the other direction is still not ok:
b.to(apu.uV / apu.m, equivalencies=E_field_equivalency)
# UnitConversionError: 'uV2 / m2' and 'uV / m' (electrical field strength)
# are not convertible

# Interestingly, if I use 
apu.add_enabled_equivalencies(E_field_equivalency)
# the Exception that is raised, is a different one:
a.to(dB_uV_m)
# <Decibel 20.0 dB(uV2 / m2)>
b.to(apu.uV / apu.m)
# AttributeError: 'DecibelUnit' object has no attribute '_is_equivalent'

```

title: Possible precision loss bug when reading FITS files with astropy.io
description:
I and my colleague @wafels encountered a possible bug when attempting to read modified julian day (MJD) values out of a FITS file using astropy.io.fits. A working example is below. For reference, the file in question can be found [here](https://drive.google.com/open?id=0B9-D4zr2735kdTN1WEZ5el90Q0E). It contains a catalogue of triggers marked 'SFLARE' detected by the Fermi mission.

```
In [2]: from astropy.io import fits
In [3]: from astropy.time import Time
In [4]: result = fits.open('browse_results.fits’)
In [5]: hdu1 = result[1]
In [6]: hdu1.data['TRIGGER_TIME'][108]
Out[6]: 55719.266
In [7]: tt = Time(hdu1.data['TRIGGER_TIME'][108],format = 'mjd')

In [8]: tt.datetime
Out[8]: datetime.datetime(2011, 6, 7, 6, 22, 30)
```

For reference, the correct time (verified from manually viewing the file, and also from the original Fermi catalogue online) for this trigger is actually: 2011-06-07 06:23:06:652

As a further test, the correct trigger time is read out by MRDFITS in IDL. As best I can tell, there seems to be some sort of precision loss when reading this file with astropy.io.fits. This can be seen here:

```
In [9]: print repr(np.float64(hdu1.data['TRIGGER_TIME'][108]))
55719.265625
```

Whereas from IDL:

```
IDL> result = mrdfits('browse_results.fits',1)
IDL> print,result[108].trigger_time,format='(d20.13)' 
 55719.2660492089999
```

Putting these numbers into a time conversion, e.g. [xTIME](https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/cgi-bin/Tools/xTime/xTime.pl) gives you the same difference in times, 55719.265625 --> 06:22:30 UT, and 55719.26604921 --> 06:23:06.652 UT

Although this example is specific to times in MJD format, it could be a more general problem - I have not tested this behaviour on other data types. Another possibility is that something is slightly non-standard regarding how the FITS file is formatted, but I am not sure what would cause this.

title: AltAz -> Galactic, with multiple observation times
description:
I created a stackoverflow question for this [here](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/39739913/astropy-coordinates-altaz-galactic-with-multiple-observation-times).

I have event tuples of `(azimuth, altitude, time)` in horizontal coordinates, which I store as 2 numpy arrays `azimuth` and `altitude`, and a `list(datetime)`. I also have an EarthLocation where these events are observed. The number of events is on the order of 100k.

Now I'd like to transform these to galactic coordinates. I tried

```
my_loc = EarthLocation.from_geodetic(...)
my_frame = AltAz(my_loc, obstime=times)
evt = SkyCoord(
        alt=my_altitude*rad, 
        az=my_azimuth*rad, 
        frame=my_frame, 
    )
evt_gal = evt.galactic
```

But each of these events apparently use the same observation time. (Judging from plots where all events are suspiciously neatly sitting on a curve).

Looking at a single event, it seems that each event has multiple observation times associated to it, which is not quite what I want.

```
e = evt[1]
print(e.frame)
<AltAz Coordinate (obstime=[datetime.datetime(2015, 5, 17, 16, 58, 17)
 datetime.datetime(2015, 12, 14, 0, 15, 26)
 datetime.datetime(2015, 9, 25, 4, 16) ...,
 datetime.datetime(2015, 9, 27, 6, 5, 9)
 datetime.datetime(2015, 2, 5, 1, 31, 8)
 datetime.datetime(2015, 12, 21, 13, 15, 49)], location=...> 
```

Supplying the obstimes directly to SkyCoord yields identical results.

```
evt = SkyCoord(
        alt=df_cscd['altitude_cscd'] * rad, 
        az=df_cscd['azimuth_random'] * rad, 
        location=my_earth_loc,
        obstime=my_times,)
```

The next idea was to _not_ pass the observation times to the frame, but to the SkyCoord:

```
frame_without_time = AltAz(location=my_location)
evt = SkyCoord(
        alt=df_cscd['altitude_cscd'] * rad, 
        az=df_cscd['azimuth_random'] * rad, 
        frame=frame_without_time,
        obstime=my_times,
)
```

But this raises a 

```
ValueError: cannot specify frame attribute 'obstime' directly in SkyCoord since a frame instance was passed in
```

It works perfectly fine if I have just a single time, e.g. `astropy.time.Time.now()`. But looping over 100k events and creating a SkyCoord instance for each of them is incredibly slow, obviously.

I don't have a pull request for this, since I wonder if there is a built-in better way to do this?

What do you think?

title: Old versions of the docs in search engines
description:
At the moment, Google sometimes returns results that point to e.g the v0.2 documentation - see e.g.:

https://twitter.com/jakevdp/status/781259020032147456

One way to deal with this is to do what yt did and make it so that only the stable docs are available at http://docs.astropy.org (not at http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable), and make sure all pages refer to the 'canonical' version of the docs: https://bitbucket.org/yt_analysis/yt/pull-requests/1693/docs-add-canonical-link-for-documentation/diff - this apparently stops search engines from indexing the non-canonical pages. However, there are I think several challenges here:
- We need to go back and re-build all the versions of the docs so that they all include this reference to the canonical version. Not unfeasible, but just means adding a commit in every maintenance branch.
- We would still break old links to the docs. However, we could in principle set up redirects so that all the old URLs still resolve to astropy.readthedocs.io/... - we can probably auto-generate these redirects, but just to say that this is not just a matter of flicking a switch.

One thing that's not clear to me with the canonical solution is what happens if you do select to browse an old version of the docs.

We do have to do _something_ though - it's pretty annoying to have v0.2 results show up in Google!

Another thing we could consider is to have a far more obvious banner at the top of the page that takes up the top third of the page that says 'you are viewing an old version' - but that won't stop Google indexing it.

cc @ngoldbaum (who suggested this on Twitter)

title: limit cache size?
description: I ran into an issue when running lots of `astroquery` queries where my cache ballooned in size to ~10s of Gb---and I didn't realize there was a cache until it was enormous, so this has caused some minor headaches with my home directory quota, etc.   I raised the issue over at [astroquery](https://github.com/astropy/astroquery/issues/759) that there should be a (perhaps user-configurable) limit on the cache size, so that old stuff gets overwritten if need be?  @keflavich suggested I make this same suggestion over here.

title: Consider allowing duplicate column names in reading ASCII tables
description:
From discussions in #5373, it might be reasonable to allow duplicate column names in an input table and automatically rename as `<colname>_<N>`, where `N` is incremented until the column name is unique.

`np.recfromtext` uses the `_<N>` convention while pandas does `.<N>`.  Both packages seem to have buggy / limited implementations in terms of handling conflicts that arise from this auto-renaming.

Implementation effort is not clear at this point.

title: Table I/O with sextractor format
description:
Loading a SExtractor output file mode fails depending on column order in the output SExtractor file. Namely, if some parameters that has several entries (like FLUX_RADIUS or ASSOC_VECTOR) is last in the SExtractor configuration, loading fails.

A following minimal example for loading some data is:

```
import astropy.table as T
assoc = T.Table.read("out_sextractor.dat", format='ascii.sextractor')
```

When the data is (e.g.)

```
#   1 X_IMAGE                Object position along x                                    [pixel]
#   2 Y_IMAGE                Object position along y                                    [pixel]
#   3 VECTOR_ASSOC           ASSOCiated parameter vector                               
#   6 FLAGS                  Extraction flags                                          
  25    50     26.1        50.1         1   0
  60    122     60.3     122.7      4   0
```

The command succeeds. However, when we have the same columns minus the FLAGS, i.e.:

```
#   1 X_IMAGE                Object position along x                                    [pixel]
#   2 Y_IMAGE                Object position along y                                    [pixel]
#   3 VECTOR_ASSOC           ASSOCiated parameter vector                               
  25    50     26.1        50.1         1   
  60    122     60.3     122.7      4   
```

loading the file fails and this error is thrown: 

```
astropy.io.ascii.core.InconsistentTableError: Number of header columns (3) inconsistent with data columns (5) at data line 0
Header values: ['X_IMAGE', 'Y_IMAGE', 'VECTOR_ASSOC']
Data values: ['25', '50', '26.1', '50.1', '1']
```

title: io.ascii.read  no longer automatically recognizes tables in fixed_width_twoline format
description:
In the past, that is pre u'1.2.dev15800, one could write an asciii table in fixed_width_two_line and then read it back (allowing the routine to guess the format), but now when you do this (possibly only when the columns are strings) it is interpreting the second line in the table (the line containing ---) as values in the columns.  

A short program and the data I was using are below:
- [foo.py.txt](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/files/516784/foo.py.txt)
- [all_stat.ls.txt](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/files/516785/all_stat.ls.txt)

I had thought that fixed_width_two_line was one of the formats that ascii.read was guaranteed to recognize (which was the reason I had selected it as my default output style), and so am surprised that this feature has apparently been "lost".   As far as I remember that is how the old documentation read.

The  new [documentaion](http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/io/ascii/index.html#guess-table-format) now appears to prefer a more basic format, but it seems like this would be an easy problem to fix, since a fixed-header is the only one that would have a line with all --

title: Astropy test customizations break pytest for affiliated packages
description:
_Moved from https://github.com/astropy/astropy-helpers/issues/258_

Every so often I make the mistake of running `pytest` (or `py.test` for old versions) instead of `python setup.py test`. title: Reshaping lost when accessing FITS_rec by field name
description:
Please consider the code below and its output. The behaviour of `FITS_rec` does not match the one of `recarray`, which feels like the correct one.

When reshaping `FITS_rec`, of initial shape `(5,)`, the new shape `(5, 1)` is properly reported. However, when accessing a field, it behaves like the reshape never happened.

Maybe a proper fix would be that reshaping a `FITS_rec` should return a `recarray`.

``` python
from os import path
from astropy.io import fits
import numpy as np

with fits.open(path.join(fits.__path__[0], 'tests', 'data', 'stddata.fits')) as hdulist:

    # As FITS_rec
    data = hdulist[2].data
    print(type(data))
    print(data.shape)
    print(data['PSFFLUX'].shape)
    data = data.reshape((5,1))
    print(data.shape)
    print(data['PSFFLUX'].shape)

    # As recarray
    data = np.array(hdulist[2].data.copy())
    print(type(data))
    print(data.shape)
    print(data['PSFFLUX'].shape)
    data = data.reshape((5,1))
    print(data.shape)
    print(data['PSFFLUX'].shape)
```

``` python
<class 'astropy.io.fits.fitsrec.FITS_rec'>
(5,)
(5, 5)
(5, 1)
(5, 5)

(5,)

title: Reshaping SkyCoord
description:
It would be very convenient to be able to reshape the coordinate arrays inside a `SkyCoord` object. Ideally, this would be an in-place reshape, similar to returning a view of an array in `numpy`.

Currently, the only way I know how to reshape an arbitrary `SkyCoord` object is to copy (`ra`, `dec`), (`l`, `b`), etc. into a flat numpy array, and then to create a new `SkyCoord`. However, something like the following would be much more efficient:

```
import numpy as np
import astropy.units as u
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord

ra = np.random.random((10,10)) * 360.
dec = np.random.random((10,10)) * 180. - 90.
coords = SkyCoord(ra*u.deg, dec*u.deg, frame='icrs')

# Reshape in place (hopefully this can be achieved by changing some strides)
coords.shape = (100,)

# Or return a view (which doesn't copy any data)
coords_view = SkyCoord.reshape((10,10))
```

title: Evaluating an array with a FittableModel

x = np.array([1,2])
simpleModel(x)
```

title: FITS headers don't update immediately?
description:
This is an issue noted on https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/5396, but is independent of that issue.

In short, given a FITS header with an invalid entry (e.g., a newline within the `'ORIGIN'` value), the following will happen:

```
fh = fits.open(fn)
fh[0].header.tostring() # produces exception
fh[0].header.tostring() # does not produce exception
```

```
>>> h = fits.open('test1n.fits')
>>> h[0].header['origin'] = 'goodval'
>>> w = wcs.WCS(h[0].header)  # <- crashes
# a repeat attempt here would (probably) not crash
```

see: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/5396#issuecomment-252687514, https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/5396#issuecomment-252699025, https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/5396#issuecomment-252700815, https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/5396#issuecomment-252701891

title: Table doc needs meta comments instructions

Someone asked me how to write out comment lines to ASCII file and I had to dig into a change log entry, then into the associated PR, and then look at the actual source code to figure it out. Something like this should be more obvious in the doc, maybe [here](http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/table/construct_table.html):

``` python
# This will turn into comment lines in output ASCII file unless
# comment=False is explicitly set in write().

                      'this and that, and i also did some other stuff',
                      'second comment line']
```

title: numpy.average not working with units
description:
While `numpy.mean` works fine with `astropy.units.Quantity`, `numpy.average` does not.

``` python
In [1]: import numpy as np

In [2]: import astropy.units as u

In [3]: a = np.linspace(0, 1, 10) * u.meter

In [4]: np.mean(a)
Out[4]: <Quantity 0.5 m>

In [5]: np.average(a)
Out[5]: 0.5

In [6]: b = np.linspace(0, 1, 10) * u.centimeter

In [7]: np.average(a) == np.average(b)
Out[7]: True
```

title: test_erfa_planet fails on i386
description:
On 32 bit x86, `TestPositionKittPeak.test_erfa_planet` fails by newer returning.
I could locate the loop in [this loop in `solar_system.py`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/coordinates/solar_system.py#L412). The absolute value of `delta_light_travel_time` here jumps between 7.91119372419e-11 AU s / m, 7.91011123661e-11 AU s / m, and 1.08248758387e-14 AU s / m.
Python version is 2.7.12, erfa 1.3.0. This didn't happen before (with Python 2.7.12rc1, erfa 1.2.0).

Full build log [here](https://buildd.debian.org/status/fetch.php?pkg=python-astropy&arch=i386&ver=1.2.1-1%2Bb1&stamp=1477058939&file=log)

Unfortunately, I have no tests in between, so it may be anything... I also just had another mystic regression on i386 (with the CPL library), so it is not excluded that it is caused by the C compiler (gcc-6.2.0) or so. But if anyone could have a look to the mentioned loop and could give some advise?

title: Add header consistency check to ECSV reader
description:
For [gamma-cat](https://github.com/gammapy/gamma-cat) we've adopted ECSV as input format for tabular data. Some of the files are generated with scripts, some are entered manually, usually by copy & pasting numbers and manually writing the header.

One issue we ran into (see https://github.com/gammapy/gamma-cat/pull/31#issuecomment-257857134, cc @adonath) is this:
```
In [13]: from astropy.table import Table
    ...: ecsv_content = """# %ECSV 0.9
    ...: # ---
    ...: # datatype:
    ...: # - {name: a, unit: m / s, datatype: int64, format: '%03d'}
    ...: # - {name: b, unit: km, datatype: int64, description: This is column b}
    ...: a b
    ...: 001 2
    ...: 004 3
    ...: """
    ...: Table.read(ecsv_content, format='ascii.ecsv')
    ...: 
Out[13]: 
<Table length=2>
  a     b  
m / s   km 
int64 int64
----- -----
  001     2
  004     3

In [14]: from astropy.table import Table
    ...: ecsv_content = """# %ECSV 0.9
    ...: # ---
    ...: # datatype:
    ...: # - {name: a, unit: m / s, datatype: int64, format: '%03d'}
    ...: # - {name: b, unit: km, datatype: int64, description: This is column b}
    ...: 
    ...: 001 2
    ...: 004 3
    ...: """
    ...: Table.read(ecsv_content, format='ascii.ecsv')
    ...: 
Out[14]: 
<Table length=1>
  a     b  
m / s   km 
int64 int64
----- -----
  004     3

In [15]: from astropy.table import Table
    ...: ecsv_content = """# %ECSV 0.9
    ...: # ---
    ...: # datatype:
    ...: # - {name: a, unit: m / s, datatype: int64, format: '%03d'}
    ...: # - {name: b, unit: km, datatype: int64, description: This is column b}
    ...: spam
    ...: 001 2
    ...: 004 3
    ...: """
    ...: Table.read(ecsv_content, format='ascii.ecsv')
    ...: 
Out[15]: 
<Table length=2>
  a     b  
m / s   km 
int64 int64
----- -----
  001     2
  004     3
```

If the CSV header row is missing, the ECSV reader silently drops the first data row!

From https://github.com/astropy/astropy-APEs/blame/master/APE6.rst#L430
> A mismatch of the number of columns will be an error.  If there is a name mismatch then it is recommended that the reader issue a warning,	but implementations are free to be either less or more strict.

@taldcroft - Would it be easy to add this check to the ECSV reader?

I would guess I'm not the only one that has made this error when writing ECSV files, and it would be very valuable to have this check.

title: Record data size in the WCS object
description:
It is clear that there are practical reasons to have a record of the original data size in the WCS object. This in the past has been recorded in public attributes `naxis1` and `naxis2` and subsequently in the private `_naxis1` and `_naxis2`.  There's  along thread on why this should  or should not be done in #4662.
More recently #5411 expanded this attribute to more than 2 axes. It also broke the ability to set the private attributes which was subsequently fixed in #5454 as a stop gap measure.

We need to fix this permanently starting with v 1.3. There are two proposed ways to do it.

1. Add public `naxisj` attributes, populated by the FITS header `NAXISj` keywords.
2. Introduce a subclass of `WCS` which adds those and leave the original WCS to represent strictly the FITS WCS standard and nothing more.

Either way a deprecation process will accompany the change.

The purpose of this issue is to collect votes. I don't want to start a new long discussion. Keep in mind that #4662 is available for reference and only share new arguments.

Since 1.3 is approaching we need to make a fast decision. So please share your preference here and volunteer for the work if possible.

title: Table join with differently named columns
description:
A use case that has come up a few times for me/others is being able to join two tables where the key is named differently in each table. At the moment, the only solution is to rename one of the columns:

```python
In [12]: from astropy.table import Table, join

In [13]: t1 = Table()
    ...: t1['a'] = [1,2,3]
    ...: t1['b'] = ['a','b','c']
    ...: 

In [14]: t2 = Table()
    ...: t2['c'] = [3,2]
    ...: t2['d'] = [4.4, 4.3]

In [15]: t2.rename_column('c', 'a')

In [16]: join(t1, t2, 'a')
Out[16]: 
<Table length=2>
  a    b      d   
int64 str1 float64
----- ---- -------
    2    b     4.3
    3    c     4.4
```

But this seems like a common use case, and changing the tables is not ideal. One idea would be to allow ``keys`` to be a dict:

```python
In [16]: join(t1, t2, {'a':'c'})
Out[16]: 
<Table length=2>
  a    b      d   
int64 str1 float64
----- ---- -------
    2    b     4.3
    3    c     4.4
```

The keys of the dictionary would be the equivalent of the current ``keys`` for the first table, and the values would be the ``keys`` for the right table.

This would be backward-compatible since there's no need to remove any of the current behavior.

title: [1.2.1] does not work with wcslib 4.24
description:
Astropy still should work with wcslib 4.24 (at least the CHANGES.rst dosn't mention a change), it does not. This makes backporting to older (Debian) versions difficult.
Quoting from the [original Debian bug report](https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=844525) (Sergio Gelato):

> In trying to backport this version of astropy to jessie, I discovered that it doesn't build against wcslib-dev 4.24 as advertised in debian/control.
>
> The reason is that astropy/wcs/src/wcslib_wrap.c and astropy/wcs/wcs.py both refer to WCSHDO_P14 which was only introduced in wcslib 5.13.  Incidentally, that means the statement in astropy/wcs/wcs.py that "versions 5.8 and later on the 5.x series are known to work" is of questionable accuracy; I guess upstream will need to be told.
>
> Browsing through version control I see that this broke in astropy 1.1.2. (I'll probably backport 1.1.1 instead, since my actual requirement is (>= 1.0) and upgrading wcslib in jessie risks breaking other things.)

It would be nice if 4.24 is still supported. If not, please document this,

title: Slicing FITS_rec objects produces unexpected dtypes.
description:
Consider the following snippet:

```python
import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits

def create_data():
    tbhdu = fits.BinTableHDU.from_columns([
        fits.Column(name='a', format='I', array=np.arange(2**16, dtype=np.int16)),
        fits.Column(name='b', format='I', bscale=1, bzero=2**15, array=np.arange(2**16, dtype=np.uint16))])
    tbhdu.writeto('test_scaled_slicing.fits')

def load_data(nonnegative=False):
    with fits.open('test_scaled_slicing.fits') as hdulist:
        data = hdulist[1].data
    if nonnegative:
        return data[data['a'] >= 0]
    else:
        return data

create_data()
t1 = load_data()
t2 = load_data(True)
assert t1['b'].dtype is np.dtype(np.uint16)
# assert t2['b'].dtype is np.dtype(np.float64)
assert t2['b'].dtype is np.dtype(np.uint16)
```

The second `assert` fails because the slicing the FITS_rec object does not trigger the mechanism that handles the scaling of the column 'b'.  In other words, some data access methods on FITS_rec trigger the scaling but some don't.

If however, I use a method that forces the scaling, then this problem goes away.  Here's an example:

```python
def load_data(nonnegative=False):
    with fits.open('test_scaled_slicing.fits') as hdulist:
        data = hdulist[1].data
    #
    # WORKAROUND
    #
    if any([c.bzero is not None for c in data.columns]):
        foo = [data[k].dtype for k in data.dtype.names]
    if nonnegative:
        return data[data['a'] >= 0]
    else:
        return data
```

That is, merely accessing the dtype of each column triggers the scaling.  Looking into the code itself, it looks like the `._converted` attribute needs to be filled in for slicing to work properly.

title: Make empty  search_around_* return arrays have reasonable units
description:
This is a follow-on prompted by @adrn's https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/5083#r69383542 in  #5083. The key question is why, when `search_around_*` yield nothing, are the units of the resulting empty vectors deg and dimensionless unscaled instead of having the dimensions of the `SkyCoord`s that they're called on?  I think the answer is simply that that seemed most straightforward to implement, but probably the better thing to do is to give back whatever unit you would have gotten if the arrays had not been empty.

Note that it would be best to make this consistent across `search_around_*` *and* `match_coordinates_*`, although the latter hasn't yet gotten the treatment from #5083 to make it yield anything in the case of empty coordinates, so this might be easier to do piecemeal.

I don't think I'll have time, but if @evertrol or @adrn might want to take a shot at this, we could try to slip it in by the feature freeze in 5 days (it's a backwards-incompatible change so can't go in a bugfix)

title: Check Table MaskedColumn for future change in MaskedArray
description: In numpy 1.13, MaskedArray views will start to share the mask with the item viewed rather than get a new copy (https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/5580). In many ways, this is much more logical, and I *think* it should pose no issues for `MaskedColumn`, but we should check. title: Need release soon to ensure leap-second fix is available before 2017
description:
Just got a note from David Kaplan asking whether the upcoming leap second (31 Dec 2016) would be in astropy. I realised I had to tell him that it would be in 1.3 and in 1.0.11, but that neither of those were likely to be available before the leap second took place. This is no good of course. Any suggestions (for those who use the bundled erfa -- most linux distributions will be fine since one gets the updated erfa automatically). My own sense is that if we do not have 1.3 out before the end of the year, we should have a 1.2.2 with just the erfa update (#5418)

The above does beg the question whether, longer-term, we should get leap second data independently from erfa -- e.g., the IERS tables that we download anyway do contain this information as well.

title: Assigning new data to an existing HDU won't update scaling consistently
description:
When creating a brand new `ImageHDU`, this:

  `im = ImageHDU(data=data, header=existing_header)`

will deal properly with the header scaling, adding or subtracting `BZERO`/`BSCALE` to fit the data type, no matter what the data type is, or whether the original header has scaling information on it or not. If we set the data *after* creation, the behavior is not consistent. Let's show this.

    >>> uint8 = np.array([[1,2,3,4],[4,3,2,1]], dtype='uint8')
    >>> uint64 = np.array([[1,2,3,4],[4,3,2,1]], dtype='uint64')

Now, let's create a new image with a data type that doesn't require scaling, and replace the data with the unsigned 64 bit array:

    >>> im = ImageHDU(uint8)
    >>> im.header
    XTENSION= 'IMAGE   '           / Image extension                                
    BITPIX  =                   8 / array data type                                
    NAXIS   =                    2 / number of array dimensions                     
    NAXIS1  =                    4                                                  
    NAXIS2  =                    2                                                  
    PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of parameters                           
    GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups                               
    >>> im.data = uint64
    >>> im.header
    XTENSION= 'IMAGE   '           / Image extension                                
    BITPIX  =                   64 / array data type                                
    NAXIS   =                    2 / number of array dimensions                     
    NAXIS1  =                    4                                                  
    NAXIS2  =                    2                                                  
    PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of parameters                           
    GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups                               
    BSCALE  =                    1                                                  
    BZERO   =  9223372036854775808                                                  

It behaves as expected. Now:

    >>> im = ImageHDU(uint64)
    >>> im.header
    XTENSION= 'IMAGE   '           / Image extension                             
    BITPIX  =                   64 / array data type                                
    NAXIS   =                    2 / number of array dimensions                  
    NAXIS1  =                    4                                               
    NAXIS2  =                    2                                               
    PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of parameters                        
    GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups                            
    BSCALE  =                    1                                               
    BZERO   =  9223372036854775808                                               
    >>> im.data = uint8
    >>> im.header
    XTENSION= 'IMAGE   '           / Image extension                             
    BITPIX  =                    8 / array data type                                
    NAXIS   =                    2 / number of array dimensions                  
    NAXIS1  =                    4                                               
    NAXIS2  =                    2                                               
    PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of parameters                        
    GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups                            
    BSCALE  =                    1                                               
    BZERO   =  9223372036854775808                                               

As we can see, scaling info is preserved, when it shouldn't. This works properly if the new array is of 16/32/64 integer (signed or unsigned), but fails with 8 bit and floating point data.

title: QTable mixin columns formatting
description:
Changing the format of a `QTable` `Quantity` mixin column results in the unit being displayed in the column output.  Example:

```
from astropy.table import QTable
import astropy.units as u

t = QTable()
t['a'] = np.arange(1, 5) * np.pi * u.km
t['a'].info.format = '0.3f'
print(t)
    a    
    km   
---------
 3.142 km
 6.283 km
 9.425 km
12.566 km
```

The column is still correctly a `Quantity` array:
```
print(t['a'])
[  3.14159265   6.28318531   9.42477796  12.56637061] km
```

so this appears to be an issue only in table output representation.  Is this a bug or am I doing something wrong?

cc: @taldcroft

title: Change make_lupton_rgb narrative docs to not use reproject
description:
As @parejkoj, @astrofrog and I discussed #5535 in and later out-of-band, a better approach for the narrative docs in #5535 might be to:

- [x] Add the reprojected files to data.astropy.org
- [x] Have the test download those, and not use reproject at all
- [x] Un-skip it in the doctest
- [ ] Write an astropy tutorial that demonstrates the combination of `SkyCoord`, `astroquery`, `reproject`, and `make_luptin_rgb` to actually do the whole thing.

That will keep the example in `astropy.visualization` focused on `make_lupton_rgb` while still showing a whole worked example for a real practical use case.

title: Convert saturated-pixel handling code from LSST for lupton_rgb
description:
Now that the basic lupton_rgb code is merged, we can look at some improvements. One of those would be to get the `replaceSaturatedPixels` method converted from lsst.afw. This is an important part of the original algorithm: smooth across saturated pixels so they look the same color as the rest of the object. This is a non-trivial amount of work, as the original code is C++ and depends on LSST objects. There may be other code in astropy we could use for this instead: I don't know what sort of saturated pixel handling currently exists in astropy, or whether it could be adapted to this use-case.

The relevant code is here:

https://github.com/lsst/afw/blob/057223eaf06faccd9bb52423f8e0505a01a9cbc6/python/lsst/afw/display/Rgb.h
https://github.com/lsst/afw/blob/057223eaf06faccd9bb52423f8e0505a01a9cbc6/python/lsst/afw/display/saturated.cc

title: Try to get the fast_reader options to give useful errors when they have no effect
description:
This came out of discussions in #5552 (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/5552#issuecomment-265195358, https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/5552#issuecomment-265363371, https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/5552#issuecomment-265535428).

The crux of the issue is this: the `fast_reader` options that get passed into `ascii.io.read` are silently ignored if the reader is not a "fast" reader.  And that's confusing because the options actually affect the output.  So it would be much clearer to have the reader *raise an exception* if the user gives `fast_reader` options but the reader is not a fast reader.

Or is there some specific reason why that doesn't happen?

I took a shot at this in https://github.com/eteq/astropy/tree/fortranexp2-fast-error but that approach doesn't seem to have worked (although maybe @dhomeier tried it and had better results?)

title: Make AstropyWarning be more informative
description:
As mentioned by @cdeil in #5586, figuring out exactly where a warning was emitted is often tricky.  The base `AstropyWarning` class seems to make this even worse by entirely suppressing line/file information in the output in favor of a cleaner display.

One thing that can help is including an appropriate `stacklevel` kwarg in the `warn` call, where this refers to the number of stack levels up where one expects the original *user* call.  Granted that is not always predictable, but in many cases it is and would then allow users to see where in their code the warning originated.  An example is in #5586 where stacklevel=3 always gets back to the user call.

title: Add lazy parsing of FITS headers
description:
As a followup to #5065 and related issues, there's another lazy-loading enhancement that could greatly speed up reading of FITS files:

When seeking through a FITS file, in order to determine how to find the next HDU the header needs to be read and parsed.  Depending on the size and complexity of the header, this is currently an expensive operation in Astropy, even considering that there's already some laziness--for example the values of header cards are not actually parsed until that value is needed (or running verify()).

However, when seeking through a FITS file, really only a few standard keywords, typically appearing (in a valid header) within the first 8 or so cards of the header, are needed.  These include: `BITPIX`, `NAXIS`, the `NAXISn` keywords (of which there may be up to 99 but are often not more than 2 or 3), and in some cases `PCOUNT` and `GCOUNT`, as well as the extension type.

Lots of efficiency can be gained by reading only that first part of the header when seeking through the file (as well as searching for the END card of the header, which is unfortunately necessary), and deferring loading of the full header until later.

One might approach this in a couple different ways.  One might be to use some kind of "minimal" header parser that only has as much functionality as one needs to parse those first few header cards.  A lot of code that's already written in the `Card` class can be used for this--the idea would be to parse one `Card` at a time, without bothering to initialize a full `Header` object (an exception would be if the required keywords are not found in the positions they're suppose to be in--this of course makes the header malformed, but it's still nice to be able to read such malformed files if possible--in this case we would switch to reading the full Header).

Another possibility would be to add some more lazy-loading capabilities to the `Header` class itself, somewhat similar to #5065, though I think it can be done more simply in the case of headers.  First I should explain how headers are currently read from a file (this is somewhat different from creating headers from scratch):

1. The [`Header.fromstring`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/bc8ddb1fdee742a4816504acbf0fc573fb0ac6ad/astropy/io/fits/header.py#L396) classmethod is responsible for reading the actual bytes of the header, from the first card through to the end card, as well as any trailing padding.  This in turn calls the worker method `Header._from_blocks` which figured out the extend of the 2880 byte blocks that comprise a header, and is responsible for locating the end card.  It looks complicated but really isn't--most of the barnacles in it have one of two sources:

    a) The same code is also used to read headers from a text file containing newlines.  This adds a bit of complication, but most of the logic for understanding the extents of a header are otherwise the same.

    b) Fallbacks for handling slightly invalid / corrupted FITS files of the sort that have appeared in the wild in the past, such as headers that are missing an END card.

2. The 2880 byte header blocks are joined into a single string and passed to the classmethod [`Header.fromstring`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/bc8ddb1fdee742a4816504acbf0fc573fb0ac6ad/astropy/io/fits/header.py#L326).  So in other words `fromfile` is just responsible for finding the bytes of a header in an actual file and returning that header as a string.  Then `fromstring` is responsible for *parsing* a header given the contents of the header as a string.  Here already there's room for improvement:  While most FITS files don't have massive headers in the first place, most of the keywords we need are going to only be in the *first* 2880 byte header block.  The only cases where they wouldn't be is if there is some huge number of axes, or in pathological cases.  So one might, say, implement a shortcut where only the *first* header block is returned and parsed at first, and on
…（以下省略）

title: Update release instructions based on 1.3 experiences
description:
A note for us to take care of this during/after release (mostly for @astrofrog as the other release maintainer) :

* When doing RCs, the steps about changing the version to ``.dev`` should be skipped (and the changelog entry additions)
* More generally, it might make sense to *not* add changelog sections in the maintenance branch?  Instead just keep track during backports. (need to think about this more - it might be more or less annoying than the current scheme...)
* ``setup.py register`` and ``setup.py upload`` no longer work!  Need to update instructions to do manual registration and upload.  Or switch to using twine (https://pypi.python.org/pypi/twine)

title: time.to_datetime() is extremely slow when there is a timezone
description:
Timezone support was added to Time.to_datetime recently (#4119).  However, it is extremely slow (~20 milliseconds, 100x slower than without timezone.)  This excess time comes from the constructor of TimezoneInfo().

```
>>> from astropy.time import Time, TimezoneInfo
>>> from pytz import utc
>>> now = Time.now()
>>> %timeit now.to_datetime()
10000 loops, best of 3: 166 µs per loop
>>> %timeit now.to_datetime(timezone=utc)
10 loops, best of 3: 23.2 ms per loop
>>> %timeit TimezoneInfo
10000000 loops, best of 3: 46.6 ns per loop
>>> %timeit TimezoneInfo()
10 loops, best of 3: 25 ms per loop
```

Limiting time conversions to 50/second is a significant performance issue (although there are workarounds.)

EDIT: See also #4124

title: Flip output of make_rgb_lupton by default
description:
At the moment, when using the ``filename`` option of ``make_rgb_lupton``, the PNG/JPEG output files are flipped the wrong way vertically (@cdeil and @parejkoj started discussing this in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/5535#issuecomment-267145197). FITS files are stored with the bottom-left origin pixels first, and other formats typically put the top right origin first. At the moment, if I open PNG/JPEG output in any viewer, the output is flipped compared to the original FITS files in any FITS viewer.

We should fix the default before 1.3 IMO.

title: Feature request: mix-in column for Table with automatic unicode conversion
description:
In Python 3, string columns in tables can take 4x the memory they really need because Numpy ``U<n>`` arrays take up 4x the memory of ``S<n>`` arrays even if only ASCII characters are present.

@embray mentioned (and provided code) in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/4829 that he wrote a ndarray sub-class that stores the data as ``S<n>`` but automatically converts to unicode when the user accesses certain elements. This made me think that we could make this into a mix-in column type for Table. I would imagine the behavior would be as follows when using this type of mix-in column:

* The data would be stored using ``S<n>`` and the encoding would be stored too
* When the user requests an item, it is decoded on-the-fly to unicode (in Python 3)
* When the user sets an item, provided it can be encoded to ASCII, it is encoded into bytes and put back into the array
* If the user sets an item to a unicode string, we could either raise an error with explicit instructions for converting the mix-in column to a full unicode column, or the mix-in column could be smart enough to 'switch' to unicode and emit a warning (to disable the warning, the user would need to explicitly ask for the conversion to be done)

With this in place, readers such as the HDF5 and FITS readers for ``Table`` could automatically make use of this mix-in column type, which would avoid unexpectedly large memory usage when reading in tables with strings.

cc @taldcroft @mhvk

title: Documentation of setting pv parameters in wcs
description:
The current documentation for setting pv parameters should be expanded. I suggest:

When setting optional pv parameters for a given projection (e.g. for an oblique SIN projection), the parameters are common to both axes in a celestial wcs. The parameters should be set with the axis specified as 0. e.g.

p = [(0, 0, par1), (0, 1, par2)]
wcsprm.set_pv(p)

title: bug in discretize_integrate_2d
description:
I'm using astropy v.1.2.1 under python 3.4.2.

The function ``astropy.convolution.utils.discretize_integrate_2d`` evaluates the model with x and y inversed. The example below evaluates an elliptical Gaussian with ``mode='oversample'`` and ``mode='integrate'``. As can be seen, ``mode="integrate"``  transposes the model (but not the array). The reason is that ``scipy.integrate.dblquad`` (used in ``discretize_integrate_2d``) takes as its first argument a function where "y must be the first argument and x the second argument.", which is opposite to the call for the astropy model (``Fittable2DModel.__call__``). A possible fix is to replace the first argument of ``dblquad`` with ``lambda y, x: model(x, y)``. 

Reproducible example:

    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from astropy.modeling.models import Gaussian2D
    from astropy.convolution.utils import discretize_model

    model = Gaussian2D(1., 10., 10., 6., 3., 0.)
    gauss_oversample = discretize_model(model, (0, 20), (0, 25), mode="oversample")
    gauss_integrate = discretize_model(model, (0, 20), (0, 25), mode="integrate")
    plt.subplot(121)
    plt.imshow(gauss_oversample, origin='lower', interpolation='none')
    plt.subplot(122)
    plt.imshow(gauss_integrate, origin='lower', interpolation='none') 
    plt.show()

title: Unable to disable remote_data test option
description:
This is a forward of a [bug in the Debian bug database](https://bugs.debian.org/849501):

The test option `remote_data` of Astropy now seems to be enabled by default and cannot be disabled (at least easily). This causes the tests of some Astropy affiliated packages to fail on Debian, e.g. [astroplan](https://ci.debian.net/data/packages/unstable/amd64/a/astroplan/20161227_031316.autopkgtest.log.gz).

title: StreamingHDU issue
description:
Hi,

I'm running Debian unstable on 64 bit machines (and hence this is version 1.3 of astropy) and have come across an issue with StreamingHDU  on 2 out of the 3 machines!

This is the test program:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

import numpy as np
import astropy.io.fits as fits

n1 = 2048
n2 = 2048
n3 = 50
hdu = fits.PrimaryHDU()
hdr = hdu.header

hdr['NAXIS'] = (3, 'its a movie')
hdr['NAXIS1'] = (n1, 'number of n1 samples')
hdr['NAXIS2'] = (n2, 'number of n2 samples')
hdr['NAXIS3'] = (n3, 'number of frames in movie')
hdr['BITPIX'] = (-32, 'np.float32')

print hdr
shdu = fits.StreamingHDU('test_shdu.fits', hdr)

data = np.zeros((n1, n2), np.float32)

for f in xrange(n3):
    data[:,:] = f
    print 'Doing frame', f, data.nbytes
    shdu.write(data)

shdu.close()
```

On two of the machines, it fails with:

```
Doing frame 25 16777216
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "./test_stream_fits.py", line 26, in <module>
    shdu.write(data)
  File "/usr/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/streaming.py", line 174, in write
    raise IOError('Attempt to write more data to the stream than the '
IOError: Attempt to write more data to the stream than the header specified.
```

If I look at the output (using ds9) when the program fails, then every odd numbered frame is filled with zero, and the even frames are 1,2,3,......24. So it seems to be writing an additional empty image out before it writes the actual data. I suspect its incidental, but the two machines it fails on are both Intel, and the one it does work on is AMD.

Any suggestions, or is it a real bug?

Thanks,

Matt

title: Better document ASCII reader for files with both tab and space delimiters
description:
EDIT: Just make the documentation more obvious is enough. See discussions below.

During the [Using Python for Astronomical Data Analysis](https://aas.org/meetings/aas229/events#workshops) workshop, there was an issue with an ASCII file using both tab and space separators. `pandas` could read it fine, but `Table.read(..., format='ascii')` threw an error until @eteq dug through the documentation and set delimiter to `\s`, leading to the thought that perhaps it is better to make that the default behavior.

p.s. Erik, I hope you don't mind that I opened this issue on your behalf.

title: SkyCoords very slow due to FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET
description:
Can we replace FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET() with a lazily-reevaluated version?  This would cure a lot of speed woes with SkyCoord.

Just creating a SkyCoords object, or accessing an attribute, is very slow (milliseconds or millions of clock cycles) regardless of whether it is one point or a thousand.   Profiling shows that the time is almost all spent in FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET() sky_coordinate.py:38 :
```
%timeit x=SkyCoord(5,5,unit=u.deg)
100 loops, best of 3: 3.03 ms per loop
%timeit x=SkyCoord(np.linspace(0,360,1000),np.arange(0,360,1000),unit=u.deg)
100 loops, best of 3: 3.07 ms per loop
x=SkyCoord(5,5,unit=u.deg, frame='fk5')
%timeit x.equinox
1000 loops, best of 3: 846 µs per loop
%prun x=[SkyCoord(5,5,unit=u.deg) for i in range(1000)]
from astropy.coordinates.sky_coordinate import FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET
%timeit FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET()
1000 loops, best of 3: 875 µs per loop
```

The profiling shows that FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET calls getattr() 252 times each time it is called, which is believable given that the code walks a tree:
```
def FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET():
    """Set of all possible frame-specific attributes"""
    out = set()
    for frame_cls in frame_transform_graph.frame_set:
        for attr in frame_cls.get_frame_attr_names().keys():
            out.add(attr)
    return out
```

To make astropy less slow, can we do some caching so that it doesn't have to be re-evaluated every single time somebody looks at a SkyCoord attribute or makes a new SkyCoord?

(Do we have to worry about invalidating the cached value?  Can we invalidate the cached value if frame_transform_graph.frame_set is changed?).

title: SkyCoord.separation is slow due to unneeded frame transform
description:
SkyCoord.separation() takes 22 milliseconds, compared to 4.5 milliseconds for Skycoord.position_angle().  This is the timing for two points in the same coordinate system.

The difference in speed is due to the fact that position_angle() checks whether the coordinate systems are the same, while separation() always does a transformation.  Since the most common use-case is to have all of the points be in the same coordinate system, this is extremely wasteful.

The code at 
`sky_coordinate.py:1060:position_angle()` and
`sky_coordinate.py:677:separation()`
should be identical, since they both serve the same function.

(Neither is fast, largely due  #5698 .  separation() calls FRAME_ATTR_NAMES_SET() 22 times causing 2717 getattr() calls).

Other comments:
I don't know why the various methods have their own import statements, e.g. `sky_coordinate.py:392`.  It probably is a minimal speed-up to put them all at the top, but it may be a stylistic convention in this project.

The following are possible enhancements (Should they go in a separate issue?  Do they already exist in some other library?):
I would also like to suggest a single function that returns both separation and posang (because that is something commonly desired). 

Also useful would be a function that takes a separation and posang to produce a new point.  (My particular use is triangulation from the InterPlanetary Network (IPN) that does timing-base localization of gamma ray bursts.  Other uses include drawing field-of-view circles and finding the midpoint between two points.)

title: SkyCoord.transform_to(other) ignores other.equinox if default
description:
Transforming from one frame to another acts differently depending on whether the destination frame's equinox was its default value or explicitly passed to the constructor.

cfk5_B1950 = SkyCoord(1 * u.deg, 0 * u.deg, frame='fk5', equinox='B1950')

The print claims that both cfk5_default and cfk5_J2000 are equinox J2000

title: Avoid code duplication for spherical <-> cartesian conversion in modeling.rotations
description:
In astropy.modeling.rotations, the following code is duplicating code that exists elsewhere:

```python
    @staticmethod
    def spherical2cartesian(alpha, delta):
        alpha = np.deg2rad(alpha)
        delta = np.deg2rad(delta)
        x = np.cos(alpha) * np.cos(delta)
        y = np.cos(delta) * np.sin(alpha)
        z = np.sin(delta)
        return np.array([x, y, z])

    @staticmethod
    def cartesian2spherical(x, y, z):
        h = np.hypot(x, y)
        alpha  = np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(y, x))
        delta = np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(z, h))
        return alpha, delta
```

This kind of transformation is already implemented both in the representation code in astropy.coordinates and in astropy._erfa (the s2c and c2s functions). It would be nice to have a set of common functions that is quantity aware that implements these transformations once and is as fast as possible. The ERFA routines are not actually as fast as the numpy implementation above due to all the overhead of preparing arrays for use in ERFA.

I think the best solution would be to create a set of functions that work in radians, written in Cython (if needed), and then have wrapper functions that are Quantity-aware. Then this set of functions could be used both from the representation code and from astropy.modeling.rotations.

title: unit module: behavior of Gauss units
description:
I am having some problem using the astropy unit module, in particular with the Gauss units (magnetic flux density). 
Let me remind you that Gauss is a cgs unit: 1 Gauss =1 cm^(-1/2) g^(1/2) s^(-1). 

Here is what I get when I define a B value:_ 
```
from astropy import units as u
B = 1*u.Gauss
print(B)
#1.0 G
print( B.cgs )
#1.0 G
```
...it looks like the G units are correctly assumed cgs.
Now I want to estimate the energy per particle, so I need to square and divide by the density:
```
n_e = 100 * u.cm**(-3)

E_mag = B**2/n_e  # forget about 4pi factors...
print(E_mag)
# 0.01 cm3 G2
```
which is correct, but units should realy be g cm2 / s2…  I guess it really likes using G!
But just to be check
```
print(E_mag.decompose())
1e-16 kg2 m3 / (A2 s4)
```
which is in MKS… Strange, for something that is defined in cos
(Gauss is cgs; corresponding MKS unit is Tesla).

Problems start if I add this energy density to another energy density, say 
the kinetic energy of a proton at 100km/s, given by:
```
from astropy.constants import m_p
m_h = m_p.cgs
v_0 = (100 * u.kilometer/u.second).cgs
E_kin = 1/2. * m_h * v_0**2
print(E_kin)
#8.363108885e-11 cm2 g / s2
```
in cgs units, as expected. But if I add the two energies I get a dimensional error
```
print(E_kin + E_mag)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/robberto/anaconda/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy/units/quantity.py", line 295, in __array_prepare__
    converters, result_unit = UFUNC_HELPERS[function](function, *units)
  File "/Users/robberto/anaconda/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy/units/quantity_helper.py",  line 290, in helper_twoarg_invariant
    return get_converters_and_unit(f, unit1, unit2)
  File "/Users/robberto/anaconda/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy/units/quantity_helper.py",  line 284, in get_converters_and_unit
    .format(f.__name__))
astropy.units.core.UnitConversionError: Can only apply 'add' function to quantities with compatible dimensions
```
Again, If I decompose
```
print(E_kin.decompose())
#8.363108885e-18 kg m2 / s2
print(E_mag.decompose())
#1e-16 kg2 m3 / (A2 s4)
```
I see that I am stuck with the Gauss behaving as a MKS unit. This seems to be an error, or at least a feature that is not well documented.

title: Skycoord __getitem__ not being applied to frame attributes
description:
I have a bunch of observations of the same object at different times (e.g. for an asteroid).  According to the [SkyCoord documentation](http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord.html)
`Inputs may be scalars or lists/tuples/arrays, yielding scalar or array coordinates (can be checked via SkyCoord.isscalar).`

So I assumed that I could have a coordinate array with the ra,dec and obstime inputs being lists:
```
path=SkyCoord([5,10],[20,30],unit=u.deg,obstime=['2017-01-01T00:00','2017-01-01T00:10'])
```

This initially seems to work:
```
In[14]: for i in range(len(path)):
...         print(path.ra[i],path.dec[i],path.obstime[i])
... 
5d00m00s 20d00m00s 2017-01-01T00:00
10d00m00s 30d00m00s 2017-01-01T00:10
```
but it actually doesn't
```
In[15]: print(path[0].obstime)
['2017-01-01T00:00', '2017-01-01T00:10']
```

And things can go bad in other ways.  The conclusion is that you can't have multiple obstimes in an array coordinate.

So to clarify the documentation, I suggest adding the word:
`**Coordinate** inputs may be scalars or lists/tuples/arrays, yielding scalar or array coordinates (can be checked via SkyCoord.isscalar).`

title: Windows ascii (and Table) fails on integer data that can't be represented as int32 (but could be as int64)
description:

```

""")['num'].astype(np.int64)
```

Could the default integer type (I know that's a mess on windows) be set to int64?

title: Can't add row to table with, e.g., SkyCoord column
description:
Starting with the [documented](http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/table/) way of making a table:
```
from astropy.table import Table
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
tm = Time(['2000:002', '2002:345'])
sc = SkyCoord([10, 20], [-45, +40], unit='deg')
t = Table([tm, sc], names=['time', 'skycoord'])
print(t)
```
gives
```
         time          skycoord
                       deg,deg
--------------------- ----------
2000:002:00:00:00.000 10.0,-45.0
2002:345:00:00:00.000  20.0,40.0
```

But if I try to add another row:
```
# Add another row
t.add_row((Time('2017:001'),sc[0]))
```
I get 
```
ValueError: Unable to insert row because of exception in column 'time':
'Time' object has no attribute 'insert'
```


Trying different things:
```
t = Table([[tm[0]],[sc[0]]], names=['time', 'skycoord'])
t.add_row([tm[1],sc[1]])
```
works giving:
```
         time                               skycoord                      
--------------------- ----------------------------------------------------
2000:002:00:00:00.000 <SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec) in deg
    ( 10., -45.)>
2002:345:00:00:00.000 <SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec) in deg
    ( 20.,  40.)>
```

So if you use astropy array objects, you can't add rows.  But if you use scalar values, you can add rows and later extract the values as a list .

title: `SkyCoord(frame=other.frame)` doesn't copy all frame attributes
description:
This may be a bug, or it may work-as-designed in which case I have a feature request.

When you have a `SkyCoord`, there is no interface defined to make another `SkyCoord` with the same frame attributes.  In particular, the `frame=` argument copies some attributes, such as `equinox`, but not others, such as `obstime`.
```
co1 = SkyCoord(10, 20, unit=u.deg, frame=FK5, equinox='B1950', obstime=Time('2017-01-01T00:00'))
co2 = SkyCoord(15, 20, unit=u.deg, frame=co1.frame)

print(co1, co2,sep='\n')
print("obstime: co1:{}, co2:{}".format(co1.obstime, co2.obstime))
```
giving:
```
<SkyCoord (FK5: equinox=B1950.000): (ra, dec) in deg    ( 10.,  20.)>
<SkyCoord (FK5: equinox=B1950.000): (ra, dec) in deg    ( 15.,  20.)>
obstime: co1:2017-01-01T00:00:00.000, co2:None
```

So if this is a bug, then this Issue is a bug report.  If this is not a bug, then I request an argument flag that tells the `__init__` to copy all the frame attributes, instead of an undocumented subset of them.  (This was touched upon in the discussion of #5702)
