title: Decide if obstime transformations of coordinates with velocities should result in motion
description:
This issues is a follow-up discussion to an unresolved question from #6219 (in that PR we are punting on the question by raising an error).

The starting point for the topic is https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6219#issuecomment-309399689 - @StuartLittlefair's position is that if you transform to a frame with a different `obstime`, a coordinate with velocities should be moved to a different position based on its velocity vector.  @StuartLittlefair added more in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6219#issuecomment-310907959 and https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6219#issuecomment-310908691 and @mhvk agreed in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6219#issuecomment-310911108

By contrast, I think this is *not* what we want and will be extremely confusing and inconsistent with the other coordinate machinery - see https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6219#issuecomment-310881737.  In https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6219#issuecomment-310906282 and https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6219#issuecomment-310908439 @adrn agreed.

This issue is hence a placeholder, because this is a somewhat significant philosophical question for `coordinates`, so we should resolve it for the next version.

title: Decide what to do about "unit<something>" representations and differentials
description:
The proximate cause for this issue was a discussion from #6289, but it's been simmering in the background of some of the coordinate stuff for a while.  Basically the question is: what is the right way to describe a "unit" representation or differential?  The prototypical example here is `UnitSphericalRepresentation` - it is conceptually "at infinity", but is modeled as being on a dimensionless radius-1 sphere.  The other two relevant examples (new in v2.0) are `RadialDifferential` and the `UnitSphericalDifferental`s, which are a bit more awkward because they aren't easy to conceptualize as "on the unit sphere".

The underlying issue is really that there's various special-casing to account for those in the coordinate transforms.  This means the builtin representations have "special status" - no user could implement a `UnitSphericalSomeOtherConventionDifferential` for example, because the special-casing wouldn't work.

For just `UnitSphericalRepresentation` it was generally ok because the "if the units are dimensionless, it's unitspherical" heuristic generally works.  But with the differentials it's now much more complicated.  So should we give these unity-representations/differentials some special status? If nothing else maybe a ".unity_component` attribute or something (bad name, but hopefully the idea is clear)?

description:

title: matplotlib 2.0.2 produces different WCSAxes format_coord() output
description:
Testing `2.0rc1` with `matplotlib-2.0.2` installed (on Python 2.7.13, 3.5.3 and 3.6.1) I found another test failure:
```
    def test_format_coord_regression(tmpdir):
        # Regression test for a bug that meant that if format_coord was called by
        # Matplotlib before the axes were drawn, an error occurred.
        fig = plt.figure(figsize=(3, 3))
        ax = WCSAxes(fig, [0.1, 0.1, 0.8, 0.8])
        fig.add_axes(ax)
>       assert ax.format_coord(10, 10) == ""
E       assert '11.0 11.0 (world)' == ''
E         - 11.0 11.0 (world)

/sw/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy/visualization/wcsaxes/tests/test_misc.py:35: AssertionError
```

Bottom line is, between `2.0.0` and `2.0.2` mpl behaviour has changed so that even before triggering a `fig.savefig()` `ax` will return these:
```
>>> ax.format_coord(10, 10)
'11.0 11.0 (world)'
>>> ax.coords[0].format_coord(10)
'10.0'
>>> ax.coords[1].format_coord(10)
'10.0'
```

One might test for `matplotlib._version.get_versions().get('version') > '2.0'` to set the expected output accordingly, but I don't know about `2.0.1` - any ideas if that info could be extracted elsewhere from `matplotlib`?

I've only tested this on OS X 10.12.6 with mpl `2.0.2` vs. `2.0.0`, but don't expect it to be any different at least on 10.11.6.

title: Can't specify differential class in frame init
description:
One of the nice things about the frame classes is that you can specify a representation class, and the expected kwarg names change accordingly:
```python
>>> icrs = coord.ICRS(x=1*u.pc, y=2*u.pc, z=3*u.pc, 
...                   representation=coord.CartesianRepresentation)
>>> icrs
<ICRS Coordinate: (x, y, z) in pc
    ( 1.,  2.,  3.)>
```

I had originally made it so that this would work with a differential class as well, but that no longer seems to be the case (because of some changes @mhvk made in #6219). An implication of this is that the velocity components *always* have to be specified with the component names corresponding to the default differential. For most frame classes, this is `SphericalCosLatDifferential`, so proper motions always have to be `coslat`. However, it would be nice to be able to do something this:
```python
icrs = coord.ICRS(ra=8.67*u.degree, dec=53.09*u.degree,
                  pm_ra=4.8*u.mas/u.yr, pm_dec=-15.16*u.mas/u.yr,
                  differential_cls={'s': coord.SphericalDifferential})
```
when someone *doesn't* want to include the `cos(dec)`.

Or, for cartesian components:
```python
icrs = coord.ICRS(x=1*u.pc, y=2*u.pc, z=3*u.pc, 
                  v_x=10*u.km/u.s, v_y=11*u.km/u.s, v_z=12*u.km/u.s,
                  representation=coord.CartesianRepresentation,
                  differential_cls={'s': coord.CartesianDifferential})
```

cc @eteq @mhvk

title: Figure out which FunctionTransformWithFiniteDifference transformations can become AffineTransform's
description:
This requires digging in to ERFA to figure out where we can switch to returning matrices and vector offsets (to use with `AffineTransform`) instead of performing the full positional transformation as a `FunctionTransform`. A good place to start could be the GCRS <--> HCRS transformation, which (nominally) is just a position and velocity offset from the Earth's surface to the center of the sun (it burns!).

cc @eteq

title: Composed AffineTransforms can be simplified
description: When all transformations through a path in the frame transform graph are `AffineTransform`'s or `MatrixTransform`'s, they can be composed into a single matrix operation and vector offset.

----- ----- -----
    1     2     3
    4     5     6

array([(4, 5, 6), (1, 2, 3)],
      dtype=[('col0', '<i8'), ('col1', '<i8'), ('col2', '<i8')])

<Table length=2>

title: Quantity constructor changes logarithmic units
description:
I like the astropy units module a lot. Thanks for this great piece of work!

I think, I encountered a bug related to the Quantities class. When I use logarithmic units, the constructor seems to change the type of the unit. This does not happen, when I simply multiply with the unit:

```python
# astropy.__version__ == '3.0.dev19502'

import numpy as np
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.units import Quantity

# define units
dimless = u.dimensionless_unscaled
dB = u.dB(dimless)

arr = np.array([1, 3, 5])

q1 = (arr * dB)         # q1.unit == Unit("dB(1)")
q2 = Quantity(arr, dB)  # q2.unit == Unit("dB")

type(q1.unit)  # astropy.units.function.logarithmic.DecibelUnit
type(q2.unit)  # astropy.units.function.mixin.RegularFunctionUnit

```

This is a problem for some of my use cases:

```python
q1.to(dimless)  # <Quantity [ 1.25892541, 1.99526231, 3.16227766]>
q2.to(dimless)  # UnitConversionError: 'dB' and '' (dimensionless) are not
                # convertible

@u.quantity_input(a=dB)
def my_func(a):
    print(a)

my_func(q1)  # [ 1.  3.  5.] dB
my_func(q2)  # UnitsError: Argument 'a' to function 'my_func' must be in
             # units convertible to 'dB'.
```

I can work-around the first problem:
```python
u.add_enabled_equivalencies(u.logarithmic())

q1.to(dimless)  # <Quantity [ 1.25892541, 1.99526231, 3.16227766]>
q2.to(dimless)  # <Quantity [ 1.25892541, 1.99526231, 3.16227766]>
```
But now the decorated function fails in both cases (with a different error!)
```python
my_func(q1)  # ValueError: Unit  is not a physical unit.
my_func(q2)  # ValueError: Unit  is not a physical unit.
```

title: Masked arrays bug in astropy.table.join
description:
Sometimes numpy masked arrays without any masked values can be created with the mask set to `nomask` (a value of False) rather than an array of booleans with the same shape as the data. This can cause problems in `astropy.table`.

For example:

```python
>>> from astropy import table
>>> test_table = table.Table([['a', 'b', 'c'], [1, 2, 3]], names=('id', 'val'), masked=True)
>>> table['val'].mask
array([False, False, False], dtype=bool)
>>> test_table['sqr_val'] = test_table['val']**2
>>> test_table['sqr_val'].mask
False
```
If you then try to join with another table, the join issues the following error:
```python
>>> other_table = table.Table([['a', 'b', 'c'], [5, 10, 15]], names=('id', 'num'), masked=True)
>>> table.join(test_table, other_table)
/Users/korandder/anaconda/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy/table/operations.pyc in join(left, right, keys, join_type, uniq_col_name, table_names, metadata_conflicts)
    183     col_name_map = OrderedDict()
    184     out = _join(left, right, keys, join_type,
--> 185                 uniq_col_name, table_names, col_name_map)
    186 
    187     # Merge the column and table meta data. Table subclasses might override

/Users/korandder/anaconda/lib/python2.7/site-packages/astropy/table/operations.pyc in _join(left, right, keys, join_type, uniq_col_name, table_names, col_name_map)
    698 
    699             if array.masked:
--> 700                 array_mask = array_mask | array[name].mask[array_out]
    701             try:
    702                 out[out_name].mask[:] = array_mask

IndexError: invalid index to scalar variable.
```
This error seems to be due to `join` expecting `array[name].mask` to be an array rather than a scaler when `False` is a valid value for `.mask' according to the `numpy.ma.MaskedArray` documentation. 

You can use `np.ma.getmaskarray` to get the full mask array:
```python
>>> np.ma.getmaskarray(test_table['sqr_val'])
array([False, False, False], dtype=bool)
```

There is possibly other code in `astropy.table` that is effected by this bug.

I'm using Python 2.7.13, NumPy 1.13.0 and Astropy 1.3.3.

title: Support vstack and similar operations for SkyCoord
description:
I use `SkyCoord` as a mixin quite a bit in tables - it's very common to have catalogs with RA/Dec coordinates as one of the axes, and of course it's convenient to just drop SkyCoord's directly into that.

However, if I try to vstack two tables with SkyCoords as one of the columns, I get the dreaded:
```
NotImplementedError: vstack unavailable for mixin column type(s): SkyCoord
```

This *seems* like it should be straightforward given that `SkyCoord`s pretty much behave like table columns... Of course I'm sure it's not that simple... but it's a pretty important use case, and maybe it's time has come?

cc @taldcroft @mhvk 

(this *might* be a duplicate of a more generic "make mixins of all types work"... but I didn't find an obvious one)

title: clobber warning could be more helpful
description:
Currently it is hard to know where the warning comes from:

title: Using LambdaCDM with emcee causes RAM to fill up very quickly
description:
I'm testing out how well astropy's own `angular_diameter_distance` works for Markov Chain inference with the `emcee` module since I'm having trouble putting it in my model myself, and upon using it (or any cosmology distance function) I noticed that my RAM was filling up very quickly, much faster than when I sample without an `astropy` function involved. Here is the relevant code:

```
import emcee as em
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from astropy.cosmology import LambdaCDM

d1 = pd.read_csv("betterdata.csv")
M_true =  0.28458426
L_true =  0.72886156
H_true = 70.01235027
c = 299792.458
z    = np.array(d1['z'])
y    = np.array(d1['mu'])
yerr = np.array(d1['dmu'])

def lnprior(theta):
    M, H, L = theta
    if (0. < M < 2. and  50. < H < 100. and 0. < L < 2.):
        return 0.0
    else:
        return -np.inf

def lnlike(theta, z, y, yerr):
    M, H, L = theta
    cosmo = LambdaCDM(H0 = H, Om0 = M, Ode0 = L)

    model = 5. * np.log10((1.+z)**2 * cosmo.angular_diameter_distance(z).value) + 25.

    return np.sum(-0.5 * ((y-model)**2/(yerr**2)) - np.log(yerr*np.sqrt(2.*np.pi)))


def lnprob(theta, z, y, yerr):
    lp = lnprior(theta)
    if not np.isfinite(lp):
        return -np.inf
    ll = lnlike(theta, z, y, yerr)
    if not np.isfinite(ll):
        return -np.inf
    return ll + lp
    

ndim, nwalkers, nsteps = 3, 6, 200    # _minimum amount of walkers is 2*ndim for demonstration purposes_
p0 = [np.array([M_true, H_true, L_true]) + 1e-2 * np.random.randn(ndim) for i in range(nwalkers)]
sampler = em.EnsembleSampler(nwalkers, ndim, lnprob, a = 4., args=(z, y, yerr), threads = 4)

sampler.run_mcmc(p0, nsteps)
```

The sampler runs perfectly fine, but again the RAM fills up very quickly and I have no idea why. I believe that `emcee` works by calling `lnprob` for each MCMC sample, so the only thing I can think of that's causing the RAM issue is that calling `cosmo = LambdaCDM(stuff)` puts something in the memory that isn't leaving, despite it not being used after a new parameter coordinate is chosen. This same thing happens when I change my model to use `cosmo.comoving_distance(z).value` as well, though for that I can use my own calculation instead.

If this issue is unfixable due to something in `astropy`, is there a working python calculation to determine Angular Diameter Distance that doesn't use something like `astropy`? I've tried `cosmolopy` and that has the same problems.

title: Add a sky coordinate parser?
description:
I want a sky coordinate parser, i.e. a function that takes a single string and makes a `SkyCoord` from it. This is partly possible with `SkyCoord` directly, e.g. this works:
```python
>>>  SkyCoord('42h 43d')
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec) in deg
    ( 270.,  43.)>
```
But I couldn't find a way to make a Galactic frame SkyCoord, e.g. for to select the Galactic center I'd like to be able to write something like:
```python
>>> SkyCoord.parse('0 0 galactic')
```

The use cases I have for this are simple-to-use end-user interfaces like
https://github.com/hipspy/hips/issues/82 or config files and GUIs where one can simply select a sky position.

So the questions I have:

1. Does this exist in Astropy core and I just don't know about it?
2. Would something like `SkyCoord.parse` be welcome? (I envision a 10 line function that splits the string "lon lat frame" and then dispatches to existing angle parsing and is limited in what frames and frame attributes it supports)
3. Does someone know of an astronomy standard or spec or good existing example of such a parser? (I only found http://simbad.u-strasbg.fr/simbad/sim-fcoo and I think it's similar to the `SkyCoord` parser, doesn't support selection of a frame within the string).

If it's not considered appropriate for Astropy core, I would start by implementing a utility function for https://github.com/hipspy/hips/issues/82 and put it there in `hips.utils` (and also write a Javascript version for a website I'm working on).

title: multiple functions from scipy.special do not work with quantities
description:
I just tried to use SciPy's error function, and Astropy politely requested that I raise this issue here:
```Python
>>> from astropy import units
>>> from scipy.special import erf, erfc
>>> r1 = 5*u.m
>>> r2 = 6*u.m
>>> erf(r1/r2)
TypeError: Unknown ufunc erf.  Please raise issue on https://github.com/astropy/astropy
>>> erfc(r1/r2)
TypeError: Unknown ufunc erfc.  Please raise issue on https://github.com/astropy/astropy
>>> erf(r1.value/r2.value)  # workaround
0.76140717068356445
```
In scipy.special, ufuncs that I would prioritize include:
- [ ] [Error function, etc](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/special.html#error-function-and-fresnel-integrals)
- [ ] [Bessel functions](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/special.html#bessel-functions)

- [ ] [Legendre functions](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/special.html#legendre-functions)

Thanks!

title: Wrong Earth radius
description:
As part of #6083 `astropy.constants` was updated, and in particular a new value for the Earth radius, called `"Nominal Earth equatorial radius"` and equal to `6.3568e6` was added:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/v2.0/astropy/constants/iau2015.py#L95

However, according to "IAU 2015 Resolution B3 on Recommended Nominal Conversion Constants for Selected Solar and Planetary Properties":

https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.07674

![screenshot-2017-7-24 - 1510 07674 pdf](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/316517/28540393-7f1ce650-70b5-11e7-85f5-e8901b7ae6ec.png)

the nominal equatorial radius of the Earth is 6.3781e6 m and the nominal polar radius of the Earth is 6.3568e6. Which means that, either the variable should read `"Nominal Earth polar radius"` or the value should be changed to `6.3781e6`.

Also, from the same report:

"If equatorial vs. polar radius is not explicitly specified, it should be understood that nominal terrestrial radius refers specifically to [equatorial], following common usage".

title: Automatically pass arguments from python setup.py test to pytest
description: At the moment, only a subset of pytest command-line arguments are available for ``python setup.py test``, and the rest need to be passed by ``-a``, e.g. ``python setup.py test -a "-x"``. It would be nice to simply pass any unrecognized arguments to pytest for simplicity.

title: Consider adding __setitem__ to SkyCoord to allow mutability
description:
From discussions in #6348, the question here is about the opportunities and implications of allowing `SkyCoord` to be mutable by adding a `__setitem__` method.  An implementation of `__setitem__` for `Time` can be seen in #6028, and this addresses some of the complications that arise in setting items in an object with non-trivial attributes (e.g. `scale` for Time or `frame`).  This issue is not mostly about implementation, we can assume that a suitable implementation can be found.

Opportunities include:
- Support table vstack and join
- Support table insert and add rows
- Making SkyCoord be more like normal arrays.  In general mutable arrays are obviously rather useful!
- Allowing resize
- Others?

Implications:
- Astropy code needs to be scrubbed to be sure that `__setitem__` clears all caches.
- Code that really depends on a SkyCoord being immutable?  Where can this introduce bugs in code?

Discuss!

title: Copying an HDUList is shallow
description:
Just a suggestion here:

It might be worth adding a deep copy method to HDUList such that is behaves in the same manner as the copy method in an PrimaryHDU object. The parent class for an HDUList has a 'copy' method but it is only a shallow copy since it inherits from a list. 

It would be convenient to have these behaviors similar because when you read in a fits file it will automatically create an HDUList and sometimes you may want to copy it without reading the file in again.

title: Should/could HDUList.info() report constant array extensions (from STScI)?
description:
I have a fits file that uses constant arrays for some of its extensions. When using ``HDUList.info()`` the following is returned:

```
No.    Name         Type      Cards   Dimensions   Format
0    PRIMARY     PrimaryHDU     229   ()              
1    SCI         ImageHDU        95   (534, 512)   float32   
2    ERR         ImageHDU        49   ()              
3    DQ          ImageHDU        41   ()
```

This implies that the ``ERR`` & ``DQ`` extensions are empty, however, this is not entirely the case. When reading the header for the ``ERR`` extension the array exists as a constant array.

```
NPIX1   =                  534 / length of constant array axis 1                
NPIX2   =                  512 / length of constant array axis 2                
PIXVALUE=        4.0400000E+00 / values of pixels in constant array     
```

This has recently lead to some confusion in believing that these arrays were not populated by [HSTCAL](https://github.com/spacetelescope/hstcal). I was wondering if perhaps ``HDUList.info()`` could display this info?

From what has been explained to me (sorry I haven't checked) these keywords and their use as a constant array is __not__ a FITS standard but that this is just an STScI convention. I can understand that this might be _the_ road blocker in this request, but here it is none the less.

title: WCS get_pc() not taking CROTA into account

*Returns the ``PC`` matrix in read-only form.  Unlike the

array([[ 1.,  0.],
       [ 0.,  1.]])
```

Also, ``to_header`` outputs a header without CROTA2.

my_dicts_2 = [ {'A': 1, 'B': 2},

my_table_2 = astropy.table.Table(my_dicts_2, names=my_dicts_2[0].keys())

KeyError                                  Traceback (most recent call last)

    648         """
    649         if data and all(isinstance(row, dict) for row in data):
--> 650             self._init_from_list_of_dicts(data, names, dtype, n_cols, copy)
    651             return
    652

/Users/tsrice/anaconda3/lib/python3.6/site-packages/astropy/table/table.py in _init_from_list_of_dicts(self, data, names, dtype, n_cols, copy)
    637                     cols[name].append(row[name])
    638                 except KeyError:

    640         if all(name is None for name in names):
    641             names = sorted(names_from_data)

ValueError: Row 0 has no value for column C

```

Basically, I think that a bug has occurred where the function "_init_from_list_of_dicts" ignores the 'names' argument that is passed in, always instead using "names_from_data" generated from the list of dicts in the following code: 

```python
ipdb> ll
    627     def _init_from_list_of_dicts(self, data, names, dtype, n_cols, copy):
    628         names_from_data = set()
    629         for row in data:
    630             names_from_data.update(row)
    631

I think the fix is probably to check that `names` is not `None` before line 628 above, so that the code between lines 628 - 639 is only ever executed if no `names` argument is passed in.

title: Velocities in cylindrical coordinates
description:
I'm trying to compute velocities in the Galactocentric cylindrical coordinate frame with astropy v2, but as far as I can tell this isn't documented anywhere. The following seems to work
```
ra= 120.*u.deg
dec= 30.*u.deg
distance= 1.2*u.kpc
pmra= 5.*u.mas/u.yr
pmdec= -3.*u.mas/u.yr
vlos= 55.*u.km/u.s
c= apycoords.ICRS(ra=ra,dec=dec,
                  distance=distance,
                  pm_ra_cosdec=pmra,
                  pm_dec=pmdec,
                  radial_velocity=vlos)
# Define GC frame
v_sun = apycoords.CartesianDifferential([11.1,245.,7.25]*u.km/u.s)
gc_frame= apycoords.Galactocentric(galcen_distance=8.1*u.kpc,
                                   z_sun=25.*u.pc,
                                   galcen_v_sun=v_sun)
cg= c.transform_to(gc_frame)
cg.representation= 'cylindrical'
print("Cylindrical: v_r/(km/s)=",cg.d_rho.to(u.km/u.s),
      ", v_phi/(km/s)=",cg.d_phi.to(u.mas/u.yr).value*4.74047*cg.rho.to(u.kpc).value,
      " v_z/(km/s)=",cg.d_z.to(u.km/u.s))
Cylindrical: v_r/(km/s)= 17.213193237684614 km / s , v_phi/(km/s)= -213.59390592255582  v_z/(km/s)= 52.07396464035026 km / s
```
This gives the right answer, but maybe this isn't how these ``d_`` attributes are supposed to be used? Also, having to manually convert ``d_phi`` from mas/yr to km/s must be wrong. Is there a way to get the velocity in the cylindrical representation out more directly that I am missing or if not, is it correct to use the ``d_`` attributes in this way?

description:

title: Document better which models currently support units
Unit of Hz defined wrong?
description:
@scottransom brought up a question that has come up several times already (most recently, #6032), of converting between `Hz` and an angular frequency. As defined in our unit system `Hz` is just `1/s`. At first, this seems quite consistent with NIST [1], which list it as such among the derived units. However, just a quick look at wikipedia yields Hz being defined as "one cycle per second" [2]. Of course, this is not the same... And least in the context of our unit system it would mean `Hz = cycle / s`. But then Hz is also logically used for count rates, etc. It seems part of the problem is that one needs to define what is being counted.

Overall, unlike in #6032, I now feel this is a bug, one that has been there since the start (and in fact is in pynbody, where the unit code came from, as well [3]).

The question is what to do. Redefine Hz as cy/s? But that might break code that now uses it differently. Define a second Hz? Add a different equivalency to help this case?

cc @adrn, @astrofrog

[1] https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/units.html
[2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertz
[3] https://github.com/pynbody/pynbody/blob/master/pynbody/default_config.ini#L222

title: Differential frame attributes can't be serialized to YAML
description:
This was first reported in #6446, although #6446 is actually two related issues - this one and a slightly different one (which I am declaring #6446 to actually be about).

This issue is that differential objects can't get written out to ECSV.  To see this in operation:
```python
import io
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy.table import Table
sc = SkyCoord([1], [2], unit='deg', galcen_v_sun=None)
t = Table([sc])
t.write(io.StringIO(), format='ascii.ecsv', overwrite=True)
```
This raises a ``RepresenterError: cannot represent an object: ( 11.1,  232.24,  7.25) km / s``

(if the ``galcen_v_sun=None`` business isn't obvious, it's that it sets that attribute to the *default* value:)
```

>>> sc1 = SkyCoord([1], [2], unit='deg')
>>> sc1.galcen_v_sun
>>> sc2 = SkyCoord([1], [2], unit='deg', galcen_v_sun=None)
>>> sc2.galcen_v_sun
<CartesianDifferential (d_x, d_y, d_z) in km / s
    ( 11.1,  232.24,  7.25)>
```

So the core problem seems to be that ``CartesianDifferential`` isn't something that ECSV can handle.  @taldcroft, is this because these features were being implemented in parallel and therefore it's an oversight? ``CartesianDifferential`` is very similar to ``CartesianRepresentation``, so I'd think it would be pretty straightforward to include?

cc @larrybradley @adrn

title: Long-term testing improvements and future directions
description:
## Purpose
This issue is intended to serve as a forum for discussing future directions and improvements to astropy's testing infrastructure. It attempts to aggregate related testing issues, and I anticipate that new, more tightly scoped, issues may result from this discussion.

## Motivation
### Test Plugins
It seems like there is general consensus that moving astropy's `pytest` plugins into separate packages would be good and useful. This would make them available _a la carte_ to affiliated packages (and even non-affiliated packages). It would help minimize the testing infrastructure we maintain since it aligns with the standard `pytest` mechanism for plugin distribution. Some work has already been done towards this end (#6384), although more work is required.

### Invoking Pytest Directly
Equally important, I would argue, is the ability to run tests directly from `pytest`, rather than relying exclusively on `./setup.py` . This currently does not work (#6424), which I would argue is a substantial shortcoming that needs to be addressed. Some work has been done to address this (#6437), but it has become clear that this will require a non-trivial refactoring of the testing infrastructure.

One reason I believe this is important is that it is the _expected_ behavior: a project that uses `pytest` for testing should be able to _just use_ `pytest` for testing (#5402).

Another argument is a little more subtle: I believe that the fact that we do not currently support invoking `pytest` directly means that _we don't use it as it is designed to be used_. In addition to being somewhat unsatisfying, I believe this makes our testing code brittle and potentially unstable in the long term. It also makes it difficult to identify testing-related issues since they might be hidden by the way that we run our tests.

To address an outstanding issue (#6392), since all `pytest` functionality is available directly from the `pytest` command line interface, the need to develop a pass-through for our `./setup.py` runner is eliminated. This is good, because after looking into this issue I believe that such a pass-through would be particularly difficult to implement.

### Other Considerations
With the move to exclusive Python 3 support in v3.0, we have an opportunity to also make potentially substantial improvements to the testing infrastructure. In considering these issues at the same time, we can hopefully minimize the number of times that affiliated packages will have to update the way that they use astropy.

## Proposal
Given the motivating assumptions above, here is an outline of the changes that I would like to propose:

1. Continue to refactor `pytest` plugins to isolate specific functionality as much as possible (see #6437)
2. Move all `pytest` plugins into separate packages
3. Move the astropy test runner to astropy-helpers or another package **-OR-** eliminate the test runner all together and rely exclusively on the `pytest` plugin mechanism for astropy-specific features
4. Make other changes to astropy itself to enable running tests directly from `pytest` (see #6449, #6450, and #6437)
5. ~~Update all tests to import astropy with absolute imports~~ This discussion has been moved to #6452 

### Moving the Plugins
The motivation for moving the plugins has been treated above. I believe this would be fairly straightforward and would require relatively small changes to astropy and affiliates.

### The Test Runner
In addition to moving the plugins out of the astropy core, I argue that it would also be beneficial to move the test runner out of the core package as well. Testing is sufficiently general to make it useful to other packages without requiring the core as a hard dependency. The astropy-helpers package seems like a reasonable destination for this functionality, although a separate test package could also be useful. This was proposed in #6362, which should probably be reopened since it is distinct from the work started in #6384.

However, it is
…（以下省略）

title: Relative vs absolute imports in tests
description:
This discussion has been moved from #6451.

Right now, it appears that nearly all tests in astropy do something like the following at the top:

```python
from ....extern.six.moves
from ....io import fits
from ....utils.data import conf, get_pkg_data_filename
```

In general, it is considered good practice to use absolute imports in unit tests so that the tests actually run against installed code when possible. This is important since it means the tests run against the same code that users will see, and it can help identify packing issues before distributing.

This proposal is primarily motivated by [this section](http://pytest.readthedocs.io/en/latest/goodpractices.html#conventions-for-python-test-discovery) of the pytest documentation.

However, there are other considerations (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/6451#issuecomment-323131897) that may prevent this from being practical for astropy. In summary, more investigation/discussion is needed.

but to get it to produce the same result as `blackbody_nu` function, I need to give the reverse of normalization used in the model evaluation (see https://gist.github.com/pllim/babea1d1337da665740439887c5b6f5f)
```python
bolometric_flux = const.sigma_sb * temperature ** 4 / np.pi
```

I can see how setting the latter as default is problematic because it depends on the other parameter, `temperature`. At the very least, this should be better documented, perhaps in `BlackBody1D` docstring. What do you think, @astrofrog ?

title: Ecliptic coordinate transformation precision
description:
At the moment, the tests for the ecliptic frame only check that things are accurate to 1 arcminute:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/coordinates/tests/accuracy/test_ecliptic.py#L29

The coordinates-benchmark [summary page](http://www.astropy.org/coordinates-benchmark/summary.html#fk5_ecliptic) also shows that Astropy's ecliptic implementation seems to disagree with all others by 10 arcseconds or more. This issue is a reminder that we should fix this. 

There is a related issue to use ERFA for the Ecliptic transformation: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/4873

I'm labelling this as a bug since I think we want to backport any fix to the 2.0 LTS series. I'm also labelling this as being high priority since I think these kinds of accuracy issues should not be present in a 'core' library.

title: Factor out Time scales into a new module, add user-defined scales
description:
Inspired by discussion in #6190 and the included [specific code example](https://gist.github.com/gahjelle/1c4e18f0df4e98a8836edcaa6dd1a7a8) from @gahjelle, it seems like it would not be too difficult to move the time scale definitions and transform functions into class definitions within a new module `time/scales.py`.

I haven't thought this all the way through, but the [main scale definitions](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/b848c2cbb24a4af7101a373cc2320cca73e68f45/astropy/time/core.py#L42) are at the top of `core.py`.  These can be moved into `scales.py` and then imported into `core.py`.

The "easy" way would be just copying the existing definitions (probably need to make `TIME_SCALES` and others mutable, either a list or set).  Then have a base metaclass `ScaleMeta` that registers the scale and updates the module `TIME_SCALES` and `MULTI_HOPS` based on a similarly-named class attributes `time_scale` and `multi_hops`.  Also have class methods that do the transforms, similar to the `_gpstai` and `_taigps` methods in https://gist.github.com/gahjelle/1c4e18f0df4e98a8836edcaa6dd1a7a8.

Finally, in the [core scale transform code](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/b848c2cbb24a4af7101a373cc2320cca73e68f45/astropy/time/core.py#L499) you just need to allow for a transform from a custom class instead of built-in ERFA.  

The slight-less-easy (but cleaner way) to do this would be to retro-fit all the ERFA transforms to use the new base class machinery.

@gahjelle - if you want to take a crack at this it would be MOST welcome!

The one thing is that for astropy core we do have to live with the unfortunate history of having `gps` already taken as a format.  In theory we might make a clean break for 3.0 and change the meaning of `gps` from format to scale.  We could then add a config item to allow `gps` to be a format instead of scale for specific applications.  But we need to be careful, and at least to start off it would be easier to develop the code using a different name e.g. `gps_scale`.

cc: @mhvk @astrofrog

title: astropy.cosmology distance functions using too much memory
description:
I regulary use distance functions of astropy.cosmology to calculate comoving distances. I noticed they consume large amounts of memory. For a couple million redshifts, my memory usage increases by ~7GB, while 3 million redshifts max out the 16GB system memory.

title: Support several SPK ephemerides at once
description:
The generic SPK files available at ftp://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/spk/planets/, which are the most useful, usually refer to the barycenter of the planetary systems that have satellites, with the sole exception of the Earth.* For example, [the README of DE430/431](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/spk/planets/aareadme_de430-de431.txt) states:

> The offset between the location of the Mars barycenter and the  Mars mass center is extremely 
small--about 20 cm--so most SPICE users could use the Mars B.C. (4) instead of the Mars mass 
center (499). But if you do wish or need to have the location of 499 available in your program, 
you must also load a Mars  satellite ephemeris such as mar097.bsp.

It would be nice to have the ability to load additional SPK files in case one wants to compute the position of other bodies, for instance those available here:

ftp://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/spk/satellites/

or even specific NASA missions:

ftp://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/MSL/kernels/spk/

I'm not sure what to do with the list of bodies given in `solar_system.py` though, perhaps it's better to leave that to the user.

title: Add support for Ecliptic coordinates in wcs_to_celestial_frame and celestial_frame_to_wcs
description:
The functions ``wcs_to_celestial_frame`` and ``celestial_frame_to_wcs`` in astropy.wcs.utils don't currently support the ecliptic frames from ``astropy.coordinates``, but this should be added. See the following paper for the conventions, in particular there are mentions of ecliptic and helioecliptic frames:

http://www.atnf.csiro.au/people/mcalabre/WCS/ccs.pdf

title: CCDData reader should check for inherit=T header card
description:
According to the [`INHERIT`](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/registry/inherit/fits_inheritance.txt) documentation an extension FITS file should inherit the Header values from the primary HDU in case the primary is non-data and `INHERIT=T` is set.

Currently only in case the primary is empty and no specific extension is given the `CCDData` will inherit (at least when #6489 is merged) the Header values from the primary - but without checking `INHERIT`.

This probably needs some thoughts and a minor (or major) restructuring of the `reader` file because `INHERIT` should be applied also when a specific extension is given and has `INHERIT=T` and the primary is non-data.

Probably breaks backwards-compatibility so it should be scheduled (if we change it at all) for 3.0.

Does someone know if `io.fits` respects the `INHERIT` conventions? I have no sample files that match the criteria so if someone knows where I can find a sample file I'll check that. :)

title: Consistency with FITS Header string types
description:
When getting text values from a FITS header, I've noticed they will not always pass simple Python 2.7 checks. For example, 
```python
from astropy.io import fits
from __future__ import (absolute_import, division, print_function, unicode_literals)
from future.builtins import bytes, int, str

hdu = fits.open(myfile)

x = hdu[1].header['DATE-OBS']
print(x, type(x), isinstance(x, str))
```
This returns: `2018-03-30T18:27:38.816Z <type 'str'> False`
However, this: 
```python
y = '2018-03-30T18:27:38.816Z'
print(y, type(y), isinstance(y, str))
```
returns: `2018-03-30T18:27:38.816Z <type 'unicode'> True`
Perhaps `astropy.io.fits.header.Header` objects should return unicode values by default under Python 2?

In my code, I can get it to work using the `six` package:
```python
from six import string_types
print(x, type(x), isinstance(x, string_types))
```
which produces: `2018-03-30T18:27:38.816Z <type 'str'> True`

I'm OK with using `six` at the moment, but wanted to mention how this fails with `future.builtins`

title: XDG_CONFIG_HOME failing silently caused confusion
description:
I ran into a group who would have benefited from #5899. However, since that is not yet possible, they tried to set two different directories for different versions of Astropy to run in parallel on the same file system on the same cluster. Otherwise, they run into a problem of `astropy.cfg` getting corrupted by the parallel attempts to write it.

Despite instructions at http://astropy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/config/index.html that says, "... if you’ve set the environment variable `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and the `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astropy` directory exists, it will instead be there," they set `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` that included the "astropy" sub-directory. As a result, the check for `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astropy` failed (because it was really looking for `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astropy/astropy`) and fell back silently to the default `~/.astropy/config`, which caused a lot of confusion.

Suggestion: If `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is defined but the desired directory is not found, raise an exception (too much?) or at least emit a warning.

title: Performance issues when writing VO tables in binary mode
description:
The following example shows two performance issues with writing VO tables:

```python
In [12]: from astropy.table import Table

In [13]: import numpy as np

In [14]: t = Table()

In [15]: t['a'] = np.random.random(1_000_000)

In [16]: %timeit t.write('test_binary2.xml', format='votable', tabledata_format='binary2', overwrite=True)
16.5 s ± 683 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

In [17]: %timeit t.write('test_binary.xml', format='votable', tabledata_format='binary', overwrite=True)
4.06 s ± 80 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

The first issue is that ``binary2`` is 4 times slower than ``binary``. The difference between the two should be the inclusion of the mask, but this shouldn't make the writing four times slower.

The second issue is that both of these are ridiculously slow and seem to indicate that there is some Python loop over the array elements. Since the whole data structure is stored as a base64-encoded string, we should be able to do this in a vectorized way (the data structure contains only data values, no VO-table-specific tags).

If someone is interested in looking into this, it would be good to profile the writer to see where things could be sped up.

I'm marking this as package-novice because I think anyone could dive in and try and profile things, but it still requires a very good knowledge of Python.

title: fitscheck checksum corrections don't work
description:
While it was originally written as a migration utility from buggy obsolete pyfits checksums to standard FITS checksums,  fitscheck was also designed as a utility simply for working with standard checksums.  It could check, add, remove, or correct FITS checksums in the standard form from the command line.   Whether they were correct or incorrect,  missing or present.   No python shell or coding required.

Sometime since 2010,  fitscheck lost the ability to correct standard checksums.   Checking still works,  but not corrections or removals of bad checksums.

I doubt it's used much so it should probably be deprecated and/or dropped.   However, another option is to fix checksum updates.   Any logic related to "nonstandard vs. standard" checksums can be dropped,  it addressed a problem that is long gone.

title: Regression with Column and units ?
description:
When running this simple code
```
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.table import Column

a = Column([1,2,3], unit='Hz')
b = 2*u.Hz
```

comparison between a & b will fail with astropy 2.0.x (tested both with 2.7 & 3.5):
* `print(a<b)` return a `UnitsError: Can only apply 'less' function to dimensionless quantities when other argument is not a quantity (unless the latter is all zero/infinity/nan)`
* `print(b<a)` return the expected array

Moreover when units are different `b = 2*u.MHz`, both will fail
* `print(a<b)` return the same `UnitsError`
* `print(b<a)` return an `AttributeError: 'Column' object has no attribute 'value'`

With astropy 1.3.3, only the last test would fail with the same exception.

title: Astropy units with fractional powers are stored incorrectly
description:
I noticed a problem when trying to store an astropy.unit in a variable that is raised to a fractional power.
If this fractional power cannot be written in terms of 'a/b' with b<=10, astropy will try to approximate the power by assigning it a power that does satisfy this rule.
So, for example,
```
>>> import astropy.units as apu
>>> A = pow(2*apu.kg, 11./14.)
>>> print(A)
```
will give me `1.7239456 kg^(7/9)`.
The value '2' was raised to the correct power, because it could be calculated immediately.
However, the unit 'kg' is not raised to the correct power.
Instead of raising it to the power of '11/14', it is raised to the power of '7/9'.
And although these two numbers are very similar, this of course doesn't work when dealing with units.

I discovered this problem because I was dealing with powers like '24/79', '11/14' and '-3/20'.
The final result should be unitless if all units along the way are stored and used correctly.
However, the final result had a really weird unit that had a power that was something like '14/41875179'.
Something that is practically zero, but not completely.


So, is this a memory issue or can this be fixed or...?


As for the software information: I tried this on Python 2.7, 3.4, 3.5 and 3.6.
I am using AstroPy version 2.0.2.
And, all other packages are up-to-date to cope with this version of AstroPy.

title: Should HDUList implement 'get' and 'keys'?
description:
The fact that `HDUList` allows ~~headers~~ HDUs to be retrieved not only by numeric index but also by extension name means it behaves in some ways like a `dict`. However, unlike `dict`, given an instance of `HDUList`, there is no `get` method to conditionally retrieve an HDU by key only if it exists. The `__contains__` method is already implemented (which allows for statements like `'NAME' in hdulist`), so it seems perfectly natural to provide a `get` method as well.

In addition, it might be useful to provide a `keys` method which would return a list of the names of all of the extensions.

title: Consider moving astropy-specific schemas and tags from ASDF to astropy core

ASDF is a data format that is capable of serializing arbitrary Python objects. While any ASDF file can be reconstructed in memory using basic Python types (strings, lists, dicts), it is often useful to recreate the original object. Currently, ASDF maintains schemas (data type definitions) and tags (implementations of serialization) for various astropy objects. It would be useful to move the astropy-specific schemas and tags to astropy, where they can be maintained and testing in parallel with the corresponding objects.

title: Improvements to changelog
description:
### Background

At the coordination meeting in NY we discussed whether the changelog could be stored in a separate format and whether it could be e.g. auto-generated from merged pull requests.

We eventually decided that a lot of these ideas would require a lot of extra engineering and also having spoken to @bsipocz, it seems the 2.0 release happened without any big issues related to the changelog, so it seems the issues we used to get in the past are gone now that @astropy-bot diligently  checks each PR for consistency. Our decision was that for now, instead of working on developing a whole new format and process we should simply try and improve interactions with the bot to better help users get the changelog entry right

### Proposal

Several ideas were discussed for improving the bot interactions with pull requests:

* If the ``CHANGES.rst`` file has not been changed at all, the bot could detect this and tell the user it would be great if they added a changelog entry, and could give an example of what a changelog entry should look like and explain how to decide where to put it in the file and remind them to add the PR number.

* If the PR does include a changelog entry but no PR number, the bot could mention that the contributor could add the PR number.

* We could have an option that if we push a PR with ``[#...]`` or similar as the PR number, the bot could automatically fill out the PR number and push a new commit to add the PR number

And as a fallback, maintainers can also simply edit the PR through GitHub to add the PR number themselves.

The idea to resolve the concern of the ambiguous name `.representation`  by doing the following:

- [ ] Change  the `.representation` attribute to `.representation_type`, and have the docs exclusively use that
- [ ] Have `.representation` remain, now but just point to `.representation_type` (both setter and getter). In a future version we may deprecate it (There's some disagreement on that point, to be resolved later)
- [ ] Have the SkyCoord and frame object constructors continue to accept the ``representation`` keyword as they do now for backwards compatibility, but change the documented use to instead use ``data`` and ``representation_type`` keywords, in parallel structure with the above.

Test()

      6         super().__init__()
      7 
----> 8 Test()

C:\Programming\Anaconda\envs\work\lib\site-packages\astropy-3.0.dev20121-py3.5-win-amd64.egg\astropy\utils\decorators.py in deprecated_func(*args, **kwargs)
    116             warnings.warn(message, category, stacklevel=2)

--> 118             return func(*args, **kwargs)

----> 6         super().__init__()

There are currently several places where we allow or should allow packages to register extensions to Astropy. For example:

- The unified I/O interface
- Custom WCS to frame/frame to WCS mappings (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/wcs/utils.py#L141)
- Custom serializations (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6619)
- Coordinate frames and transformations

The current workflow is for a package to append something to a list or call a register function. However, this is not ideal because it means the user has to know to explicitly import the package first. For example, let's say sunpy defined a ``.solar`` file format (I'm making this up, but hey).

If I just did:

```python
from astropy.table import Table
t = Table(...)
t.write('myfile.solar')
```

this wouldn't work. I'd need to do:

```python
from astropy.table import Table
import sunpy.io  # making this up
t = Table(...)
t.write('myfile.solar')
```

The standard way around this kind of issue is to consider using entry points to set up a plugin system. With entry points, sunpy could then say it has plugins for file formats and provide the entry point to set up those file formats. This then allows astropy to discover plugins without the user having to import other packages explicitly (installing is enough).

To avoid a proliferation of ways of doing this, we should probably decide if we want to do this and then come up with standard entry point categories, e.g. ``[astropy.table.serialization]``, ``[astropy.table.formats]``, ``[astropy.coordinates.frames]`` and so on.

Note that if we had one entry point per Table format, we could also use entry points in the core package itself to register reader/writers instead of doing this ugly hack: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/58fdc0115d0204c5bb64a36b5a24939190e4c396/astropy/table/__init__.py#L54

As a bonus, for Table formats, this could mean loading entry points only when the format is requested, which could improve import-time performance.

I'm opening this here to get some initial feedback - not sure if this should become an APE, or if this + astropy-dev discussion would be enough. Maybe we can see how controversial this idea is 😆

title: The brightness temperature equivalence is confusing
description:
The `astropy.units.equivalencies.brightness_temperature()` is very confusing. According to the documentation, it defines a conversion between Jy/beam and the brightness temperature in Kelvins. It is defined as:
![capture d ecran 2017-10-05 a 11 53 38](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95471/31221405-e40ad9c2-a9c3-11e7-9d80-7a026d686ae2.png)
where S_nu the flux density, usually expressed in Jy/sr. The documentation also says that the beam area is essential for this computation: the brightness temperature is inversely proportional to the beam area. 

However, by definition, the brightness temperature does *not* depends on the beam size: it is simply defined as the temperature of a black body with the same flux density (note that equation above is only valid in the Rayleigh-Jeans approximation). It is *not* inversely proportional to the beam area (there is perhaps a confusion with the beam temperature, which is a different thing).

I think this equivalence should define a conversion between Jy/sr (or equivalent units) to Kelvins, which does not depend on the beam. The beam is only needed to convert between Jy/sr and Jy/beam, but this is straightforward.

cc @keflavich

title: Further work related to the FITS Time standard, FITS WCS and astropy native objects
description:
This is just a list of things to remind ourselves that there is work yet to be done (following the work that I did in the summer):

1. Use ``GreenBank`` convention to store vector ``location`` of `~astropy.time.Time`:
    This is fairly simple and I will get to it as soon as possible.
2. Simplify the current implementation for reading time coordinate keywords: 
    Avoid repetitive checks for time coordinate keywords (io/fits/column.py and io/fits/fitstime.py)
    As suggested by @mhvk, this will improve time complexity. This seems fairly easy, but the 
    exact details are still difficult to evaluate. I will try to do so whenever possible.
3. Make use of ``TCRVL`` (reference value) and ``TCDLT`` (delta time) for precise calculation 
    of time coordinate values:
    This will be especially useful when dealing with multiple time coordinate columns in a single 
    FITS binary table HDU (all of these relative to a reference time value MJDREF, JDREF or 
    DATEREF each interpreted using the column-specific time scale). This might require much 
    more efforts.
4. Interpret time column formats using reference time and time scale:
    This is a minor modification but will still be helpful.
5. Store ``Mixins`` using ECSV technique. This was suggested by @taldcroft; @taldcroft and 
    @mhvk are the best people to do so. I will be happy to be of any assistance in doing this.
6. Extend this to ``SkyCoord`` and ``Earthlocation``:
    This will probably constitute another GSoC 😛 . Nevertheless, I will try to work on it when I 
    get the time (of course along with @taldcroft @mhvk and @hamogu or someone else willing to 
    work on the same).

If there is anyone willing to work on any of these issues, I'll be happy to tag along.

title: Table column print format cache bug
description:
The column format is currently cached in a global dictionary keyed with the format and `id()` of the column.  The problem is that when the table/column get garbage collected, a totally different column can be later placed in the same memory location and thus have the same `id()`.  That may seem unlikely, but I've been encountering this seemingly random bug in real code (and in `photutils` CI testing).

The specific issue that I'm having is that a mixin `Quantity` column caches the formatter to use the one for `Quantity` objects: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/units/quantity.py#L121

Later, a regular non-mixin `Column` cannot be printed because it's trying to use the `Quantity` formatter.  This is because the initial column has been garbage collected and the later `Column` has the same `id()` -- thus it uses the cached formatter.

This was frustrating to debug in actual code because it was hard to reliably reproduce, but here's a contrived example showing the bug:

https://gist.github.com/larrybradley/57185c001ae12647d74d9a73a53f6a5e

My suggestion would be to cache the formatter in the column `info` object, as suggested in #5804.  I don't understand the concern about the case when the column does not yet have data. Perhaps I missed something, but it appears that the caching occurs only when the first item of the column is printed, so the column must have data in order for the format to be cached.  Also, how does one even set the column format without having defined the column object?

Also related to:  #5800 and #5803

CC: @taldcroft, @mhvk

description:

WARNING: The following header keyword is invalid or follows an unrecognized non-standard convention:
FIX4 2                                                                           [astropy.io.fits.card]
```

I'm not sure if that ever worked or when that regression was introduced. But should such a card be fixable?

title: pytest needed as (runtime) requirement?
description: pytest is now listed as `install_requires` in setup.py, and also included as 'run requirement' in the conda recipe. I think it's better to use `tests_require`  (see http://setuptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/setuptools.html) for setup.py, and not include it in the recipe. In general I don't think test packages should be dependencies, people that want to test will either have this in their environment already, or will read the documentation.

title: skyCoord() and masked fields
description:
Hi,
I stepped over unexpected behaviour of skyCoord(). After importing a VOTable into the code below, the script works fine. Unless there is invalid data in a field: in this case skyCoord() does neither raise an error or a warning, but instead treats the data in the masked fields as zeros -- which is not a NULL value at all, but a valid value for a position. 
Attached you will find a VOTable with invalid fields as .txt file. 

```
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy.io.votable import parse_single_table
from numpy.ma import masked as Masked

table=parse_single_table("example.txt").to_table()
for index,row in enumerate(table):
  position=SkyCoord(row["RA"]*u.deg, row["DEC"]*u.deg, frame="icrs")
  print position
```

So far I use the following workaround using numpy masked arrays by replacing the upper buggy code with the following:

```
 try: 
    if row["RA"] is Masked or row["DEC"] is Masked:
      raise ValueError("Missing coordinate")
    else: 
      position=SkyCoord(row["RA"]*u.deg, row["DEC"]*u.deg, frame="icrs")
      print position
  except ValueError as error:
    print error 
```

[example.txt](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/files/1422919/example.txt)

title: Why doesn't astropy use ~/.config/astropy by default (on Unix-like systems)?
description: If `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set, astropy will look for configuration files in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astropy/`.  However, it will **not** look for configuration files in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astropy/config/`.  Similarly, if `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` is set, astropy will look for cache files in `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/astropy/`, not `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/astropy/cache`.  Why does the layout of `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astropy/` have to be different from the layout of `$HOME/.astropy/`, which contains `config/` and `cache/` directories?  Unless one knows that the layout is different, one would expect that `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/astropy/config/` and `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/astropy/cache/` would be the directories to contain configuration and cache files.

title: Add a way to write comments to FITS table columns
description:
It would be nice, if descriptions of astropy.table.Table columns were used somehow, and also saved to FITS files. A simple idea for the latter would be to add FITS comments to the TTYPE keywords.

Example:
```python
from astropy.table import Table

a = [1, 4, 5]
b = [2.0, 5.0, 8.2]
c = ['x', 'y', 'z']
t = Table([a, b, c], names=('a', 'b', 'c'), meta={'name': 'first table'})
t['a'].description = 'some numbers'
t['b'].description = 'some floats'
t['c'].description = 'these are strings!'
print(t)
t.write('tabletest2.fits')
```

The FITS file written gets this header:
```
XTENSION= 'BINTABLE'           / binary table extension
BITPIX  =                    8 / array data type
NAXIS   =                    2 / number of array dimensions
NAXIS1  =                   17 / length of dimension 1
NAXIS2  =                    3 / length of dimension 2
PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of group parameters
GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups
TFIELDS =                    3 / number of table fields
TTYPE1  = 'a       '
TFORM1  = 'K       '
TTYPE2  = 'b       '
TFORM2  = 'D       '
TTYPE3  = 'c       '
TFORM3  = '1A      '
NAME    = 'first table'
END
```

It could write this instead:
```
TTYPE1  = 'a       '           / some numbers
TFORM1  = 'K       '
TTYPE2  = 'b       '           / some floats
TFORM2  = 'D       '
TTYPE3  = 'c       '           / these are strings!
TFORM3  = '1A      '
```

Of course, these would be cut off when the descriptions are long, but something may be better than nothing.

title: FittingWithOutlierRemoval doesn't work for model sets
description:
Attempting to use `FittingWithOutlierRemoval` in place of a simple `LinearLSQFitter` instance produces a `ValueError: Input argument u'x' does not have the correct dimensions in model_set_axis=0 for a model set with n_models=4176`. This blocks the very common use case of fitting each row of an image with rejection, as in IRAF's ``fit1d``. One could, of course, fit each row with a separate model instance, but that would be much slower -- and even _with_ model sets, fitting already seems unpleasantly slow compared with IRAF, so it probably wouldn't be viable.

Unfortunately, I think fixing this might be non-trivial: Within `FittingWithOutlierRemoval`, L557 (also L567-568) selects only good points from an input array of `x` co-ordinates, like so:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/667b7ab621dfa80290fbe36cd711ad0a427ca272/astropy/modeling/fitting.py#L556-L559

Obviously the rejected points will differ from one row/model to another, which means that `FittingWithOutlierRemoval` cannot simply pass the underlying `Fitter` a single array of `x` co-ordinates (in N-1 dimensions) to use for every model. Unlike model evaluation, I _think_ fitting of model sets in general only works with a common `x` array for all the models, so `LinearLSQFitter` and friends may need substantial changes for this to work. Moreover, I believe the matrix equation solved by the underlying `np.linalg` routine assumes a 2D Vandermonde matrix, corresponding to a single set of points in `x` -- I'm not even sure (off the top of my head) that the problem can be expressed in a form that the back-end solver can work with, which would be rather unfortunate.

Would you mind confirming that this is a correct analysis, @nden (assuming you know off hand)? I've always had a bit of a hard time discerning from the documentation exactly what dimensionality of inputs the models and fitters accept under different circumstances.

title: Equivalencies are not used on compound models with units
description:
The following works:
```python
>>> from astropy.modeling.functional_models import Scale

>>> scl1 = Scale(1*u.arcsec)
>>> scl1.input_units_equivalencies = {'x': u.pixel_scale(0.6*u.arcsec/u.pix)}
>>> scl1(3*u.pix)
'<Quantity 1.7984670000000003 arcsec>'

The following does not:
```python
>>> scl1 = Scale(1*u.arcsec)
>>> scl1.input_units_equivalencies = {'x': u.pixel_scale(0.6*u.arcsec/u.pix)}

>>> scl2 = Scale(1*u.arcsec)
>>> scl2.input_units_equivalencies = {'x': u.pixel_scale(0.6*u.arcsec/u.pix)}

>>> scale = scl & scl2

>>> scale(3*u.pix, 3*u.pix)
(<Quantity 3.0 arcsec>, <Quantity 3.0 arcsec>)

```python
>>> scale(3*u.pix, 3*u.pix, equivalencies={'x': u.pixel_scale(0.6*u.arcsec/u.pix),

            pm_ra_cosdec=4.8*u.mas/u.yr, pm_dec=-15.16*u.mas/u.yr,

hcrs.transform_to(LSR)

title: Bug in Table with unicode sandwich when dealing with masked columns
description:
When comparing masked columns in bytes and unicode, the result is different when comparing two unicode columns compared to comparing a unicode and a bytes column:

```python
In [1]: from astropy.table import Table
   ...: 

In [2]: t1 = Table(masked=True)
   ...: t1['a'] = ['z', 'b', 'c']
   ...: t1['a'].mask = [1, 0, 0]
   ...: t2 = Table(masked=True)
   ...: t2['a'] = ['a', 'b', 'c']
   ...: 

In [3]: t2['a'] == t1['a']
Out[3]: 
masked_array(data = [-- True True],
             mask = [ True False False],
       fill_value = True)

In [4]: t1 = Table(masked=True)
   ...: t1['a'] = ['z', 'b', 'c']
   ...: t1['a'].mask = [1, 0, 0]
   ...: t2 = Table(masked=True)
   ...: t2['a'] = [b'a', b'b', b'c']
   ...: 

In [5]: t2['a'] == t1['a']
Out[5]: 
masked_array(data = [False True True],
             mask = [False False False],
       fill_value = True)
```

In the second case, the first mask item should be ``True``. This is a separate issue from https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/6838 (but I had to do ``t2['a'] == t1['a']`` instead of ``t1['a'] == t2['a']`` to avoid running into that issue).

title: Add a velocity convenience property to frames
description:
Following from some discussions (with @adrn and @mhvk) about things people find confusing in the new velocity machinery, we are now thinking there should be a set of attributes that're basically just:

```
def velocity(self):
    return self.cartesian.differentials['s']
```

and similar for `proper_motion` and `radial_velocity`.  The iffy part is that `radial_velocity` *already* exists and yields a *quantity*, not a `RadialDifferential`.  Probably that's OK though, because it's not that useful to use `RadialDifferential`?

title: Physical types in units could be improved
description:
For other contexts (specifically in `astropy.coordinates`, where we the `Unit*` representation and differential classes), it would be useful to have a concept of `dimensional_unscaled` units (compare
 to `dimensionless_unscaled`). But it occurred to us that this is actually a physical type! It may be that we want to make the physical types in astropy.units into objects themselves that behave like dimensional but unscaled units that cancel and combine properly.

cc @mhvk

title: Make erfa functions ufuncs instead of using custom wrappers?
description: In some of the work on distributions @eteq and I have been discussing, a bottleneck is the assumptions the current erfa wrappers make about the inputs; it would be great if those could be overridden. One possible way, which I note here mostly as a reminder, is to make all the erfa functions `ufunc` (or perhaps `gufunc` where reductions over axes take place). That way, any array can in principle override them using `__array_ufunc__` and we could have `Quantity` helpers that take care of units. An advantage would be that broadcasting and iteration would be taken care of by the ufunc machinery (now a lot of duplicated code).

title: test runner with -t option fails on python 3.5
description:
Sometime in the last month or so, *something* has caused the ``-t`` command on the test runner to start failing in Python 3.5.  I've included a test run below.  A few relevant facts:

* It happens on Pytest 3.1.2 or 3.2.1
* It does *not* seem to happen if you give a path to a directory instead of a file.  E.g., the traceback below is for ``python setup.py test -t astropy/io/fits/tests/test_checksum.py``, but ``python setup.py test -t astropy/io/fits/tests`` works just fine.
* It works on Python 3.6.x
* It happens pretty much anywhere in the test suite, but the fail is always wherever the first relative import is.

title: Write a Cython/C in-place rstrip function to speed up writing of FITS tables
description:
I was profiling writing of FITS tables with string columns (which has terrible performance at the moment) and I found that one of the bottlenecks is the following function in ``fitsrec.py``

```python
def _rstrip_inplace(array, chars=None):
    """
    Performs an in-place rstrip operation on string arrays.
    This is necessary since the built-in `np.char.rstrip` in Numpy does not
    perform an in-place calculation.  This can be removed if ever
    https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/6303 is implemented (however, for
    the purposes of this module the only in-place vectorized string functions
    we need are rstrip and encode).
    """

    for item in np.nditer(array, flags=['zerosize_ok'],
                                 op_flags=['readwrite']):
        item[...] = item.item().rstrip(chars)
```

At the moment,  https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/6303 hasn't been implemented yet, but it should be reasonably easy to write a C or Cython function that would implement something like this ourselves for now. Specifically, we need a function that loops over elements of a string array and replaces trailing spaces with null. I think the changes to Numpy would be a lot harder to do.

This could speed up writing FITS tables with character arrays by a factor of ~10x or more when combined with some other changes I'm preparing locally (PR forthcoming)

title: Is astropy.units essential in more fields than just astronomy?

I am very new to this project and I don't want to step on any toes. Still, I can't help but wonder if `astropy.units` should be "advertised" as bigger than only astronomy. A subset of possible mechanisms for this includes moving the module outside the `astropy` namespace, and/or listing a variety of other domains for which it's a great fit in the documentation, and/or writing an official blog post (though I don't believe Astropy has a blog?).

Generally, What do you all think?

title: Improve memory usage/performance with masked Table
description:
At the moment, even if the data from a table (e.g. a FITS table) is memory-mapped when loaded into Table, if the table is masked (due e.g. to TNULL in a FITS file) we construct masks using ``t[column] == null_value`` which creates an array in memory. For large tables this may not be negligible. One way to improve this would be to make it so that masks can also be arrays that dynamically return True/False by comparing the value on-the-fly to a null value. More generally speaking one could have lazy masks that check e.g. if the value is larger/smaller than a threshold, and so on. We do this in spectral-cube:

http://spectral-cube.readthedocs.io/en/latest/masking.html

This would make it possible to not use much additional memory for masks that can be represented with this (including columns from FITS tables masked with TNULL).

We could build this mask infrastructure to also work with NDData. I think we want lazily-evaluated Numpy boolean array subclasses basically.

title: Add documentation of YAML serialization of astropy core objects in Table
description:
Using ECSV (#6181) and FITS (#6912), and hopefully others such as HDF5, one can serialize a Table object with mixin columns (astropy core objects like SkyCoord, Time, and Quantity).  This is done via a set of extension representer/constructor pairs in YAML along with a recursive algorithm to encode a table with mixins into a "plain" table with only column objects, along with a nested dict structure that provides required info to later decode back to the same table with mixins.

This is evolving to a defacto astropy standard and should be documented.  That would allow for non-astropy implementations to *fully* read these files.

title: update wcslib for 3.0 release
Make units be consistent with versioned constants
description:
This motivation for this issue is fixing a subtle but important inconsistency that can now appear because constants are versioned (new feature in v2.0).  The basic problem is that some units are effectively tied to constants.  For example `units.solMass` exists, but so does `constants.M_sun`.  Right now with the default units they are consistent, but *if* someone uses the constant versioning machinery to update e.g. M_sun, they become inconsistent.

There are a couple possible fixes here:
* Tie the units to the constant values so that if a particular constant is set as the "current" version, the unit is assumed to have that value (I think that is more "right" but probably requires subtle and/or major changes to `units`).
* Make unit conversion factors versionable, and provide helper functions or just instructions for how to sync them up (possibly easier, but means manual intervention is required).

On the "what is new"  page for 2.0

`astropy.coordinates.Galactocentric` uses a left-handed convention (x increases from the galactic centre to the Sun). In that case the U component of v_sun should be negative

title: download_file() bug with cached results from a mirror
description:
This is something I stumbled on when I was having connection issues with data.astropy.org but not the mirror: when using `download_file()`, my download times were very long because it tries to connect several times before giving up and switching to the mirror. When it then finally decides to use the mirror, it works, downloads the file, and caches it. But because the file gets cached using the *mirror* url, if I run `download_file()` again with the same exact filename, it won't read it from the cache because the first URL it tries is with data.astropy.org, so then the same timeout issues happen again.

This isn't a serious issue, because I suspect the failure mode is pretty rare: this will only happen if connections to data.astropy.org timeout. If the connection is explicitly blocked, it should quickly fall back to the mirror. But it should probably first check the cache for all possible URLs before doing any internet connection.

title: Add unit of electron-volts that is specifically a temperature
description:
The [electron-volt](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt) (eV) is an extremely common unit of temperature in plasma physics.  Units of eV, keV, and so on are often used as a measure of the thermal energy per particle.  A quantity with units of eV can be converted to temperature by dividing by the [Boltzmann constant, k<sub>B</sub>](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann_constant).

Despite my honest opinion about this usage (see https://github.com/PlasmaPy/PlasmaPy/issues/131 for my grumblings), many in the plasma physics community would benefit from a unit of electron-volts that is specifically a temperature (perhaps called `eV_temp`).  Including this unit would also allow us to clean up a lot of code within [PlasmaPy](https://github.com/PlasmaPy/plasmapy). 

The ways to currently do this are:
```Python
>>> kT = 1.4 * units.eV
>>> kT.to(units.K, equivalencies=units.temperature_energy())
<Quantity 11604.522060401008 K>
```
and
```Python
>>> units.set_enabled_equivalencies(units.temperature_energy())
>>> kT.to(units.K)
<Quantity 11604.522060401008 K>
```

The proposed usage would allow usage like:
```Python
>>> kT = 1.0 * units.eV_temp
>>> kT.to(units.K)
<Quantity 11604.522060401008 K>
```
One of the biggest benefits is that we would not need to explicitly do a conversion step before we put a quantity with these units into a formula.  This would also greatly reduce the ambiguity for when units of eV are used as temperature.  

However, units of eV can also correspond to [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt#Mass), [momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt#Momentum), [distance, and time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt#Distance) as well as energy.  This ambiguity is part of the reason why I generally recommend against using units of eV in general (along with having silent factors of k<sub>B</sub>, c, c<sup>2</sup>, etc.).  If we decide to have units of `eV_temp`, then we might want to consider units of `eV_mass` and `eV_momentum` as well.

Thank you!  
-Nick

title: Simplify table creation and column handling
description:
_From @embray on July 17, 2014 21:30_

This ticket is mostly a stub--I will add more as I think of it.

The main point of this is that table creation really needs to be simplified. Users ought not understand the details of FITS column formats in order to create a table. Instead, it should be sufficient to just pass in a numpy array with fields and have a table created from it. Furthermore, it should be possible to create a table from a two-dimensional array of any sort, plus some column names and optionally column formats (otherwise the format can be inferred). To an extent this is already possible, but it's still not as easy at it could be.

Also, any tables containing columns that are not homogenous or otherwise incompatible with the FITS spec would be rejected with a friendly error message. It also be possible to allow some conversion functions to convert incompatible data to a FITS-compatible format.

Original ticket: https://aeon.stsci.edu/ssb/trac/pyfits/ticket/67

title: Add Header event notification system
description:
_From @embray on May 20, 2013 20:19_

It would be endlessly useful if headers had an event notification subscription system.  Any change on a header such as an addition of a keyword, a removal of a keyword, a change in value, a change in comment, etc. should publish an event to any and all subscribed listeners.  Listeners should probably be stored on the Header instance as weakrefs to avoid reference cycles and various sorts of zombism.

Such a system would have a great many uses and would be very helpful for maintaining internal consistency of FITS files.

title: HDU Improvement Checklist
description:
_From @embray on May 20, 2013 19:41_

This is a broad overall checklist of things that need to be fixed and cleaned up a bit in the pyfits HDU API.  Some of these reference existing issues, and some of them are new topics for which issues should be created.  I will update this checklist as I think of more items.
- [ ] Split verification into input verification and output verification phases; include support for full verification upon opening a file (see https://trac.assembla.com/pyfits/ticket/182, astropy/astropy#873, https://trac.assembla.com/pyfits/ticket/205)
- [ ] Work on a specialized ndarray subclass for FITS data that has built-in support for features like scaling and other types of transformations required for FITS data (such as 'T'/'F' -> True/False on boolean columns.  This could be used for both table columns and image arrays.
- [ ] Perhaps as sort of a specialized subclass of the above mentioned FITS data array type, support a way to decompress tile-compressed images one tile at a time. This would support something like https://trac.assembla.com/pyfits/ticket/100 and might support or supersede https://trac.assembla.com/pyfits/ticket/187)
- [x] Add a `.ver` attribute in addition to `.name` and keep `.name` and `.header['EXTNAME']` as well as `.ver` and `.header['EXTVER']` fully synchronized (see https://trac.assembla.com/pyfits/ticket/185) Should also add support for the EXTLEVEL keyword and a `.level` attribute.
- [ ] Relatedly, detect when HDUs in the same HDUList have an identical EXTNAME/EXTVER/EXTLEVEL combination.  Although the FITS standard does not forbid this but does, for obvious reasons, recommend that they be unique. So when they're not unique this should at least produce a warning.  This will be easier to tackle when #14 is implemented.
- [ ] Streamline handling of mandatory/reserved keywords on standard HDU types.  Each HDU type should have perhaps as one or more class-level attributes a set of all its reserved keywords and specify the constraints on those keywords.  This would be similar to what is already specified in each HDU type's `._verify` but made more declarative.
- [ ] It might be nice if all valid HDUs had a `.dtype` attribute returning Numpy `dtype` object specifying what the type of the data array would be even if the data hasn't been read (this might also allow an iterable of dtypes to support tables though it's not clear yet whether or not multi-field dtypes will be sufficient for this purpose)
