title: `table_to_hdu` warns about reserved keywords 'NAXIS', 'NAXIS1', but does not ignore them
description:
### Description
When converting a table with existing keys with reserved keywords in `table.meta`, `table_to_hdu` duly warns
`Meta-data keyword NAXIS1 will be ignored since it conflicts with a FITS reserved keyword`
but does not in fact ignore or update them to the correct values.
### Expected behavior
E.g. on writing such a table, the header should be written with the correct dimensions, but instead
```
>>> spec = Table([np.arange(5.), np.ones(5)], names=['wave', 'flux'], meta={'NAXIS1': 42, 'EXPTIME': 80.0})
>>> spec.write('table.fits', format='fits', overwrite=True)
WARNING: Meta-data keyword NAXIS1 will be ignored since it conflicts with a FITS reserved keyword [astropy.io.fits.convenience]
>>> fits.open('table.fits')[1].header
XTENSION= 'BINTABLE'           / binary table extension                         
BITPIX  =                    8 / array data type                                
NAXIS   =                    2 / number of array dimensions                     
NAXIS1  =                   42 / length of dimension 1                          
NAXIS2  =                    5 / length of dimension 2                          
PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of group parameters                     
GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups                               
TFIELDS =                    2 / number of table fields                         
TTYPE1  = 'wave    '                                                            
TFORM1  = 'D       '                                                            
TTYPE2  = 'flux    '                                                            
TFORM2  = 'D       '                                                            
EXPTIME =                 80.0
```
Similarly, a conflicting `NAXIS = 1` key gives a warning, but in this case fails the final verification before writing the file:
```
astropy.io.fits.verify.VerifyError: 
Verification reported errors:
HDU 1:
    NAXISj keyword out of range ('NAXIS2' when NAXIS == 1)
    'PCOUNT' card at the wrong place (card 5).
    'GCOUNT' card at the wrong place (card 6).
    'NAXIS' card has invalid value '1'.
```
whereas `NAXIS2` is replaced with the correct table dimension; so this seems to be updated at a later point.

It appears that the responsible block in
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/io/fits/convenience.py#L564
```
    for key, value in table.meta.items():
        if is_column_keyword(key.upper()) or key.upper() in REMOVE_KEYWORDS:
            warnings.warn(
                "Meta-data keyword {} will be ignored since it conflicts "
                "with a FITS reserved keyword".format(key), AstropyUserWarning)
```
may just be missing a `continue` after the warning...

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
`astropy.__init__._check_numpy()` is supposed to check for a compatible version of numpy, but it gives a misleading error message if numpy isn't installed at all.  This is not impossible: it can happen that numpy & astropy are installed, then numpy is removed.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
I would expect `_check_numpy()` to actually raise the `ImportError`  from `import numpy` instead of `pass`ing on that error and raising a message that the *version* is incompatible.


### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
`raise ImportError("Numpy version {} or later must be installed to use "
               "Astropy".format(__minimum_numpy_version__)`

command. -->

### Description
Plotting a figure to a WCSAxes when `CDELT1` != `CDELT2` results in a 1:1 aspect ratio for the pixes, but *not* a 1:1 aspect ratio in 'coordinate space'. I think it should by default set a 1:1 aspect ratio in coordinate space (ie. stretch the pixels in one direction), or at least it should be documented how to achieve this effect.

### Actual behavior
The second image with the code below (with `CDELT1` = 2`CDELT2`) is shown here. Note that the axes labels are correct, but the aspect ratio is no longer 1:1, as 30' on the x-axis is the same distance as 15' on the y-axis.
![Unknown-2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6197628/67082215-917d3f80-f190-11e9-9bc8-a358ee71ee0c.png)

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from astropy.wcs import WCS
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.utils.data import get_pkg_data_filename

filename = get_pkg_data_filename('galactic_center/gc_msx_e.fits')

hdu = fits.open(filename)[0]
header = hdu.header
wcs = WCS(header)

plt.figure()
plt.subplot(projection=wcs)
plt.imshow(hdu.data, vmin=-2.e-5, vmax=2.e-4, origin='lower')

# Scale one of the axes by a factor of 2
header['CDELT1'] = header['CDELT1'] * 2
wcs = WCS(header)
plt.figure()
plt.subplot(projection=wcs)
plt.imshow(hdu.data, vmin=-2.e-5, vmax=2.e-4, origin='lower')

```

description:

If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

At the time of writing, http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/modeling/add-units.html#fitting and the actual implementations of `_parameter_units_for_data_units` all use `OrderedDict`. Example from `Gaussian1D`:
```python
def _parameter_units_for_data_units(self, inputs_unit, outputs_unit):
    return OrderedDict([('mean', inputs_unit['x']),
                        ('stddev', inputs_unit['x']),
                        ('amplitude', outputs_unit['y'])])
```

Since Python 3.6, `dict` is already insertion-ordered. In addition, I don't see how the order could/should affect the results.

Furthermore, if your model only has one parameter anyway, you definitely don't need `OrderedDict`, as the ordered and unordered results would be the same.

### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

I asked about this on Slack and @nden seemed to agree but @astrofrog did not have time to investigate. So I decided to open an issue so we can revisit this in the future.

title: Support IAU 1976 ellipsoid for geodetic coordinates
Allow formatting of Time using __format__ or to_string
description: This would partially address also formatting in Table - see #7902.  The big question for `__format__` is how to deal with a combination of multiple possible formats, both string and numeric, the meaning of precision, etc. Also, should it work only for scalars, or also for arrays? title: USNO IERS services going down for 6 months (SOLVED: Upgrade astropy)
description:
There's a big red warning on both http://maia.usno.navy.mil/ and http://toshi.nofs.navy.mil/ saying that they will be down for maintenance from Oct. 24 2019 until April 30 2020 (6 months!).

I'm not sure if there are other sites that will serve the files astropy relies on, but I believe that these two are the only ones astropy currently looks at.

The astropy functionality that depends on the availability of these IERS tables is mission critical for several telescopes so I think we need some ways to handle this.

### Description
While working on issue #8995 I wondered whether there is sufficient test coverage for the binary (FITS, BINARY and BINARY2) serializations.  The non-binary serialization (TABLEDATA) tests seem to have good coverage.  I would like to look at whether those tests should be replicated for the binary cases, or whether the existing tests of the converters are sufficient to show that the various data types and shapes (array values) are being handled consistently across the different serializations.

In addition, PR #9505 made it clear that we could be more complete in covering the subtle aspects of VOTable format and semantics.  This is important because some aspects of the VOTable spec are subject to interpretation, and more test cases could demonstrate the understanding or assumptions that were made in the implementation.

title: Distribution.pdf_* methods should be functions, not properties
description:
@eteq - while looking at the code again, I noticed that things like `.pdf_mean` are properties, not methods. I think this is a mistake, as it is too different from `.mean()` and `.std()`, etc. In general, I'd use methods if real calculations are being done, and in this case I also wonder if we shouldn't be a bit more future-proof by at least in principle allowing extension with arguments (even if just an `out` argument, or for `pdf_std` to pass on `ddof` to the underlying `ndarray` method).

My sense is that we should still change this - since `uncertainty` is not used that much yet, it is probably the last change we have...

title: Issues with the default value for `clip` in `ImageNormalize`
description:
The [documentation for `ImageNormalize`](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.visualization.mpl_normalize.ImageNormalize.html) is confusing because it provides conflicting information about the default value for `clip` (which is True).  The call string and the parameter list correctly note that the default is True, but the text below that, which looks to be copied from Matplotlib's `Normalize`, states that the default is False because it otherwise "silently defeats" other functionality and "is likely to lead to surprises".

I agree with the sentiment the default should be `clip=False`.  I'll note that this was changed in #7800 due to a different inconsistency in the claimed defaults, but there may have been insufficient discussion about what the default ought to be.

Even if the consensus is that the default should be `clip=True`, the documentation still needs to be made consistent.  I'm not clear how the Matplotlib text is being pulled into the documentation.

title: Decision for some __array_function__ overrides
description:
Separating some things out of #8825, since these are important to decide upon before 4.0, since after we cannot seriously change it any more: for a number of numpy functions, a decision still needs to be made, mostly on whether to stick exactly to the numpy docstring or to make adjustments to parameter defaults that make the function more useful for `Quantity`
- [ ] `np.isclose`, `np.allclose`: these were never all that useful since internally they calculate `abs(a - b) < atol + rtol * abs(a)` and `atol` is given as a small number, which is interpreted as dimensionless. For `Quantity`, we could either set it to `0` or assume the units of `a`, but in either case it would become inconsistent with the docstring that users actually see.
- [ ] `np.broadcast_arrays` and `np.broadcast_to` by default return plain arrays, needing `subok=True` to work for `Quantity`. We could change the default if a `Quantity` is present. Again, the possible issue is that the docstring will no longer be correct.

My own sense is to adjust `isclose` and `allclose`, since that allows things to "just work". But the question is how (0 or small number times unit of first).

For `broadcast*`, though, I think there may be code relying on it always returning plain `ndarray`, so probably it is best not to change the default.

cc @adrn

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

To create a cython version of `biweight_midcorrelation` because the current implementation is very slow.  For example, `pandas` has `nancorr` and `nancorr_spearman` which are EXTREMELY fast compared to the normal pairwise iterations that could be done using `scipy`.

Would it be possible to add this functionality to `astropy`? Currently, I am unable to use this robust metric for my actual datasets that are quite large.  I can only use this for test datasets because it takes very long. 


### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

Here's an example of the `nancorr` function implemented in cython: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/master/pandas/_libs/algos.pyx

```python
# Pairwise correlation/covariance


@cython.boundscheck(False)
@cython.wraparound(False)
def nancorr(const float64_t[:, :] mat, bint cov=0, minp=None):
    cdef:
        Py_ssize_t i, j, xi, yi, N, K
        bint minpv
        ndarray[float64_t, ndim=2] result
        ndarray[uint8_t, ndim=2] mask
        int64_t nobs = 0
        float64_t vx, vy, sumx, sumy, sumxx, sumyy, meanx, meany, divisor

    N, K = (<object>mat).shape

    if minp is None:
        minpv = 1
    else:
        minpv = <int>minp

    result = np.empty((K, K), dtype=np.float64)
    mask = np.isfinite(mat).view(np.uint8)

    with nogil:
        for xi in range(K):
            for yi in range(xi + 1):
                nobs = sumxx = sumyy = sumx = sumy = 0
                for i in range(N):
                    if mask[i, xi] and mask[i, yi]:
                        vx = mat[i, xi]
                        vy = mat[i, yi]
                        nobs += 1
                        sumx += vx
                        sumy += vy

                if nobs < minpv:
                    result[xi, yi] = result[yi, xi] = NaN
                else:
                    meanx = sumx / nobs
                    meany = sumy / nobs

                    # now the cov numerator
                    sumx = 0

                    for i in range(N):
                        if mask[i, xi] and mask[i, yi]:
                            vx = mat[i, xi] - meanx
                            vy = mat[i, yi] - meany

                            sumx += vx * vy
                            sumxx += vx * vx
                            sumyy += vy * vy

                    divisor = (nobs - 1.0) if cov else sqrt(sumxx * sumyy)

                    if divisor != 0:
                        result[xi, yi] = result[yi, xi] = sumx / divisor
                    else:
                        result[xi, yi] = result[yi, xi] = NaN

    return result
```

title: Ordering of leap second update can lead to import warnings
description:
After #9365 was merged, @taldcroft [noticed](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9365#issuecomment-546683559) that "In a clean build of master right now I'm seeing this:"
```
In [1]: from astropy.io import ascii
WARNING: leap-second auto-update failed due to the following exception: ImportError("cannot import name 'convert_numpy'",) [astropy.time.core]
```
???

Clearly, import order is important in ways it shouldn't be.  I'll investigate but suggestions would be most welcome...

EDIT: reason it is tricky: many of the most common time formats need an up-to-date leap-second table (e.g., `Time.now()` uses `TimeDatetime`, which, like `TimeISO*` calls `erfa.dtf2d`, which needs leap second information. But the `LeapSecond` class subclasses `QTable`, so needs to import `astropy.table`. `Table` itself only imports `Time` locally, so is safe, but some parts of `io.ascii` import `Time` on top and therefore are not.

Possible solutions:
1. Make `LeapSeconds` a class independent of `Table` - which means also moving it out of `iers`. That means parsing the files outside of `io.ascii` and having very IERS-like configuration elsewhere; this seems a horrible duplication of work.
2. Ensure `Time` is imported only locally in `io`. But it seems rather annoying not to be able to count on being able to import such a fundamental class.
3. Ensure `erfa` is imported only locally in `Time`, `iers`, etc., and move the update back there. More than a little annoying, since used a *lot* in `time.formats`. Also, is a very basic package that should just be importable (and is not currently causing the problems).
4. Ensure the leap-second update is only done on first *use* of `Time`.

Option (4) may be the best. Should I do this with something in `Time.__new__`?

cc @taldcroft, @eteq

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
After converting the unit of a `MaskedColumn` with `convert_unit_to`, subsequent manipulations of the column use the old unit.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
The new unit should be used with the converted values. E.g. if after conversion from km to m the value is 300 m, then 300 m * 2 = 600 m

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
The old unit was used with the converted value. E.g. if after conversion from km to m the value is 300 m, then multiplying by 2 results in 300 m * 2 = 600 km.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use tripe backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

Example triggering the bug:
```python
>>> from astropy.table import MaskedColumn
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> c = MaskedColumn([3.5,2.4,1.7], name='test', unit=u.km)
>>> c
<MaskedColumn name='test' dtype='float64' unit='km' length=3>
3.5
2.4
1.7
>>> c.convert_unit_to(u.m)
>>> c
<MaskedColumn name='test' dtype='float64' unit='m' length=3>
3500.0
2400.0
1700.0
>>> # all looks fine up to this point, now for the bug...
>>> c*2.0
<MaskedColumn name='test' dtype='float64' unit='km' length=3>
7000.0
4800.0
3400.0
>>> # unit should be 'm' not 'km'
```

This does not occur with `Column`:

```python
>>> from astropy.table import Column
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> c = Column([3.5,2.4,1.7], name='test', unit=u.km)
>>> c.convert_unit_to(u.m)
>>> c
<Column name='test' dtype='float64' unit='m' length=3>
3500.0
2400.0
1700.0
>>> c*2.0
<Column name='test' dtype='float64' unit='m' length=3>
7000.0
4800.0
3400.0
```

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

Upon construction, all Time objects contain two double-precision values, `jd1` and `jd2`. These satisfy, and are tested to satisfy, the invariant that `jd1` is an integer, `abs(jd2)<=0.5`, and if `abs(jd2)==0.5` then `jd1` is even. This is enforced by application of the not-publicly-documented function `day_frac`. 

When a Time object is converted from one timescale to another, though, under some circumstances `abs(jd2)>0.5`. 

```python
>>> from astropy.time import Time
>>> t = Time(2441316.5, 0, scale='tai', format='jd')
>>> t.tcb.jd2
0.500344155968967
```

This was revealed by #9532 .

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

`t.tcb.jd2` should be made less than 0.5 by calling `day_frac`.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

The value violates the invariant.

title: Add alternate constellation names / boundaries
description:
The constellation names and data we have in astropy.coordinates are derived from [this vizier page](http://vizier.u-strasbg.fr/vizier/VizieR/constellations.htx) and [Roman 1987](http://cdsarc.u-strasbg.fr/viz-bin/Cat?VI/42), however, there are some spelling differences between these names and, e.g., the [list maintained on the IAU site](https://www.iau.org/public/themes/constellations/), which references [Davenhall 1989](http://vizier.cfa.harvard.edu/viz-bin/VizieR-3?-source=VI/49/bound_20) (contains its own list of constellation boundaries). For example, in our constellation data it is "Ophiucus" but the IAU page spells it as "Ophiuchus". Should we default to the IAU list? Should we support both? 

cc @eteq

In [4]: t = Time([1, 2, 3], format='jyear', scale='tai')                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         

In [5]: t.argsort()                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
WARNING: ErfaWarning: ERFA function "utctai" yielded 3 of "dubious year (Note 3)" [astropy._erfa.core]
Out[5]: array([0, 1, 2])
```

This seems unnecessary, and is the source of many warnings in e.g. the table tests (in particular relating to indexing). Even for end users, this kind of warning is confusing since it is not needed and also not clear how to solve.

title: Consider changing `sort()` to not update columns in-place
description:
From #9536.

The current Table behavior was based on how numpy behaves both with respect to sorting a single array in place and sorting a structured array (with tbl.sort(order='sort_col')). In the latter case in particular a ref to a column is not lost during the sort operation.

My guess was that pandas would do the same, but I just tried df.sort_values('sort_col', inplace=True) and found that it does indeed make new column references.

So there is not an unambiguous precedent, though numpy and astropy Table have historically kept references. BTW, for Table it used to be the case that replacing a column in the table was slow, but no longer.

One thing I that I just appreciated is that take is actually make a deep copy of all the info attributes (e.g. meta). From that perspective we are already paying for a full independent copy of the Column or mixin, so maybe just using the new column always is better?

This would be a real API change.

### Description

In principle, `ccache` could dramatically speed up compilation of C code for very little extra effort - provided that its cache survived between runs. The Travis builds do persist the build, but do not actually use `ccache` in any compilation (so the persisted cache is empty). 

### Expected behavior

Examine the Travis logs for a run. It will have a fold-away button marked `ccache` on the right side, but when unfolded the button reveals nothing was done.

title: Persist astropy cache
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md .
Please be sure to check out our code of conduct,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . -->

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

When `astropy`  downloads remote files, it can store them in a global cache; it can then avoid re-downloading them unless explicitly requested. For normal use this cache persists between astropy runs and can save time and load on remote servers (only some of which are associated with Astropy).

Currently when we run the test suite, we run the entire thing with the cache in a temporary location, so all remote files must be re-downloaded for every test run. For testing `astropy.utils.data`, which actually implements the caching mechanism, as of #9182 this is unnecessary, as it uses its own temporary caches for tests where they matter. For any other tests that require remote data, we simply don't run them unless explicitly requested by the user; if the user does request them, all files are re-downloaded every time. 

I suggest that `astropy` *not* reset its cache to point somewhere temporary on every run. This will not affect `astropy.utils.data`, whose test suite demonstrates that `astropy`'s caching and downloading mechanisms work correctly. All other tests that require remote data can then be set (by adding flags to their `download_file` calls) to:

1. use cached data if available, not touching the server at all in this case,
2. never use the cache because the requested data is different every time, or
3. update the data in the cache if it is excessively old.

This will immediately improve the user experience when running `astropy` with `--remote-data=astropy` or `--remote-data=any`. Travis jobs that require remote data can then also be set to persist the Astropy cache, making them both more reliable and faster (for all tests in categories 1 and 3).

This will have the additional advantage that running the `astropy` test suite will populate the user's cache with things like the IERS tables; they can use this as a first pass at preparing for disconnected operation. 

It is probably a good idea to add testing flags to use a temporary cache or to clear the cache (instead of running tests) so that users can easily cope with strange behaviour that comes about if cached files are changed online (though currently users simply stumble over such situations without guidance in normal operation). 

One early step of any PR would be to note the volume the cache was populated with after a full `--remote-data=any` run, which would help decide whether keeping the cache around was a good idea.

title: Decide if it's acceptable to add the User-Agent:astropy and Accept:*/* headers into file download functions
description:
This is a follow-on from #9508, with more details in: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9508#discussion_r343211648 and https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9508#pullrequestreview-311403515

Short version: we should decide if we want to have `User-Agent:astropy` and `Accept:*/*` in the request headers for *all* uses of `download_file`/`get_readable_fileobj`, or just the IERS (where it is known to be necessary). As of #9508, no change is necessary for the "all" case, so we can close this without PR if agreement is to stick with that.

Relevant text from the HTTP/1.1 spec: is here: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2616#section-14.43 - "User agents SHOULD include this field with requests." The example shown includes a string "libwww" that suggests to me that it is reasonable practice for this header to include "library" information in the header.  So I conclude from this that it the spec is recommending we do things as-is.

cc @pllim @aarchiba @adrn

title: Use sources keyword of download_file in IERS
description:
I'm not entirely sure if this should be milestoned 4.0, but since it came out of #9508 I thought that was a safer bet.

The gist is: #9508 was merged (or hopefully will be soon...) without using the ``sources`` keyword introduced in #9182, to get master working again.  But the IERS machinery should be re-worked to use ``sources`` since that should be more robust.

cc @pllim @aarchiba @adrn

title: Change table.cstack to table.dstack before 4.0?
description:
`Table.cstack()` is short for depth-wise stacking, by analogy to `vstack` and `hstack`.  I don't quite remember why it got named `cstack` instead of `dstack`.  I think that `table.cstack` is conceptually similar to `np.dstack` : "Stack arrays in sequence depth wise (along third axis)."

Before the 4.0 release can we just change this?

title: No way to silence Bayesian Blocks warning when computing histogram
description:
There is no way to silence the following warning (without just filtering it with the warnings module):

```
In [4]: from astropy.stats import histogram                                                                    

In [5]: histogram([1, 2, 3], bins='blocks')                                                                    
WARNING: p0 does not seem to accurately represent the false positive rate for event data. It is highly recommended that you run random trials on signal-free noise to calibrate ncp_prior to achieve a desired false positive rate. [astropy.stats.bayesian_blocks]
Out[5]: (array([3]), array([1., 3.]))
```

This warning is due to the following code in the bayesian blocks implementation:

```
    def __init__(self, p0=0.05, gamma=None, ncp_prior=None):
        if p0 is not None and gamma is None and ncp_prior is None:
            warnings.warn('p0 does not seem to accurately represent the false '
                          'positive rate for event data. It is highly '
                          'recommended that you run random trials on signal-'
                          'free noise to calibrate ncp_prior to achieve a '
                          'desired false positive rate.', AstropyUserWarning)
        super().__init__(p0, gamma, ncp_prior)
```

By default p0 is set and if p0 is set and the other arguments aren't, the warning is emitted. The ``histogram`` function provides no way to set these parameters, resulting in the warning.

In https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/4927#issuecomment-311650474, @jakevdp mentioned it might make sense to just remove the warning and describe this in the docs instead. I'm going to also cc @Quantum-cross as the original author of this warning (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/commit/969446239709f539ce878e6e9e5be5a4ad3c03c8). Any suggestions on the best way to proceed?

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
Per the documentation at http://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.wcs.WCS.html#astropy.wcs.WCS.to_header
it seems like astropy wcs does not write out PC matrix header keywords when they differ from the unit matrix.

This can sometimes cause undesirable behaviour when reading in FITS files produced with astropy using other languages.  The well-established extast.pro routine (part of the Goddard IDL library) for instance assumes a default value of zero for non-specified keywords.  Since this has been the cornerstone of FITS WCS in IDL for many years it is integral to many data pipelines (e.g., SDSS MaNGA/eBOSS).

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

Given a FITS file produced by astropy I would expect full WCS information to be attached in an unambiguous manner (i.e., not skipping keywords) such that they can be properly interpreted by other standard FITS libraries.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

Given a FITS file with CRPIX values outside the actual image footprint, and a PC matrix in which only PC1_1=-1 is provided, astropy routines assume that PC2_2=1 and correctly compute the RA/DEC values for any given pixel.  IDL libraries however assume that PC2_2=0 and can return RA/DEC values that are in error by a degree or more.  Simply adding PC2_2=1 to the header keywords completely fixes the issue.

title: pep8 line length
description:
The *recommended* line length in pep8 (https://pep8.org/#maximum-line-length) of 79 characters is not respected consistently in Astropy, depending on the sub-packages and their original authors. This is slightly annoying when using flake8 in your preferred editor.

The trendy formatting tool *Black* defaults to 88 characters per line, and I was curious to see how many of the flake8 errors it would solve in Astropy. (https://github.com/psf/black#line-length)
Having used Black for some time, increasing the line length from 80 to 88 is often a good way to avoid splitting lines, and is also a good compromise to not have too long lines.

So I made this ([code](https://gist.github.com/saimn/4c4018e1b11ae913d5e4195cdba1d6d0)):
![Figure_1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/311639/68521227-bccde880-027d-11ea-93d7-c2888db6ac78.png)

Increasing to 88 chars would remove 72% of the flake8 errors, and would then make it possible to fix the other lines to respect this rule and have a more consistent coding style :).

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

Although python's datetime objects support microsecond resolution, and Time objects support sub-nanosecond resolution, conversion and arithmetic between the two can be off by tens of microseconds. (By design datetime objects do not support leap seconds, so UTC cannot be expected to work. The problems described here are for non-UTC timescales like TAI.) 

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

Computing the difference between two datetime objects then converting to a TimeDelta should give the same result as converting the datetime objects to Time objects and subtracting, to within a couple of microseconds.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->

In fact PR #9532 demonstrates several examples where the difference exceeds 20 microseconds. 

### Steps to Reproduce
```python
def test_datetime_difference_agrees_with_timedelta_no_hypothesis():
    scale = "tai"
    dt1 = datetime(1235, 1, 1, 0, 0)
    dt2 = datetime(9950, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 890773)
    t1 = Time(dt1, scale=scale)
    t2 = Time(dt2, scale=scale)
    assert(abs((t2-t1) - TimeDelta(dt2-dt1, scale=scale)) < 25*u.us)

title: Use Sphinx ref links or URLs in docstrings?
description:
I noticed that there's some raw URL links pointing to http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable from class docstrings such as `astropy.table.Table`:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/e22110689b7bd95d7e674b720620e07b97d2d714/astropy/table/table.py#L338

or `astropy.uncertainty.Distribution`:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/297589cd9b3f087795803cd698d8410c46cac0eb/astropy/uncertainty/core.py#L30

This can be problematic, since it takes users to a different docs version, when reading an older docs version. Since Astropy isn't changing much, in practice it's probably OK, but it could happen that links break, and generally I think users will be surprised if docs version changes when clicking around in the docs.

Most other projects use Sphinx ref links to generate relative links in the HTML (or PDF if generated) within a given docs version. Example:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1495f69242646d239d89a5713982946b8ffcf9d9/sklearn/linear_model/ridge.py#L599

Should we change to relative links?
(I'm +1 to do that, and could send a PR if it's the way to go.)

Or was there a deliberate decision to put raw URLs to http://docs.astropy.org/en/stable ?
(there is the advantage that from the help docstring in `python`, `ipython`, `Jupyter` one can get the URL quickly)

title: Improve ERFA warnings about dubious years to give more user-friendly information
description:
As discussed in some other issues (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/9587#issuecomment-552538314; https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9593#discussion_r345521069) it would be good if ERFA warnings could be more user-friendly. For example, this tells me nothing much as a user:

```
WARNING: ErfaWarning: ERFA function "utctai" yielded 3 of "dubious year (Note 3)" [astropy._erfa.core]
```

A better warning would be:

```
WARNING: conversion between the utc and tai scales is may be inaccurate as dates in the utc scale outside of the range ... to ... are not well defined
```

In general whenever I get ERFA warnings I basically never really understand them and also don't know how to fix them. Clearer messages such as the above would really help in that regard.

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
In the documentation [here](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/io/fits/usage/headers.html#continue-cards) it notes that `CONTINUE` keywords are not part of the FITS specification, but are supported by Astropy. This is no longer true; the proposal is now officially part of the 4.0 standard. For details, see Section 4.2.1.2 of [the specification](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/fits_standard.html).

As noted in the docs, the convention is supported in Astropy, but it would be nice to update them to reflect that it is part of the format.

I also recently encountered a `fits.VerifyError` warning, saying that the`CONTINUE` keyword is invalid and it was inserting a missing "=" character (which is not present with the `CONTINUE` keyword), but I can't find it in the source so maybe that has been removed.

### Description

In #6028 it became possible to initialize Time objects using masked arrays to represent missing data. There's a hitch that occurs though when you try to change the format of a Time object which contains missing data. This hiccup was encountered while tackling astropy/astroplan#398.

### Expected behavior

```python
from astropy.time import Time
import numpy as np

jd = [np.nan]

title: Failure of unicode sandwich for multi-dimensional columns
description:
We allow comparisons of unicode with byte-valued columns using a unicode sandwich, but this fails in the corner-case where the column is multidimensional and we take a single element from it:
```
from astropy.table import Column
c = Column([[b'a', b'b'], [b'c', b'd']], name='c')
print(c == ['a', 'b'])
# [[ True  True]
#  [False False]]
print(c[0] == ['a', 'b'])
# False  # expected [True, True]
```
EDIT (2024-01-11): now gives `[False, False]` so still an issue.

The reason is that for multi-D columns, access of any given `Column` row just returns a plain `ndarray`, which does not know about the unicode sandwich: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/table/_column_mixins.pyx#L54-L55

A fix might be to convert the result to unicode or to use an `ndarray` subclass that still contains the unicode sandwich (but is otherwise a plain `ndarray`).

cc @taldcroft

p.s. Found while trying a new `Masked` class for creating a new `MaskedColumn`.

command. -->



### Description
Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona is on Mountain Standard Time. However, unlike the standard US convention, it does not follow Daylight Savings Time. Therefore, the UTC Offset for the observatory remains constant at -7 hours throughout the year, and it does not oscillate back and forth twice a year due to  historical idiosyncrasies. 


### Expected behavior
The UTC offset is -7 throughout the year, therefore it is Mountain Standard Time in the winter months, and on Pacific Time in the summer.


### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use tripe backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

```python
from astropy.coordinates import EarthLocation
from astropy.time import Time
import datetime
import pytz

location = EarthLocation.of_site('KPNO')
timezone = location.info.meta['timezone'] # The output of this is 'US/Mountain' which is technically correct, if not for the fact that there is this sub-zone of regions within this timezone which remains fixed w.r.t to UTC and does not follow the Daylight Saving sham. 

print('December offset = {}'.format(pytz.timezone(timezone).localize(Time('2019-12-1').datetime).strftime('%z'))) #This outputs -7 hrs which is correct
print('April offset = {}'.format(pytz.timezone(timezone).localize(Time('2020-04-1').datetime).strftime('%z'))) #This outputs -6 hrs which is incorrect
```

title: Incorrect derivative in Defining New Model Classes documentation
description:
Hi, maybe I am missing something, but I believe the 'Defining New Model Classes' example (https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/modeling/new.html) in the documentation has the incorrect derivatives for the 1DGaussian function. This comes under the section 'A step by step definition of a 1-D Gaussian model'.

 For the Gaussian defined as:

amplitude * np.exp((-(1 / (2. * stddev**2)) * (x - mean)**2))

The derivatives should be:

d_amplitude = np.exp((-(1 / (2.*****stddev**2)) * (x - mean)**2))
d_mean = (amplitude *
              np.exp((-(1 / (2.*stddev**2)) * (x - mean)**2)) *
              (x - mean) / (stddev**2))
d_stddev = (amplitude *
                np.exp((-(1 / (2.* stddev**2)) * (x - mean)**2)) *
                ((x - mean)**2) / (stddev**3))

In the online example, the factor of 2 multiplying stddev inside the exponential is missing - for all derivatives. And the factor of two multiplying the amplitude (in d_mean and d_stddev) should not be there. Online version is:

d_amplitude = np.exp((-(1 / (stddev**2)) * (x - mean)**2))

d_mean = (2 * amplitude *
              np.exp((-(1 / (stddev**2)) * (x - mean)**2)) *
              (x - mean) / (stddev**2))

d_stddev = (2 * amplitude *
                np.exp((-(1 / (stddev**2)) * (x - mean)**2)) *
                ((x - mean)**2) / (stddev**3))

### Description
I'm running astropy on an offline computer.  I need the added accuracy that the de430 ephemerides provide, and so at the beginning of the utility, I call
```python
astropy.coordinates.solar_system_ephemeris.set('file://path/to/local/copy/de430.bsp')
```

Sometimes, I'm in a hurry to get things done, and so I'll fire off multiple copies of my utility from the shell (use moar cores!), and the processes will often (but not always) will decide that the file is out of date and start copying it ("downloading") from the path above into /tmp, start fighting over the lock for the cache directory, then barf, etc.  I end up with most of my runs failed, a /tmp directory full of abandoned files, and a bunch of frustration.

I have discovered that if I set XDG_CACHE_HOME to a directory that is mounted locally (/tmp is my only option) instead of through NFS, I can no longer trigger the bug.  I assume that the lock is assuming file existence is atomic, near as I can tell NFS only guarantees directory creation to be an atomic operation.

### Expected behavior
I expected the file to be "downloaded" at most once and everyone else to wait their turn.
I would prefer that there were a way to disable downloading/caching entirely (perhaps similar to how the IERS util in astropy allows pointing at a local finals2000a.all)

### Actual behavior
```bash
   File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/astropy/coordinates/solar_system.py", line 175, in _get_kernel
    return SPK.open(download_file(value, cache=True))
  File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/astropy/utils/data.py", line 1122, in download_file                   _acquire_download_cache_lock()
  File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/astropy/utils/data.py", line 1405, in _acquire_download_cache_lock
    raise RuntimeError(msg.format(lockdir))
RuntimeError: Unable to acquire lock for cache directory (/home/mcbeth/Sites/astropy/download/py2/lock exists). You may need to delete the lock if the python interpreter wasn't shut down properly.
```

### Steps to Reproduce
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

import astropy.coordinates as coords
from astropy.time import Time

coords.solar_system_ephemeris.set('file:///home/mcbeth/astropy_caching/de430.bsp')
print(coords.get_sun(Time.now()))
```

The issue is that when I build a datalink object from that votable:

`datalink = vo.dal.adhoc.DatalinkResults.from_result_url(url)`

I get a warning:

``` 
WARNING: W35: None:6:6: W35: 'value' attribute required for INFO elements [astropy.io.votable.tree]

That warning is incorrect, as it is true that the INFO element in a votable requires the value attribute to be present, but nowhere in the VOTable specs is written that the value attribute cannot be an empty string.

title: Inconsistency behavior in APE14 WCS API implementations
description:
### Description
This issue encompasses a few problems that have cropped up when interfacing with the WCS API wrapper classes (and presumably the APE14 API implementations in GWCS and FITS WCS).

The first issue is in pixel to world values transformation for a sliced wcs (e.g. a wcs wrapped with `SlicedLowLevelWCS` object:

```
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-7-ccda0c3ea9df> in <module>
----> 1 print(arr_sliced.wcs.pixel_to_world([1, 2]))

~/projects/astropy/astropy/wcs/wcsapi/high_level_api.py in pixel_to_world(self, *pixel_arrays)
    213 
    214         # Compute the world coordinate values
--> 215         world = self.low_level_wcs.pixel_to_world_values(*pixel_arrays)
    216 
    217         if self.world_n_dim == 1:

~/projects/astropy/astropy/wcs/wcsapi/sliced_low_level_wcs.py in pixel_to_world_values(self, *pixel_arrays)
    160                 ipix_curr += 1
    161                 if self._slices_pixel[ipix].start is not None:
--> 162                     pixel_arrays_new.append(pixel_arrays[ipix_curr] + self._slices_pixel[ipix].start)
    163                 else:
    164                     pixel_arrays_new.append(pixel_arrays[ipix_curr])

TypeError: can only concatenate list (not "int") to list
```

It looks to be that it tries to concatenate a `list` and `int` when the pixel values are not passed as an ndarray. Replacing line 162 with

```
pixel_arrays_new.append(list(np.array(pixel_arrays[ipix_curr]) + self._slices_pixel[ipix].start))
```

fixes this issue (presuming that we would want to add the start of slice as an offset to the pixel values).

The second and third problems are a bit more nuanced and have to do with the implementation of `pixel_to_world_values` in GWCS and FITS WCS.

The `pixel_to_world_values` on a gwcs and fits wcs object return different things. For gwcs, it returns a list with a single ndarray containing the world values (e.g. `[array([1, 2])]`), while in fits wcs, it returns just the ndarray (e.g. `array([1, 2])`). This seems to be important because when `SlicedLowLevelWCS` is initialized the pixel dimensions (and world dimensions) to be kept are calculated based on the correlation matrices. In the case of a 1d array wcs, it's just the 0th dimension. This `world_keep` value is applied to the return value of the `pixel_to_world_values` call; in the gwcs case, it correctly gets `array([1, 2])`, but for fits wcs, it returns 1.
Relatedly, applying the index for the kept pixel dimension is done inside a list comprehension, meaning that for gwcs the final returned world values are `[[1, 2]]`. For fits, this means `[1]`.

### Expected behavior
Sliced wcs objects behave consistently.

### Actual behavior
Sliced wcs objects do not behave consistently.

### Steps to Reproduce

The comparison between the gwcs and fits wcs behaviors is demonstrated in this [notebook](https://gist.github.com/nmearl/6ff8b2a239fa017b70bdcd2053b3248d).

### System Details

Python 3.7.0 (default, Jun 28 2018, 07:39:16)
[Clang 4.0.1 (tags/RELEASE_401/final)]
Numpy 1.17.4

description:
That is a problem specific for those who use the system's library for erfa: The version in astropy incorporates liberfa/erfa#49, which is not merged or released yet. The function `eraSetLeapSeconds()` is then used in `_erfa/ufunc.c` and causes a build failure:
```
astropy/_erfa/ufunc.c: In function ‘get_leap_seconds’:

      |     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~

 9719 |     count = (npy_intp)eraGetLeapSeconds(&leapseconds);
      |                       ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
astropy/_erfa/ufunc.c:9733:59: error: ‘eraLEAPSECOND’ undeclared (first use in this function); did you mean ‘dt_eraLEAPSECOND’?
 9733 |     memcpy(PyArray_DATA(array), leapseconds, count*sizeof(eraLEAPSECOND));
      |                                                           ^~~~~~~~~~~~~
      |                                                           dt_eraLEAPSECOND

description:

issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

There seems to be no easy way to determine which parameters are connected to which by introspection on a model. That is because the parameter **tied** is  a dictionary of `{parameter_name: callable}`. So on introspection, all we know is that the parameter is tied to another. We don't know which one and how. This is okay if it's your own home-built compound model, but it's a problem if it's a compound model that someone else has provided.

It might be too big a change to fix this universally, but a partial solution could be to 
create a helper class or set of helper classes and then encourage in the documentation that people use it when linking parameters together. I could imagine a base class, e.g. `TiedParameters` that keeps track of the names of the parameters. Then subclasses like `MultiplicativeTiedParameters` would have their own `__call__` and `__init__` methods to take in the multiplicative factor and apply it. So instead of writing your own custom function as now shown in the documentation, a user would link two parameters by a multiplicative factor by instantiating the class: 

``` 
my_tie = MultiplicativeTiedParameters(model,parameter_name_1,parameter_name_2,factor)
```

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

On arm64/aarch64 (essentially alternative names for the same ABI, one of two implemented on the 64-bit ARM CPUs in modern phones and Raspberry PIs) double precision calculations do not have access to the hidden extra 16 bits that they do on Intel machines, and long double is actually quadruple precision, alas implemented in software. As a result a number of floating-point differences arise, chiefly when using Time to push the limits of available precision. (In fact np.longdouble here has more precision than Time.) PR #9407 will add arm64 tests to CI but unfortunately amr64 support on Travis and on PyPI is limited (no compiled wheels for anything, no conda) so that can't be implemented yet. But some arm64 machines are affordable, so I ran our test suite and uncovered a number of problems, mostly in  the test suite.

A few of the errors below are our usual test failures when run with remote data, a few are tests that assume long doubles are less precise than Time, a few result from different float error handling, but I've included everything because it wasn't clear to me which was which or whether there was another category.

title: "output_verify" option forced to "exception" when using fits.open() in a "with" block
description:
### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
Astropy has different behavior when using the `fits.open()` command in the following two ways (which I expected to be equivalent):
```python
hdulist = fits.open('file_with_non_compliant_header_card.fits", "update") 
    # make some changes and flush the results with: 
    hdulist.flush(output_verify="warn")
hdulist.close(output_verify="warn")
```
```python
with fist.open('file_non_compliant_header_card.fits", "update") as hdulist:
    # make some changes and flush the results with:
    hdulist.flush(output_verify="warn")
```
### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
In both cases, I expected Astropy to warn me about the non-compliant header card, but not raise an exception (as I don't care about the value of the card in question, and can't do anything about it since it's archival data).

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
The expected behavior works in the first code form, but not the second; in the second case, I got a warning as expected from `flush()`, but then astropy raised an exception (`astropy.io.fits.verify.VerifyError`) upon exiting the `with` block. (This also occurs when using the "ignore" option, without the warning obviously.)

I first found this bug in 3.2.3, as I'd been using the `file = fits.open`...`file.close()` form with explicit `output_verify='warn'`, and changed it to a `with` block, when I suddenly started getting the `VerifyError`s. The bug persisted in 4.1.dev27006 when I cloned the repo. 

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use tripe backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

I don't have specific steps to reproduce, but from looking at the code in `astropy/io/fits/hud/hdulist.py` I think I know why it's happening: the `HDUList.close` method takes an `output_verify` argument, but the `HDUList.__exit__` method which handles leaving a `with` block only calls `self.close` without any arguments. Thus, leaving a `with` block essentially calls `close` with its default `output_verify="exception"` argument, regardless of what the user may have used in the interim. This makes it impossible to use `with fits.open...` with a less restrictive `output_verify` option than 'exception'.

I don't think having 'exception' be the default when using a `with` block is bad, per se (errors should never pass silently, unless explicitly silenced!), it would just be nice to be able to change it. I'm not quite sure how to do so; perhaps having an optional `output_verify` argument to `HDUList.__init__` which could set some sort of instance-spcific `self._verify_level` attribute, the value of which could be passed by `__exit__` to the `close` method? Leave the default as 'exception' and the current behavior would still be the default, while also allowing the user to set whatever level of verification they want. I could try and take a stab at it myself to see if that would work.

### System Details

title: bzip2 fits append/update
description:
The [documentation of it.fits](https://docs.astropy.org/en/v3.2.3/io/fits/index.html#working-with-compressed-files) states that bzip2 does not support update/append. While the [`bz2` python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bz2.html) states that it's supported.

So we might investigate if we can add update/append for io.fits with bzip.

title: Make table's `Row` a mapping?
description: Right now, `Row` is registered as a `collections.abc.Sequence`, but arguably it makes more sense as a `Mapping`, since the way `__getitem__` is implemented is much more like a `dict`. Indeed, `Row` could gain `keys()`, `items()`, and `.values()` methods which would make it very similar to a `dict` (and allow "splatting" with `**row`). The only inconsistency might be in `Row.__iter__`, which currently iterates over values rather than keys.

title: visualization's norms should ignore nan by default
description:
astropy.visualization's norm operations break when given any NaN input by default.  It would be much more reasonable to have them ignore NaNs by default.

example:
```
x = np.random.randn(5,5)
x[2,2] = np.nan
logn = visualization.ImageNormalize(stretch=visualization.LogStretch(), interval=visualization.PercentileInterval(99.95))
bad = logn(x) # logn now has vmin, vmax = nan
```
The right approach would have vmin, vmax be determined using, e.g., `nanpercentile` instead of `percentile` under the hood.  Presumably this affects some (but I haven't checked if it hits all) interval & stretch measurers.  

This could be a lot of work and could have performance implications, but usually with visualization tools the stats aren't the bottleneck.

Up to someone else to evaluate whether this is a feature request or a bug report.  I suspect this should be a pretty easy fix, but I'd like to see discussion here about whether there are good reasons to avoid the `np.nan<stat>` methods.

### Description

We define a number of custom Frames for analysis of IACT data.
These are mostly intermediate steps between detector coordinates and `AltAz`.
These frames have attributes like `obstime`, `focal_length` and `pointing_direction`
to be able to transform e.g. from a coordinate in `CameraFrame` to a coordinate in `AltAz` or `ICRS`.

However, often we need to instantiate a sky coord with a frame before knowing `focal_length` or `obstime`, just to know in what frame these coordinates live.

When that information is later avaible, this is not easily changed.

I guess it boils down to the question, why `FrameAttributes` are immutable.
Even just allowing updating from the default would be very helpful or
passing a frame instance and additional frame attributes to `SkyCoord`.

Am I missing something here? 

Or is this not how `SkyCoords` and custom `Frames` are supposed to be used?

Any help would be appreciated.

title: Is change in behavior of quantity.value for scalars deliberate?
description:
## Description

There is a change in behavior between Astropy 3.2 and Astropy 4.0 that is breaking some of our code. I'm flagging this in case it wasn't deliberate:

### Astropy 3:

```
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> import numpy
>>> a = 5 * u.s
>>> type(a.value)
<class 'float'>
```

### Astropy 4

```
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> import numpy
>>> a = 5 * u.s
>>> type(a.value)
<class 'numpy.float64'>
```

So for scalar quantities the type has changed from standard float to numpy float. 

It's entirely possible that this is deliberate so that array values and scalar values have the same type.  I was asked to file this on Slack just in case it was a side effect of something.

The impact for us is that something which serialized to YAML without any issue now breaks because YAML does not understand what to do with a numpy object. We can of course fix our code to trap this case.

cc/ @mhvk

converters_bad = {

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

The context managers `paths.set_temp_cache` and `paths.set_temp_config` are supposed to let users temporarily reset the locations of the astropy cache and config file. These are used in the test suite but are also user-visible. Unfortunately, as context managers, if an exception occurs in their `__enter__` methods, their `__exit__` methods are never called; these exit methods are what is supposed to reset the values to their original state, so if an exception is produced, say because something is badly wrong with the requested cache setup, the bogus cache setup is left behind.

This appears as bug #9634 and PR #9703 revealed and should fix the problem; there should be an example in the code for it.

description:
### Description
#9652 has introduced a more concise `ModuleNotFoundError` for `io.fits` if bzip2 is not available. For consistency, `get_readable_fileobj` should raise the same exception, analogously for missing `lzma` support (this had already been changed, but reverted in 7795c8d in order not  to change the API in a bugfix PR). title: ENH: add lzma (.xz) support to io.fits
description:
### Description
Loosely related to #9652 and #9685, is there a specific reason why `io.fits` does not support `lzma` compression? title: astropy way of setting dtype of CCDData
description:

so you do not need to remove them! -->

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . -->

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->
Most CCD images on ground-based at least are in 16-bit, and traditionally flat-fielded images, as well as their uncertainty frames have only 32-bit (float32), and that's enough. astropy's CCDData by default converts every numerical data after, e.g., flat division or combining processes, to at least 64-bit (float64). 

As far as I know, this has not been addressed yet (e.g. [this issue](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/9056) in ccdproc is the last one I know). This 64-bit convention doubles the disk space required for data storage, as well as the memory in many occasions.

I had to make my own code snippet to do this task like this:
```python
def CCDData_astype(ccd, dtype='float32', uncertainty_dtype=None):
    ''' Assign dtype to the CCDData object (numpy uses float64 default).
    Parameters
    ----------
    ccd: CCDData
        The ccd to be astyped.
    dtype: dtype-like
        The dtype to be applied to the data
    uncertainty_dtype: dtype-like
        The dtype to be applied to the uncertainty. Be default, use the
        same dtype as data (``uncertainty_dtype = dtype``).

    Example
    -------
    >>> from astropy.nddata import CCDData
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> ccd = CCDData.read("image_unitygain001.fits", ext=0)
    >>> ccd.uncertainty = np.sqrt(ccd.data)
    >>> ccd = yfu.CCDData_astype(ccd, dtype='int16',
    >>>                          uncertainty_dtype='float32')
    '''
    nccd = ccd.copy()
    nccd.data = nccd.data.astype(dtype)

    try:
        if uncertainty_dtype is None:
            uncertainty_dtype = dtype
        nccd.uncertainty.array = nccd.uncertainty.array.astype(
            uncertainty_dtype)
    except AttributeError:
        # If there is no uncertainty attribute in the input ``ccd``
        pass

    return nccd
```

But maybe it should be generalized and/or implemented in a more organized way to astropy. How do you think?

description:
`Table` has `.keys()` and `.values()` which work like expected, producing results similar to what a `dict` would. So far, though, it does not also have `.items()`, which probably make sense if only for completeness. If we do this, we should be sure to also add it to `Row`.

A related question (though one that doesn't have to be solved at the same time), is whether this also makes `Table` compatible with a mapping - the answer for `Table` is arguably "no", since, e.g., its length is the number of rows, not the number of entries returned by `.keys()` or `.values()`. For `Row`, though, it arguably is a mapping.

title: astropy.wcs.get_include() incorrect when astropy compiled against system libaries
description:
Astropy has a ``astropy.wcs.get_include()`` function for other Python packages to build against WCSLIB using the WCSLIB header files bundled with astropy (for examples where this is used see https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9729#issuecomment-563726445).

However at the moment the implementation of ``get_include()`` doesn't seem to take into account that astropy may have been built against a system install of WCSLIB in which case it should probably return the system headers:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/wcs/__init__.py#L30

Is it correct that this would need to be fixed? Or should it not matter? (we've never had reports of issues and this code has been there for a long time, so mabye in practice it's not a problem?)

title: quantity_support machinery should provide a way to include axis labels that still know the units
description:
Right now the `quantity_support` machinery is a bit awkward to use in the "one plot" (i.e. just one quantity on x and y rather than multiple y's with the same unit) case because even though it conveniently shows the unit, it does *not* provide a way to see something like `frequency [Hz]`, which is what is usually desired on a publication-quality plot.  Of course one can just do that manually by unit-formatting... But it then defeats part of the point of the auto-uniting.

There are a few possible solutions I could imagine - 
1. have `quantity_support` (optionally) add `[unit]` at the *end* of whatever goes into `*label`
2. have a magic format option that gets filled in. I.e., the user would do `ax.set_xlable('flux [{xunit}]')`

I think I like 1 more, but am curious if there are other thoughts?

The correct namespace for VOTable 1.4 is `"http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3"`.  The schema location is optional, and if specified can be either `http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/VOTable-1.4.xsd` or `http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3`.  The former will always point to the VOTable 1.4 standard, whereas the latter will resolve to the backward-compatible schema for VOTable 1.5(+) when/if they are approved as standards.

So these are all legal VOTABLE elements:
```xml
<VOTABLE version="1.4" xmlns="http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3">
```
```xml
<VOTABLE version="1.4" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" 
xmlns="http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3" 
xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3 http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/VOTable-1.4.xsd">
```
```xml
<VOTABLE version="1.4" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" 
xmlns="http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3" 
xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3 http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.3">
```
### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
Instead, the VOTABLE element looks like this:
```xml
<VOTABLE version="1.4" xmlns="http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.4"
xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="http://www.ivoa.net/xml/VOTable/v1.4">
```

A WCS object that describes longitude/latitude, and a `CAR` projection, should have independent axes. This means moving along the x-pixel of the images, only longitude changes, and not latitude (and vice versa for moving along the y-pixel).

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

Attempting to read in a file with Table.read() under the 'no_header' format but get an error. The exact code was previously working, but now is not. I did do an astropy update recently, but really cannot pin that as the sole change between when it was/was not working. 

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

The text file should be read into a Table object without error.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

I get an error.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use tripe backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

I was able to reproduce the error by first making a text file 'testfile.txt': 

a,1.0
b,2   
1.0    2.0    abc 
2.0    3.0    def 
3.0    4.0    ghk

where the first two lines are some metadata to be ignored, and the third row and on is the table I would like to read. 

To read it in I am doing: 

```
from astropy.table import Table

Table.read('test_fileread.txt',format='ascii.no_header',delimiter='\t',data_start=2,guess=False)
```

but get back an error: 

```
InconsistentTableError: Number of header columns (1) inconsistent with data columns in data line 0
```

title: Consider declaring package data in MANIFEST.in
description:
As @saimn mentioned in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9729, and as mentioned in [APE 17](https://github.com/astropy/astropy-APEs/blob/master/APE17.rst#package-data-and-entry-points), there are two main ways of specifying the package data, both of them mentioned in the setuptools docs:

https://setuptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/setuptools.html#including-data-files

Essentially, we can either define the package data in ``setup.cfg``, or we can use the ``MANIFEST.in`` and then just set ``include_package_data=True`` in ``setup.cfg``. I don't have very strong opinions, but ``MANIFEST.in`` might give us more flexibility in terms of e.g. including data files recursively.

Do people have strong opinions one way or another?

title: Split out ERFA Python wrappers from core package
ASDF serialization of polynomial models missing domain (causing incorrect evaluation)
description:
When saving & reloading a polynomial model, the `domain` information gets lost (also `window`?), causing the reloaded model to produce different results from the original one.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from astropy.modeling import models, fitting
>>> import asdf

>>> x = np.arange(0, 9)

>>> af = asdf.AsdfFile({"model" : model})
>>> af.write_to("testdom.asdf")

>>> newmodel = asdf.open("testdom.asdf")['model']

>>> print('Fwd before {}, after {}'.format(model.domain, newmodel.domain))
Fwd before (0, 9), after None

>>> print('Inv before {}, after {}'.format(model.inverse.domain,
>>>                                        newmodel.inverse.domain))
Inv before [0.1, 4.6], after None

>>> print('y before:', model(x))
y before: [0.1 0.6 1.1 1.6 2.1 2.6 3.1 3.6 4.1]

>>> print('y after:', newmodel(x))

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
The gauss unit does not decompose at all into the cgs base system, unlike e.g. StatCoulomb.

### Expected behavior
Perform unit conversions according to gaussian cgs units

### Actual behavior

Minimal example:

```python
import astropy.units as u

u.Gauss.decompose(bases=u.cgs.bases)
```

results in:
```
UnitConversionError: Unit A can not be decomposed into the requested bases
```

where it should be:
` Unit("g(1/2) / (cm(1/2) s)")`

See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_(unit)

...

So apparently python only allows built-in category names from the environment variable.

Maybe this is because I do not know how to use PYTHONWARNINGS environment -- any suggestions?

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

I have been using astroplan to plan some observing and specified midnight as 24:00:00. This is defined/allowed by the ISO standard 8601: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601

e.g. 2019-01-19T24:00:00

"Midnight is a special case and may be referred to as either "00:00" or "24:00". The notation "00:00" is used at the beginning of a calendar day and is the more frequently used. At the end of a day use "24:00". "2007-04-05T24:00" is the same instant as "2007-04-06T00:00" (see Combined date and time representations below)."

This issue appears to be a feature of python date/datetime, so documentation is probably the solution.

See: https://github.com/psycopg/psycopg2/issues/278 which reports:

"PostgreSQL can store time (with or without TZ) values from 0:00:00 to 24:00:00 while Python datetime.time only accepts values up to 23:59:59"

Looking at python.date/datetime formats:

https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#strftime-and-strptime-behavior

```
%H | Hour (24-hour clock) as a zero-padded decimal number. | 00, 01, ..., 23
```

Digging into: astropy `core.py`
```python
   def strptime(cls, time_string, format_string, **kwargs):
        """
        Parse a string to a Time according to a format specification.
        See `time.strptime` documentation for format specification.

        >>> Time.strptime('2012-Jun-30 23:59:60', '%Y-%b-%d %H:%M:%S')
        <Time object: scale='utc' format='isot' value=2012-06-30T23:59:60.000>
```
It seems odd to use "23:59:60" as the example but maybe the author of the example had encountered the 24:00:00 issue?

your code snippet. -->

  File "/Users/rgm/anaconda2/envs/py37/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astropy/time/core.py", line 570, in strptime
    tt, fraction = _strptime._strptime(to_string(time), format_string)

title: Order of configuration import
description:
Hey, 

I have been (successfully)  using `astropy` in multiple projects of mine. Lately, I have used it for the first time on Windows where I encountered really strange issues when importing the package: 
```
In [1]: %time import astropy  
Wall time: 4min 13s     
```
IT TAKES **4 MINUTES** JUST TO IMPORT THE PACKAGE!!! 

I started investigating the issue: it seems it is about system variables (I will simply copy part of  astropy.config.paths.py (38 - 52)): 
```
    elif os.name == 'nt':  # This is for all modern Windows (NT or after)
        if 'MSYSTEM' in os.environ and os.environ.get('HOME'):
            # Likely using an msys shell; use whatever it is using for its
            # $HOME directory
            homedir = os.environ['HOME']
        # Next try for a network home
        elif 'HOMESHARE' in os.environ:
            homedir = os.environ['HOMESHARE']
        # See if there's a local home
        elif 'HOMEDRIVE' in os.environ and 'HOMEPATH' in os.environ:
            homedir = os.path.join(os.environ['HOMEDRIVE'],
                                   os.environ['HOMEPATH'])
        # Maybe a user profile?
        elif 'USERPROFILE' in os.environ:
            homedir = os.path.join(os.environ['USERPROFILE'])
```
I am using Windows so I fall inside the if statement.  My suggestion here is to move the `'HOMESHARE'` to the end so that it is checked as the last one. Setting the network drive as `homedir` will make everything superslow. Is there any reason why it is the second?

Thanks for help!

title: rounding a Table or QTable in astropy to a specified number of significant digits
description:
### Description
Is it currently possible to round an entire astropy `Table` or `QTable` to a certain number of significant digits?

### Additional context
In pandas a simple `df.round` will achieve this:

```
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'a':[1.11, 2.22, 3.33, 5.55, 6.66], 'b':[9.99, 8.88, 7.77, 6.66, 5.55]})
df.round(1)
```
I have already tried this in astropy with a QTable but get an error:

> AttributeError: 'QTable' object has no attribute 'round'

I have also tried:

`my_qtable.info.format='0.1f'`

But this does not seem to help. Is there a way to do this? If not would it be easy to implement?

title: get_constellation() should use exact HMS, DMS boundaries, not 4-decimal approximations
description:
### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
IAU's official constellation boundaries are defined using HMS / DMS coordinates in 
E. Delporte | Délimitation scientifique des constellations, cartes, Cambridge University Press, London 1930.

But the data that drives the astropy `get_constellation()` routine is derived by Roman et al. (1987) from Delporte's work, using a lossy conversion to decimal hourangles and degrees with just 4 decimal places.

Roman's data is archived at http://cdsarc.u-strasbg.fr/viz-bin/Cat?VI/42
astropy's copy is in `constellation_data_roman87.dat` file.

For example, the 4th line is:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/51c619e5ffe7aaf748e7c34d08c6336762decc74/astropy/coordinates/data/constellation_data_roman87.dat#L4

It represents an edge between Ursa Minor (`UMi` there) and Cepheus.

It matches data on page 14 of Delporte's book, as reproduced at http://www.atlascoelestis.com/del%20inice%20cost.htm, where
 the corresponding data shows up as the 2nd line after the Ursa Minor sequence starts:

> Paralléle de 86° 10' de 21 h. o m. à 23 h. o m.

We thus see that the original parallel at dec 86° 10' was rounded off by Roman to 86.1667.

(Note that edges are listed twice in Delporte's book, once for each constellation, so it also shows up on page 39 for UMi.)

A better digital representation of Delporte's IAU constellation standard is provided in multiple formats at [Pierre Barbier's Constellation Boundaries](http://pbarbier.com/constellations/boundaries.html)

For example, line 195 of his edges_18.txt file shows the same edge represented exactly in the native sexagesimal format:

```
318:319 P+ 21:00:00 +86:10:00 23:00:00 +86:10:00 CEP UMI
```

Based on the roundoff, astropy thus would find the wrong constellation for coordinates like 22h 86.16668°

While trying to demonstrate this, I ran across what seems to be another issue that I understand less well. `get_constellation()` calls `PrecessedGeocentric(equinox='B1875')` which throws the coordinates off a bit as I document below, interpreting them as geocentric with a distance inferred somehow I guess.

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/b1addf5ae4ae8c18b048940c460a3be2735f5392/astropy/coordinates/funcs.py#L235

While this might make sense for a SkyCoord pointing to a comet or other solar system object, it makes no sense to me when trying to figure out which constellation a distant variable star is in. Perhaps there is a more appropriate way to call the functions, but the methods I'm using below are similar to those in `test_constellations()` in `test_funcs.py`, so I'm still confused.  Note that those tests don't test the edge case (pun intended) that I'm discussing there. I have some additional tests which will, which I'll add to that file in a PR.

To be precise:

### Actual behavior

```
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord, FK5, get_constellation, PrecessedGeocentric
from astropy import units as u

print('Coordinate\tTransformed\tConstellation\tHand annotation')

for dec in [86.16, 86.1666, 86.16668, 86.1668]:
    c = FK5(22*u.hour, dec*u.deg, equinox='B1875')
    constel = get_constellation(c)
    pg = c.transform_to(PrecessedGeocentric(equinox='B1875'))
    print(f'{dec:<10.8}\t{pg.dec:.8}\t{constel}')
```

Annotated output:
```
Coordinate      Transformed     Constellation   Hand annotation
86.16           86.164512 deg   Cepheus     # Right
86.1666         86.171112 deg   Ursa Minor  # Wrong
86.16668        86.171192 deg   Ursa Minor  # Right for wrong reason
86.1668         86.171312 deg   Ursa Minor  # Right
```

### Expected behavior

I expected the 2nd row (86.1666) to properly be located in Cepheus.
I expected the transformed column (showing the values that are actually looked up in the table, currently generated when PrecessedGeocentric has been applied to the coordinate) above to match the Coordinate column.
After the issue with PrecessedGeocentric is resolved, I expect the 3rd row to continue to show up in

title: Properly support different electromagnetic unit systems.
description:
## Description

Currently, astropy does not really handle different electromagnetic unit systems.
There are definitions for units in different cgs systems and natural constants 
have properties to access them.

But e.g. the Gauss does not decompose into cgs bases, because it is only defined as
1e-4 Tesla, see #9830.

There are probably other cases I don't yet know about the require different decompositions depending on the unit system.

Many papers in astronomy still use gaussian cgs units.

I think it is desirable, to have a nice top level API to switch between unit systems.
E.g. deciding whether `u.Gauss` decomposes into `u.Tesla` or the cgs base units.

E.g.

```python
import astropy.units as u

u.use_system('gauss')
```

Or 

```python
with u.system('gauss'):
    # do stuff

```

### Additional context
Problems relating to the cgs units occured in #5879 and #5736.
