title: Parallel build failure on CircleCI
Safer BaseCoordinateFrame?
description:
Dear `astropy` developers,

first let me thank you for the great job you have done here :) I have been using the `astropy.coordinates` package for some time now and find it very convenient. Yet I have a few concerns which I discuss below.

The intent of `BaseCoordinateFrame` w.r.t. mutability is not clear to me. On one side the class restricts changing `self.data` (by not implementing the corresponding property setter) but on the other side the low level data are `numpy.ndarray` which are actually mutable. Furthermore, the class uses as cache which can get invalid without any notice.  This can lead to strange bugs, for example as following:

```python
>>> from numpy import zeros                                                       
>>> from astropy.coordinates import BaseCoordinateFrame, CartesianRepresentation                 

>>> z2 = zeros(2)                                                  
>>> frame = BaseCoordinateFrame(CartesianRepresentation(z2, z2, z2))       
>>> frame.spherical.distance  # This gets cached                                               
<Quantity [0., 0.]>                                                        

>>> frame.cartesian.x[:] += 1 # Someone modifies the coordinates in-place                 
>>> frame.spherical.distance  # The cached value is used                                               
<Quantity [0., 0.]> 
```
Explicitly clearing the cache (e.g. with `self.cache.clear()`) before the 2nd call to `frame.spherical` would solve the problem in this specific case. However, in a less obvious situation where the two calls are largely separated (e.g. in different functions implemented by different users) this can get really messy and error prone.

In order to prevent these types of errors a simple solution to me would be an option to disable the cache. This would allow for a more robust, yet less efficient, frame version.

Another confusing point to me is that in the previous example `frame.cartesian` while differing from the `frame.data` representation actually gets references to the data instead of copies. For example: 
 
```python
>>> frame.cartesian is frame.data
False
>>> frame.cartesian.x is frame.data.x
True
```
To me it would be safer if the representation like attributes of a frame (`frame.cartesian`, `frame.spherical`, ...) would always return a copy of the data, instead of references when matching the data representation.  If one explicitly wants a reference to the coordinates data then there is the `frame.data` property whose name clearly indicates that one is manipulating the initial data. Though, such a change could have a significant impact on the performances of existing codes :(

title: Special-case iterable of Time for Time initialization.
description:
Currently, lists/tuples of `Time` instances are special cased in `_make_array` since the `np.array` call will give a warning for them in numpy >1.18 that being turned into object arrays is going to change. We should perhaps special-case iterable of `Time` so it never gets to this place. For more discussion, see https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9719#discussion_r354242779

EDIT (2022-08-28): the specific case that is a problem is for a combination of scalars and arrays that, perhaps somewhat oddly, we support (i.e., we concatenate inputs):
```
from astropy.time import Time
t = Time('2000-01-01')
t2 = Time([t, t])
t3 = Time([t, t2])
t3
# <Time object: scale='utc' format='iso' value=['2000-01-01 00:00:00.000' '2000-01-01 00:00:00.000'
 '2000-01-01 00:00:00.000']>
np.array([t, t2])
<ipython-input-5-da7e2abbe6df>:1: VisibleDeprecationWarning: Creating an ndarray from ragged nested sequences (which is a list-or-tuple of lists-or-tuples-or ndarrays with different lengths or shapes) is deprecated. If you meant to do this, you must specify 'dtype=object' when creating the ndarray.
  np.array([t, t2])

int64 int64 int64

description:
### Description
It would be helpful if one could test if a specific model is used (included) in a compound model by a class (type) or model name.

Currently, the default behavior is as follows:
```python
>>> from astropy.modeling.models import Scale, Shift

title: Listing compound submodels
description:
### Description
A useful feature in modeling would be to be able to inspect a model  without "breaking apart" constituent compound models into basic models. Let's consider the following model:

```python
>>> from astropy.modeling.models import Scale, Shift
>>> s1 = Scale(1, name='first')
>>> s2 = Scale(2, name='second')
>>> s3 = Scale(2, name='third')
>>> c1 = s1 | s2
>>> c1.name = 'comb1'
>>> c = c1 | s3
```

I would like to be able to do see if `'comb1'` is a part of `c` as suggested in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/9887#issuecomment-577696389:

```python
'comb1' in c.submodel_names
```
Currently this does not work:
```python
>>> c.submodel_names
('first', 'second', 'third')
```
The name of `c1` seems to be completely ignored/irrelevant.

title: fitting fails when model supports units and has custom inputs/outputs labels
description:
When trying to define a custom Fittable1DModel with custom labels for inputs/outputs that also supports units/quantities, the fitting fails. 

I am writing a fittable model for which I would like the inputs/outputs labels to be something other than x and y. I would also like this model to support units. As a simplified version of the issue I'm encountering, here is a simple model called 'CustomModel' that is fittable and supports units. The input/output units are called 'inn' and 'out' (rather than x & y).

```
from astropy.modeling.core import Fittable1DModel, Parameter
from astropy.modeling import fitting
from astropy import units as u
import numpy as np

class CustomModel(Fittable1DModel):
    
    a = Parameter(default=1.0)
    b = Parameter(default=1.0)
    
    def __init__(self, a=a, b=b):
        super().__init__(a=a, b=b)
        
        self.inputs = ('inn',)
        self.outputs = ('out',)
        
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate(inn, a, b):
        return a*inn + b
    
    @property
    def input_units(self):
        if self.a.unit is None and self.b.unit is None:
            return None
        else:
            return {'inn': self.b.unit / self.a.unit}

    def _parameter_units_for_data_units(self, inputs_unit, outputs_unit):
        return {'a': outputs_unit['out'],
                'b': outputs_unit['out'] / inputs_unit['inn']}

```

This model can be evaluated successfully:

```
>>>modd = CustomModel(a=1*u.m/u.s, b=2*u.m)
>>>modd(10 * u.s)
12m
```
However, fitting fails. Here I pass in some perfectly linear data hoping to get slope and intercept 10.5 and 7.2 back in the fit: 

```
>>>fitter = fitting.LevMarLSQFitter()
>>>x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100) * u.m
>>>y = 10.5*x + 7.2*u.m
>>>fit_custom_model = fitter(m, x, y)

-------------------------------------------------------------------
KeyError                          Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-12-81aa8227aaed> in <module>
----> 1 fit_custom_model = fitter(m, x, y)

~/packages/astropy/astropy/modeling/fitting.py in wrapper(self, model, x, y, z, **kwargs)
    123                 if model.input_units is not None:
    124                     if isinstance(x, Quantity):
--> 125                         x = x.to(model.input_units['x'], equivalencies=input_units_equivalencies['x'])
    126                     if isinstance(y, Quantity) and z is not None:
    127                         y = y.to(model.input_units['y'], equivalencies=input_units_equivalencies['y'])

KeyError: 'x'
```

When I try the above steps but omit the step where I rename inputs and outputs, everything works as expected. Similarly, when the input/output units are renamed but the units support is removed, everything works. 

It looks like this issue is stemming from the fact that when unit support is enabled, fitting works internally with 'x' and 'y' and expects them to be named exactly that. 

The simple solution would be to just work internally with x & y, and rename the inputs/outputs at the end or just document what they should be - this is my solution for the time being. However, there are several existing non-fittable models (i.e those in rotations) that rename the inputs/outputs right away and work internally with those units, so I think it makes more sense to expect the same functionality here. I can work on a fix for this if it truly is a bug.

title: Undeclared (?) limitation of FITS ASCII table integer field width
description:
### Description
According to the FITS standard (section 7.2.5):

"This Standard does not impose an upper limit on the number of digits of precision, nor any limit
on the range of numeric values. Software packages that read or write data according to this Standard could be limited, however, in the range of values and exponents that are supported (e.g.,
to the range that can be represented by 32-bit or 64-bit binary numbers)."

My expectation was that AstroPy would choose an underlying data-type suitable for the range of values being read, but that appears not to be the case. This file:

[i10_test.zip](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/files/4122596/i10_test.zip)

for example reads fine with the FITS reference software (fv, fitsverify, fdump etc.) but in AstroPy the values of 4294967295 are read incorrectly as -1. It looks like integer values in ASCII tables are constrained to be 32-bit signed integers - is this correct? I understand I can use offsets etc. but I couldn't see this limitation written down, so wanted to confirm.

### Expected behavior
Valid FITS files to be read as expected.

### Actual behavior
Values outside of the range of a 32-bit signed integer are incorrectly read.

title: deprecated_renamed_argument fails for a removed keyword (not solved: when it is called as positional argument)
description:
**UPDATE:** It is still unsolved for when function below is called as `myfunc(1, 200)`.

<hr/>

`deprecated_renamed_argument` allows one to deprecate a removed keyword argument.  However, when doing so, the deprecated keyword cannot be set.  It is always given its default value:

```python
>>> from astropy.utils.decorators import deprecated_renamed_argument

>>> @deprecated_renamed_argument('b', None, '4.1')
>>> def myfunc(a, b=3):
>>>     print(a, b)
>>>     return

>>> myfunc(1, b=200)
1 3
WARNING: AstropyDeprecationWarning: "b" was deprecated in version 4.1 and will be removed in a future version.  [warnings]
```

The deprecated keyword value can be changed from the default if it is used as a positional argument, but in that case the deprecation warning is not raised:

```python
>>> myfunc(1, 200)
1 200
```

title: Incorrect transformation of coordinates with SkyCoord
description:
Hello everyone,

I was trying to transform galactic coordinates in Cartesian coordinates but when I go back from Cartesian to galactic, the coordinates of the source has changed (see the code below).
```python
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy import units as u

lon = 251
lat = -26
dist = 5 

coord = SkyCoord(lon, lat, dist, frame="galactic", unit=(u.deg, u.deg, u.Mpc))
print(coord)

coord = coord.cartesian
print(coord)
x, y, z = coord.x.value, coord.y.value, coord.z.value

coord = SkyCoord(x, y, z, unit=u.Mpc, representation_type="cartesian")
print(coord)
print(coord.galactic)
```
output:
```
<SkyCoord (Galactic): (l, b, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    (251., -26., 5.)>
(-1.46309359, -4.24913233, -2.19185573) Mpc
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (x, y, z) in Mpc
    (-1.46309359, -4.24913233, -2.19185573)>
<SkyCoord (Galactic): (l, b, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    (354.46656629, 12.84625821, 5.)>
```

I made a test and it seems that the galactic longitude and latitude are interpreted as right ascension and declination. Indeed, in the next code I put my galactic longitude and latitude as RA, Dec and I obtain the same results as before:
```python
coord = SkyCoord(ra=lon, dec=lat, distance=dist, unit=(u.deg, u.deg, u.Mpc))
print(coord.cartesian)
print(coord.galactic)
```
output:
```
(-1.46309359, -4.24913233, -2.19185573) Mpc
<SkyCoord (Galactic): (l, b, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    (354.46656629, 12.84625821, 5.)>
```

It appears that during the transformation, the galactic coordinates are always read as ICRS coordinates. I don't know if the problem occurs with other system of coordinates (I didn't try) but I guess the reference system is not taking into account during transformation.

Right now, I solved the problem by first converting the galactic coordinates in ICRS and then converting it in cartesian.
```python
coord = SkyCoord(lon, lat, dist, frame="galactic", unit=(u.deg, u.deg, u.Mpc))
RA, DEC = str(coord.icrs.to_string('hmsdms')).split(" ")
coord = SkyCoord(ra=RA, dec=DEC, distance=dist, unit=(u.deg, u.deg, u.Mpc))
print(coord.cartesian)
print(coord.galactic)
```
output:
```
(-0.11744916, 3.60221526, -3.46558089) Mpc
<SkyCoord (Galactic): (l, b, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    (251.00000002, -25.99999998, 5.)>
```

Cheers,
Thomas

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

When slicing rice tile compressed image, the output data are invalid. In some cases this gets magically fixed if `scale_back=True` flag is passed when opening the fits file, but on some other cases it has no effect.

To clarify what I mean by valid and invalid data, see attached examples. 

### Expected behavior

This is what I would expect to get:

And this is what is produced:

(obviously the data are totally wrong, but the images show this much better than tables)

### Steps to Reproduce

This can be easily reproduced by:

```python
        outfile = "compressed_cut.fz"
        infile = "ADP.2020-02-12T10_26_25.400.fits.fz" # you can get the input file from http://dataportal.eso.org/dataPortal/file/ADP.2020-02-12T10:26:25.400
        hdus = fits.open(infile)
        slices = tuple([slice(start, stop) for (start, stop) in [(0, 4090), (0, 2040)]])
        hdus[1].data = hdus[1].data[slices]
        new_hdus = hdus[0:2]
        new_hdus.writeto(outfile, overwrite=True)
        hdus.close()
```

It's also pretty easy to see that the actual data saved to the file, are not what you'd expect. If we extend the above example to:

```python
        outfile = "compressed_cut.fz"
        infile = "ADP.2020-02-12T10_26_25.400.fits.fz"  # you can get the input file from http://dataportal.eso.org/dataPortal/file/ADP.2020-02-12T10:26:25.400

        hdus[1].data = hdus[1].data[slices]
        new_hdus = hdus[0:2]

        print(hdus[1].data[1][0:100]) # data we're reading back from file

We get two very different sets of data printed out, even though they should be the same.

I tried using the `do_not_scale_image_data=True` and  `scale_back=True` flags but they have no effect.

Am I doing something wrong here?

title: nicer way to write table to fits file when a column contains arrays of variable length
description:
It doesn't seem like theres a nice way to write a table to a fits file when one of the columns contains arrays of variable length. For example:
```
colA = [1, 2]
colB = [np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])]
fits.BinTableHDU(tab)
```
fails because colB contains arrays of different lengths. A workaround for this is possible by deconstructing each table column into a Column object, then creating a BinTableHDU from these:
```
colaa = fits.Column(name='ColA', format='I', array=colA)
colbb = fits.Column(name='ColB', format='PD', array=colB)
tab_hdu = fits.BinTableHDU.from_columns([colaa, colbb])
```
This works and the table is able to be written out. However, if you would like to modify the table you just wrote out, after reading it in you have to go through the clunky process of creating individual columns again to write it back out as none of the table > fitsrec/hdu functions work out of the box. I have a helper function to do this and obscure it in my code, but it might be helpful to have this in here (maybe in table_to_hdu?). 

(In my real use case, the arrays do have to be variable length, I can't just set them to the max length of any array in the table. for historical reasons.)

title: Instantiating a Time from a Time looses the location
description:
As found by @luojing1211 in https://github.com/nanograv/PINT/issues/609, initializing a table column from a list of time instances loses the location. Further investigation showed that more generally, initializing a `Time` from another `Time` instance causes loss of location, and that likely the fact that it now happens in `Table` reflects a change in how tables initialize from list:
```
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy.table import Table
t = Time('J2010', location=(45, 45))
print(t.location)
# (3194419.14506057, 3194419.14506057, 4487348.40886592) m
print(Table([[t]])['col0'][0].location)
# None
print(Time(t).location)
# None
```
Looking back, in versions prior to 4.0 (checked 3.2.x and 3.1), the `Table([[t]])` kept the location, but the `Time(t)` already did not.

title: Cache locked errors when download cache dir is on NFS
description:
### Description

We use Astropy on the LIGO-Caltech computing cluster on which users' home directories are shared across all worker nodes using NFS. We are finding that when users are running many Python scripts at once that use Astropy, a large fraction of the jobs are failing with the error:

```
RuntimeError: Cache is locked after 5.02 s. This may indicate an astropy bug or that kill -9 was used. If you want to unlock the cache remove the directory /home/leo.singer/.astropy/cache/download/py3/lock. Lock claims to be held by process 14764.

The error even happens if we run the script once first on the submit node to pre-populate the cache before running it on the worker nodes.

We know that we could work around this issue by setting environment variables to put the cache directory on a non-NFS  filesystem (e.g. in /tmp). However, this is a new issue in the most recent version of Astropy: we are _only_ seeing this error with Astropy 4.0, and not with 3.2.3. `astropy.stats.sigma_clipping.sigma_clipped_stats` may be inappropriately using `numpy.nanfunctions` when masked arrays are involved.

This issue is intended to open up the discussion of whether `sigma_clipped_stats`, and any other functions that are using the `nanfunctions`, should switch to the standard, non-nan, functions when masked arrays are involved.

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
By design, `clear_download_cache()` completely removes the cache, including any lock that may be held. Unfortunately, if the cache is recreated, the new lock file has the same name as the old, and so processes that think they have the lock from before the cache was cleared can remove it while processes started after the clearing hold it, breaking their lock.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
Unclear what good behaviour in this setting would look like.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
`clear_download_cache()` while other processes are running can cause cache problems.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

1. Process A acquires the lock.
2. Process B runs `clear_download_cache()`
3. Process B acquires a lock on the new cache.
4. Process A releases the lock, now on the new cache.

Now Process B thinks it has the lock but doesn't. Double unlocks are usually harmless, but other problems can occur.

Suggested mitigation: do not use no-argument `clear_download_cache()` (or delete the Astropy cache) while jobs are running.

title: radial_velocity_correction needs more careful handling of obstime for objects with high proper motion
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md .
Please be sure to check out our code of conduct,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . -->

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
Whilst working on #9645 I noticed a subtlety in the radial velocity correction that is important at the metres/second level for objects with high proper motion (arcsecs/year).

The issue is that, in order to calculate the RV correction one needs to know the ICRS position of the source *at the time of observation*. To do this, one needs to apply space motion of the ```SkyCoord``` itself, in order to find the position of the source at the observation time. However, this requires knowing the epoch of the coordinates. 

At the moment, we apply no space motion - i.e we assume the epoch of the coordinates is equal to the RV observation time. We need a way of knowing both the ```obstime``` of the RV measurement and the epoch of the coordinates.  However, at the moment, only one Time is allowed for the whole calculation, which is the time of observation of the radial velocity. In fact, if the user tries to fix this and supplies ```obstime``` argument when the ```SkyCoord``` already has an obstime set then we raise an error.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
What I think should happen is this:

##### Case 1 (User supplies a single ```obstime``` argument, ```SkyCoord.obstime``` is set):
Assume ```SkyCoord.obstime``` is the epoch of the coordinates, apply space motion to find position of source at ```obstime```.

##### Case 2 (User supplies no ```obstime``` but ```SkyCoord.obstime``` is set):
Assume epoch and RV observation time are the same. Do not apply space motion.

##### Case 3 (User supplies ```obstime``` but ```SkyCoord.obstime``` is not set):
This is the only awkward case. We could assume the epoch is equal to the equinox and apply space motion, or we could assume case 2 and apply no space motion. Either way I think we ought to warn the user they are potentially doing something inaccurate.

The documentation for this method will also need changing to clarify what is happening.

title: Default FITS WCS has CRPIX set to 0
description:
### Description

This is not really a bug nor can I call it a feature request. It is about the default value of `CRPIX` of a `WCS` object just constructed with default parameters `WCS()`.

While `CRPIX` is a 1-based pixel position, the default constructor create a WCS with `CRPIX1` and `CRPIX2` set to 0.0.

```python
In [1]: from astropy.wcs import WCS
   ...: w = WCS()

In [2]: w
Out[2]:
WCS Keywords

Number of WCS axes: 2
CTYPE : ''  ''
CRVAL : 0.0  0.0
CRPIX : 0.0  0.0
PC1_1 PC1_2  : 1.0  0.0
PC2_1 PC2_2  : 0.0  1.0
CDELT : 1.0  1.0
NAXIS : 0  0
```

This is _strange_ because if I wanted to compute world coordinates at the `CRPIX` location I would have to do:

```python
In [3]: w.wcs_pix2world(0, 0, 1)
Out[3]: [array(0.), array(0.)]

In [4]: w.wcs_pix2world(-1, -1, 0)
Out[4]: [array(0.), array(0.)]
```
Image pixel at `-1, -1`???

### Expected behavior
```python
In [5]: WCS()
Out[5]:
WCS Keywords

Number of WCS axes: 2
CTYPE : ''  ''
CRVAL : 0.0  0.0
CRPIX : 1.0  1.0
PC1_1 PC1_2  : 1.0  0.0
PC2_1 PC2_2  : 0.0  1.0
CDELT : 1.0  1.0
NAXIS : 0  0
```

This is not really a bug. But I think it would be more valuable from the didactic point of view to have `CRPIX` set to `(1, 1)` to re-iterate that `CRPIX` is 1-based.

title: Minor issues related to polynomial domain & window
description: Following PRs #9906, #9941, #9956 to fix issues #9942, #9795 & #9809 (not a one-to-one correspondence), a few minor outstanding issues have been left for later. I think the following are still pending , if I have kept track of them correctly: - Polynomial models don't do any checking of their `domain` & `window` (or `x_domain` / `y_domain` / `x_window` / `y_window`) arguments, so those can be set to whatever value you like, causing errors when you later try to use the model. In particular, if the user provides a tuple, it works as expected but then gets serialized to `asdf` as a list instead, so if a model is saved and reloaded, its `domain` and `window` are not identical before and afterwards (eg. in a test comparison `[-2, 2] != (-2, 2)`). The tentative consensus was that the `domain` & `window` arguments should be checked and converted to 2-tuples in the corresponding attributes (though the current documentation defines their values as lists). - In `Model._format_repr`, an optional model argument/attribute gets included in the printed output only if its value is not the default (as provided by the calling `__repr__` implementation). In `Model._format_str`, however, the same argument/attribute gets printed whenever the value is `not None`, which is not correct the default eg. for `window`. Thus (once #9941 is merged), `window` will **always** get printed by `str`, unlike `domain` and also unlike `window` in `repr`. Presumably this is not the intended behaviour and `_format_str` should have a `defaults` parameter like the one in `_format_repr`, which should then get passed by `PolynomialModel.__str__` and `OrthoPolynomialBase.__str__` () (or the equivalent methods of their child classes). - Similar to the previous point, in the asdf tag code for `PolynomialTypeBase`, the `window` will **always** get serialized given the condition `not None` -- unlike the `domain` -- because the value is never None, defaulting to `[-1, 1]`. This should be harmless but is obviously not the intended behaviour. Likewise for `x_window` / `y_window`. For `Polynomial1D`/`Polynomial2D`, it looks like the `domain` will always get serialized as well. These might be good problems for a new contributor, eg. at PIA?

### Description
The parameters `fill_include_names` and `fill_exclude_names` in [astropy.io.ascii.read](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.io.ascii.read.html#astropy.io.ascii.read) don't work as expected.

### Expected behavior
Setting a column name in `fill_exclude_names` should exclude that column from the `fill_values` mask.

### Actual behavior
It works in a confusing way.

### Steps to Reproduce
```python
from astropy.io import ascii

test_data = """
ID  x  y
1   99  3.0
99  5.2  6.1
7   1.8  99
"""
fill_msk = [('', '0'), ('99', '0')]
```

1. Works as expected: all columns are masked
```
data = ascii.read(test_data, fill_values=fill_msk)
 ID  x   y 
--- --- ---
  1  -- 3.0
 -- 5.2 6.1
  7 1.8  --
```
1.  Works as expected: only the `x` column is excluded from the mask
```
data = ascii.read(test_data, fill_values=fill_msk, fill_exclude_names='x')
 ID  x    y 
--- ---- ---
  1 99.0 3.0
 --  5.2 6.1
  7  1.8  --
```
1.  Works as expected: only the `y` column is excluded from the mask
```
data = ascii.read(test_data, fill_values=fill_msk, fill_exclude_names='y')
 ID  x   y  
--- --- ----
  1  --  3.0
 -- 5.2  6.1
  7 1.8 99.0
```
1.  Works as expected: only the `ID` column is excluded from the mask
```
data = ascii.read(test_data, fill_values=fill_msk, fill_include_names=('x', 'y'), fill_exclude_names='ID')
 ID  x   y 
--- --- ---
  1  -- 3.0
 99 5.2 6.1
  7 1.8  --
```
1. **Does not** work as expected: the `y` column is excluded from the mask when a different name was given
```
data = ascii.read(test_data, fill_values=fill_msk, fill_exclude_names='nny')
 ID  x   y  
--- --- ----
  1  --  3.0
 -- 5.2  6.1
  7 1.8 99.0
```
1. **Does not** work as expected: the `ID` column is **not** excluded from the mask
```
data = ascii.read(test_data, fill_values=fill_msk, fill_exclude_names='ID')
 ID  x   y 
--- --- ---
  1  -- 3.0
 -- 5.2 6.1
  7 1.8  --

Hi,

We run astropy in a Docker container on an HPC system using the Shifter container-running platform.  In Shifter, the container's filesystems are all read-only.  We have pre-loaded a number of cached files required by astropy (eg, IERS).  But even though the file already exists in the cache directory, it fails because the filesystem is read-only!  This seems not ideal.

```
$ python -c "from astropy.time import Time; Time.now()"
CacheMissingWarning: Not clearing data cache - cache inaccessible due to OSError: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/root/.astropy/cache/download/py3/lock' [astropy.utils.data]
CacheMissingWarning: Not clearing data cache - cache inaccessible due to OSError: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/root/.astropy/cache/download/py3/lock' [astropy.utils.data]
Downloading https://www.ietf.org/timezones/data/leap-seconds.list [Done]
```

### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

ps, weird thing is, strace shows it looks for an "urlmap" file, and then trying to create a lock

```
stat("/root/.astropy/cache/download/py3/urlmap", 0x7fffffff3d70) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
mkdir("/root/.astropy/cache/download/py3/lock", 0777) = -1 EROFS (Read-only file system)
```

but in the cache dir there are files `urlmap.dat` and `urlmap.dir`....

### EDIT: Workaround

Set `astropy.utils.iers.conf.auto_download = False`. Also see https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10003#issuecomment-594034005

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
Using `float` or `numpy.float` on a complex number results in a `TypeError`.  Using `float` or `numpy.float` on that complex number represented as a dimensionless `Quantity` results in the real part being returned and a `ComplexWarning` being issued.  The consequence is that code using complex numbers and complex quantities may behave differently, so it may be necessary to write separate code to handle complex numbers and complex quantities.  Code that relies on the current behavior for quantities should instead use `numpy.real`. 

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

I would expect that using `float` or `numpy.float` on a complex number represented as a dimensionless `Quantity` would raise a `TypeError` also. 

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

Using `float` on a complex number multiplied with `astropy.units.dimensionless_unscaled` returns the real part while issuing a `ComplexWarning`.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

```Python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> complex_number = 5 + 6j
>>> complex_quantity = complex_number * u.dimensionless_unscaled

>>> float(complex_number)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: can't convert complex to float

>>> float(complex_quantity)  # would expect a TypeError for consistency
/media/Scratch/namurphy/envs/empty_for_astropy/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/units/quantity.py:1077: ComplexWarning: Casting complex values to real discards the imaginary part
  return float(self.to_value(dimensionless_unscaled))
5.0
```

The `TypeError` came from [this line in quantity.py](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/3c88b57e39cbda39b6f604c7472e7b3e40c9d690/astropy/units/quantity.py#L1077).

title: Add option to use first identifed reader from registry
description:
This comes from https://github.com/astropy/specutils/issues/171 - currently specutils has a priority system built in to its wrapper of astropy.io.registry (it does dig into the internals of astropy.io.registry, but that's a separate thing). However, were I to do `Spectrum1d.read("test.fits")`, if there were multiple readers which could handle the file (the case I hit was the SDSS loader and the IRAF loader both are found to work), astropy/specutils would claim the format was ambiguous. If there was a option in `read` to specify to load the first reader found (which will be the one with the higher priority via specutils priority system), such as `use_best_format` or similar, `Spectrum1d.read("test.fits", use_best_format=True)` would load the file as an SDSS spectrum.

I'm happy to create a PR adding this, but I'd like to have some agreement on the API before creating it.

title: confusion about precise definition of galactic and galactocentric reference frames
description:
I noticed a minor but puzzling discrepancy in conversion between ICRS, Galactic and Galactocentric coordinates, namely, in the position of the "so-called" Galactic center:

```
import astropy.coordinates as coord, astropy.units as unit
coord.Galactic(l=0*unit.degree,b=0*unit.degree).transform_to(coord.ICRS)
```
produces
```
<ICRS Coordinate: (ra, dec) in deg
    ( 266.40498829, -28.93617776)>
```
but
```
coord.Galactocentric(x=0*unit.kpc,y=0*unit.kpc,z=0*unit.kpc).transform_to(coord.ICRS)
```
produces
```
<ICRS Coordinate: (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, kpc)
    ( 266.4051, -28.936175,  8.3)>
```
the difference is fairly small, 0.3 arcseconds, but why is it there at all?
To clarify, this is _not_ the difference between the "so-called" Galactic center as defined by the Galactic coordinate system, and the actual position of Sgr A* - the latter is offset from origin by ~10 pc or more than 4 arcminutes. Which is, of course, very annoying, but it's another story.

title: Please support TAI time expressed as unix seconds
description:
### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->

I would like astropy.time.Time to directly support expressing TAI date in unix seconds. This would allow manipulating the value returned by TAI_CLOCK on linux. It is also a standard used by the LSST for timestamps for telescope control.

At present astropy.time.Time seems to think that any time in unix seconds is always UTC. Thus the two asserts in the following code pass, but if this feature was implemented then they would not -- the two times would differ by 37 seconds (on 2020-03-19):

```
import time
import astropy.time
unix_time = time.time()
date1 = astropy.time.Time(unix_time, scale="tai", format="unix")
date2 = astropy.time.Time(unix_time, scale="utc", format="unix")
assert date1 == date2
now = astropy.time.Time.now()
assert now.tai.unix == now.utc.unix
```

It is currently quite painful to obtain TAI time in unix seconds from astropy.time,
and even more painful to go in the other direction. 

### Additional context

Here is the code I am using to obtain TAI unix seconds:
```
def tai_from_utc(utc_unix):
    """Return TAI in unix seconds, given UTC in unix seconds."""
    astropy_utc = astropy.time.Time(utc_unix, scale="utc", format="unix")
    try:
        dt_utc = astropy_utc.utc.to_datetime()
        dt_tai = astropy_utc.tai.to_datetime()
    except ValueError:
        # datetime cannot have 60 in the seconds field; back off a second
        astropy_utc = astropy_utc - 1 * u.second
        dt_utc = astropy_utc.utc.to_datetime()
        dt_tai = astropy_utc.tai.to_datetime()
    tai_minus_utc = (dt_tai - dt_utc).total_seconds()
    return utc_unix + tai_minus_utc
```
If this feature was implemented this code would become:
```
def tai_from_utc(utc_unix):
    """Return TAI in unix seconds, given UTC in unix seconds."""
    return astropy.time.Time(utc_unix, scale="utc", format="unix").tai.unix
```
I have not yet figured out tolerable code to go in the other direction though I have cobbled something together that works.

You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

`astropy.modeling.custom_model` provides following example in its docstring:

```python
>>> from astropy.modeling.models import custom_model
>>> import numpy as np
>>> def sine_model(x, amplitude=1., frequency=1.):
...     return amplitude * np.sin(2 * np.pi * frequency * x)
>>> def sine_deriv(x, amplitude=1., frequency=1.):
...     return 2 * np.pi * amplitude * np.cos(2 * np.pi * frequency * x)
>>> SineModel = custom_model(sine_model, fit_deriv=sine_deriv)
```

However, according to the documentation, `fit_deriv` should "return a sequence where each element of the sequence is the derivative with respect to the corresponding argument".

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

If I understand correctly, the actual `sine_deriv` implementation should be:
```python
>>> def sine_deriv(x, amplitude=1., frequency=1.):
...     return [np.sin(2 * np.pi * frequency * x), 
...             2 * np.pi * amplitude * x * np.cos(2 * np.pi * frequency * x)]
```

First element is the derivative with respect to the amplitude, second is the derivative with respect to the frequency (assuming `col_fit_deriv == True`, the default). According to a quick test, this implementation of the derivative seems to work correctly (whereas the current one does not, although it only raises a `TypeError` when fitting). 

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

The current implementation seems to return only the derivative with respect to the frequency, and on top of that it seems to be lacking an extra factor `x`.

I can provide a pull request if wanted. If so: should another line break be included? The example is double indented, and the last line (of the derivative) would be at 86 characters (instead of the current 80), above the PEP8 limit. Possibly the argument of the sin/cos can be cached into a variable to save computation and line space.

EDIT: I am using astropy v3.2.1, but the bug is still there in the master branch.

title: Questions about UTC<->TAI conversions
description:
### Description

Leap second correction is applied gradually on the day of a leap second, leading to questions about conversion between UTC and TAI time. [EDIT by @taldcroft]

### Expected behavior

The leap second correction should be applied one second before the new day.

### Actual behavior

The leap second is applied gradually throughout the day.

### Steps to Reproduce

Here is a simplified example halfway through the day of the most recent leap second.  `tai_minus_utc1` is a variant of the code I usually run, which handles the leap second correctly. `tai_minus_utc2` is the code I would rather use, because it is simpler. See https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10052 for another variant that is also simple, but fails in the same way as `tai_minus_utc2`:
```
import astropy.time

def tai_minus_utc1(ap_time):
    try:
        dt_utc = ap_time.utc.to_datetime()
        dt_tai = ap_time.tai.to_datetime()
    except ValueError:
        # datetime cannot have 60 in the seconds field; back off a second
        ap_time = ap_time - 1 * u.second
        dt_utc = ap_time.utc.to_datetime()
        dt_tai = ap_time.tai.to_datetime()
    return (dt_tai - dt_utc).total_seconds()

def tai_minus_utc2(ap_time):
    return (ap_time.tai.mjd - ap_time.utc.mjd) * 24 * 60 * 60

ap_time = astropy.time.Time("2016-12-31 12:00:00", scale="utc", format="iso")
print(f"tai_minus_utc1: {tai_minus_utc1(ap_time)}")
print(f"tai_minus_utc2: {tai_minus_utc2(ap_time)}")
```
produces:

tai_minus_utc2: 36.499994387850165  # wrong

title: TimeDatetime does not roundtrip properly
description:
Bug reported by Joris Kersten via @kelle:
> I recently noticed that some of my scripts that were developed with Astropy 3 fail with Astropy 4.
The problems seem to be related to tables with Time objects in them. Writing and reading a Table does not work and opening the table in a browser (Firefox in my case) fails.
>
> I wrote two small example scripts, which I attached to this email. These scripts give no error for me with Astropy version 3.2.3 , but do give errors with Astropy version 4.0. I use Windows 10 and Anaconda with Python 3.7 and NumPy 1.18.1 .
>
> First I believed that Time objects created from datetime objects were the cause. Indeed, this is the case that breaks reading the written table. Reading with other Time objects works well. (See script.) However, show_in_browser fails also for t4 = Time('1999-01-01T00:00:00.123456789') objects, but not for # t5 = Time([1, 2, 3], format='unix') objects. So, the problem is wider than just with datetime objects. Also interesting: show_in_browser does not fail if jsviewer=False is set.

```
from datetime import datetime
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy.table import Table

# Time object initiated from datetime objects.
timelist = Time([datetime(2020, 4, 1),
                 datetime(2020, 4, 2),
                 datetime(2020, 4, 3)])

timetable = Table([timelist], names=("timestamp",))

print(timetable)

# The read action below fails with Astropy 4.
timetable.write("DateDatetimeTable.ecsv", format='ascii.ecsv', overwrite=True)
tablefromfile = Table.read("DateDatetimeTable.ecsv", format='ascii.ecsv')
```

Also a problem (not just for `datetime`)
```
timetable.show_in_browser(jsviewer=True)
# AttributeError: 'Time' object has no attribute 'dtype'
```

title: LombScargle occasionally returns all-NaN powers
description:
### Description
I want to use LombScargle to calculate the spectral window function of my observations, but sometimes I get an array of NaNs returned for powers. I'm not sure what governs the conditions for this error, but so far I've only encountered it when the input `y` grid is populated with a single value.

### Expected behavior
Input an array `t` and a same-sized array `y` where all y-values are 1, get back some powers corresponding to the window function.

### Actual behavior
Sometimes this works as expected. Other times, the output powers are an array of NaNs and the following warning is raised:

> /Users/mbedell/miniconda3/envs/exoplanet/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/timeseries/periodograms/lombscargle/implementations/fast_impl.py:125: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in true_divide
>  power /= YY

### Steps to Reproduce
Here is a snippet of code that reproduces the error:

```python
from astropy.timeseries import LombScargle
np.random.seed(42)
N = 180
xs = np.arange(N) + np.random.normal(0., 0.1, N)
ys = np.ones_like(xs)
frequency, power = LombScargle(xs, ys).autopower(method='fast')
np.isfinite(power).any()
```
(should raise a warning and return `False`)

Changes to the above code that do not fix the error:
- changing autopower method (I have tried 'slow' and 'chi2' with same results)
- changing the random seed/rerunning the randomization
- specifying a frequency grid as an input
- making the `xs` grid perfectly uniformly spaced (no random perturbations)

Changes to the above code that *do* fix the error and return sensible powers:
- changing `N` to nearly any other integer (I haven't tried an exhaustive list but for example 179 or 181 work just fine, as do other random ones I've tried. However, `N = 180` is definitely not the only number that can reproduce this bug - `N = 256` behaves similarly.)
- scaling `ys` by some factor - this fixes the error if and only if the factor is not a multiple of 180, as far as I can tell. That is, `ys = np.ones_like(xs)/100` fixes the error, but `ys = np.ones_like(xs)/180` does not. Again, I haven't tried factors exhaustively, so take that theory with a grain of salt.
- making the values of `ys` different from each other, e.g.:
`ys = np.ones_like(xs) * np.random.normal(1., 0.01, N)`

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
CompoundModel slicing depends on the tree structure, and this structure does not permit all valid slicing operations. In particular, for long chains of models combined with |, the valid slices depend on the order in which this chain was constructed. So if I construct `m = A | B | C`, where A, B, and C are models, then I can slice to get `m[:2] = A | B`, but not `m[1:] = B | C`.

I can create `m = A | (B | C)`, which allows me to slice `m[1:] = B | C` but now I can't do `m[:2] = A | B`. This might be reasonable behaviour, since I have explicitly connected B and C and suggested they're inseparable, but the first example _should_ allow all slices. The problem, of course, is that it's constructed like `m = (A | B) | C` because every operator produces a `CompoundModel` that creates a tree node, but in reality there are really three leaves springing from a single top node.

## Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
I expected to obtain a valid slice that combined the last two submodels.

### Actual behavior

`IndexError: No appropriate subtree matches slice`

title: SkyCoord.directional_offset_by only allows a single vector input
description:
### Description
It would be useful to allow giving `SkyCoord.directional_offset_by` and similar functions multiple vector inputs and have them return ND matrices.

### Expected behavior
Ideally I'd like to be able to offset vector coordinates by multiple angles and directions and get a multidimensional `SkyCoord` back (without needing to loop over anything).

For example, say I have a telescope with a field of view of 10 arcminutes. For a set of points I want to find the extent of the field, i.e. the northernmost/southernmost/easternmost/westernmost point visible, which means offsetting by 10 arcminutes with angles of [0,90,180,270] degrees.

This works for a single coordinate:

```python
>>> from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
>>> from astropy import units as u

>>> coord = SkyCoord(0*u.deg, 0*u.deg)
>>> angles = [0, 90, 180, 270]*u.deg
>>> coord.directional_offset_by(angles, 10*u.arcmin)
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec) in deg
    [(0.00000000e+00,  1.66666667e-01), (1.66666667e-01,  1.02053756e-17),
     (0.00000000e+00, -1.66666667e-01), (3.59833333e+02, -3.06161268e-17)]>
```

But this isn't currently simple for multiple coordinates. The neatest way of doing that (I think) would be:

```python
>>> coords = SkyCoord([0,10,20,30]*u.deg, [0,10,20,30]*u.deg)
>>> angles = [0, 90, 180, 270]*u.deg
>>> coords.directional_offset_by(angles, 10*u.arcmin)
...
```

Here I'd like back a 4x4 matrix, with each of the four input coordinates moved in the 4 directions. 

### Actual behavior

Right now if you do the above you get back a 4x1 SkyCoord. In this case the 1st point has been moved north, the 2nd point has been moved east etc. It's mapping the `i`th angle to the `i`th coordinate. 
```python
>>> coords = SkyCoord([0,10,20,30]*u.deg, [0,10,20,30]*u.deg)
>>> angles = [0, 90, 180, 270]*u.deg
>>> coords.directional_offset_by(angles, 10*u.arcmin)
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec) in deg
    [( 0.        ,  0.16666667), (10.16923775,  9.99995726),
     (20.        , 19.83333333), (29.80755009, 29.99986005)]>
```

And if `len(coords) != len(angles)` then it raises a `ValueError`. If for example I only wanted to move north and south:

```python
>>> coords = SkyCoord([0,10,20,30]*u.deg, [0,10,20,30]*u.deg)
>>> angles = [0, 180]*u.deg
>>> coords.directional_offset_by(angles, 10*u.arcmin)
ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (2,)
```

And likewise if I had more coordinates. This matters for survey telescope trying to operate on a grid of tiles, we might want to pass in several thousand coordinates and find the extent of the FoV at each point.

### Current workaround

Now to be clear the behaviour the function currently has is still useful, so I wouldn't want to break that. And there are also ways around this to do what you want: you can loop over the coordinates or the angles, and then with a bit of reshaping I could get what I was was looking for:

```python
>>> coords = SkyCoord([0,10,20,30]*u.deg, [0,10,20,30]*u.deg)
>>> angles = [0, 180]*u.deg
>>> SkyCoord([coords.directional_offset_by(angle, 10*u.arcmin) for angle in angles]).reshape(len(angles),len(coords)).T
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec) in deg
    [[( 0.,  0.16666667), ( 0., -0.16666667)],
     [(10., 10.16666667), (10.,  9.83333333)],
     [(20., 20.16666667), (20., 19.83333333)],
     [(30., 30.16666667), (30., 29.83333333)]]>
```

There would have to be some other option in `directional_offset_by` to return a matrix instead of mapping one-to-one.

And for completeness I believe this could apply to `position_angle` and `separation` too. If you had a set of N coordinates and wanted to find the separation to M targets you'd currently have to loop though one or the other, it would be nice if you could create the matrix instead.

title: Resource error when accessing IERS data using multiprocessing
description:
*From https://stackoverflow.com/questions/61043112/astropy-multiprocessing-access-to-iers-data, this looks like a IERS issue related to multiprocessing:*

We are using astropy to perform large SKA simulations running in Dask on single nodes or cluster. We use both Time and astroplan.Observer in our calculations. Some fraction of the time, we see errors in access of the IERS data. For example:
```
rascil/processing_components/visibility/base.py:275: in create_blockvisibility
570     from astroplan import Observer
571 /usr/local/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astroplan/__init__.py:32: in <module>

576     with _open_shelve(urlmapfn, True) as url2hash:
577 /usr/local/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astroplan/utils.py:322: in _open_shelve
578     shelf = shelve.open(shelffn, protocol=2)
579 /usr/local/lib/python3.7/shelve.py:243: in open

None of these have helped. We still see the same gdbm errors.

### Description

The current documentation makes it seem like it should be possible to have a column with quantities that are masked. `QTable` for example allows for `masked=True`. There are many examples throughout the documentation (for example [here](https://astropy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/table/masking.html#table-creation)) which show a masked column in a `QTable`.

### Expected behavior
```python 
from astropy.table import QTable, MaskedColumn
import astropy.units as u

tbl = QTable(masked=True)
tbl.add_column(MaskedColumn([1, 2] * u.keV, mask=[True, False]))

 2.0
```

<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
```python 
from astropy.table import QTable, MaskedColumn
import astropy.units as u

tbl.add_column(MaskedColumn([1, 2] * u.keV, mask=[True, False]))
print(tbl)

output
col0
keV 
----
 1.0
 2.0
```

Given that masked Quantities arrays are not a thing (see #1852), I would recommend that there be a note or warning adding to the documentation to make it crystal clear that it is currently not possible to make a `MaskedColumn` with quantities. I might even go so far as to issue a warning when a user tried to create a `MaskedColumn` with quantities.

title: Support surface brightness in units of mag/arcsec2, etc.
description:
Request from @robertoabraham - support surface brightness in magnitudes.

This may be rather tricky to get right, with surface brightness often quoted in terms of `mag/arcsec2`, which is a very strange unit in that conversion to `mag/arcmin2` implies not multiplication by 3600 but rather subtraction of `-2.5*log10(3600)`, so effectively one has to think of the `/arcsec2` as being part of the physical unit of the magnitude zero reference flux. Supporting it may require a separate class, though perhaps we can get away with being careful about just surface area (cannot think about any other physical unit for which this is done...).

Right now, for proper magnitude units, it simply fails, while for `u.mag` it does the wrong thing:
```
u.ABmag/u.arcsec**2
# UnitsError: Cannot divide a function unit with a physical dimension by any unit.
(20*u.mag/u.arcsec**2).to(u.mag/u.arcmin**2)
# <Quantity 72000. mag / arcmin2>
```

title: API enhancement: Provide a standard "variance" property in all NDUncertainty classes, accessible to the parent NDData
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md .
Please be sure to check out our code of conduct,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . -->

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->
The abstraction of `nddata.uncertainty` to different classes is a good one, but makes writing generic code difficult. If I have an `NDData` instance and want to plot the data with errorbars based on the `uncertainty`, I need to write code to modify the `uncertainty.array` according to the class of the uncertainty. Similarly, if I want to combine multiple `NDData` instances with some sort of weighting based on their uncertainties (e.g., inverse-variance is commonly used) I also need to have such code.

I therefore propose that all NDUncertainty classes have a property that returns as uniform as possible a measure of uncertainty, where such a thing can be defined. "variance" and "standard deviation" are suitable candidates, which are well-defined for the three existing classes and Poisson statistics. This property can be accessed by the parent NDData, so I can do the following

```
var = ndd.variance
```

instead of

```
unc = ndd.uncertainty
if isinstance(unc, StdDevUncertainty):
    var = unc.array ** 2
elif isinstance(unc, VarUncertainty):
    var = unc.array
elif isinstance(unc, IVarUncertainty):
    var = 1. / unc.array
else:
    var = None
```

If the variance (or whatever statistical property is chosen) is well-defined (as it is here), then it can/should also be settable on the NDData, simply passing it to its `uncertainty` to handle via the inverse calculations to those listed above. If the property is not well-defined, then `None` can be returned (which the parent NDData can return if its `uncertainty` raises an Exception because this hasn't been implemented).

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

Currently the `__setitem__` support for `BaseFrame` and `SkyCoord` require that frame attributes are exactly the same in the object being updated and the right hand side value.  Some WIP code that would help in making things somewhat more flexible is shown below and was removed from #9857  in 8b161db70.  See also https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/9857#pullrequestreview-385950530.

For instance there is no reason that one should not be able to do:
```
sc1 = SkyCoord([1]*u.deg, [2]*u.deg, obstime='J2001')
sc2 = SkyCoord([3]*u.deg, [4]*u.deg, obstime='J2010')
t1 = Table([sc1])
t2 = Table([sc2])
table.vstack([t1, t2])
```
### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

```
@contextlib.contextmanager
def _set_time_writeable_true(obj):
    """Context manager to allow __setitem__ to operate on frame attributes.

    Not used in current implementation which just insists that they are
    equivalent but see commit 4e3f99943.
    """
    is_time = isinstance(obj, Time)
    try:
        if is_time:
            writeable = obj.writeable
            obj.writeable = True
        yield
    finally:
        if is_time:
            obj.writeable = writeable

def _frame_attribute_setitem(frame, attr, item, value):
    """Set a frame attribute ``frame.attr[item] = value```

    This is not used in the current implementation of __setitem__ but here in
    the WIP for reference of what might be possible.

    The trick is that frame attributes can be scalars and they might need to be
    broadcast to the SkyCoord shape.  For example if a SkyCoord ``sc1`` has
    shape=(3,) with scalar equinox='B1999', and ``sc2`` has equinox='B2015',
    then setting ``sc1[1] = sc2[2]`` needs to make sc1.equinox into shape=(3,)
    and result in ['B1999', 'B2015', 'B1999'].

    It isn't obvious if this can cause problems, so don't do that without
    some discussion.
    """
    _attr = '_' + attr
    frame_attr = getattr(frame, _attr)
    value_attr = getattr(value, _attr)
    frame_attr_shape = getattr(frame_attr, 'shape', ())

    # If all the same then do nothing
    if np.all(frame_attr == value_attr):
        return

    # At this point we need to ensure frame_attr has the same shape as frame
    # because ``item`` is referenced to frame shape and we will set frame_attr[item].
    if frame_attr_shape == ():
        frame_attr = frame_attr.take(np.zeros(frame.shape))
        setattr(frame, _attr, frame_attr)

    elif frame_attr_shape != frame.shape:
        # How to broadcast a ShapedLikeNDArray subclass like Time. E.g.
        # an obstime attribute with shape (3,) and the frame has shape (10, 3).
        raise NotImplementedError('help me @mhvk!')

    # Finally do the setting
    frame_attr[item] = value_attr
```

I obtained the FITS files from  the [SDO JSOC](http://jsoc.stanford.edu/ajax/lookdata.html?ds=hmi.Ic_720s) but this requires users to register email and learn how to request data. I have the file temporarily available [here ](https://arg.usask.ca/wheels/SDO/hmi.Ic_720s.20170530_000000_TAI.3.continuum.fits) if you want to replicate the problem. 

I actually think this is not really a bug in astropy.io.fits but is due to the SDO HMI team using NaN values which is beyond the FITS standard (I think). Unfortunately this is a good idea and they obviously have FITS software that lets them create these files.  From a pragmatic point of view it might make sense for astropy.io.fits to also support the option, which seems to be relatively straight forward,  so it can keep up with other FITS software out there. 

I have done some diagnostics outlined below and I have hacked my version of astropy to allow me to keep on working with the SDO HMI data.


### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
I hoped astropy.io.fits  would read the SDO HMI continuum FITS file  without issue. It consists of one 2-D image, 4096x4096 numbers. 

The problem seems to be that the SDO HMI people have encoded "nan" values into some of the  CARD values used in their FITS file.  This is not supported by astropy.io.fits and may not be part of the FITS standard. Unfortunately it is used by the HMI instrument.

Other people have seen this problem and reported issues on [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/59450462/getting-nan-values-while-trying-to-convert-fits-file-to-ndarray-using-astropy). 

The sample code is straight-forward but must use SDO HMI data files.  The example is shown below. The fits.open line works without issue but crashes on the line data = hdul[1].data.

```
    from astropy.io import fits
    
    fullname='hmi.Ic_720s.20170530_000000_TAI.3.continuum.fits'
    hdul =  fits.open(fullname)
    data =  hdul[1].data
```
Curiously the code does not always crash when using the PyCharm/Python debugger environment. I suspect the debugger is calling many @Property based values when it displays variable values and this is circumventing the normal internal caching and checking going on inside the FITS code. Definitely complicates debugging.

The code always crashes when it runs without a debugger. The following errors are output when executing the last line,

I am relying on SkyOffsetFrame to do some of the coordinate transformation to describe an array of detectors on the sky, then I found the code does not perform in a predicable fashion. After some tracking, I was able to come up the code (listed below) to demonstrate the bug.

In short, SkyOffsetFrame is implemented as a factory, which means classes like `SkyOffsetFrameICRS`, `SkyOffsetFrameAltAz`, etc. are created on the fly. One issue with this is that both these classes have a `CoordinateAttribute` named `origin`, and this is registered into the global `frame_transform_graph` (an instance of `TransformGraph`) though the `frame_attrs_from_set` convenient function, which does an iterative dict update according to the classes listed in `frame_transform_graph.frame_set`. When both `SkyOffsetFrameICRS` and `SkyOffsetFrameAltaz` are present in this set, the order of dict update is undetermined. As a consequence, the `frame_transform_graph.frame_attributes` sometimes contain `origin` object from the former, sometimes the latter.

### Description

<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->
I was investigating a bottleneck in a Python library and found that converting UTC unix seconds to TAI unix seconds using AstroPy was surprisingly slow.

I wrote some custom Python code that uses bisect (and the leap second table from AstroPy) and got a factor of 350 better performance (which was enough to fix our bottleneck).

I expected AstroPy to be somewhat slower, because it is more general; but I did not expect such a large discrepancy. I am hoping if would be practical to improve AstroPy's performance using a similar algorithm.

I am happy to work on that if it seems practical, but I didn't want to go diving into the code without some feedback from experts as to whether it seems feasible.

### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

Here is the code, including timing comparison to two simple AstroPy variants:
```python
"""Time three ways to convert UTC unix seconds to TAI unix seconds:

1: Custom code that uses bisect and the leap second table from AstroPy.
2: Simple astropy.time code using MJD.
3: Even simpler astropy.time using a custom time scale class from "mhvk".

On my macOS system I get (with some fluctuation, naturally):
tai_from_utc1: iter/sec=701879
tai_from_utc2: iter/sec=1858: 378 times slower than 1
tai_from_utc3: iter/sec=1576: 1.18 times slower than 2
"""
import bisect
import datetime
import itertools
import math
import time

import astropy.time
import astropy.utils.iers


class TimeUnixTAI(astropy.time.TimeUnix):
    """unix_tai time scale from mhvk

    https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10052
    """

    name = "unix_tai"
    epoch_scale = "tai"


SECONDS_PER_DAY = 24 * 60 * 60

# MJD - unix seconds, in seconds
MJD_MINUS_UNIX_SECONDS = (
    astropy.time.Time(0, scale="utc", format="unix").utc.mjd * SECONDS_PER_DAY
)


def make_leap_second_table():
    ap_table = astropy.utils.iers.LeapSeconds.auto_open()
    lp_list = [
        (
            astropy.time.Time(
                datetime.datetime(row["year"], row["month"], 1, 0, 0, 0), scale="utc"
            ).unix,
            row["tai_utc"],
        )
        for row in ap_table
        if row["year"] >= 1972
    ]
    lp_list.append((ap_table.expires.unix, None))
    return lp_list


LEAP_SECOND_TABLE = make_leap_second_table()


def tai_from_utc1(utc_unix):
    """Convert UTC unix seconds to TAI unix seconds.

    Use bisect and a leap second table from AstroPy.
    """
    i = bisect.bisect(LEAP_SECOND_TABLE, (utc_unix, math.inf))
    if i == 0:
        raise ValueError(f"{utc_unix} < {LEAP_SECOND_TABLE[0][0]}")
    if i >= len(LEAP_SECOND_TABLE):
        raise ValueError(f"{utc_unix} > {LEAP_SECOND_TABLE[-1][0]}")
    utc0, tai_minus_utc0 = LEAP_SECOND_TABLE[i - 1]
    utc1, tai_minus_utc1 = LEAP_SECOND_TABLE[i]
    if utc_unix + SECONDS_PER_DAY > utc1 and tai_minus_utc1 is not None:

title: A model that maps multiple models via array mask?
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,

Please be sure to check out our code of conduct,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . -->

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

I am working on creating a model to describe a set of detectors which are grouped in to three arrays, denoted as a0, a1, and a2.

For the three arrays, I have models m0, m1 and m2, respectively, to convert the (x, y) positions to a common coordinate frame (dlon, dlat).

To do that, I have created the following model:

```
class ArrayProjModel(ProjModel):
    """A model that transforms the detector locations per array to
    a common instrument coordinate system.

    """
    n_inputs = 3
    n_outputs = 2

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        # omitted definition of m0, m1, and m2
        m_projs = dict(a0=m0, a1=m1, a2=m2)
        self._m_projs = m_projs
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.inputs = ('array_name', 'x', 'y')
        self.outputs = ('dlon', 'dlat')

    def evaluate(self, array_name, x, y):
        out_unit = u.deg
        x_out = np.empty(x.shape) * out_unit
        y_out = np.empty(y.shape) * out_unit
        for n in self.array_names:
            m = array_name == n
            xx, yy = self._m_projs[n](x[m], y[m])
            x_out[m] = xx.to(out_unit)
            y_out[m] = yy.to(out_unit)
        return x_out, y_out

    @property
    def array_names(self):
        return ['a0', 'a1', 'a2']

    def prepare_inputs(self, array_name, *inputs, **kwargs):
        # this is necessary to handle the array_name inputs
        array_name_idx = np.arange(array_name.size).reshape(array_name.shape)
        inputs_new, broadcasts = super().prepare_inputs(
                array_name_idx, *inputs, **kwargs)
        inputs_new[0] = np.ravel(array_name)[inputs_new[0].astype(int)]
        return inputs_new, broadcasts
```

I am just wondering if there is any better solution than what I have above. I feel that this paradigm is encountered quite often, so we may want to make a helper function or a new composition operator to create a conditional model using a list of models.

One thing that I noticed is the gwcs LableMapper/RegionSelector machinery, which happens to hide the label-to-model mapping details in the implementation, which is similar to what I used in the above code. In fact, in their documentation https://gwcs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gwcs/ifu.html , it mentions that one could define a custom model storing transforms in a dictionary on their own.

On a separate note, the `prepare_inputs` override is necessary to work around the issue that there is a `np.asarray(input, float)` call, which does not work for non numerical data as input. This may also be a restriction that should be lifted. A related issue on this is #9892

title: Matrix transforms for coordinate frames don't handle velocities for non-inertial frames correctly
description: ### Description I noticed this when implementing the TEME coordinate frame in #10149, which is a simple matrix rotation of IRTF around the pole. You would think that a ```DynamicMatrixTransform``` would be the correct one to use here, but if you do that, the velocities come out incorrectly. ### Additional context I believe the issue arises because the transformation is between frames that are non-inertial. For example, the transform between TEME and IRTF is (roughly) to rotate IRTF by the GMST around the pole. But IRTF is a non-inertial frame with it's own velocity, so the correct transform is: However, because the DynamicMatrixTransform doesn't have any of this context about inertial or non-inertial frames, the transform [actually performed](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/coordinates/representation.py#L1139) is: My work-around was to use a finite-difference transform instead, but we should check if this issue affects any current transforms, and perhaps thing about fixing it. A fix is non-trivial though, since the transformation code is implemented on the ```Representation```, which is unaware of what frame owns it, but the knowledge of the inertial nature of the frame, should be held at the frame level....

title: Citing the literature in the narrative documentation
description: I realized while writing some documentation today that we don't have best practice guidelines for citing the academic literature. The numpydoc guidelines do give a recommendation on citations in https://numpydoc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format.html (basically using e.g. [1] and then having a ``References`` section in the docstring) but it would be nice to make sure we agree on a similar set of guidelines for narrative docs. So a concrete proposal is to use numerical references as done for example in https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/timeseries/lombscargle.html, except that we would rename the references section to just 'References' instead of 'Literature References'. Another option (or maybe complementary since this may be more about how to manage the references) is to look into something like [sphinx-bibtex](https://sphinxcontrib-bibtex.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). We should also decide what style we want for citations, preferably a style that can be exported from ADS? And should we include DOI or ADS links?

The goal of the [CodeMeta Project](https://codemeta.github.io/) is to standardize metadata for software packages.  A librarian friend of mine strongly suggested that open source software projects have a CodeMeta file in order to facilitate greater discoverability.  In the future, I'm expecting CodeMeta files to be able to be used for auto-populating uploads to Zenodo, so this could eventually end up making the process of uploading a release to Zenodo more automated.

title: Consider creating coordinate frames that map on to standard velocity frames
description:
As part of the work on https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10185, the issue came up a few times about how we should deal with different velocity frames in astropy, which aren't already covered by existing coordinate frames. For example, while ICRS can be used to represent a frame that is stationary relative to the solar system barycenter, we don't have any frames at the moment which co-move with the LSRK or LSRD velocity frames or other commonly used frames (e.g. the WCS standard also defines a galactocentric velocity frame, a local group velocity frame, and a CMB dipole velocity frame).

So in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10185, we create specific coordinate instances that can represent such velocity frames:

```python
    LSRK_GORDON1975 = FK4(x=0 * u.km, y=0 * u.km, z=0 * u.km,
                          v_x=-20 * u.km / u.s * np.cos(270 * u.deg) * np.cos(30 * u.deg),
                          v_y=-20 * u.km / u.s * np.sin(270 * u.deg) * np.cos(30 * u.deg),
                          v_z=-20 * u.km / u.s * np.sin(30 * u.deg),
                          representation_type='cartesian',
                          differential_type='cartesian',
                          equinox='B1900')
```

In fact, this is a specific point in space, but we can use it as a proxy for defining the LSRK reference frame. The downside of this is that the user will never actually see the words 'LSRK' spelt out when introspecting ``SpectralCoord`` objects:

```python
    >>> sc_ttau.with_observer_in_velocity_frame_of(sc_ttau.LSRK_GORDON1975)  # doctest: +REMOTE_DATA +FLOAT_CMP
    <SpectralCoord [200.01903338, 210.01998505, 220.02093672, 230.02188838,
                    240.02284005, 250.02379172, 260.02474339, 270.02569506,
                    280.02664673, 290.0275984 , 300.02855007] GHz
        observer:
          <FK4 Coordinate (equinox=B1900.000, obstime=2019-04-24T02:32:10.000): (x, y, z) in m
              (-1.27820157e+11, -7.20621074e+10, -3.12431755e+10)
           (v_x, v_y, v_z) in km / s
              (1.51824951e-05, 17.32048573, -9.99998236)>
        target:
          <ICRS Coordinate: (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, pc)
              (65.497625, 19.53511111, 144.321)
           (pm_ra_cosdec, pm_dec, radial_velocity) in (mas / yr, mas / yr, km / s)
              (1.37949782e-15, 1.46375638e-15, 23.9)>
        observer to target (computed from above):
          radial_velocity=12.506991149252126 km / s
          redshift=4.171970213029397e-05>
```

Instead, they see an FK4 object. Just to put a couple of possible solutions out there for discussion:

**Option 0:** Status quo, don't change anything, which means no additional development but will almost certainly frustrate users.

**Option 1:** In principle we could create a whole new set of classes that represent pure velocity frames with no origin, and to somehow allow velocities to optionally be defined in a separate frame than the location, so for example:

```python
          <ICRS Coordinate: (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, pc)
              (65.497625, 19.53511111, 144.321)
           (v_x, v_y, v_z) in km/s
              LSRK: (1.0, 2.2, -3.1)>
```

The default would be the current behavior of interpreting them in the same frame of reference. This has the benefit that a user can easily say e.g. 'I want to set up an object with Galactocentric coordinates XYZ and with a velocity relative to LSRD of VXVYVZ', a task that is extremely difficult for anyone but the astropy.coordinates developers at the moment.

**Option 2:** An alternative is that we could consider using regular coordinate frames (perhaps based on ICRS) that differ only in their velocities to defined velocity frames, so for example we could define ``ICRS_LSRK`` or ``ICRS_LSRK_GORDON1975`` which is the ICRS coordinate system which moves relative to ``ICRS`` using the ``LSRK`` velocities. This is not a perfect solution because really the velocities aren't ICRS any more than Galactic - they are just define

title: Serialization of mixin columns can fail due to unexpected name clashes
description:
Simple example:
```
from astropy.coordinates import EarthLocation
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.table import Table
el = EarthLocation([0, 1]*u.deg, [0, 1]*u.deg)
q = [2., 3.]*u.m
t = Table([q, el], names=['x', 'el'])
t.write('a.fits', format='fits', overwrite=True)
Table.read('a.fits').colnames
# ['el']
# Oops, column 'x' disappeared.
```
The column only disappears when its name matches one of the `EarthLocation` components (which is why this was likely not caught earlier; I was trying to save `SphericalRepresentation` in `fits/tests/test_connect.py`, which also saves `lon` and `lat`, and they both disappeared).

The problem is in reading, not writing: `a.fits` does contain `x`. The same happens for `ecsv`, so it is likely in `serialize.py`.

@taldcroft - if you have any immediate clue, let me know.  I'm stuck in zoom for most of the day.

title: SkyCoord lose their differentials when written/read back as table columns
description:
Split out from https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10210#issuecomment-620527211 by @taldcroft:
```
>>> sc = SkyCoord([270] * u.deg, [30] * u.deg, [10] * u.Mpc, radial_velocity=[20] * u.km / u.s)
>>> t = Table([sc])
>>> t['col0']
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    [(270., 30., 10.)]
 (radial_velocity) in km / s
    [(20.,)]>
>>> t.write('junk.ecsv', overwrite=True)
>>> t2 = Table.read('junk.ecsv')
>>> t2['col0']
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    [(270., 30., 10.)]>
```
Oops, the differentials are gone...

This is because in `SkyCoordInfo`, only the regular components are looked at for serialization. Indeed, things sort-of work with the following patch to `SkyCoordInfo` (in `sky_coordinate.py`):
```
    def _represent_as_dict(self):
         obj = self._parent
-        attrs = (list(obj.representation_component_names) +
-                 list(frame_transform_graph.frame_attributes.keys()))
-
+        attrs = list(obj.representation_component_names)
         # Don't output distance if it is all unitless 1.0
         if 'distance' in attrs and np.all(obj.distance == 1.0):
             attrs.remove('distance')
 
+        diff_s = obj.data.differentials.get('s')
+        if diff_s is not None:
+            attrs += [name for (name, diff_comp_name)
+                      in obj.get_representation_component_names('s').items()
+                      if hasattr(diff_s, diff_comp_name)]
+
+        attrs += list(frame_transform_graph.frame_attributes.keys())
+
```

However, in the example above one gets extraneous columns popping up:
```
In [2]: sc = SkyCoord([270] * u.deg, [30] * u.deg, [10] * u.Mpc, radial_velocity=[20] * u.km / u.s)

Out[4]: 
{'ra': <Longitude [270.] deg>,
 'dec': <Latitude [30.] deg>,

 'radial_velocity': <Quantity [20.] km / s>,

In [5]: sc.info._represent_as_dict()

{'ra': <Longitude [270.] deg>,

 'pm_dec': <Quantity [-4.68402043e-20] mas / yr>,

This seems to be related to some representation changes being done while trying to access all coordinate and frame-transfer graph attributes on the `SkyCoord`. (Not yet had time to investigate which is the culprit.)
