title: Requesting two additional built-in frames.
description:
Issue #1: The positions of the bodies are returned in the GCRS and there appears to be no way to easily transform them to topocentric astrometric positions. By this I mean simply the difference in the ICRS position of the body compensated for light time and the ICRS position of the observer. This is rather important if one wishes to place the body on a background map in the ICRS. It is also the only way to compare the output of AstroPy's ephemerides with that of JPL Horizons or Brandon Rhodes' Skyfield. Why isn't there a built-in frame for doing this?

Issue #2: Currently, there is also no built-in frame for transforming the returned positions to classical apparent place. By this I mean the topocentric position with respect to the true equator and equinox of date. This is quite important to people such as myself who still like their origin of right ascension to be an actual location on the sky rather than a convenient mathematical construct. It allows one to point an equatorial mounted telescope using the local sidereal time to calculate the hour angle. And again, this is the only way to compare the output of AstroPy's ephemerides with that of JPL Horizons or Skyfield. It is also quite simple to do. Just adjust the CIRS right ascension by subtracting the equation of the origins. Note: I did find a function for doing this in solar_system.py, _apparent_position_in_true_coordinates(), but it feels sort of kludgy to use this. There should be a built-in frame for this.

title: Requesting local earth rotation angle and one additional built-in frame
description:
Just as I find it frustrating that the Time package provides local sidereal time, but the coordinate package doesn't currently include a built-in frame providing topocentric position with respect to the true equator and equinox of date (issue #10230), I find it equally frustrating that the Time package doesn't provide the local earth rotation angle to complement the coordinate package's built-in CIRS frame. When working with an equatorial mounted telescope both a set of equatorial coordinates and its complementary time or angle are required in order to calculate the hour angle necessary to point the telescope. The Time package should be enhanced to provide the local earth rotation angle. 

In this regard, it would also be nice to provide a built-in frame to transform CIRS coordinates to observed equatorial coordinates to complement the AltAz built-in frame. This should provide both declination and hour angle (or right ascension if the local earth rotation angle is available) adjusted for refraction and polar motion. This would be very simple as the same function that is used by AltAz (atioq()) provides these also.

title: Add equivalency for converting relativistic redshift to velocity

                pm_ra_cosdec=0 * u.mas/u.yr, pm_dec=0 * u.mas/u.yr,

title: Longitude.std() does not drop to Angle
description:
For `Longitude` and `Latitude`, the intent is that any arithmetic operation drops them back to `Angle`, since, e.g., the standard deviation of a longitude is not a longitude anymore (with wrapping making little sense). But:
```
from astropy.coordinates import Longitude
import numpy as np
l = Longitude(np.arange(10.), 'deg')
l.std()
# <Longitude 2.87228132 deg>
```
The method -> `_wrap_function` -> `_result_as_quantity` -> `_new_view` path bypasses `_no_angle_subclass` in `__array_ufunc__`. It will need some careful thought about how to proceed.

(Found by @astrofrog [while trying to implement `SpectralQuantity`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10185#issuecomment-622109800).)

title: Add high accuracy reference tests for SpectralCoord
description: The accuracy tests added for ``SpectralCoord`` in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10185 are currently limited by the precision of the output files from Starlink (currently we test down to 20m/s). It would be good to create more stringent tests of the accuracy of SpectralCoord transformations to different velocity frames. Just to be clear, I believe the implementation in ``SpectralCoord`` is more accurate than 20m/s, but this is currently a limitation in the accuracy testing.

title: Make sure SpectralCoord implementation properly supports relativisic velocities
description:
Currently the implementation of SpectralCoord from https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10185 does correctly support inputting relativistic redshifts and converting them to the 'correct' velocities, and we do take care in a few places to add velocities using the relativistic velocity addition formula. However, there are still some cases (e.g. https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10185#discussion_r418511614) where we should be using the relativistic approach too - the remaining cases appear to be mostly related to when the observer and target are relativistic.

The bottom line is that we should go through the code in SpectralCoord carefully to determine which operations need to be updated, and add appropriate tests. Because the differentials framework in astropy.coordinates does not support relativistic calculations, we will have to hard-code some operations that we currently rely on differentials for.

Ideally it would be good to try and fix this before the final 4.1 release, but in case we don't manage, I have added a warning in the docs in #10185 regarding some unsupported relativistic cases.

title: How to deal with various LSR definitions?
description:
The wonderful new `SpectralCoord` PR (#10185) also introduced two new frames, `LSRK` and `LSRD`, and in hindsight I wonder if it is the right approach to define two new frames rather than, like for `GalactoCentric` allow the user to specify the assumed LSR velocity via a `ScienceState` - https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/coordinates/galactocentric.html

This in part since I'm not sure our current definitions are entirely consistent: e.g., `LSRK` defines the velocity vector in `FK4` - isn't it strictly defined as co-moving with `FK4` then? It's quite likely that in practice this does not matter, but I worry a bit about mixing rough and fairly precise items in our transform graph.

Anyway, this mostly simply as a question, though one that we should answer before 4.1, hence the milestone. cc @astrofrog, @eteq, @adrn.

title: Organize to avoid circular imports?
description:
In #10210, we had a travis CI windows run hang because of what seems to have been a circular import issue (still somewhat unclear why the PR mattered for it, but @pllim certainly solved the problems by moving imports in-line). This issue is mostly one about organization - can we somehow decide which packages should be considered "lower" and therefore always importable, and which "higher" and thus better done in-line. I've certainly found that `iers` is a culprit, needing the high-level `table`, but needed itself in the lower-level `time`

Anyway, as in @pllim's fix one of the "culprits" was `convert_numpy`, maybe that one at least can move from `io` to `utils`.

title: Adjust get_body to take into account location on Earth
description:
In https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10230#issuecomment-622655253, @mkbrewer noted that our `solar_system._get_apparent_body_position`, which is used in `get_body`, corrects for travel time to the center of the Earth rather than the actual location of the observer. While in general the resulting differences of a ms is not going to affect any of the locations of the planets at a level one likely cares about, the actual travel time is iterated on until it is less than `10 ns`, which is suggesting better precision. And the [docstring for `get_body`](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.coordinates.get_body.html#astropy.coordinates.get_body) also seems to suggest the actual location of the observer is used. cc @StuartLittlefair 

Also, crossref https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10230#issuecomment-622659492, in which @ayshih mentions a sunpy routine that calculates light-travel times for an arbitrary observer.

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
I obtain an incorrect conversion when involving `astropy.constants` (h) in a custom equivalency

### Snippet to reproduce
```python
import astropy.units as u
import numpy as np
from astropy.constants import m_e, h

mec2 = m_e.to("erg", equivalencies=u.mass_energy())
epsilon_equivalencies = [
    (u.Hz, u.Unit(""), lambda x: h * x / mec2, lambda x: x * mec2 / h)
]
nu = np.logspace(23, 28, 10) * u.Hz
# dimensionless energy in electron rest mass energy units
epsilon = (h * nu / mec2).to("")
print("manual conversion: ", epsilon)

epsilon = nu.to("", equivalencies=epsilon_equivalencies)
print("equivalencies conversion: ", epsilon)
```
The output reads
```bash
manual conversion:  [8.09329979e+02 2.90858114e+03 1.04528986e+04 3.75657700e+04
 1.35004377e+05 4.85180576e+05 1.74364858e+06 6.26634810e+06
 2.25200874e+07 8.09329979e+07]
equivalencies conversion:  [8.09329979e-05 2.90858114e-04 1.04528986e-03 3.75657700e-03
 1.35004377e-02 4.85180576e-02 1.74364858e-01 6.26634810e-01
 2.25200874e+00 8.09329979e+00]
```
The difference is a factor `1e-7`, which is exactly the factor between `h` in SI and cgs units.
The issue can be avoided by explicitly converting h in cgs inside the equivalency
```python
epsilon_equivalencies = [
    (u.Hz, u.Unit(""), lambda x: h.cgs * x / mec2, lambda x: x * mec2 / h.cgs)
]
```
Why the equivalency cannot handle the simplification correctly?

title: Seamless integration of WCS with coordinates
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,

issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
WCS objects should work with astropy coordinates, i.e. `all_world2pix` should accept a coordinate (vector) on input and `all_pix2world` should return a coordinate object.

Here is an example:
```
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy import wcs
import astropy.units as u

# For this example, I build a WCS from scratch so that the issue can be run easily
# but in reality I would load a WCS from a fits image
w = wcs.WCS(naxis=2)
w.wcs.crpix = [165.5,-34.7]
w.wcs.cdelt = [-0.066667, 0.066667]
w.wcs.crval = [0, -90]
w.wcs.ctype = ["RA---AIR", "DEC--AIR"]
w.wcs.set_pv([(2, 1, 45.0)])
```
I can do:
```
myobj = SkyCoord(*w.all_pix2world(123, 234, 0), unit=u.deg)
```
but would it not be much easier if the WCS already returned a coodiante?

The same is true the other way around:
```
twhya = SkyCoord.from_name('TW Hya')
w.all_world2pix(twhya.ra.deg, twhya.dec.deg, 0)
```
The following would be a lot more integrated, but fails:
```
w.all_world2pix(twhya, 0)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-184-7c8278221f9c> in <module>
----> 1 w.all_world2pix(twhya)

/nfs/melkor/d1/guenther/soft/anaconda/envs/ciao412/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astropy/wcs/wcs.py in all_world2pix(self, tolerance, maxiter, adaptive, detect_divergence, quiet, *args, **kwargs)
   1859                 adaptive=adaptive, detect_divergence=detect_divergence,
   1860                 quiet=quiet),
-> 1861             'input', *args, **kwargs
   1862         )
   1863 

/nfs/melkor/d1/guenther/soft/anaconda/envs/ciao412/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astropy/wcs/wcs.py in _array_converter(self, func, sky, ra_dec_order, *args)
   1310             "dimension, and the origin argument). Instead, {2} arguments were "
   1311             "given.".format(
-> 1312                 self.naxis, self.naxis + 1, len(args)))
   1313 
   1314     def all_pix2world(self, *args, **kwargs):

TypeError: WCS projection has 2 dimensions, so expected 2 (an Nx2 array and the origin argument) or 3 arguments (the position in each dimension, and the origin argument). Instead, 1 arguments were given.

```
### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->
We don't want to break backwards compatibility for a function as basic as this one, but we could do the following:

- for `all_world2pix` check if input is an instance of SkyCoord and treat that correctly
- for `all_world2pix`have a keyword like `return_coord_object = True`.

Note that this does not collide with APE14, which adds an WCS interface layer, but does not prohibit lower-level, existing WCS implementations to understand coordinates.

    854         if not hasattr(col_cls.info, 'new_like'):

title: Changes to SkyCoord equality incompatible with a SkyCoord frame attribute
description:
In sunpy one of the frame attributes we set on some of our frames is an `observer` attribute, which is itself a `SkyCoord`. The recent changes to coordinate equality checking in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10154 break some functionality however, because `sc1 != sc2` now errors instead of returning `False` if `sc1` is in a different frame to `sc2`.

In particular, a traceback where we are now seeing errors is
```
>       assert_quantity_allclose(implicit.separation_3d(explicit2), 0*u.AU, atol=1e-10*u.AU)

sunpy/coordinates/tests/test_transformations.py:500: 
_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _
../astropy/astropy/coordinates/sky_coordinate.py:1054: in separation_3d
    if not self.is_equivalent_frame(other):
../astropy/astropy/coordinates/sky_coordinate.py:970: in is_equivalent_frame
    if np.any(getattr(self, fattrnm) != getattr(other, fattrnm)):
../astropy/astropy/coordinates/baseframe.py:1656: in __ne__
    return np.logical_not(self == value)
_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _

self = <HeliographicStonyhurst Coordinate (obstime=2019-06-01T00:00:00.000): (lon, lat, radius) in (deg, deg, AU)
    (0., -0.72605048, 1.01396311)>
value = <HeliographicStonyhurst Coordinate (obstime=2019-12-01T00:00:00.000): (lon, lat, radius) in (deg, deg, AU)
    (0., 0.94857499, 0.98618233)>

    def __eq__(self, value):
        """Equality operator for frame.
    
        This implements strict equality and requires that the frames are
        equivalent and that the representation data are exactly equal.
        """
        is_equiv = self.is_equivalent_frame(value)
    
        if self._data is None and value._data is None:
            # For Frame with no data, == compare is same as is_equivalent_frame()
            return is_equiv
    
        if not is_equiv:
>           raise TypeError(f'cannot compare: objects must have equivalent frames: '
                            f'{self.replicate_without_data()} vs. '
                            f'{value.replicate_without_data()}')
E           TypeError: cannot compare: objects must have equivalent frames: <HeliographicStonyhurst Frame (obstime=2019-06-01T00:00:00.000)> vs. <HeliographicStonyhurst Frame (obstime=2019-12-01T00:00:00.000)>
```

Because `is_equivalent_frame`  checks all the attrs in this line:
```
../astropy/astropy/coordinates/sky_coordinate.py:970: in is_equivalent_frame
    if np.any(getattr(self, fattrnm) != getattr(other, fattrnm)):
```
it will check our observer attribute, but now the `!=` call raises an error instead of just returning `False`, when `self` and `other` are not in the same frame.

I'm not entirely sure what the best way to solve this is. One the one hand, I see conceptually why an error is now raised when trying to compare coordinates in two different frames. On the other hand, I'm not sure how to practically solve this new issue, without making `!=` return `True` when the two frames are different.

title: Account for distance properly in aticq and atciqz
description:
Both of these routines include a call to `erfa.ld` to account for light deflection from the Sun. However, in both routines we ignore any distance information and therefore treat objects in front of the Sun as if they were at large distances.

These routines need updating to fix this problem, and as a result the GCRS-ICRS transforms may need re-working, since the first step in this chain is to drop distance information and treat all objects as if they are at large distances, handling parallax separately.

cc @mhvk @mkbrewer

title: Let frames/coordinates have (internal?) has_distance function
description: In a fair number of places inside our coordinate machinery, we have to deal with coordinates with and without distances, and are testing this somewhat haphazardly - checking whether the representation is `UnitSphericalRepresentation` *or* whether it is `Spherical` and the distance is all unity. We should normalize these tests, and ideally also ensure that the second case simply doesn't happen (so that the test can be very simple).

Several `coordinates` tests now chronically fail. They pull `sites.json` from data server and are marked as "remote data" but the server is now denying access. I don't know if they would work again once the CI traffic decreases or not; i.e., if the blacklist is temporary or permanent. Because of these failures, maintainers might miss real "remote data" failures that need to be fixed (e.g., #10297 and #10299).

What are these tests really testing? Do they really need to be on the whim of internet? Can we use a local copy of `sites.json` and not mark them as "remote data"?

title: Request: way to have development testing set up with pinned test dependencies
description:
Over at #10275, @taldcroft [wrote](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10275#issuecomment-623654560):

> I have been just suggesting that the environment installed by `pip install -e .[test]` include at least some pinning (in particular on pytest which seems notorious for breaking things in ways that are inscrutable) so that local developer testing does not break suddenly for mysterious reasons. 

which is clearly better in a separate issue than in a closed one! So herewith.

Basically, the request is to have some standard way in which one can set up an environment in which one can edit code and *quickly* run the appropriate tests to see if changes worked, i.e., just to `pytest <path-to-test>`. Right now, the above `pip install -e .[test]` sometimes fails as test dependencies are upgraded, and it would be good to have a way to get an environment with a known-to-work combination.

From what @bsipocz [wrote](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10275#issuecomment-623044847):

> To reuse the env: tox creates a .tox directory for the virtualenvs inside. Run tox once to set up everything and then you can manually run the activate script to bring up the same environment and then iterate on the individual tests.

It seems this is already possible with `tox`, although at least for me it was not immediately clear how to actually do that (and be able to edit regular source code). Anyway, this "feature request" may simply be a docs update so that we all can share the best practice. For now, labeling it as such.

title: Expose wcsprm.aux in astropy.wcs
description:
WCSLIB 7.1 includes auxiliary parameters on an ``auxprm`` object:

```
  - Support Solar keywords RSUN_REF, DSUN_OBS, CRLN_OBS, CRLT_OBS,
    HGLN_OBS, and HGLT_OBS by accomodating them within an auxiliary
    struct, auxprm, within the wcsprm struct.  Now filled by the header
    parsers, wcspih() and wcsbth() and handled routinely by wcsinit(),
    wcssub(), wcscompare(), wcsfree(), wcsprt(), wcsset(), and wcshdo().
    Requested by Stuart Mumford (SunPy) with input from Bill Thompson.
```

We should expose these parameters in ``astropy.wcs``, either as an ``Wcsprm.aux`` or ``Wcsprm.auxprm`` property or a ``Wcsprm.get_aux`` method.

I gave this a try, but my C-foo isn't quite there yet, so I'd rather leave this to someone else more experienced with the inner workings of astropy.wcs! (cc @nden @mcara @MSeifert04)

The repo at https://github.com/taldcroft/astropy-changelog shows a proof of concept for changing the basis of the astropy changelog from the `CHANGES.rst` file to a new `CHANGES.yml` file.  Please see the README there for details.  The driver for this and initial discussions were captured in an astropy-dev email thread in Oct 2016 (subject "Proposal for a new changelog system"). 

This was discussed in more detail at the 2019 coordination meeting in Socorro, with the agreement at the time that @bsipocz and @Cadair would develop a different system that uses information embedded in the PR description and/or GitHub metadata. While arguably a better solution, 6 months have passed with no progress, and in fact the details of the better solution were not captured in any written form. @bsipocz has stated in private conversation that she does not have time to spend on this given many other higher priorities and is OK with the YAML solution.

I propose moving forward on the YAML solution unless @Cadair can commit to developing the better solution in the next few months. All details of the YAML solution and how it gets implemented (both code and process) are certainly open for discussion here.

The problems in the current CHANGES.rst implementation are real and persist. I personally had to rebase at least 5 times due to a changelog conflict in the last few weeks (including once literally ten minutes after the last rebase), and now I see the 5-day old #10296 is already blocked from merge because of a changelog conflict. title: Of required and optional dependencies
description:
## Description

As `astropy` grows over the years, we now have different kinds of dependencies:

* Absolutely required and documented as such: `numpy`
* Required for certain jobs, e.g., building docs and testing.
* Declared optional but really required for some subpackages, such as but not limited to:
    * `matplotlib` for `visualization.wcsaxes`
    * `asdf` for `io.misc.asdf` (this one is even cyclic, i.e., we also depend on it for schemas version or something)
    * `PyYAML` for `io.misc.yaml` and maybe even `io.fits` (see #7783) 
* Truly optional, i.e., there is a fallback alternative if the dependency is missing -- Do we really have this? Need to double check.

All the dependencies are declared in [the installation page](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/install.html) but unfortunately this page is purely informational and does not enforce anything code-wise; i.e., it will not automatically downloads `asdf` for you if you use `astropy.io.misc.asdf`. (But do we even want that?)

The complexity of these dependencies occasionally cause problems when they are missing or incompatible, resulting in but not limited to:

* Unable to use part of the code directly.
* Unable to use code in downstream package that uses our affected code.
* Unable to test the code effectively, causing bugs to slip through during development process. (Either forget to test with or without the dependency.)
* #12121

Some workaround to make the dependency optional also caused performance issue; e.g., #10302 .

## Things we could do to improve the situation

* Import-only test job as discussed in #7939 . Such a job will ensure things like, but not limited to:
   * `pytest` not required at runtime.
  * Optional dependencies don't cross-pollinate; e.g., `io.fits` would work even if `PyYAML` is not present, or `visualization.wcsaxes` is not affected by the presence or lack of `asdf`.
  * Importing `astropy` without any optional dependencies will not cause `ImportError`.
  * Defining special cases where `ImportError` is acceptable; e.g., `io.misc.asdf` can throw `ImportError` if `asdf` is not installed.
    * However, will this accidentally let real problems through?
    * Can we overload `__doctest_requires__` for this purpose or is subpackage `conftest.py` incantation sufficient?
    * Perhaps even a new `__doctest_subpackage_requires__` directive in `pytest-doctestplus` to avoid recursion into a subpackage.
* Skip test collection in `setup_package.py` to avoid problem with requiring `extension-helpers`; e.g. #10246 .
* Do not use `pytest.importorskip` in non-test code; e.g., #10302 vs #10325.
* Avoid `try ... except ...` imports in subpackage; e.g., `io.misc.asdf` should always assume `asdf` is importable.
* Parse `__init__.py` with AST rather than importing them? (This idea was given with a 😉)

What else?

## Other related issues/PRs not mentioned above

* #10260 (deemed impractical and was rejected)
* astropy/pytest-doctestplus#100
* astropy/pytest-doctestplus#110

## Disclaimer

The information here is put together from multiple discussions with many people. Feel free to comment/edit if I missed something.

title: TimeDelta comparison with float "works"
description:
Found by @paulray in https://github.com/nanograv/PINT/pull/702:
```
from astropy.time import TimeDelta

TimeDelta(1) < 10
# True
```
The reason is that `Time` tries to initiate an instance of itself in doing the comparison, so it treats numbers as `days` (default format for `TimeDelta`). I think the easiest is to be a bit less generous and simply only accept for a comparison what we actually know works, i.e., another `Time` or, for `TimeDelta`, a `Quantity`.

p.s. I see the blame is mine - clearly, in 2013, I was too enchanted with duck typing...

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/223d9c38114af67743081eabfe96566067ac8bfe/astropy/time/core.py#L2018-L2027

title: CIRS is not at the ultimate accuracy
description:
Copying @mkbrewer's https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10230#issuecomment-629491534:

>It is unfortunate that you only implement geocentric position for your CIRS frame. You use apci() and apio() rather than the more rigorous apco() which builds the observer's topocentric position and velocity (if present) right in. This has two side effects. In going from ICRS to CIRS light deflection doesn't take into account a topocentric observer's position and velocity and in going from CIRS to AltAz the less rigorous simple first-order vector expression for diurnal aberration as mentioned in paragraph 4.7 of the SOFA Astrometry Tools document is used.

It sounds like we could improve things fairly simply since GCRS seems OK:

> On the other hand, your GCRS frame does implement topocentric position rigorously. Therefore, I find it curious that you don't derive your CIRS frame from GCRS. After all, with GCRS you are just one step of applying the CIO based BPN matrix from true topocentric CIRS intermediate (apparent) place. The call to apcs() in this transform properly sets up the ASTROM data structure for rigorously calculating gravitational light deflection, diurnal aberration and diurnal parallax including the observer's position and velocity (including taking the observer's velocity into account in beta - 1). I particularly like the way that diurnal aberration is naturally included in Ab() this way, so that the transformation from topocentric CIRS to AltAz can be done without resorting to the use of astrom->diurab.

```python
import numpy as np
import os
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.io.fits.hdu.hdulist import fitsopen

filepath = os.path.expanduser("~/Downloads/foo.fits")

title: Change warn_or_raise() to vo_warn() for output.
description:
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/4d754b4b37c84602a75cc0b78138aae608c32622/astropy/io/votable/converters.py#L353

The above `warn_or_raise()` is not effective because it is used in a converter `output()` method.  Those methods do not accept the `config` arg, so do not honor the `pedantic` options (which were intended for parsing not writing).

The current behavior is OK in this case since it will warn any time this condition is detected, and will never raise an exception.  To make the code more explicit however, change the call to `vo_warn()` so that it doesn't imply that an exception is possible.

This code can trigger the warning as it writes a non-ASCII character to a `char` FIELD.

```
from astropy.io.votable.tree import VOTableFile, Resource, Table, Field

# Create a new VOTable file...
votable = VOTableFile()

# ...with one resource...
resource = Resource()
votable.resources.append(resource)

# ... with one table
table = Table(votable)
resource.tables.append(table)

# Define some fields
table.fields.extend([
        Field(votable, name="filename", datatype="char", arraysize="*")])

# Now, use those field definitions to create the numpy record arrays, with
# the given number of rows
table.create_arrays(1)

# Now table.array can be filled with data
table.array[0] = ('zła')

# Now write the whole thing to a file.
# Note, we have to use the top-level votable file object
votable.to_xml("new_votable.xml")

```

title: Initialising Table with structured dtype produces inconsistent/confusing results
description:
### Description
A discussion in the Facebook group brought up that a new, empty table can be constructed from an existing table by passing its `dtype`:
```
>>> oldtable.dtype
dtype([('wavelength', '<f8'), ('flux', '<f4'), ('uncertainty', '<f4')])
>>> Table(dtype=oldtable.dtype)
<Table length=0>
wavelength   flux  uncertainty
 float64   float32   float32  
---------- ------- -----------
```
and it is equally possible to initialise it in the more pedestrian manner
```
>>> newtable = Table(names=oldtable.colnames, dtype=[dt for n, dt in oldtable.dtype.descr])
```
but directly using the old `dtype` if `names` are already specified throws these exceptions:
```
 >>> newtable = Table(names=oldtable.colnames, dtype=oldtable.dtype)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/derek/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/table/table.py", line 621, in __init__
    self._check_names_dtype(names, dtype, n_cols)
  File "/Users/derek/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/table/table.py", line 873, in _check_names_dtype
    raise ValueError(f'{inp_str} must be a list or None')
ValueError: dtype must be a list or None

>>> newtable = Table(names=oldtable.colnames, dtype=oldtable.dtype.descr)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/derek/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/table/table.py", line 1088, in _convert_data_to_col
    col = col_cls(name=name, data=data, dtype=dtype,
  File "/Users/derek/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/table/column.py", line 879, in __new__
    self = super().__new__(
  File "/Users/derek/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/table/column.py", line 254, in __new__
    if np.dtype(dtype).char == 'S':
TypeError: data type 'wavelength' not understood
```
The same happens when the `Table` is initialised with a structured array.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
`Table` should either raise a more meaningful error, or (perhaps preferably) accept the structured `dtype`, possibly with a warning that `dtype.names` will be replaced with the specified `names`.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
See above. While the recommended method in the docs `newtable = oldtable[:0].copy()` works (and has the advantage of additionally copying any `unit` properties), the discrepant behaviour between specifying `dtype` alone, and together with `names` is potentially confusing, and the exceptions not very clear.

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/eeb9b7ac0e18b262fae64cd2fa46d0e1cff1e4d5/astropy/table/table.py#L592-L594

"unpacks" the `dtype` automatically when no other `names` information is available, and the same might be done with `names` set (but discarding `dtype.names`, since `names` should certainly take priority).
 
On a slightly related note, it would be convenient to have a method to directly get all units for the table columns in a form that could be passed as `units=`. Of course one can return to the `newtable = oldtable[:0].copy()` method, but if modifying names or dtypes is desired, such an option would come in handy.

title: Performance: quantity comparison to 0 is incredibly expensive
description:
Quantities with units can be compared to 0 without a unit, in accordance with the interpretation that quantities are products of values and units.

However, this operation is forbiddingly expensive compared to the simple accessing of the value property:

```
In [1]: import astropy.units as u                                                                         

In [2]: q = 5 * u.m                                                                                       

In [3]: %timeit q != 0                                                                                    
42 µs ± 1.17 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10000 loops each)

In [4]: %timeit q.value != 0                                                                              
607 ns ± 28 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000000 loops each)
```

description:

Out[9]: 
WCSAXES =                    2 / Number of coordinate axes                      
CRPIX1  =                  0.0 / Pixel coordinate of reference point            
CRPIX2  =                  0.0 / Pixel coordinate of reference point

This doesn't seem desirable, especially setting the date to 1858 by default at the end.

When testing Astropy v4.1rc1 on Windows 10/WSL2 + Ubuntu 18.04 (if you don't know WSL, it's basically "windows inside linux"), I see the following test failure in Astropy v4.1rc1:
```

self = <astropy.utils.iers.tests.test_leap_second.TestDefaultAutoOpen object at 0x7f434d88bad0>
tmpdir = local('/tmp/pytest-of-erik/pytest-6/test_system_file_used_if_not_e0')

    @pytest.mark.skipif(not os.path.isfile(SYSTEM_FILE),
                        reason=f'system does not have {SYSTEM_FILE}')
    def test_system_file_used_if_not_expired(self, tmpdir):
        # We skip the test if the system file is on a CI and is expired -
        # we should not depend on CI keeping it up to date, but if it is,
        # we should check that it is used if possible.
        if (iers.LeapSeconds.open(SYSTEM_FILE).expires <= self.good_enough
                and ON_CI):
            pytest.skip("CI system leap second file is expired.")

        self.remove_auto_open_files('erfa')
        with iers.conf.set_temp('system_leap_second_file', SYSTEM_FILE):
            ls = iers.LeapSeconds.open()
            assert ls.expires > self.good_enough
            assert ls.meta['data_url'] in (iers.IERS_LEAP_SECOND_FILE,
                                           SYSTEM_FILE)

            # Also check with a "built-in" file that is expired
            fake_file = make_fake_file('28 June 2017', tmpdir)
            iers.LeapSeconds._auto_open_files[0] = fake_file
            ls2 = iers.LeapSeconds.open()
            assert ls2.expires > Time.now()
>           assert ls2.meta['data_url'] == SYSTEM_FILE
E           AssertionError: assert 'https://hpie...ap_Second.dat' == '/usr/share/z...-seconds.list'
E             - /usr/share/zoneinfo/leap-seconds.list
E             + https://hpiers.obspm.fr/iers/bul/bulc/Leap_Second.dat

miniconda3/envs/test-ap41/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astropy/utils/iers/tests/test_leap_second.py:269: AssertionError

the `/usr/share/zoneinfo/leap-seconds.list` file on this setup ends at 37 (the one at the end of 2016), which is up-to-date...

The test itself actually confuses me though - I don't understand why the `SYSTEM_FILE` would be the same as the `fake_file`... Perhaps it's that this Leap_Second.dat expired at a time not expected by this test? (@mhvk may have some insight of the intent of the test here...)

res = fitter(model, x, y)

title: Stop bundling jquery?
description:
While looking at what makes astropy so big (21MB), I wondered about `jquery` (~1MB). Looking at old issues, I realize it is big in part because we need to include the actual source, but why is it included in the first place? It is used only for `table/jsviewer`, and that ignores the source if one is on-line. Would it not make more sense to just move it to the "extra" packages, so that users who really use this feature a lot *offline* can get it if they want? Or is it difficult to install? (I see a `jquery` on pypi, but that perhaps is not the same thing.)

Ping @taldcroft - for reference, `astropy/table` itself is also ~1 MB...

title: Possible bug in setting shape of Time, Representation, etc.
description:
Currently, setting the shape of a `Time` or `Representation` ~`SkyCoord`~ (edit: frames and sky coordinates cannot have their shape set) implies going through all attributes and trying to set their shape in turn, reverting if there is any `AttributeError` for items for which the shapes stride imply that the shape change is not possible. title: Change order of operations in setup.py
description:
In the ``setup.py`` file we should make sure that the checks for the ``test`` and ``build_docs`` commands come *before* the extension-helpers imports, otherwise contributors who don't have extension-helpers installed will see an import error when trying to run ``python setup.py test`` rather than the help messages. This will also need to be fixed in the coordinated packages and the package template.

(cc @aarchiba since this affected you today!)

### Description
When interactively changing vmin and vmax of an image shown with imshow, using astropy wcsaxes in the Qt5Agg MPLBACKEND figure editor python exits and an exception is raised. This happens with matplotlib 3.2.1.

### Expected behavior
Successful change of vmin and vmax.

### Actual behavior
Crash of python with backtrace:

### Steps to Reproduce

Consider this script:
```python

from astropy.visualization.wcsaxes.frame import EllipticalFrame

_, pix_b_max = w.all_world2pix(0,  89.9, 0)

plt.figure()
plt.subplot(projection = w, frame_class=EllipticalFrame)

title: Kernels allow silent overwriting of arrays
description:
For any `convolution.Kernel2D` subclass (probably 1D also), if you give an `array=` parameter, it will overwrite the underlying array and not populate the kernel as expected.  This shouldn't be allowed.  All subclasses of `Kernel2D` should catch and reject `array=` keywords.

Example:
```
x = np.ones([10,10])
kernel = Airy2DKernel(2)
normalized_ones = Airy2DKernel(2, array=x)
```

`normalized_ones` will not be an Airy2DKernel!

title: x-axis missing on WCSAxes whole sphere plot
description:
### Description
When plotting a full sphere plot (in this case it happens to be a map of the Sun), WCSAxes does not draw the x-axis when the whole map is shown. Example code is given below.

The issue is that the x-axis lies at -180deg, which is technically the same longitude as 180deg. When WCSAxes tries to work out if a given pixel location is within the valid bounds of the transformation
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/64bc74b1cef62ddf9fe764282a18ade3e879028a/astropy/visualization/wcsaxes/wcsapi.py#L356-L358
, it round trips the transformation, ie. for the bottom left corner of the bottom left pixel:
```python
pixel = (-0.5, -0.5)
world = wcs.pixel_to_world_values(*pixel)
pixel2 = wcs.world_to_pixel_values(*world)
```
`pixel2` comes out as `(array(359.5), array(-0.5))` however, which is different to the input pixel, so WCSAxes treats this as invalid, and does not draw x-axis because it thinks the spine has invalid coordinates. I think it is actually on the edge of valid pixel locations, so should be drawn.

Downstream issue at https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/3611


### Expected behavior
x-axis is drawn.

### Actual behavior
x-axis isn't drawn:
![Figure_1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6197628/83689056-4ceec900-a5e6-11ea-92f5-51600df3e6d2.png)

title: Inconsistent handling of `obstime` in FK4 transformations
description:
It appears that most transformations involving `FK4` or `FK4NoETerms` ignore the value of the `obstime` frame attribute.  The only transformations that appear to take that attribute into account are the `FK4NoETerms`<->`FK5` transformations.  Thus, you get inconsistent behavior such as:
```python
>>> from astropy.coordinates import FK4NoETerms, FK5
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> fk4 = FK4NoETerms(ra=1*u.deg, dec=2*u.deg)
>>> fk4
<FK4NoETerms Coordinate (equinox=B1950.000, obstime=B1950.000): (ra, dec) in deg
    (1., 2.)>

# A change in equinox is respected in the loopback
>>> fk4.transform_to(FK4NoETerms(equinox='J2000', obstime='B1950'))
<FK4NoETerms Coordinate (equinox=J2000.000, obstime=J2000.000): (ra, dec) in deg
    (1.6406186, 2.27827139)>

# A change in obstime is ignored in the loopback
>>> fk4.transform_to(FK4NoETerms(equinox='J2000', obstime='J2000'))
<FK4NoETerms Coordinate (equinox=J2000.000, obstime=J2000.000): (ra, dec) in deg
    (1.6406186, 2.27827139)>

# An explicit transformation through FK5 forces the change in obstime to be respected
>>> fk4.transform_to(FK5).transform_to(FK4NoETerms(equinox='J2000', obstime='J2000'))
<FK4NoETerms Coordinate (equinox=J2000.000, obstime=J2000.000): (ra, dec) in deg
    (1.64058557, 2.27833187)>
```

title: TST: Revisit tests marked as remote data that can now use offline IERS
description:
This is a follow-up of #10311: A reminder that we should revisit some remote data tests that are currently marked as remote data only because they access IERS somehow (e.g., `time`, `coordinates`). Now, with `astropy.utils.iers.conf.auto_download = False` by default in the test suite, these tests no longer needs to be remote data tests as long as they can live with possibly outdated results and have their outputs adjusted accordingly.

On the other hand, for cron jobs it would be good to keep running with new random seeds every time. (see also https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10428#issuecomment-637893577 and following)

description:

command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
As discussed with @Cadair regarding the GSoC `glue-solar` project, we found the following potential bug and would like to see if it can be fixed upstream. This bug report concerns the `__init__()` function's implemenation of the `WCSAxes` class as in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/visualization/wcsaxes/core.py#L48. Basically we are concerned with the following in particular: 

```python
def __init__(self, fig, rect, wcs=None, transform=None, coord_meta=None,
             transData=None, slices=None, frame_class=None,
             **kwargs):
    """
    """

    super().__init__(fig, rect, **kwargs)
    self._bboxes = []

    if frame_class is not None:
        self.frame_class = frame_class
    elif (wcs is not None and (wcs.pixel_n_dim == 1 or
                               (slices is not None and 'y' not in slices))):
        self.frame_class = RectangularFrame1D
    else:
        self.frame_class = RectangularFrame

    if not (transData is None):
        # User wants to override the transform for the final
        # data->pixel mapping
        self.transData = transData

    self.reset_wcs(wcs=wcs, slices=slices, transform=transform, coord_meta=coord_meta)
    self._hide_parent_artists()
    self.format_coord = self._display_world_coords
    self._display_coords_index = 0
    fig.canvas.mpl_connect('key_press_event', self._set_cursor_prefs)
    self.patch = self.coords.frame.patch
    self._wcsaxesartist = _WCSAxesArtist()
    self.add_artist(self._wcsaxesartist)
    self._drawn = False
```

We have a use case for the `glue` package where we would like to use `RectangularFrame1D` in the following code snippet to plot the 1D spectrum at a pixel extracted from a cross-section of a data cube:  

```python
self.axes.frame_class = RectangularFrame1D

    if ref_coords is None or isinstance(ref_coords, LegacyCoordinates):
        self.axes.reset_wcs(slices=self.state.wcsaxes_slice, wcs=get_identity_wcs(self.state.reference_data.ndim))
    else:
        self.axes.reset_wcs(slices=self.state.wcsaxes_slice, wcs=ref_coords)
```
However, as is, the code would automatically hide the y-axis as it has been found that even though we have set in the above `self.axes.frame_class = RectangularFrame1D`, this information has not been picked up and this `_hide_parent_artists()`:

```python
def _hide_parent_artists(self):
    # Turn off spines and current axes
    for s in self.spines.values():
        s.set_visible(False)

    self.xaxis.set_visible(False)
    if self.frame_class is not RectangularFrame1D:
        self.yaxis.set_visible(False)
```
As a result, the `self.yaxis.set_visible(False)` case becomes the default behavior and in our use case the y-axis has been unexpectedly hidden from view. 

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
We expect the y-axis in our use case to remain visible after the initialization of the `WCSAxes` class for a `RectangularFrame1D` frame. 

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
The y-axis has been hidden from view as described above. We had to manually add in the line of code 
```python
self.axes.yaxis.set_visible(True)
```

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
I have a several fits file that have 

CTYPE1  = 'DEC--TAN'           / X (Column) Axis Projection                     
CTYPE2  = 'RA---TAN'           / Y (Row) Axis Projection       
                 
which is the reverse of the "normal" order.
When using WCS and cutout2D to produce cutouts, the RA and DEC values do not point to the correct object in the image due to Astropy's handling of this reverse. 

I notice this has been discussed before but not (#4976) addressed?

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

Fits file that has reversed ctype: [http://das.sdss.org/imaging/3325/41/corr/5/fpC-003325-r5-0374.fit.gz](image)

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from astropy.visualization import LogStretch
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.nddata import Cutout2D
from astropy import wcs
from astropy import units

def _normalise(image: np.ndarray):
    m, M = np.min(image), np.max(image)
    return (image - m) / (M - m)


log_stretch = LogStretch(10000.)

filename = 'imaging/fpC-003325-r5-0374.fit.gz'
ra = 39.812583
dec = 0.47847746

img, header = fits.getdata(filename, header=True)

w = wcs.WCS(header)
print(w.wcs.ctype)

position = SkyCoord(ra*units.deg, dec*units.deg, frame="icrs")
position = wcs.utils.skycoord_to_pixel(position, wcs=w)
stamp = Cutout2D(img, position, (128, 128), copy=True)

# wrong cutout
plt.imshow(log_stretch(_normalise(img)), origin="lower", aspect="auto")
stamp.plot_on_original(color='white')
plt.show()

# correct cutout
plt.imshow(log_stretch(_normalise(img)), origin="lower", aspect="auto")
stamp = Cutout2D(img, position[::-1], (128, 128), copy=True)

stamp.plot_on_original(color='white')
plt.show()

title: Keywords' values are not replaced in fits.Header when keywords end in space
description:
### Description
Normally, when a keyword in `astropy.io.fits.Header` is set twice second value replaces previous value of the same keyword. This does not happen when keywords end in space (`' '`)

### Expected behavior
I would expect that setting a keyword value of a keyword like `'KEY '` to 1 (first time) and to 2 (second time), the second value would replace the first value.

### Actual behavior
When setting a keyword value of a keyword like `'KEY '` to 1 (first time) and to 2 (second time), the second value **does not** replace the first value. Instead the header has two cards with the same keyword with two different values (1 and 2 in this case).

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
In [1]: from astropy.io import fits
   ...: print("--- FIRST iteration ---")
   ...: hdr = fits.Header()
   ...: hdr['KEY1'] = 1
   ...: hdr['KEY2 '] = 2
   ...: print(repr(hdr))
   ...: hdr['KEY1'] = 3
   ...: hdr['KEY2 '] = 4
   ...: print("--- SECOND iteration ---")
   ...: print(repr(hdr))
   ...: print("value of 'KEY2 ' is: {}".format(hdr['KEY2 ']))
--- FIRST iteration ---
KEY1    =                    1
KEY2    =                    2
--- SECOND iteration ---
KEY1    =                    3
KEY2    =                    2
KEY2    =                    4
value of 'KEY2 ' is: 2
```
I would expect the value of `'KEY2 '` to be 4 and that there were just one entry for this keyword in the header.

If space character is supported in keyword names (i.e., if it is simply ignored, like `strip()`), then the behavior should be as expected by me. If space at the end is not supported, then I would expect to see a warning like in the following situation:
```python
In [2]: hdr['a#'] = 9
WARNING: VerifyWarning: Keyword name 'a#' is greater than 8 characters or contains characters not allowed by the FITS standard; a HIERARCH card will be created. [astropy.io.fits.card]

In [3]: hdr['a '] = 9  # No warning!

In [4]:
```

title: Consider moving away from docker based figure test builds
description:
I recently spent a day (yes really) looking into the figure test builds for sunpy, specifically surrounding how we pin the version of freetype to minimize differences with the reference images (for sunpy they are hashes of the figures so have no tolerance unlike the currently astropy test setup). This is documented in https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/pull/4271.

What I learned is that matplotlib actually does a very good job of managing its own freetype versions under normal (pip) operations. When you install matplotlib from wheels a version of freetype is included, which is determined by matplotlib. More interestingly though is that is is also true when compiling matplotlib from a git checkout, and optionally true when compiling matplotlib from a release tarball (controlled by an environment variable).

Therefore, what I think is a good compromise between reliability and simplicity is to rely on these versions of freetype as provided by matplotlib, and not use docker etc on the CI, but to have tox install a known version of matplotlib, which will have an enclosed known version of freetype. To support this approach in sunpy we also check the version of freetype at runtime, and then stop the test run before the figure comparison fails.

The upshot of this is that, as long as you run the figure tests with tox, you should always get the right version of matplotlib and freetype to be able to accurately reproduce the reference figures.

title: Should ascii.fixed_width be able to infer column start (or end) positions only from header?
description:
### Description
#10481 presented an example of a somewhat exotic table that could be parsed as `fixed_width` but would not be detected automatically. I found however that much simpler examples of tables are not always parsed as I at least expected. Take a file
```
a   b    
1   2.3  
 4  5.6e7
```
that can be read in by setting the `delimiter` option to a blank value like `None` or `' '`, which will however determine both column positions _and widths_ from the header entries:
```
>>> ascii.read(t, format='fixed_width', delimiter=None)
<Table length=2>
  a     b  
int64 int64
----- -----
    1     2
   --     5
```
One may reasonably want to read in the full content of the rows (assuming each column ends just before the start of the next one), but presently this requires explicitly specifying all column positions:
```
>>> ascii.read(t, format='fixed_width', col_starts=[0, 4])
<Table length=2>
  a       b     
int64  float64  
----- ----------
    1        2.3
    4 56000000.0
```
For (more machine- than human-readable) fixed-width tables it is not even uncommon for the content to completely fill the rows
```
a   b    
10242.345678
00425.606e07
```
to be read as
```
<Table length=2>
  a       b     
int64  float64  
----- ----------
 1024   2.345678
   42 56060000.0
```
So what I propose is a modification to `get_fixedwidth_params` allowing it to return the column `starts` only from the header entries (and infer the `ends` from them, just as if the `col_starts` argument had been given). Questions:

1. Would the column start positions indicated by the header names be enough as the typical case, as in the example above, or would we also want a complementary option determining the ends only (i.e. for right-aligned captions)?

2. If the `col_starts` case is enough, would it be acceptable to make this the default for `delimiter=None`? `delimiter=' '` could still reproduce the present behaviour, so the only case that would no longer work that way would be a table requiring the generic 'blank' delimiter (e.g. for a mix of space and `\t` separators).

I have let the `io.ascii` and `table` tests run with the 1. option made default for `delimiter=None` without any failures, so at least in the tests there seems to be no conflicting use of that delimiter setting.

Some tests may make the proposed behaviour clearer:
```
table = """\
| Col1 |  Col2     |  Col3     |  Col4     |
| 1.2  | "hello"   |  1        |  a        |
| 2.4  | 's worlds |         2 |         2 |
"""
dat = ascii.read(table, Reader=ascii.FixedWidth)


def test_read_header_col_starts():
    """Table with blank delimiter with column start positions demarked by header"""
    table = """
  Col1   Col2         Col3        Col4      
  1.2    "hello"      1           a         
  2.4    's worlds           2           2  
"""
    tab = ascii.read(table, Reader=ascii.FixedWidth, delimiter=None)
    assert_equal(tab.colnames, dat.colnames)
    for c in dat.colnames:
        if dat[c].dtype.kind == 'f':
            assert np.allclose(dat[c], tab[c])
        else:
            assert np.array_equal(dat[c], tab[c])

    # Compare delimiter=None (defining start positions) to delimiter=' ' (start and end)
    table = """
Col01  Col02   Col3 
    100  1.2345XA
    200123.4e+12A03b
"""
    tab = ascii.read(table, Reader=ascii.FixedWidth, delimiter=None)
    assert np.array_equal(tab['Col01'], np.arange(1, 3) * 100)
    assert np.allclose(tab['Col02'], np.array([1.2345, 1234]))
    assert np.array_equal(tab['Col3'], np.array(['XA', '2A03b']))

    tab = ascii.read(table, Reader=ascii.FixedWidth, delimiter=' ')
    assert np.array_equal(tab['Col01'], np.arange(1, 3))
    assert np.allclose(tab['Col02'], np.array([1.2, 123.4]))
    assert np.array_equal(tab['Col3'], np.array(['XA', '2A03']))
```

description:

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

When astropy is run on a cluster, many processes operate at once, often nearly simultaneously. If data from the Net is required, all processes are liable to request it nearly simultaneously, which is likely to cause problems. This can usually be detected when a torrent of error and failure messages appear, and prevented by loading the appropriate files into the astropy cache from a single process, up front. A key exception is when the IERS data becomes too old and needs to be refreshed; this is not easy for users to anticipate and can cause surprising problems with a job that ran fine yesterday.

Specifically:

- Request IERS data from astropy in a single process.
- Submit a cluster job that requires that same IERS data from many machines.
- Set the `auto_max_age` configuration variable to `0`.
- Re-submit the same cluster job that requires that same IERS data from many machines.

Probably only detectable after solving #9970 

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

Re-submitted jobs succeed, or fail in some way that the user can understand and that either loads the cache or tells the user how to do this.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

Many downloads are attempted at once, hammering the server and causing at least some of them to fail, producing exceptions in many jobs describing problems accessing a particular server.

Also triggers concurrency problems even with #10437 - though an extension to that might be able to resolve this issue.

title: Modernize documentation on how to use virtualenv
description:
### Description
The page on [virtualenv](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/development/workflow/virtualenv_detail.html) in the development documentation (which I believe I might have originally written most of), while still a good thing to have, is pretty outdated and should be cleaned up at some point.  A few points to highlight

* [x] In the usage instructions it still mentions the `--distribute` flag which has long been deprecated and is no longer relevant.
* [x] At the time of its original writing I don't think conda existed yet, or was not widely used.  For most beginners I would recommend conda (which we do elsewhere in the documentation) but it would be good here to clarify the relationship between conda environments and virtualenv environments (and why the former precludes use of the latter).
* [x] It would also be good to mention `venv` more prominently since it is more widely used these days, but also clarify its relationship with `virtualenv` (and why the latter is more flexible), but the former is also still useful in a pinch.
* [x] Maybe some mention of [Pipenv](https://pipenv.pypa.io/en/latest/)?
* [x] Clean up most of the documentation on using virtualenv with IPython; although there already is a notice to this effect, most of this documentation is long obsolete and would better be removed to reduce confusion.  Still, some note on how to use IPython/jupyter notebooks in a virtualenv would be good to have. 

**Update:** It turns out there is also already a newer page on working with different types of virtual environments: https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/development/workflow/virtual_pythons.html#virtual-envs  I would probably just integrate I listed above that's missing from that page, and then either remove the old page or change it to a redirect to the new one.

title: Add copy=False option to Quantity.to
description:
### Description
Currently `Quantity.to` always makes a copy of the data, even if the target unit is the same. It would be useful to call `q.to(u.m, copy=False)` which would only copy if necessary.

### Additional context
While the newish `<<` operator helps to reduce copies, it can lead to mistakes because it does two unrelated things:
1. If the left side is a quantity, it performance unit conversion (like `Quantity.to`, but only copying if necessary);
2. If the left side is some other array-like, it performs Quantity construction (like `*`, but only copying if necessary).

If a function is supposed to take a Quantity and uses `<<` to ensure that it is working in a particular unit (maybe so that future arithmetic operations won't need to do conversions, or so that unit errors are caught early), the user could accidentally pass a plain ndarray (which could be in any units) and instead of failing, it will be assumed that it's in whatever units are being converted to.

Additionally, `<<` is not convenient for working with equivalencies.

title: DOC: Update doc testing doc to reflect switch to RTD PR builder
description:
### Description

We have stopped using CircleCI + Giles to test doc build in a PR. Now, we use RTD PR builder. The main difference is that, now `[skip travis]` isn't really the right directive anymore to skip CI *except* for doc build. This is because that would still run CircleCI, which is now unnecessary.

In fact, even `[ci skip]` will not stop RTD PR builder from running. However, this might change in the future, see readthedocs/readthedocs.org#871. But until it is implemented over there, `[ci skip]` is now the right thing to do to skip CI on a PR *except* the doc build.

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

`fitscheck` uses `astropy.tests.helper.catch_warnings`:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/49708febbdaa1d1bf53f96981bf1f1d71295d33d/astropy/io/fits/scripts/fitscheck.py#L134

It should not be using a function from "test helper" module because that makes `pytest` a compulsory dependency whenever this import happens:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/49708febbdaa1d1bf53f96981bf1f1d71295d33d/astropy/io/fits/scripts/fitscheck.py#L47

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

Any non-test function should not be using stuff in `astropy.tests`.

### Blocker

An attempt to replace it with `warnings.catch_warnings` failed in #10504 , which @saimn explained beautifully at https://github.com/astropy/sphinx-astropy/issues/21#issuecomment-653692416 : 

*Basically Astropy's `catch_warnings` is overwriting the warnings defined in `setup.cfg` for pytest, by calling `treat_deprecations_as_exceptions` in its `__exit__` method. So the global `error` clause in pytest's config was ignored once Astropy's `catch_warnings` was called... When using `warnings.catch_warnings` this does not happen, so the global `error` clause is there, and the checksum verification in `io.fits` is issuing warning when the checksum is wrong, which turns into errors, which break the code's logic...*

title: Backport pyerfa#39 for astropy 4.1
description:
As discussed in #10329, the problem described in liberfa/pyerfa#38 is true for the still bundled _erfa directory:

> `erfa_generator.py` uses the locally provided headers and c sources despite PYERFA_USE_SYSTEM_LIBERFA is specified. The way it is described, one would expect that only the global headers form the system's `erfa-devel`, `liberfa-dev` or whatever it is called in the distribution package would be needed. But `erfa_generator.py` is called with `ERFA_SRC` before the check for the library.

So liberfa/pyerfa#39, which closes that issue should probably be backported to astropy and included into the 4.1 release

title: Performance of Table creation from Python lists
description:
This is mostly a question to understand what is causing the following performance hit in initialization of a table from Python lists:

```python
In [238]: import numpy as np
     ...: from astropy import table
     ...: time = list(np.random.randint(0, 1000000, 100000))
     ...: rate = list(np.random.randint(0, 1000000, 100000))
     ...: error = list(np.random.randint(0, 1000000, 100000))

In [239]: %timeit table.Table([time, rate, error], names=["time", "rate", "error"])
673 ms ± 14.5 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

In [240]: %timeit data = table.Table([np.array(time), np.array(rate), np.array(error)], \
     ...:                             names=["time", "rate", "error"])
17 ms ± 224 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```
That was with:
```
astropy: 4.2.dev360
numpy: 1.18.0
```
With updated `numpy` to `1.19.0`, timing difference is even larger:
```
In [2]: %timeit table.Table([time, rate, error], names=["time", "rate", "error"])
861 ms ± 7.78 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

In [3]: %timeit table.Table([np.array(time), np.array(rate), np.array(error)], \
   ...:                     names=["time", "rate", "error"])
16.5 ms ± 401 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```

title: Lossless gzip compression of floating-point fits image data puts incorrect ZQUANTIZ header value
description:

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
Writing floating point image data with lossless gzip compression (specifying `quantize_level=0.0`) sets `ZQUANTIZ='NO_DITHER'` in the compressed HDU header.  This is incompatible with cfitsio and funpack, which expects `ZQUANTIZ='NONE'` for unquantized data.  If you run `funpack` on a file compressed in this way you get garbage data (but no error is raised).  Note that this bug is only triggered when you explicitly set `quantize_level=0.0`, and is not triggered when quantization is automatically turned off when the fits writer cannot compute a good RMS.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
What I expect is that compressed data written by `astropy.io.fits` is readable by other standard fits readers.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
What actually happens is that you get garbage data when running `funpack` on an image compressed in this way.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

The following code assumes that `funpack` is available in the system path.

```python
import astropy.io.fits as fits
import numpy as np
import subprocess
import os
import mmap


arr = np.random.normal(size=(1000, 1000), loc=100.0, scale=10.0)

hdu_list = fits.HDUList()
hdu = fits.CompImageHDU(data=arr, header=fits.Header(),
                        compression_type='GZIP_2', quantize_level=0)
hdu_list.append(hdu)
hdu_list.writeto('test_gzip_compressed_image.fits.fz', overwrite=True)

arr2 = fits.getdata('test_gzip_compressed_image.fits.fz', ext=0)

# This test succeeds because astropy.io.fits can read these files
np.testing.assert_array_almost_equal(arr2, arr)

# Use funpack to uncompress test_gzip_compressed_image.fits.fz
if os.path.isfile("test_gzip_compressed_image.fits"):
    os.unlink("test_gzip_compressed_image.fits")
subprocess.run(["funpack", "test_gzip_compressed_image.fits.fz"])

arr3 = fits.getdata('test_gzip_compressed_image.fits', ext=0)

# This will fail because the funpack uncompress failed (silently)
np.testing.assert_array_almost_equal(arr3, arr)

# Replace the ZQUANTIZ= 'NO_DITHER' header value with NONE
# Do this manually because the Z* header keywords are reserved
with open('test_gzip_compressed_image.fits.fz', "r+b") as f:
    mm = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0)
    loc = mm.find(b"ZQUANTIZ= 'NO_DITHER'")
    if loc >= 0:
        mm.seek(loc)
        mm.write(b"ZQUANTIZ= 'NONE     '")

# Use funpack to uncompress the updated version
if os.path.isfile("test_gzip_compressed_image.fits"):
    os.unlink("test_gzip_compressed_image.fits")
subprocess.run(["funpack", "test_gzip_compressed_image.fits.fz"])

arr3 = fits.getdata('test_gzip_compressed_image.fits', ext=0)

# The following test works, the arrays are equal.
np.testing.assert_array_almost_equal(arr3, arr)
```

title: Will parsing FITS time strings with scale continue to be supported?
description:
If one does
```python
astropy.time.Time(''2000-01-01T00:00:00.000(TAI)", format='fits')
```
a warning is raised:
```python
E           astropy.utils.exceptions.AstropyDeprecationWarning: FITS time strings should no longer have embedded time scale.
```
This is fair enough, but does not specify whether support will continue for parsing these strings or not (this warning was introduced in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/7870). Either the warning should be clear that support will remain, or should provide an alternative for users that want to parse these strings (should I remove the scale? is there another argument I can pass the scale as?). I'm happy to put in a PR to improve the warning if there is guidance on what to do.

title: Add the ability to calculate the Jacaboian matrix to `astropy.wcs`.
description: ### Description A useful feature for handling coordinate transformations is the Jacobian matrix. Primarily, it allows for a local determination of how the transformation modifies area elements (by the eigenvalues/determinant) and basis orientation (by the eigenvectors). The prototypical application is to determine in the xy coordinates which directions are North and East. at a particular point in the image. In the simple case, this would just be reporting the elements of `CDi_j` correctly packed in an array, but when distortion is relevant the local Jacobian should be modified by this. This should correctly handle all of the special cases, though, like when the header specifies two scales and an angle. Ideally, the signatures of the functions should follow the coordinate transform functions. Something like `Jac_all_world2pix`, with the same arguments and meanings as the `all_world2pix` function, but which returns an `N` by `NAXIS` by `NAXIS` array, instead of just `N` by `NAXIS`. ### Additional context My primary use case is overlaying text on a ds9 image and getting the text to display upright. When the fits file does unusual things with the data axis order (i.e. the Jacobian has a reflection) and/or a 90 degree rotation, it can make the text display upside-down (even when the text angle is specified relative to the fk5 coordinates as 0.0). It would also make it more straightforward to generate compass roses to overlay on non-ds9 images.

title: BUG: `constants.pc` definition does not use small angle approximation
description:
### Description
As reported on the [mailing list](https://mail.python.org/pipermail/astropy/2020-July/004772.html) the definition of the parsec in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/28349153fcc25a9ca01bb5e563c86177c50aed1d/astropy/constants/iau2015.py#L29
uses the exact distance for a 1"-parallax object `c.au / np.tan(u.arcsec.to('radian'))` rather than the small-angle approximation `c.au / u.arcsec.to('radian')`. However the [IAU 2015 resolution B2](https://www.iau.org/static/resolutions/IAU2015_English.pdf) states (footnote 4) that 
> The parsec is defined as exactly (648 000/π) au (e.g. Cox 2000, Binney & Tremaine 2008).

([small-angle approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsec#cite_note-11)).
### Expected behavior
```
from astropy import constants as apc
from astropy import units as apu
print(apc.au.value * 180 * 3600 / np.pi)
3.085677581491367e+16 
```
### Actual behavior
```
print(apc.pc.value)
print(apc.au.value / np.tan(np.pi / (180 * 3600)))
3.0856775814671916e+16
3.0856775814671916e+16
```

Fixing the value in `iau2015.py` is trivial; perhaps to be discussed if the change should also be copied into `iau2012.py` (which implicitly certainly assumed the same definition, but did not state this).
Also `equivalencies=u.parallax()` will probably need to be adapted as well.

title: Documentation, tests, follow-up of Quantity.__array_function__
description:
Coverage of numpy functions for `Quantity` is now complete, but there are a few left-overs in the long tracking issue (#8825), which seem sufficiently separate that it is better to create a new one. This also allows to add something new, which is documentation (clearly needed, given e.g. #10573).

- [ ] Have some way to document what the expectations are for `Quantity` input for different numpy functions. Should be auto-generated and ideally uses docstrings from the routines `astropy/quantity_helpers/function_helpers`. An explicit example that has come up is `np.logspace` - see #10573; edit (2024-01-24): could use the same mechanism as done for `Masked`; see https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/utils/masked/index.html#module-astropy.utils.masked.function_helpers.
- [ ] Would be good to have some tests for `LogQuantity` such as `Magnitude`
- [ ] Also test `Angle`s such as `Longitude`
- [x] Implement support for the `like` argument to `np.zeros`, `np.ones`, `np.empty`, `np.arange`, and other functions (new in numpy 1.20; see https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/16935)

title: Document custom logarithmic units
description:
Another issue with `LogUnit`, but not specifically array-related like #10575 that came up on the mailing list a while ago:
On [defining custom **negative** log units](https://mail.python.org/pipermail/astropy/2020-June/004766.html) (in dex, not mag) – basically the OP already figured out a way to solve this by creating a custom unit type as
```
ndex = u.function.mixin.RegularFunctionUnit(['ndex'], -u.dex)                                                                                                                
ndex._function_unit_class = u.function.logarithmic.DexUnit                                                                                                                    
zhPa = ndex(u.hPa)
```
but I still felt there might be a more direct solution, which I just realised would be
```
zhPa = u.LogUnit(u.hPa, '-1 dex')
```
This is described in the docstring of `u.DexUnit`, but that gets rather little exposure in https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/units/logarithmic_units.html
Alternatively it seems the identical result (almost, except for the subclass inherited) can be obtained with
```
zhPa = u.DexUnit(u.hPa, '2.5 mag')
```
or even some chimera like
```
zhPa = u.MagUnit(u.hPa, '-10 dB')
```
- Is there still some other method to define such a unit using `u.dex` directly?

- If not, how is the canonical solution best documented?

title: BlackBody does not include change-of-variables factor when given wavelength units.
description: ### Description A blackbody function should return a power per area per solid angle per *input unit*, where the input unit is typically in wavelength or in frequency. The example on this page: [https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.modeling.physical_models.BlackBody.html ](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.modeling.physical_models.BlackBody.html ) returns a blackbody spectrum with an input in wavelength and an output in power per area per solid angle per *Hz*. Because it's a density and is typically used under an integral, one needs to include the factor that converts to , which means multiplying by a factor of (e.g., the Jacobian is missing). ### Expected behavior That the linked demo of the blackbody function would return a spectral density commensurate with input units. ### Actual behavior The linked demo returns a spectral power density appropriate only for frequency as an input. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. title: Time creation for unix time is very slow
description:
This issue is very likely related to #5846 and #10167.

When using `astropy.time.Time` to convert unix timestamps (or utime) to datetime, it's more than factor 1000 slower than using `datetime.utcfromtimestamp()`.

I benchmarked converting 2000 values, which is not even much when reading fits files
```python
Time(times[i], format="unix")  # 1.61s
datetime.utcfromtimestamp(times[i])  # 998µs

Time(times[i], format="utime")  # 1.74s
datetime.utcfromtimestamp(times[i] + offset)  # 2ms, offset being set to Time(0, format="utime").to_value("unix")
```

Astropy does some special checks for leap seconds and so on, but I haven't found an example where the native conversion differs from astropy using seconds as the smallest unit.. is there any at all? If not, would it be feasible to convert those two formats using the native `datetime` module? If not, what is causing this huge difference..? seems a bit strange to me
