title: ECSV array/object-valued column support
description:
The ECSV format is, as far as I know, defined by [APE6](https://github.com/astropy/astropy-APEs/blob/master/APE6.rst).  That lists the permitted datatypes as `bool`, `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64`, `uint8`, `uint16`, `uint32`, `uint64`, `float16`, `float32`, `float64`, `float128`, `complex64`, `complex128`, `complex256`, and `string`, and it says on the topic of array-valued columns (as it calls them _"Multidimensional columns"_):

> Multidimensional columns are not supported in version 0.9 of the ECSV format.
>
> None of the available text data formats supports multidimensional columns with more than one element per row. Although in many cases having such data would indicate using a binary storage format, there is utility in supporting this for cases where the column shape is "reasonable", perhaps with no more than about 10 elements.

_(parenthetically: VOTable listed as one of the comparison formats earlier in the document does support array-valued columns, though it's not really a text format)_

However, if you ask `astropy.table` to write a table with array-like columns (lists, tuples, numpy arrays) to ECSV format, it will output ECSV tables using the undocumented datatype `object`.  Such columns produce string values when read back in.  See the following code:

```
from astropy.table import Table

# Create table column data
column_float  = [10., 20., 30.]
column_string = ['xx', 'yy', 'zz']
column_list   = [[2.0, 3.0, 4.0], [5.0], [8.5, 1.1]]

# Create Astropy table and get info
table = Table([column_float, column_string, column_list],
              names=('num_col', 'txt_col', 'list_col'),)

# Write ecsv table with multiple elements per cell
table.write('tsimp.ecsv', format='ascii.ecsv', overwrite=True, delimiter=',')

# Read it back in
tr = Table.read('tsimp.ecsv', format='ascii.ecsv')
print([type(c) for c in tr[0]])
print(tr)
```
which writes the following output:
```
[<class 'numpy.float64'>, <class 'numpy.str_'>, <class 'str'>]
num_col txt_col     list_col   
------- ------- ---------------
   10.0      xx [2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
   20.0      yy           [5.0]
   30.0      zz      [8.5, 1.1]
```
and produces the following ECSV file:
```
# %ECSV 0.9
# ---
# datatype:
# - {name: num_col, datatype: float64}
# - {name: txt_col, datatype: string}
# - {name: list_col, datatype: object}
# delimiter: ','
# schema: astropy-2.0
num_col,txt_col,list_col
10.0,xx,"[2.0, 3.0, 4.0]"
20.0,yy,[5.0]
30.0,zz,"[8.5, 1.1]"
```

Is this intended behaviour?  At present my (java STIL/TOPCAT) ECSV reader fails to read such tables because they have an unknown datatype `object`.  I'd say that's an ECSV output bug given the documentation at APE6.

However, as it happens this got noticed during some discussion within DPAC (the Gaia data processing consortium) about whether array values could be stored in ECSV tables, which is an enhancement requested by some DPAC members for use with both Astropy and TOPCAT.  The suggestion was that the existing behaviour could be extended with some additional metadata (new `datatype` or array flag) to provide array-valued column support in ECSV.

On a related topic, I see #11155, which is pursuing a different approach to serializing array values into ECSV.  That may not be suitable for the Gaia use case, since (a) it only supports fixed-size array values and (b) from the metadata in the example file it seems to be intended as an astropy-specific convention.

So: fix `object` datatype output?  Extend it to support array-valued columns? Or should I just patch my ECSV parser to cope with undocumented datatypes?

Hi guys,

It seems to me there is a logic bug in tokenizer.c at line 602.
From https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/io/ascii/src/tokenizer.c#L602

```C
static inline int ascii_tolower(int c)
{
    if (c >= 'A' || c <= 'Z') /* this conditions is always true */
    {
        return c + ('a' - 'A');
    }

    return c;
}
```

The condition is always true and it seems it should have been logical-and (&&) instead of logical-or (||) ?
I don't think this has much effect, but it may work different from what was originally envisioned, so I wanted to give you a heads up.

title: FITS header indexing should support numpy ints. Incorrect error type
description:
### Description
Indexing an `astropy.io.fits.Header` using elements of an integer `numpy` array fails because `np.int64` is not `int`.

### Expected behavior
I would expect numpy integers to be treated/accepted as valid header indices.

### Actual behavior
Attempting to index a header using, i.e., `np.int64` raises `ValueError` which seems to be the wrong type of error to raise. I think it should have been `TypeError`.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
In [1]: import numpy as np

In [2]: from astropy.io import fits

In [3]: hdr = fits.Header([('card1', 1), ('card2', 2)])

In [4]: hdr
Out[4]:
CARD1   =                    1
CARD2   =                    2

In [5]: hdr[np.int64(1)]
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-5-f794962e8ec2> in <module>
----> 1 hdr[np.int64(1)]

~/virtualenv/py37/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astropy/io/fits/header.py in __getitem__(self, key)
    154             keyword = key
    155
--> 156         card = self._cards[self._cardindex(key)]
    157
    158         if card.field_specifier is not None and keyword == card.rawkeyword:

~/virtualenv/py37/lib/python3.7/site-packages/astropy/io/fits/header.py in _cardindex(self, key)
   1698         else:
   1699             raise ValueError(
-> 1700                 'Header indices must be either a string, a 2-tuple, or '
   1701                 'an integer.')
   1702

ValueError: Header indices must be either a string, a 2-tuple, or an integer.
```

I think that when an `isinstance` check fails the more natural error to raise is a `TypeError` instead of the `ValueError` - see https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/d971b1c48231d38665229d0d18b4245766b4b033/astropy/io/fits/header.py#L1708-L1730

title: Have relative and absolute temperature units?
description: In #11204, we had to work around temperature units because K and C, F do not have the same origin. In principle, temperature *differences* are much easier to deal with and it might be worth having those be treated differently.  Or have an offset unit class based on the functional units.

title: Velocities in spherical coordinates
description:
Hi, I'm converting some positions and velocities from ICRS to Galactocentric, and then turning that into a spherical representation. The velocities are given as angular velocities, which is a little strange since I would have expected them in km/s. 

```python
c = coord.SkyCoord(
        ra = ra * u.deg, 
        dec = dec * u.deg, 
        pm_ra_cosdec = pmracosdec * u.mas/u.yr, 
        pm_dec = pmdec * u.mas / u.yr, 
        radial_velocity = vrad * u.km / u.s, 
        distance = dist * u.kpc,
        frame = 'icrs',
    )
cg = c.transform_to(coord.Galactocentric())
cgs = cg.represent_as('spherical')
diffs = cgs.differentials['s']
diffs
<SphericalDifferential (d_lon, d_lat, d_distance) in (mas / yr, mas / yr, kpc mas / (rad yr))
    (-0.17801241, -0.06221044, -12.62912254)>
```
**How can I get these in km/s?** For `d_distance` I can do 
```python
cgs.differentials['s'].d_distance.to(u.km/u.s)
```
but for `d_lon` and `d_lat` I can't do the conversion, even when I multiply by the distance:
```python
(cgs.differentials['s'].d_lon * dist * u.kpc).to(u.km/u.s)
``` 
gives the following error:
```python
UnitConversionError: 'kpc mas / yr' and 'km / s' (speed) are not convertible
```
Thanks.

title: DOC: Have a formal policy on what goes in LTS or not
description:
LTS maintenance is not trivial and introduces burden to release managers who are already stretched thin. As LTS branch and dependencies continue to diverge from dev, backports become more involved. Two years is a long time for a software and many things can break as LTS minversion stays stagnant. For instance, some Numpy compatibility that is overlooked in dev (because we have bumped the minversion) can become a time sink in LTS debugging rabbit hole.

One proposal is to only have backports on demand. The reasoning is that maybe LTS isn't used that much anyway (perhaps only by a few pipelines here and there) and people who use it will let us know exactly what needs to get backported on a as-needed basis, or better still, help us do the backport via PRs.

title: ANN: New WCSLIB 7.5 released
description:
New WCSLIB release found.

Version: 7.5 (2021/03/20)

#### Change log

WCSLIB version 7.5 (2021/03/20)
-------------------------------

The C code in WCSLIB is moving piecemeal to the C99 standard.  In fact,
various indispensible C99 constructs have been used in WCSLIB for many
years: the long long int data type (in fitshdr() only); stdint.h,
inttypes.h, and the use of PRI formatting control (in wcsprintf(), which
is widely used by the library); and the C99-extended library function
vsnprintf() (used by wcserr for a decade).  Flex-generated C code also
uses C99 extensions, though with workarounds if they are not available.

Except in the header prologues, which are formatted in a special way for
generating the user manual, comments were changed en masse to C99 style
in release 7.3.1, and variable declarations in code that I have occasion
to modify will transition to the more general placement allowed by C99.
However, I have no plans to use any of the more esoteric features of
C99.

* C library

  - New function, wcsccs(), changes the celestial coordinate system of a
    wcsprm struct, for example, from equatorial to galactic coordinates.
    The parameters that define the spherical coordinate transformation
    must be provided.  This allows WCSLIB to provide this functionality
    without needing to know anything about specific celestial coordinate
    systems, and has the advantage of making the routine completely
    general.  Requested by Mohammad Akhlaghi.

    Modified test program twcsfix also to test wcsccs().

  - Fixed a problem common to all of the Flex code (fitshdr, wcsbth,
    wcspih, wcsulex, and wcsutrn) that made it thread-unsafe.  Reported
    by Cyril Richard.

    Added a new test program, tpthreads, to test thread safety.  It is
    only used for code development, and not exercised as part of the
    standard test suite.

  - In fitshdr(), fixed a problem that potentially could arise on
    systems where sizeof(long long int) is greater than 8 (64 bits).

* Fortran wrappers

  - Match changes to the C library: added a wrapper for wcsccs(), and
    modified twcsfix.f.

  - Because null addresses cannot be passed to functions in Fortran,
    wcssub_() now interprets *nsub == -1 && *axes == -1 as a signal to
    do a deep copy of one wcsprm struct to another.

* Utilities

  - New utility, sundazel, computes the local time of the Sun's passage
    through the specified apparent longitude or latitude in a user-
    defined coordinate system.  It can also perform several other Solar
    related calculations.  (It is unrelated to FITS WCS, and does not
    use WCSLIB.)

* Installation

  - Added an 'uninstall' rule to the makefiles.  Suggested by
    Cyril Richard.



(For complete change log information, see https://www.atnf.csiro.au/people/mcalabre/WCS/CHANGES .)

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
In a file with more than one WCS (in this case a Chandra events table), some WCS parameters are assigned to the wrong WCS. Standard Chandra event files have four independent WCS per file (for chip coordinates, detectors coordinates, ..., and importantly for sky coordinates). Mostly, I care for the "sky coordinates". The issue is that one of the other coordinate systems has a "lonpole" set and that lonpole gets used for **all** WCS that are read in. As a workaround, the file can be modified before passing it to the `WCS` constructor. *Instructions for workarounds below.*
I did considerable debugging and will provide details below, but it is not clear to me how to resolve this, since it might have to be addressed in the C code which I'm not familiar with. (An easier workaround is prevented by #11412. )

The effects of this bug can be seen in the following comments, but it took me several hours to isolate this problem to the point that I can describe it here:

- https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/7180#issuecomment-624978278
- https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/8389#issuecomment-805177589

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
If one of the independent coordinate systems has a lonpole or latpole (or possibly other keywords that I did not test) set, then that keyword is only applied to the WCS in question, not to all axes.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
Instead of a three WCS with 2 axes each, a single WCS with 6 axes is constructed. That WCS has only a single setting for latpol/lonpole and the value set in there is valid only for a subset of axes.

title: On-sky rotations of coordinates with NaN distance are NaN
description:
### Description

Coordinate transformations that don't require the distance will return incorrect results if the distance value is set to NaN. This is different than if the value is not specified, presumably because a UnitSpherical representation is being used, while it is not for the NaN case.

### Expected behavior

Coordinate transformations that don't require the distance are not affected by the value of the distance. This is not a problem for most values, but NaN is clearly a special case because 2 * nan / nan = nan, not 2.

**ps. I just noticed this is also true for ``np.inf``.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
print(coord.ICRS(ra=1*u.deg, dec=2*u.deg).transform_to(coord.Galactic()))  # works
print(coord.ICRS(ra=1*u.deg, dec=2*u.deg, distance=np.NaN*u.pc).transform_to(coord.Galactic()))  # does not
```

### Thoughts on a solution

Maybe for these classes of transformations any NaNs in the distance array could changed to a special value, then be changed back to NaN after the transformation. We kind of need a NaN for which 2 * nan / nan = 2.

Something super hacky that works for transforming from ICRS to Galactic is:

```
c = coord.SkyCoord(ra=[0, 1]*u.deg, dec=[2, 3] * u.deg, distance=[4, np.nan]*u.pc)
distance = c.distance
c.frame._data = c.frame.data.represent_as(coord.UnitSphericalRepresentation)

c = c.galactic
_data = c.frame.data.represent_as(coord.SphericalRepresentation)
_data._distance = distance
c.frame._data = _data
print(c)
```

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

In several contexts there are problems with the automatic checking of the leap second file via internet queries:
- Using astropy in a non-networked environment for a large team of non-expert users.
- Using astropy on an HPC cluster.
- Difficult debugging during Time sub-package development (since it catches exceptions during import in a way that continually confuses me)

There are workarounds, but nothing really clean. From my perspective the auto-leap second has been a frequent source of problems. A number of issues have come up related to this, and informal polling of a few people at the 2021 Coordination Meeting shows strong agreement on disabling this feature by default.

The specific proposal is to make automatic updating of the leap second file be an opt-in feature via the config file.

[EDIT - see the discussion for a slight evolution of the proposal]

title: Add RadialRepresentation to SphericalRepresentation
description:
### Description

When two ``SphericalRepresentation`` are added, the distance components are correctly summed. A SphericalRepresentation + RadialRepresentation could be equivalent to summing two ``SphericalRepresentation``, with the same lon, lat.

Ex:
```
>>> coord.SphericalRepresentation(1*u.rad, 0.2*u.rad, 3) + coord.RadialRepresentation(5)
<SphericalRepresentation (lon, lat, distance) in (rad, rad, )
    (1., 0.2, 8.)>
```


### Additional context

This would be useful for generalizing #11444 to allow for offsets in the transformation machinery to be a RadialRepresentation.

title: Allow setting astropy cache directory via an environment variable
description:
### Description

In some conditions (e.g. certain HPC clusters or special purpose system users) the home directory of the current user is not writable or even existing.

In that case, astropy raises a couple of warnings due to the cache directory not being writable.

Under such conditions, it would be great, if the location of the cache would be configurable via environment variables, e.g. `ASTROPY_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/my/custom/cache`.

title: Seasonal Variations in Altitude Missing
description:
### Description
I am converting the coordinates of a source to Alt-Az and see the expected variations in altitude over the course of a day that are caused by the rotation of Earth. But when I do the conversion over the range of a whole year I would expect to see additional variations due to the tilt of the Earth axis, but I don't.

See daily and annual variations in altitude above the horizon for a given source.

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

description:
Now that `matplotlib` dev bugs are fixed upstream, there are real failures in the CircleCI `mpldev` job that we need to fix, namely updating the data files, as they have bumped from 3.3.dev to 3.4.dev. You will see errors like this until this is fixed:

```
UserWarning: Downloading http://data.astropy.org/testing/astropy/2019-08-02T11:38:58.288466/3.4.x/....png
failed: HTTP Error 404: Not Found
```

The data are in https://github.com/astropy/astropy-data/tree/gh-pages/testing/astropy/2019-08-02T11:38:58.288466 but I am not familiar with the procedures to do this update myself.

* Do you create a new dir with new timestamp or a new subdir under this timestamp? When do you choose to or not to create new dirs with new timestamps?
* If copying the expected outputs from `3.3.x` to `3.4.x` is insufficient, how do we update the data files? I don't see the CircleCI job for `mpldev` uploading any artifacts into CircleCI itself in the failed job: `Uploading /root/project/results to results... No artifact files found at /root/project/results`
* Are we supposed to update the CircleCI `mpl` test matrix too? Currently, it only runs `302`, `310`, and `dev`. When do we choose to update matrix and how to we pick the versions that are deemed important enough to test in CI?

The `mpldev` job isn't as critical as other jobs but we should still fix this as soon as possible, because it is failing for unrelated PRs, causing unnecessary stress when PR authors see the ❌ .

title: Misleading behavior in SkyCoord.is_transformable_to()
description:
Elsewhere in SkyCoord, we allow string aliases of the coordinate frames, for example:
```python
>>> import astropy.coordinates as coord
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> c = coord.SkyCoord(90*u.deg, -11*u.deg)
>>> c.transform_to('galactic')
<SkyCoord (Galactic): (l, b) in deg
    (217.12716293, -16.34634219)>
```
However, in `SkyCoord.is_transformable_to()`, strings fail the test silently, even though the input is technically invalid. 
```python
>>> c.is_transformable_to(coord.Galactic())
True
>>> c.is_transformable_to('galactic')
False
```

We should either add support for turning a string frame alias to a frame class, or raise an exception.

title: SkyCoord/BaseFrame.represent_as does not treat differentials very logically
description:
Right now, things get transformed a bit too eagerly to having all velocity components present, while really we should not make up numbers:
```
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy import units as u

sc = SkyCoord(10*u.deg, 10*u.deg, radial_velocity=-10*u.km/u.s)
sc
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec) in deg
    (10., 10.)
 (radial_velocity) in km / s
    (-10.,)>

sc.data.differentials
{'s': <RadialDifferential (d_distance) in km / s
     (-10.,)>}

sc.represent_as('spherical')
<SphericalRepresentation (lon, lat, distance) in (rad, rad, )
    (0.17453293, 0.17453293, 1.)
 (has differentials w.r.t.: 's')>

sc.represent_as('spherical').differentials
{'s': <SphericalDifferential (d_lon, d_lat, d_distance) in (km rad / s, km rad / s, km / s)
     (2.22044605e-16, -2.22044605e-16, -10.)>}
```
Here, there is no reason to move to a `SphericalDifferential` and set the proper motions to zero - rather, just stick with the `RadialDifferential` since that is compatible with `SphericalRepresentation`. Needs some adjustment in `BaseFrame.represent_as` (and perhaps in `_get_repr_classes`).

p.s. The current process is blocking #11467.

title: Surprising differences in stats due to effects of FITS-endianness
description:
### Description
I was experiencing some really strange issues where a fit would only succeed when executed in a process-pool, but fail in single threaded mode. Digging down, it appears the divergence was due to non-identical output from `sigma_clipped_stats` between single and multi-process execution.
The reason for that boils down to FITS-images being read as dtype `>f4` (big endian, non-native on x86), which when passed directly to bottleneck for mean/median will default to the numpy implementation of `nanmean`/`nanmedian`. In the process of pickling, the array is converted to `<f4` and ends up in the bottleneck implementation.
As far as I can tell, bottleneck performs a straight sum over all elements, while numpy seems to use some form of compensated summation scheme, to decrease numerical error.

### Actual behavior
As bottleneck gets automatically selected by astropy if available, the choice between a accuracy and speed is potentially hidden from the user. This may well be a case of "works as intended" but the chance of reading FITS and unintentionally triggering a conversion to a (on most machines) native array format only under specific circumstances seems rather high. This may cause a lot of headscratching for people that see different results for the same data in seemingly equivalent programs. 

This could plausibly also be considered a bug or unexpected behaviour in bottleneck as the library gives the impression of being a complete drop-in replacement for certain numpy routines.

### Expected behavior
I'm not exactly sure what the best resolution is here. The fact that numpy supports non-native byteorder without explicit conversion/warnings complicates things a bit. Obviously for the user it would be the easiest if all array-operations would have the same results, irrespective of byte-order, but that would possibly cause issues with mmap or performance.

Some kind of warning or note, either when applying `sigma_clipped_stats` to a non-native byteorder or when a FITS file is read, or at least a disclaimer in the docs for `io.fits` about this possible gotcha would help.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import requests
from astropy.stats import sigma_clipped_stats
import warnings

r=requests.get('https://gist.github.com/krachyon/7408a4029fd9cca83f5a8c6ecbeb1173/raw/0ba5cc3e5a0d0eb02a2a4da3d04ec16ee8aa4267/repro_array.npy')
with open('repro_array.npy','wb') as f:
    f.write(r.content)

arr = np.load('repro_array.npy')

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', '.*Input data contains invalid values.*', append=True)

    print('as_is: ', sigma_clipped_stats(arr))
    print('native: ', sigma_clipped_stats(arr.astype(np.float32)))
    print('higher precision: ', sigma_clipped_stats(arr.astype(np.float64)))
    print('')
    print('delta:', np.array(sigma_clipped_stats(arr))-np.array(sigma_clipped_stats(arr.astype(np.float32))))
    print('dtype resolution:', np.finfo(np.float32).resolution)
```

native:  (2523.126220703125, 2519.47998046875, 50.6502799987793)
higher precision:  (2523.1193250563483, 2519.4801025390625, 50.650290905964354)

delta: [-6.83593750e-03  0.00000000e+00  1.14440918e-05]

### Description
A deep copy should lose any link to the original object, so that one can modify the copy with no side effects on the original object. In a Jupyter notebook, something happens that makes this fail.

I would expect that a deepcopy would allow to modify the copy without any change happening to the original model.

The original model gets changed when I change the parameters of the new model in place (e.g. with _fitter_to_model_params).
It turns out that, _when I run the method in a Jupyter notebook_, the parameter array in the copied version is _not_ a deepcopy, but a reference to the original parameter array, as demonstrated below.

title: DOC: remove references to RandomState
description:
### Description

I propose here to remove from the documentation any reference to `RandomState` and wrong (not best practice) usage of random number generators.

We went through this in SciPy. More on the PR https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/13778

Let me know if you would accept this contribution and I would propose to do it 😃 

### Additional context

Since NumPy 1.17 (and as far as I understand, the supported minimal version here is 1.17), the [canonical way](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/index.html) to create random numbers is:

```python
import numpy as np
from numpy.random import default_rng
rng = default_rng()
```
And If a seed is to be used. User should not use a common value such as 0 or 123456. This is to prevent bias (everyone is using the same values) and ensure sufficient entropy for the generator. More [details](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/bit_generators/index.html#seeding-and-entropy). The good practice (from NumPy's doc) is to generate a seed like this:

```python
from numpy.random import SeedSequence
print(SeedSequence().entropy)
```

Then you can use the value like
```python
rng = default_rng(my_seed_generated_and_not_common_value)
```

### Description

Not sure whether this is a bug, a missing feature, or just my problem:

Plain Table columns may come with a unit that is not always kept:

>>> from astropy.table import Table
>>> t = Table({'foo': [1,2,3]*u.deg)
>>> print(np.copy(t['foo']))

title: Improve support for unit systems in astropy.units
description:
The [current support for unit systems in Astropy](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/units/decomposing_and_composing.html#converting-between-systems) is pretty minimal and only extends to major unit systems like CGS, SI, Imperial (as modules with implemented units). There have been various related feature requests, discussions, and attempts to improve this. For example:
- Feature request for more specific galactic/extragalactic unit systems #703
- Experimental port of `UnitSystem` class from my `gala` package to Astropy #6065
- Feature request for setting the global unit system as a science state, to control (globally) output from any unit-aware function ([this comment](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6065#issuecomment-676838647))
- Being able to (de)compose in prefix units (#5615).

Let's use this issue as a new meta-issue for discussing improving support for unit systems in astropy.units!

cc @mhvk @eteq @nstarman

title: Have basic ascii table writing include units if they are present
description:
This is coming from the discussion whether or not to close #756 - after reading that I realized the one thing still not solved in my original issue description is that when one writes a basic ASCII table when the units are present, those units are lost.  I think it is desirable for those units to be written out somehow by default (although it certainly should be an option to not do that, and maybe even the default?).

My thinking here is that users (i.e., some of my collaborators!) just do a quick `table.write('filename', format='ascii')`, and that drops the units, which is not desirable for cases where the table is relying on the units for important information (most relevant here is tables with "RA" where it's never clear if it's hours vs degrees).  So defaulting to having the units written if they're present I think is a Good Thing :TM:. So it should default to something like:
```
#id RA Dec
#None hour  degree
NGC1234 1.2 3.4
NGC9876 9.1 2.3
```

Note, that, unlike #756, I am *not* expecting round-tripping here or any standardization.  That's already been achieved by ECSV. This is entirely about "human-readable-headers".

title: Avoid very strange SI unit decompositions
description:
Taken from #8398, to just focus on the actual problem:
```
from astropy import units as u

(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.Angstrom).si
# Unit("1e+07 Pa / s")
```
This decomposition is very unfortunate and it would be nice if it could be more sensible, perhaps by using physical type or so.

EDIT: A specific suggestion might that if a given unit has an associated physical type, then the unit of that physical type is used (which I think is always SI).
EDIT2: the above suggestion doesn't work easily, since the unit system has no direct way to know which one it is:
```
(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.Angstrom).physical_type
PhysicalType({'power density', 'spectral flux density wav'})
```
Though even `W/m3` would be nicer than `Pa/s`...

title: Meta issue for Masked class follow-up
description:
#11127 introduced a new `Masked` class. Here are items that were left out or were postponed for later:
- [x] Decide what to do with the `nanfunctions`. In principle, one could decide to treat all masked values as `nan`, but it is a bit tricky for non-float dtype (#12454; all masked values are skipped, sum and prod never give a masked result)
- [ ] Resolve what `argmin/argmax` should do for all-masked slices. Just return the index of the first masked element (i.e., 0), or maybe a masked 0? (Raising an exception would be strange if `axis` is passed in).
- [X] Ensure that `Table` turns `MaskedQuantity` into `MaskedColumn` and `QTable` does vice versa. See https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11127#issuecomment-817791389; solved by #16500.
- [ ] Check that `Distribution` and `Masked` can operate properly, since both try to be at the bottom of the class hierarchy (`Masked` should probably be below, since masking could be different for different trials in the distribution).
- [x] Replace the Time masking using `nan` with `Masked` (#15231)
- [X] Provide some sort of general mask-gathering and mask-setting facility for coordinate representations, frames, and `SkyCoord`. Need to consider whether this should just be data or also frame attributes. 2024-06-07: Also need to decide what a mask really means. Maybe be important to have proper motion, radial velocity and distance individually being masked, to be able to represent arrays of coordinates from catalogues, where often one or more of these are missing. (#17016)
- [ ] Provide a replacement `MaskedColumn`?
- [ ] Provide `.reduceat` and `.at` functionalities for ufuncs. After this is fixed, enable the performance test that was skipped in https://github.com/astropy/astropy-benchmarks/pull/135 .

title: Creating a PhysicsSphericalRepresentation with NaNs raises RuntimeWarning
description:
### Description

This is not exactly a bug, but inconsistent behavior between the different spherical representations. For example, the following code will raise a RuntimeWarning (and thus error in pytest) if the representation is PhysicsSpherical, but not Spherical. 

```python
from astropy.coordinates import PhysicsSphericalRepresentation
from astropy.coordinates.matrix_utilities import rotation_matrix
import astropy.units as u
import numpy as np

s1 = PhysicsSphericalRepresentation(
    phi=[1, 2] * u.deg, theta=[3, 4] * u.deg, r=[5, np.nan] * u.kpc)
matrix = rotation_matrix(-10, "z", u.deg)

# THIS PART RAISES THE WARNING
expected = (s1.to_cartesian().transform(matrix).represent_as(PhysicsSphericalRepresentation))
```

The reason for this is in the initialization of ``PhysicsSphericalRepresentation``

```python
    if np.any(self._theta < 0.*u.deg) or np.any(self._theta > 180.*u.deg):
```

I use this example because it fails the test suite in #11444.  @mhvk @adrn 

Which is not NaN-"protected".

### Expected behavior

A  NaN-"protected" check of the angular domain.

### Actual behavior

title: TST: Do not use random seed in doctest
description:
See https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10644#pullrequestreview-634247783 from @tupui 

<hr/>

We did this (#10644) in SciPy and the only difference is that we removed all seeding from examples. This is to enforce best practices. Using small seeds is bad for the entropy of the generator and also common values like 0, 42, 12345 end up in every code which leads to bias in results. Seeing should only be used for testing.

Here I am proposing to remove the seed and just allow variation in the results to pass the doctests (in SciPy I can add `# random` or `# may vary`, I am not sure if this is standard or not. Maybe this is your `# doctest: +FLOAT_CMP`?).

I can do a PR on this branch if you want some help. Also, I would suggest to add somewhere in the doc a paragraph about seeding. See what we did for example https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/tutorial/stats.html#random-number-generation.

title: Please support os.PathLike
description:
### Description

When I try to open a FITS file with a [path like object](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html?highlight=pathlike#os.PathLike) which is not dircetly a `pathlib.Path`, I get a failure:

```Python
import os

class DummyPath(os.Pathlike):
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.path = path

    def __fspath__(self):
        return str(self.path)
```

With the normal open, this works fine:
```Python
>>> p = DummyPath('foo.txt')
>>> fp = open(p)
>>> print(fp.read()
A big brown fox
```
But it does not work with `astropy.io.fits`:

```Python
>>> from astropy.io import fits
>>> f = DummyPath('foo.fits')
>>> fits.open(f)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/hdulist.py", line 164, in fitsopen
    return HDUList.fromfile(name, mode, memmap, save_backup, cache,
  File "/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/hdulist.py", line 401, in fromfile
    return cls._readfrom(fileobj=fileobj, mode=mode, memmap=memmap,
  File "/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/hdulist.py", line 1052, in _readfrom
    fileobj = _File(fileobj, mode=mode, memmap=memmap, cache=cache)
  File "/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/astropy/utils/decorators.py", line 535, in wrapper
    return function(*args, **kwargs)
  File "/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/astropy/io/fits/file.py", line 177, in __init__
    self._open_filelike(fileobj, mode, overwrite)
  File "/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/astropy/io/fits/file.py", line 541, in _open_filelike
    raise OSError("File-like object does not have a 'write' "
OSError: File-like object does not have a 'write' method, required for mode 'ostream'.
```
Having `os.PathLike` supported would make it easy to implement f.e. a cache, where  `__fspath__()` could handle the creation or download of a requested file before opening.

For fits, I would guess that the problem is that `pathlib.Path` is hardcoded: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/8d26b90c5b71276d0d1ab750f774bfa7aa68a8ea/astropy/io/fits/file.py#L134-L136

This could be replaced with checking for `os.PathLike`, and accessing the string with `__fspath__()` instead, but there may be other places as well. A simple grep shows that `isinstance(…, pathlib.Path)` is used here:
 * `io/registry.py`
 * `io/fits/util.py`
 * `io/fits/convenience.py`
 * `io/fits/file.py` (this is the one shown above)
 * `io/fits/diff.py`
 * `config/configuration.py`

### Description

When `astropy.io.fits.open` receives a `LocalFileOpener` instance (a wrapper class used by https://github.com/intake/filesystem_spec to facilitate serialization, i.e., for distributed execution on workers with a shared networked filesystem), it is able to read the headers correctly but silently garbles the data it loads.

### Expected behavior

The header and data should be loaded correctly, or an exception should be raised when that is not possible.

### Actual behavior

Headers and shapes are correct, but the contents of the data attribute on the HDU are nonsense. @martindurant of fsspec did some debugging here https://github.com/intake/filesystem_spec/issues/613 and it seems to be related to the use of raw file handles.

### Steps to Reproduce

**To reproduce:**

1. Save this script as `repro.py`

```python
import numpy as np
import fsspec
from astropy.io import fits

def main():
    data = np.arange(10, dtype=float)
    fits.PrimaryHDU(data).writeto('ex.fits', overwrite=True)
    print('\nUsing builtin open()')
    with open('ex.fits', 'rb') as fh:
        hdul = fits.open(fh, mode='readonly', memmap=False)
        hdul.info()
        print(hdul[0].data)

    print('\nUsing fsspec.open() with local path')
    with fsspec.open('ex.fits', 'rb') as fh:
        hdul = fits.open(fh, mode='readonly', memmap=False)
        hdul.info()
        print(hdul[0].data)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

python -m venv env
source env/bin/activate
pip install astropy fsspec

title: Add narrative documentation on physical types
description:
### Description

In #11204 we made the `physical_type` attribute of units into instances of the new [`PhysicalType`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/4a289db09ac1026b038d156c1e1139223a762590/astropy/units/physical.py#L199) class.  Before this, `physical_type` returned a string.  It's now possible to do dimensional analysis along the lines of:
```Python
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> length = u.m.physical_type
>>> area = u.get_physical_type("area")
>>> length * area
PhysicalType('volume')
```
There are descriptions on how to use physical types in the docstrings for `PhysicalType`, `get_physical_type`, and `UnitBase.physical_type`.  Following a [suggestion](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11204#pullrequestreview-636754774) in #11204, it would be helpful to add a discussion of physical types in the narrative documentation for `astropy.units`.  

It might be helpful to write out or have a table of all of the names of physical types.  I'm not sure if this would be best in the narrative documentation or in the docstring for `get_physical_type`.

```python
    ticklabels = cb.ax.get_ymajorticklabels()

title: Provide an easy way to generate random coordinates spatially uniform distributions
description:
This is a follow-on from #10241 and some related discussion.  While I think we settled there that `zeros` is not that compelling, having a way to randomly sample coordinates *is* - in fact I think several of the tests do this already in various ways.

So this issue is to suggest adding some helper functions to auto-generate random coordinates that are either:

1. uniform on the sky (but without any specific 3D distribution - i.e. `UniformSphericalRepresentation`
2. uniform density in a fixed 3D volume

While we could get away with just, say, 2, and say the user can drop the r-coordinate, I'd advocate for both since there's a factor-of-a-few performance difference (see https://gist.github.com/eteq/2c1b9c5b5ba04cb8d36a8f4df78087b9 for proof of this).

One could argue as in #10241 that this could be a `SkyCoord` `classmethod`, but I'm inclined more towards a regular function.

cc @astrofrog @adrn @mhvk

title: Make PhysicalType instances support string methods with deprecation warnings
description:
### Description

Prior to #11204, the `physical_type` attribute of units was a string with the name of the unit.  #11204 transformed the `physical_type` attribute into instances of the new `PhysicalType` class.  #11204 did preserve much of the behavior of the string API (such as having `==` work between `PhysicalType` instances and strings), but there were a few ways that it did not. title: Add option to preserve input order on table joins
description:
### Description

joins sort the resulting table by the join key. This is not documented in the actual API documentation of join here:
https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.table.join.html

and just mentioned in passing here:
https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/table/operations.html#join

This is undesired in many circumstances. There should be an option to preserve the input order, at least for left/right joins.

### Additional context


Example:
```python
from astropy.table import Table, join
import numpy as np
import astropy.units as u

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

N_EVENTS = 10
N_TELESCOPES = 3
events = Table({
    'event_id': np.arange(N_EVENTS),
    'tel_id': rng.integers(0, 3, N_EVENTS),
})
telescopes = Table({
    'tel_id': np.arange(N_TELESCOPES),
    'x': rng.uniform(-100, 100, N_TELESCOPES) * u.m,
    'y': rng.uniform(-100, 100, N_TELESCOPES) * u.m,
})


events = join(events, telescopes, keys='tel_id', join_type='left')

print(events)
```

title: Documentation reorganization
description:
This issue is to discuss a number of issues related to reorganization of the Astropy documentation as well as themeing.

* [x] There has been some discussion between @adrn and I, as well as on Slack, about possibly adopting the [pydata-sphinx-theme](https://github.com/pydata/pydata-sphinx-theme) for Astropy.  It is now used by NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, and several others in the "PyData" ecosystem.  Of course, we would probably like to tweak the theme a bit to keep Astropy's styling (e.g. I would like to keep the existing color scheme, with a dark nav bar, etc.).  This is also discussed in #11520 and @tupui has offered to help.
  * [x] @pllim also requested a "dark mode" which would be nice, but I think that's a feature that should be added directly to pydata-sphinx-theme if at all.

* [x] Adapting the pydata-sphinx-theme is also a good opportunity to redo the top navigation bar a bit.  #8320 relates to this insofar as using the nav bar from astropy.org.  For the documentation I'm not sure using it exactly as-is is necessarily what we want (e.g. having the "Documentation" menu on the docs themselves would be redundant.  But keeping links like "About" and "Affiliated Packages" might be good.

* [ ] The NumPy, SciPy, and Pandas docs all have an "API reference" link on their nav bars.  Astropy doesn't currently have a top-level API reference page.  Rather, most of the existing documentation pages are thematic by sub-package.  They contain some narrative documentation about the sub-package, and typically have some API reference at the bottom.  I think we should keep this format, though it would also be nice to have a single index of all API docs for all sub-packages, ordered alphabetically.  I have often wanted this myself, as a quick way to find API docs for a specific package, rather than having to scroll through all the narrative docs to find the API reference for that package.  See also #9277

* [x] Add a top-level page for the development docs.  Improving the development docs is actually the issue that originally prompted this discussion. In short, rather than having an index of the development docs directly on the main documentation index as we have currently (see https://docs.astropy.org/en/v4.2/#developer-documentation) it would be good to have a top-level development page featuring a sort of "quick start" guide at the top-level, followed by a table of contents for more detailed pages.  This aspect is tracked in more detail at #11621.

All of the above issues are intertwined on some level.

title: Development docs reorganization
description:
As discussed with @adrn and others on Slack, we would like to reorganize the Astropy developer docs.

The key points are to:

* Add a top-level landing page for development documentation.  For this we take inspiration particularly from NumPy's development docs: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/dev/index.html  (I would not mind even going so far as to borrow some of their text almost verbatim).  It would feature a clean and direct guide to getting started on Astropy (much less jumbled than [this page](https://docs.astropy.org/en/v4.2/development/workflow/development_workflow.html).

* At the bottom of the top-level page, add a table of contents for sub-pages that contain more detailed discussions.  Most of those would be the same as the existing development pages, though some of them might merit additional reorganization/rewriting.

* I like some aspects of the SciPy developer docs as well, especially the "ways to contribute" section: http://scipy.github.io/devdocs/dev/index.html

* The [matplotlib documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/devel/index.html) is also a good inspiration.  In particular we like the "choose your own adventure" style with prominent links for where to get started for different types of contributions.

* Maybe rename from "Developer documentation" to "Contributor documentation" or "Contributor guide"?

title: astropy.io.fits read failure for variable-length arrays with THEAP
description:
### Description
`astropy.io.fits` fails to read a FITS BINTABLE with variable-length array columns (P/Q TFORM descriptors) and a non-default THEAP.

### Expected behavior
I'm looking at the file [theap-gap.fits](https://github.com/Starlink/starjava/raw/master/fits/src/testcases/uk/ac/starlink/fits/theap-gap.fits).  `astropy.io.fits` ought to be able to read the content of the BINTABLE in HDU#1.

### Actual behavior
I see a stacktrace with the error:
```
OSError: Could not find heap data for the 'arr' variable-length array column.
```

### Steps to Reproduce
```
from astropy.io import fits
f = fits.open("theap-gap.fits")
f[1].data
```

### Additional information
This file **fails verification** by the `fverify` command in FTOOLS (e.g. from CFITSIO 3.340).  However, the verifier is wrong in this case; the file is valid FITS.  I have confirmed this with Bill Pence and the NASA FITS support office (ticket FTOOLS 4219).  I could forgive you for being sceptical ... if you want to wait to address this issue until fverify is updated to agree with me, I don't blame you.

What's unusual about the file, and what confuses `fverify` (and possibly what confuses `astropy.io.fits`) is its use of the THEAP keyword to move the heap start to a non-default position (it is offset from the end of the table data).  As described in sec 7.3.5 of the FITS 4.0 standard, in that case the PCOUNT keyword gives the size of the heap plus the pre-heap gap; `fverify` is incorrectly taking PCOUNT to mean the size of the heap alone.  There is a bit more discussion at Starlink/starjava@dec145cab (in which I decided not to write files like this in the future).

I did succeed in getting the `fitsio` package to read it:
```
>>> import fitsio
>>> f = fitsio.FITS('theap-gap.fits')
>>> t = f[1]
>>> t

  file: theap-gap.fits
  extension: 1
  type: BINARY_TBL
  rows: 500
  column info:
    i                   i4
    arr                 i4  varray[5]
>>> t[497]
array([(497, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4])], dtype=[('i', '>i4'), ('arr', '>i4', (5,))])

```

### System Details
Linux-5.4.0-73-generic-x86_64-with-Ubuntu-18.04-bionic
Python 3.6.9 (default, Jan 26 2021, 15:33:00)
[GCC 8.4.0]
Numpy 1.19.5
astropy 4.1
Scipy 0.19.1
Matplotlib 2.1.1

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

The `yaml` library (provided by PyYAML) is central to the serialization functionality used for losslessly storing Table data to ECSV, FITS and HDF5 formats.  The ECSV format in particular is seeing fairly wide usage, and is now supported in the StarLink java library STIL and TOPCAT. To this point we have accepted having `yaml` as an optional dependency, but this means that it cannot be used in any required parts of astropy.

A recent example was to improve the storage of cosmological model parameters. This would nicely be done as an ECSV table, but the `yaml` dependence was a stopper.

While we do not intend to go down a slippery slope of adding many dependencies, it seems like `yaml` is justified and would enable future enhancements to astropy core using ECSV or YAML-based storage of data within the package itself. 

From the Python packaging perspective this is a small package and should not measurably change the package footprint for a typical astropy installation.

Joining tables, with an outer join or vstack,  does not always preserve the fill_value of a masked column.

### Expected behavior

masked columns should preserve fill_value for outer join and vstack. If identical columns have different fill_values, the first defined value should be taken.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->

The outer join preserves the fill_value for non identical masked columns, but not for identical masked columns.
vstack does not preserve any fill_value for masked columns.

<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->

```python
from astropy.table import Table, vstack, join, MaskedColumn
t1=Table()
t2=Table()

t1["a"]=MaskedColumn([1,2],fill_value=0)

t2["b"]=MaskedColumn([3,4],fill_value=0)

tv=vstack([t1,t2])
print("vstack")
print("a  t1:",t1["a"].fill_value,"tv:",tv["a"].fill_value)
print("b  t2:",t2["b"].fill_value,"tv:",tv["b"].fill_value)

<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

We want to save multiple FITS images in parallel, and when multithreading it seems there's a significant time loss when saving compressed images compared to uncompressed (more than you'd expect from just compressing the data - see the examples below).

From a bit of research we found that CFITSIO needs a particular flag set when used in multi-threaded environments (https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/software/fitsio/c/c_user/node15.html), but it's hard to tell if that's set with the version bundled with Astropy. Even installing CFITSIO separately with the flag enabled and then installing Astropy with `ASTROPY_USE_SYSTEM_CFITSIO=1` seemed to not make any difference to the timing.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
Writing images in parallel is faster than writing them in serial.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
When compressing images writing out in parallel using multithreading takes longer than doing the same in serial.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

1) Setup, create two simple output functions and some test data.

```python
import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits

def write_fits(image, i):
    hdu = fits.PrimaryHDU(image)
    hdulist = fits.HDUList([hdu])
    hdulist.writeto(f"/tmp/uncompressed_{i}.fits", overwrite=True)

def write_compressed_fits(image, i):
    hdu = fits.CompImageHDU(image)
    hdulist = fits.HDUList([fits.PrimaryHDU(), hdu])
    hdulist.writeto(f"/tmp/compressed_{i}.fits", overwrite=True)

image = np.random.randint(0, 2**8, (8000, 6000)).astype("i2")
```

2) Time the functions, note that writing a compressed file takes ~5x longer than uncompressed.
```python
%time write_fits(image, 1)
# CPU times: user 72.5 ms, sys: 80.8 ms, total: 153 ms
# Wall time: 153 ms

%time write_compressed_fits(image, 1)
# CPU times: user 712 ms, sys: 73.2 ms, total: 785 ms
# Wall time: 785 ms
```

3) Try writing out 8 files in series. Again the compressed case takes ~5x longer, as expected.

```python
%time for i in range(8): write_fits(image, i)
# CPU times: user 477 ms, sys: 604 ms, total: 1.08 s
# Wall time: 1.17 s

%time for i in range(8): write_compressed_fits(image, i)
# CPU times: user 5 s, sys: 546 ms, total: 5.55 s
# Wall time: 5.55 s
```

4) Now using a ThreadPool try writing out the images in parallel. For uncompressed images this reduces the time to ~60% of the above serial case, but when compressing images it actually takes several seconds longer!

```python
from itertools import repeat
from multiprocessing.pool import ThreadPool

with ThreadPool() as pool:
    %time pool.starmap(write_fits, zip(repeat(image),list(range(8))))
# CPU times: user 522 ms, sys: 725 ms, total: 1.25 s
# Wall time: 710 ms

with ThreadPool() as pool:
    %time pool.starmap(write_compressed_fits, zip(repeat(image),list(range(8))))
# CPU time
…（以下省略）

title: wcs.pixel_to_world is seriously wrong for Equatorial coordinates.
description:
python 3.8.5
numpy 1.19.2
astropy 4.0.2

I find that the conversion of pixel positions to RA will dilate the angular size of all pixels by a factor of more than 3! The conversion to DEC is correct, however. 

For example, if I get the WCS from an input fits image that has more than 2500 pixels along each of the two axes through:

wcs = WCS(hdul[0].header)

Using print(hdul_N[0].header), I get the following wcs parameters:

CTYPE1  = 'RA---TAN'           / name of the coordinate axis                    
CTYPE2  = 'DEC--TAN'           / name of the coordinate axis                    
CRPIX1  =         1.300500E+03 / coordinate system reference pixel              
CRPIX2  =         1.630500E+03 / coordinate system reference pixel              
CROTA1  =         0.000000E+00 / coordinate system rotation angle               
CROTA2  =         0.000000E+00 / coordinate system rotation angle               
CRVAL1  =         1.868108E+02 / coordinate value at reference pixel            
CRVAL2  =        -7.153672E+01 / coordinate value at reference pixel            
CDELT1  =        -1.111111E-03 / coordinate increment along axis                
CDELT2  =         1.111111E-03 / coordinate increment along axis                

It means the pixel shape is square, and its size is 0.0011111 degree. Then, I try to convert two pixels that are separated equally in RA and DEC, e.g.,

wcs.pixel_to_world([1000,2000],[1000,2000])

I should expect to get equal separations in both RA and DEC of 1.11111 degree. However, what I get is

<SkyCoord (FK5: equinox=2000.0): (ra, dec) in deg
    [(187.9013224 , -72.2331139 ), (184.40632521, -71.10960646)]>

which means the separation in RA is unexpectedly expanded by a factor of >3. This is totally wrong!!!

Even for the DEC, the separation is 1.12350744 deg, which is still 1.1% larger than the nominal separation. I understand that this should be a projection effect at this high DEC range.

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
Use case: I have some Jupyter widgets displaying time series data (TESS lightcurves). It is very slow in the [`ipywidgets.fixed()`](https://ipywidgets.readthedocs.io/en/latest/examples/Using%20Interact.html#Fixing-arguments-using-fixed) call, e.g
```python
  # lc is a TimeSeries object of a typical TESS lightcurve 
  ...
  fixed(lc)
```

In my test of a time series data with ~15000 data points, the elapsed time is as follows

Calling `fixed(object)` with ...
| object type | time |
| ----------- | ---- |
| TimeSeries | 60s |
| Table with `Time` | 7s |
| Table without `Time`| < 0.01s |
| `Time`| < 0.01s |

In other words, calling `fixed()` with 
- TimeSeries object: very slow
- Table containing `Time` type column: slow
- `Time` object itself: fast

### Steps to Reproduce
```python
import numpy as np

from astropy.table import Table, QTable
from astropy.timeseries import TimeSeries
from astropy.time import Time

from ipywidgets import fixed

import timeit

# TimeSeries
# very slow (60s)
# also showed a warning -- table.py:3183: FutureWarning: elementwise == comparison failed and returning scalar instead; this will raise an error or perform elementwise comparison in the future.
tab = TimeSeries(time=Time(100 + np.arange(15000), format='mjd'))
print(timeit.timeit(lambda: fixed(tab), number=1))

# Table with Time as a column
# slow (6s)
tab = Table()
tab['time'] = Time(100 + np.arange(15000), format='mjd')
print(timeit.timeit(lambda: fixed(tab), number=1))

# Time object itself 
# fast (< 0.01s)
print(timeit.timeit(lambda: fixed(Time(100 + np.arange(15000), format='mjd')), number=1))

# A table without Time column, simulating the dimension of the original data
# fast (< 0.01s)
tab = Table()
for i in range(1, 24):
    tab[f'col{i}'] = np.ones(15000)
print(timeit.timeit(lambda: fixed(tab), number=1))
```

Calling `Table.to_pandas()` yields `TypeError: data type '>I4' not understood` in a specific situation:

See https://github.com/lightkurve/lightkurve/issues/1043 for a downstream issue that is affected by this one.

Workaround: before calling `to_pandas()`, change the dtype to comptaible types that work, e.g., for `>i4`, change the dtype to `np.int32`

```python

title: Use chained exceptions instead of combining them
description:
Following up on https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11569/files#r621502335, in quite a few places in the code we do things like:
```
try:
    ...
except Exception as exc:
    raise TypeError(f'could not convert column {col.info.name!r} to string: {exc}')
```
Here, we benefit by telling the user what went wrong, but lose the traceback of the original problem. More typically recommended seems to be to chain the exceptions by adding `from exc`.  We should try to use that (`astropy.units` parsing being a particularly good example where this should help reduce the *very* lengthy and hard-to-comprehend tracebacks).

title: Representing Fields (ie scalar, vector, etc.)
description: ### Proposal Add a new module to coordinates to represent fields — scalar, vector, and tensor — and leverage Astropy coordinates to handle transforming representation types. 2) add a new class ``Field`` to handle collections of fields that share the same set of points. This would leverage ``QTable`` to hold the data, enable easy I/O, and potentially even make the Fields class useful for catalogs. @mhvk @adrn @taldcroft @eteq Current example code : https://github.com/nstarman/astropy/blob/coord_vectorfield/astropy/coordinates/field.py ### Motivation Any time you have a table of coordinates and a property for each of those coordinates. For scalars, like a gravitational potential field, ``Field`` is just a very convenient way to package the information, but for vectors like the corresponding acceleration field, transformations between representation types would be extremely nice. ### Implementation It's a change-of-basis. Astropy's Representation machinery can do it already, it just needed some tweaking for this new use case. ### Potential Future Extensions Expanding ``Field`` to handle CoordinateFrame transformations on the fields. ### Examples The basis is ``BaseFieldRepresentation``, which defines the components of a field at a point: ```python >>> from astropy import table, coordinates as coord, units as u >>> import numpy as np >>> points = coord.CartesianRepresentation(x=np.linspace(0, 10) * u.kpc, ... y=np.linspace(-1, -11) * u.kpc, ... z=np.linspace(-3, 3) * u.kpc) >>> fr = coord.CartesianFieldRepresentation(np.linspace(0, 10) * u.km / u.s**2, ... np.linspace(10, 100) * u.km / u.s**2, ... np.linspace(100, 1000) * u.km / u.s**2, ... points=points) >>> fr[:3] ``` Codewise, BaseFieldRepresentation is less than 200 lines of code (excluding docstrings), but could probably be shorter since a fair bit is only lightly modified from ``BaseRepresentationOrDifferential``. It's designed for multiple inheritance so that making new field representations is very easy. For example, this is how I made ``SphericalFieldRepresentation`` ```python class SphericalFieldRepresentation(FieldRepresentationBase, SphericalRepresentation): pass ``` Since ``BaseRepresentationOrDifferential`` (and therefore ``BaseFieldRepresentation``) can be columns in a QTable, this enables the ``Field`` class, which holds in a table: pointes (a Representation) and an arbitrary number of fields, scalar or vector (or hypothetically tensors, if extended). As an example ```python >>> field = coord.Field(points, ... mass=1 * u.solMass, # scalar field ... vector=np.c_[np.linspace(0, 10), # vector field ... np.linspace(10, 100), ... np.linspace(100, 1000)] * u.km / u.s**2) >>> field[:5] ``` The Field has both attribute and item access to all the fields in the table. The Field can be transformed between representation types and it uses the above machinery to not only transform the points, but also all the vector fields (scalar fields are invariant). ```python >>> Field.fieldtypes mappingproxy({'mass': 'scalar', 'vector': 'vector'}) ``` Showing a transformation: ```python >>> field.represent_as("spherical").vector[:3]

title: Modernize random number generation (i.e., stop using np.random.seed/get_state/set_state)
description:
`numpy` has gone away from the `np.random.seed`/`np.random.set_state`/`np.random.get_state` models for random number generation.  `astropy` should follow suit where possible.  This in practice means the following tasks:

- [ ] Stop using our home-grown `RNGContext` in the tests and replace with the newer `numpy` mechanism.
- [ ] Replace anywhere that `np.random.*` is used currently with something that uses the new mechanism (e.g. the random functions in #11628 ), which may require some API additions to let the new numpy generators be passed into functions.
- [ ] ? Deprecate our home-grown `RNGContext` and replacing it with the "new" numpy mechanism.  Note it is *not* currently clear to me if we can do this.  I don't think the numpy scheme supports a context manager a la our `ScienceState` approach. In that case we have to decide if we think it's worth supporting this long-term, trying to get this into `numpy` or just deciding it's better to use the `numpy` approach anyway.

For some backstory/justification on the `numpy` shift see:
* https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/index.html - the paragraph beginning with "Since Numpy version 1.17.0"
* https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/new-or-different.html#new-or-different
* https://towardsdatascience.com/stop-using-numpy-random-seed-581a9972805f

cc @adrn @lpsinger @mhvk (as discussers from #11628)

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/main/astropy/io/fits/hdu/table.py#L939 which pads FITS binary tables that variable-length columns out to the necessary multiple of 2880, can be triggered even when `data._gap == 0`.  That is, `fileobj.write(b'')` is not a no-op.

This padding may also be needed if a table or image is not itself an exact multiple of 2880 bytes, so it may be possible to trigger this even when there are no variable-length columns.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

Don't trigger a filesystem write if there is nothing to write:
```python
if data._gap > 0:
    fileobj.write((data._gap * '\0').encode('ascii'))
```

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

The Lustre filesystem has a known issue that is triggered when zero-length writes are attempted.  This bug report is an attempt to provide a workaround, and in general raise consciousness of corner cases that can happen in certain filesystems.

title: Add short worked examples to demo intended usage for each built-in coordinate frame
description:
I am attempting to simulate visibility of a low-Earth-orbit satellite from a fixed ground station.  The satellite elevation angles are all coming out around -17 degrees.  This is not believable.  As the satellite travels around the earth, the elevation angles should vary widely, and the satellite should at least occasionally be visible to the ground station (positive elevation angle).  I'm assuming that I'm doing something wrong, but it is possible that there is a documentation issue here.  My code follows.

```
# This script calculates visibility of a satellite to a single ground station.

# Section 1: Imports and constants.

from numpy import arange, empty, pi
from pdb import set_trace

import cartopy.crs as ccrs
from cartopy.feature.nightshade import Nightshade

from astropy import coordinates, time, units as u
from astropy.coordinates import AltAz, CartesianRepresentation, EarthLocation

from poliastro.bodies import Earth
from poliastro.twobody import Orbit, propagation
from poliastro.frames.fixed import ITRS
from poliastro.frames.equatorial import GCRS

RAD2DEG= 180 / pi


# Section 2: Simulate orbit.

a  = 7578.1 * u.km  # semi-major axis
ecc= 0      * u.one # eccentricity
inc= 63.4   * u.deg # inclination of the orbit plane
raan= 50    * u.deg # right ascension of the ascending node
argp= 270   * u.deg # argument of perigee
nu  = 0     * u.deg # true anomaly at epoch

T_sim_hrs= 24
T_step_min= 3

epoch= time.Time("2021-05-05 10:43")
orbit= Orbit.from_classical(Earth, a, ecc, inc, raan, argp, nu, epoch=epoch)

# Create time steps covering the duration of the simulation:
times= arange(0, 60*T_sim_hrs+1, T_step_min) * u.min

xyz= propagation.propagate(
  orbit,
  time.TimeDelta(times),
  method=propagation.cowell,
  rtol=1e-10,
)

epoch_times = epoch + times

# Calculate Earth-fixed (non-inertial) coordinates `itrs_xyz`:
gcrs_xyz = GCRS(xyz, obstime=epoch_times, representation_type=CartesianRepresentation)
itrs_xyz = gcrs_xyz.transform_to(ITRS(obstime=epoch_times))

# Convert satellite positions from Cartesian to spherical coordinates (radians and km):
sat_lat_lon= coordinates.cartesian_to_spherical(itrs_xyz.x, itrs_xyz.y, itrs_xyz.z)


# Section 3: Calculate satellite elevation angles.

# Reference: https://learn.astropy.org/rst-tutorials/Coordinates-Transform.html#transform-frames-to-get-to-altitude-azimuth-altaz

ground_station= EarthLocation.from_geodetic(
  lat   = 30 * u.deg,
  lon   = 30 * u.deg,
  height= 0  * u.km)

elevation= empty(len(sat_lat_lon[0]))

for i in range(len(sat_lat_lon[0])):
   satellite  = EarthLocation.from_geodetic(
     lat   =sat_lat_lon[1][i],
     lon   =sat_lat_lon[2][i],
     height=sat_lat_lon[0][i])

   # In the following call to `transform_to`, it is unclear why time is needed as an input.
   result= satellite.get_itrs().transform_to(AltAz(obstime=time.Time('J2010'),
     location=ground_station))

   elevation[i]= result.alt.value

set_trace()
```

title: Many Table formats deserialize None to a string
description:
### Description

When a column if full of `None`, many formats will deserialize the column to a string instead of None.

These are the problematic formats: {'aastex',  'ascii',  'ascii.aastex',  'ascii.basic',  'ascii.commented_header',  'ascii.csv',  'ascii.fast_basic',  'ascii.fast_commented_header',  'ascii.fast_csv',  'ascii.fast_no_header',  'ascii.fast_rdb',  'ascii.fast_tab',  'ascii.fixed_width',  'ascii.fixed_width_no_header',  'ascii.fixed_width_two_line',  'ascii.html',  'ascii.ipac',  'ascii.latex',  'ascii.no_header',  'ascii.rdb',  'ascii.rst',  'ascii.tab',  'csv',  'html',  'ipac',  'latex',  'rdb',  'votable'}

### Expected behavior

Table/Column correctly roundtrips the data type.

### Actual behavior

`None` becomes a string.

### Steps to Reproduce

Here is an illustrative example
```python
from astropy import table

t = table.Table(dict(a=[0], b=[None]))
print(t["b"][0], type(t["b"][0]))

t.write("temp.csv", format="ascii.fixed_width", overwrite=True)
t2 = table.Table.read("temp.csv", format="ascii.fixed_width")
print(t2["b"][0], type(t2["b"][0]))
```
None <class 'NoneType'>
None <class 'numpy.str_'>

And this will produce the full list of problematic formats
```python
bad_formats = set()
table_formats = set(get_formats(table.Table, "Write")["Format"])
# these are problematic for other reasons
table_formats -= {"pandas.html", "fits", "pandas.csv", "ascii.qdp", "asdf", "jsviewer", "pandas.json", "hdf5"}

t = table.Table(dict(a=[0], b=[None]))

for fmt in table_formats:
    t.write("temp.csv", format=fmt, overwrite=True)
    t2 = table.Table.read("temp.csv", format=fmt)
    if t2[t2.colnames[-1]][0] is not None:
        bad_formats.add(fmt)

bad_formats
```

title: Unable to open regular file when it has an extension indicating it's compressed
description:
### Description
If a FITS file has an extension that indicates it's a compressed file, but it's not actually compressed, Astropy can't open the file. This is because in line 441 of https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/main/astropy/io/fits/file.py, Astropy determines file type based on the extension, so if the file has .gz at the end of it, it’ll get uncompressed regardless of whether it’s actually compressed or not.

### Expected behavior
I would expect AstroPy to be able to understand that the file isn't actually compressed, and be able to open the file.

### Actual behavior
I get the following error:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/edbraun/opt/anaconda3/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/hdulist.py", line 173, in fitsopen
    return HDUList.fromfile(name, mode, memmap, save_backup, cache,
  File "/Users/edbraun/opt/anaconda3/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/hdulist.py", line 408, in fromfile
    return cls._readfrom(fileobj=fileobj, mode=mode, memmap=memmap,
  File "/Users/edbraun/opt/anaconda3/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/io/fits/hdu/hdulist.py", line 1113, in _readfrom
    raise OSError('Empty or corrupt FITS file')
OSError: Empty or corrupt FITS file
```

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a regular FITS file (example.fits) and rename it to add a .gz extension (example.fits.gz). DO NOT actually compress the file.
2. Try to open the file in AstroPy, e.g., with the following script:

```python
from astropy.io import fits
hdu = fits.open('example.fits.gz')
```

`astropy.visualization.wcsaxes.SphericalCircle` should accept a coordinate object for its `center` parameter. `center` is a tuple of two angle objects, describing the position on the sky, e.g. RA, DEC. title: Make _fitter_to_model_params public available to all users
description:
When subclassing fitters in order to override the `objective_function` method, one needs to use `_fitter_to_model_params` (or, alternatively implement a long hack). It is unfortunate that this function is "private" (`_`) and this poses some dangers when subclassing this class.

Would it be possible to make it public?

title: Allow fitters to work with "vector-models"
description: Currently it is impossible to use fitting machinery to fit multi-dimensional vector-models (functions) to multi-dimensional data. There are all kinds of restrictions in modeling that checks that `x`, `y`, and `z` all have the same shape. It would be very helpful if such checks could, for the very least, be disabled in order to allow subclassing fitters in order to implement custom `objective_function` for arbitrary dimensionalities.

title: Replace our custom calc_moon with new moon98 in SOFA 18
description:
The latest SOFA has a new `moon98` routine that calculates position and velocity using the Meeus algorithm. This can replace our own Meeus implementation in `coordinates.orbital_elements` - should give the same (or very similar) results and has the benefit that we'll also get velocities.

Milestoning 5.0 since pyerfa will definitely be up to that state by then (ERFA update is waiting for review; https://github.com/liberfa/erfa/pull/84).

title: Clarify definition of `modeling.separable`
description:
The [definition of `astropy.modeling.separable`](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/modeling/reference_api.html#module-astropy.modeling.separable) says:

> Functions to determine if a model is separable, i.e. if the model outputs are independent.

But this definition isn't clear to me, in particular if the model outputs are independent of *what*? It would be good to clear this up to include a watertight definition of what `separable` means in the context of a model.

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
When `SkyCoord.apply_space_motion()` for a coordinate without distance specified, astropy emits the following warning:

```python
WARNING: ErfaWarning: ERFA function "pmsafe" yielded 1 of "distance overridden (Note 6)" [astropy._erfa.core]
```

- The warning happened on the latest `main`. It was also on 4.1 release
- The issue seems to be related to #10092. But it appears that the resolution of #10092 does not make the warnings go away. The codes now just emit a different (albeit more comprehensible) warning.

- In jupyter, it emits two warnings that refer to the same problems:
```python
WARNING: ErfaWarning: ERFA function "pmsafe" yielded 1077 of "distance overridden (Note 6)" [astropy._erfa.core]
WARNING:astropy:ErfaWarning: ERFA function "pmsafe" yielded 1077 of "distance overridden (Note 6)"

The warning should not be there.

```python
import astropy
from astropy import units as u

title: The output of SkyCoord.apply_space_motion() can have a different differential type than its input
description:

by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
If `sc=SkyCoord()` is specified in ICRS with `differential_type='sphericalcoslat'` (i.e. with `pm_ra_cosdec`), then the output of `sc.apply_space_motion()` will have `differential_type='spherical'` (i.e. it will have `pm_ra`).

Furthermore, if `sc` is specified in Galactic coordinates, then `sc.apply_space_motion()` will always have `differential_type='sphericalcoslat'`, i.e. the output will always have `pm_l_cosb` and never `pm_l`.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
The output of the function `SkyCoord.apply_space_motion()` should have the same differential type as its input.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy.time import Time

obstime = Time('1988-12-18 05:11:23.5')
c = SkyCoord(ra=10*u.degree, dec=45*u.degree, distance=100*u.pc,
                       pm_ra_cosdec=34*u.mas/u.yr, pm_dec=-117*u.mas/u.yr,
                       obstime=obstime)
c.apply_space_motion(new_obstime=obstime)
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, pc)
    (10., 45., 100.)
 (pm_ra, pm_dec, radial_velocity) in (mas / yr, mas / yr, km / s)
    (48.08326112, -117., -4.88614875e-15)>
```
```python
c = SkyCoord(l=10*u.degree, b=45*u.degree, distance=100*u.pc,
                      pm_l=34*u.mas/u.yr, pm_b=-117*u.mas/u.yr,
                      frame='galactic',
                      differential_type='spherical',
                      obstime=obstime)
c.apply_space_motion(new_obstime=obstime)
<SkyCoord (Galactic): (l, b, distance) in (deg, deg, pc)
    (10., 45., 100.)
 (pm_l_cosb, pm_b, radial_velocity) in (mas / yr, mas / yr, km / s)
    (24.04163056, -117., 0.)>

```

### The issue

Ensuring that the output will always have the same differential type as the input is quite simple, but it would cause problems to existing code that is adapted to current behavior. This means that any change must be introduced gently, if at all.

It might be a good idea to temporarily add a new boolean keyword argument to `SkyCoord.apply_space_motion()`. The default value would result in the current behavior and also emit a warning, but explicitly changing the value would ensure that the differential types of the input and output are indeed the same.

title: HeaderDiff doesn't recognize ignore_keywords for keyword_count
description:
Astropy 4.2.1

Consider the following:

```
>>> h1 = fits.Header()
>>> h2 = fits.Header()
>>> h1['foo'] = 'bar'
>>> h2['foo'] = 'bar'
>>> h1['foo2'] = 'baz'
>>> diff = fits.HeaderDiff(h1, h2, ignore_keywords=['foo2'])
>>> diff.identical
False
>>> diff..diff_keyword_count
(2, 1)
```

Based on the [documentation for HeaderDiff](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/io/fits/api/diff.html#headerdiff) I would have expect these to be found to be identical. As shown above they are not identical because they have a different number of keywords, even though I'm trying to ignore one of them.

I did a quick check of some of the other `*Diff` methods and they seem to all suffer from the same issue.

Thanks.

>>> h1 = fits.Header()
>>> if fits.HeaderDiff(h1, h1): print('These are the same')
... 
>>> 
```

Nothing is printed. 

The culprit is in `_BaseDiff.__bool__`:
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/e183e398d8bdbbe5c7ccec7a793afed2ecdac4e1/astropy/io/fits/diff.py#L74-L80
