title: BUGs: Inconsistencies with `Distance`
description:
### Round-tripping

1) The redshift is not actually stored, even if passed to the Distance constructor. This means the distance is recomputed every time and only to the accuracy of ``z_at_value``. While this accuracy is high enough for actual astronomy purposes, the following fails:

```python
>>> from astropy.coordinates import Distance
>>> from astropy.cosmology import Planck18
>>> d = Distance(z=100, cosmology=Planck18)
>>> d.z == 100
False
```

2) For large redshifts the default values of `zmin` and `zmax` mean the redshift cannot even be computed.

```python
>>> from astropy.coordinates import Distance
>>> from astropy.cosmology import Planck18
>>> d = Distance(z=4e3, cosmology=Planck18)
>>> d.z
CosmologyError: Best guess z=999.9999999676769 is very close to the upper z limit 1000.
Try re-running with a different zmax.
```

### Inconsistent cosmology

Distance doesn't store the cosmology when initialized with a redshift, even if that cosmology is explicitly passed as an argument.

Consider the following:

```python
>>> import astropy.coordinates as coord
>>> import astropy.cosmology as cosmology
>>> d = coord.Distance(z=100, cosmology=cosmology.Planck18)
>>> cosmology.default_cosmology.set("WMAP7")
>>> d.z
98.78242384189551
```

I think that if Distance is initialized with a redshift, that it should be tied to the cosmology, especially if the cosmology is also passed as an argument. This can be solved by storing the cosmology used at initialization (if initialized by `z`).

### Conceptual

I think there might be a deeper conceptual problem. Calculating cosmological redshifts on distances smaller than 0.01 are pretty much meaningless because we are locally disconnected from the Hubble flow. Conversely, parallax measures on scales larger than 0.01 have and probably will never be observed. 1 AU is just too small a baseline.
While it's nice to have 1 class that does all distance measures, it doesn't make much as much sense physically given the difference in applicable scales.

### Possible Solution

My thought is that there should be a new class: ``CosmologicalDistance``, with ``.value`` as the redshift. The physical distance would be accessible by some attribute, kind of the opposite of ``Distance``.  Now ``Distance.z`` would return a ``CosmologicalDistance``.  When ``Distance`` is initialized with a redshift it internally stores a ``CosmologicalDistance`` that also keeps the cosmology. Keeping the ``CosmologicalDistance`` synced to the retaining ``Distance``  would be a bit tricky, but not insurmountable. The ``CosmologicalDistance`` can have other nice attributes, like ``comoving_distance``, since it stores the cosmology. Additionally, like ``SpectralQuantity`` (#10263), ``CosmologicalDistance`` can have (and provide) equivalencies like ``with_H0`` and from https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10143 (when merged)

description:
(Migrated from #10673, which I closed)

- [x] #11345 : Separating all the cosmology realizations (and controller `default_cosmology`) to a separate file — `realizations`
~I've currently called this `builtin`, but `realization` might be better.~ 

2.  upgrade `default_cosmology` to be a registry (a la `galactocentric_frame_defaults`) so users can add their own cosmology realizations and set them as the default.

- [ ] change the parameters file to an ECSV (if pyyaml becomes a dependency, JSON otherwise). #11517

4.1 Add entrypoints to the realizations, so that third-party packages can add specific cosmology realizations and users can access them straight through astropy.

4.2 Also allow auto-import of user-defined realizations from a file(s).

  - [ ] JSON & ECSV I/O  #11559 
  - [ ] #11517 
  - [ ] configuration parameter for parameter files location.

4. Enhance the `Cosmology` class so it initializes the default cosmology, with any user-passed modifications. This centralizes the cosmology creation process for any "perturbations" about the default cosmology. Finally a use for the base class.

    - [x] : step 1 is #11515 
    - [ ] : step 2 is #11518 

5. [Not in this PR] Add entrypoints to `core`, where the `Cosmology` classes are defined, so that  third-party packages can add cosmologies and have them integrate well with the realizations machinery.

At the end, astropy will provide a core set of cosmology classes and realizations, but be highly extensible to allow user-defined realizations, and aggregate third-party cosmologies and realizations.

These PRs might also might partially alleviate the lack-of-maintainer problem. Instead of programming more `Cosmology` classes, we let third-party packages demonstrate user need. If a Cosmology class becomes stable & popular enough then it could be added as a built-in.

title: Problems with ``logspace`` and dimensionless units.
description:
### Description


The following works:

```python
>>> np.logspace(1, 1, 1)
array([10.])
```

But the equivalent statements with units do not:

```python
>>> np.logspace(1*u.one, 1*u.one, 1)
```

and

```python
>>> np.logspace(np.log10(10*u.one), np.log10(10*u.one), 1)
```

### Actual behavior

``logspace`` with units only accepts ``Dex`` inputs.

If ``log10(x*unit)`` returned ``log10(x.value) * Dex(unit)`` that would fix this problem. But this solution doesn't make much sense for dimensionless units, for which ``log10(x*u.one)`` should still return units of ``u.one``. Then this would still break for ``logspace``, which is why dimensionless units might need to be special-cased in ``logspace`` and similar functions.

title: `fits.getdata` overrides `ext=0` argument
description:
### Description
Reported in the Facebook group:
For an HDUList with empty primary HDU, getdata intransparently returns data from the first extension, even if called explicitly as `fits.getdata(filename, ext=0)`.

### Expected behavior
Should raise an exception or at most return `None` as `hdulist[0]` has no data.

### Actual behavior
Returns data array, which turns out to be `hdulist[1].data`.

### Steps to Reproduce
See above and [Facebook post](https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=2974167039576138)

This is caused by the fallback in
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/c58ad0a6590d591b7b43cbd155b43891e9b44f6e/astropy/io/fits/convenience.py#L193-L206

There are a number of problems with this:
1. The docs state that the extension has to be specified or defaults to the primary HDU only.
2. Defaulting to the first non-empty HDU is reasonable, but only if no other has been explicitly requested, i.e. for the (default) `ext=None`. But since `_getext` already expanded `ext=None` to `extidx=0` that bit of information is lost at that point. Also _if_ looking for an HDU with data, there is no reason not to proceed all the way unto the first non-empty HDU rather than just to no. 1 (although there might be no sensible use case of a FITS file with an empty extension HDU).
3. The exceptions and error messages are misleading; the first states "No data in this HDU." when no HDU exists at that index, the second raises an `IndexError` when in fact there are no data (which probably should be a `ValueError`?).

Since it is not documented, it might make sense to remove that fallback altogether, but as it may still have been used, it could also be fixed and adequately documented (this would probably require saving the original `ext` setting from the `getdata` *args).

### System Details
Confirmed with 4.2.1 on macOS 10.14

description:

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

I was recently working on some time series data in which the time was in the Reduced Julian Date format, or `rjd` for short.
I wanted to convert `rjd` to other formats, however sadly looking at https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/time/index.html#id3, I found that `astropy.time` doesn't has support for `rjd`, although it does supports Julian Date `jd` and the Modified Julian Date `mjd`.

There is a small Python library called `Julian` (see: https://github.com/dannyzed/julian/blob/master/julian/julian.py) which provides conversions to and from different Julian Dates, and I ultimately utilised its functionalities.
Since, Astropy is the de-facto library one looks for when doing astronomy work in Python, I think it would be nice have this added  feature of `rjd` format in `astropy.time`

Changes required to incorporate this are not much since, RJD differs only minutely from the MJD format.

- RJD = JD − 2400000
- MJD = JD − 2400000.5

See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day

### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

There are many datasets that record Time in the RJD format, esp. in the Solar and Stellar field. Having the `rjd` format in `astropy.time` will also enable Time Format conversions in TimeSeries objects (https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/timeseries/times.html), something which the non-integrated `Julian` library cannot do.

title: "No velocity defined on frame" warning is deceptive?
description:
This code specifies an observer and a target with a radial (line-of-sight) velocity and an "observed" frequency, then computes the rest frequency in the frame of the target:

```python
from astropy.coordinates import SpectralCoord, EarthLocation, SkyCoord
location = EarthLocation.of_site('VLA')
from astropy.time import Time
vla = location.get_itrs(obstime=Time('2019-10-15T17:00:30'))
ic860 = SkyCoord('13h15m03.520s +24d37m07.9s', frame='icrs',radial_velocity=3867*u.km/u.s,distance=53.3*u.Mpc)
sc_feat = SpectralCoord(45.6*u.GHz,observer=vla,target=ic860)
sc_feat_rest = sc_feat.with_observer_stationary_relative_to(sc_feat.target)
```

It raises the warning
```python
WARNING: NoVelocityWarning: No velocity defined on frame, assuming (0., 0., 0.) km / s. [astropy.coordinates.spectral_coordinate]
```
which seems very worrying, since we did specify the velocity on the target!  However, it's referring to the _observer_ object:
```python
# this is the line in astropy/coordinates/spectral_coordinate.py that raises the warning:
obj._observer = cls._validate_coordinate(observer, label='observer')
```

However, it appears that the calculation is taking into account the rotation of the Earth and its orbit around the sun.  If I redo the calculation with `v_target=0`:
```python
ic860_zero = SkyCoord('13h15m03.520s +24d37m07.9s', frame='icrs')
sc_feat_zero = SpectralCoord(45.6*u.GHz,observer=vla,target=ic860_zero)
sc_feat_zero_rest = sc_feat_zero.with_observer_stationary_relative_to(sc_feat_zero.target)
((sc_feat_zero_rest - 45.6*u.GHz) / (45.6*u.GHz) * constants.c).to(u.km/u.s)
# -7.27 km/s, reasonable for Earth motion at a glance
```

So I think this warning is telling us that we have (unwittingly) specified that our observer is fixed with respect to the ITRS frame, which I'd say should be expected of any observatory besides, say, SOFIA.

Is my interpretation correct?  Should we therefore include v_x,y,z = 0 in the specification of site locations?  Or can we rephrase this warning to make it clearer?

cc @jmangum, who raised this question to me

### Description
I am using astropy.io.fits to work with fits files from GOES/SUVI. Those fits files have an issue with the CONTINUE convention, which is implemented incorrectly. Until astropy version 4.2, I was able to use the .tostring() method to convert the corrupt fits header to a string, fix it, and convert it back to a corrected fits header. Starting with astropy version 4.2.1, this is no longer possible: the .tostring() method now seems to do a fits header validity check and will not allow me to access the header. Setting verify to "ignore" does not help, but maybe I am using it wrong. 

Is this the desired behaviour? For me this means I am no longer able to fix the corrupt fits header. I believe that if it is known that a fits header is not compliant with the fits standard, there should at least be an option to ignore the validity check so it is still accessible and can be fixed. 

### Expected behavior

title: FITS table documentation uses non-standard FITS unit
description:
### Description

While reading the documentation about fits table data, I noticed that there is a non-standard unit used: 
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blame/main/docs/io/fits/usage/table.rst#L346
```python
   >>> col2 = fits.Column(name='counts', format='J', unit='DN', array=counts)
```

### Expected behavior

I'd expect that the documentation sticks to the standard.

### Actual behavior

`DN` is not a standard FITS unit, and even not directly supported by `astropy.units`. For example, the following does not work:
```
counts = [0., 1.]
col2 = fits.Column(name='counts', format='J', unit='DN', array=counts)
tbl = QTable([col2])
```

It may sound nitpicking, but we should not encourage people to use phantasy units. The name "counts" would suggest as unit `count`.

title: u.format.fits.Fits.to_string() throws the wrong exception with bad argument
description:
### Expected behavior

An bad unit argument in `u.format.fits.Fits.to_string()` should raise a `TypeError` (or a `ValueError` if the type is correct).

### Actual behavior

It raises an `UnboundLocalError`

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import astropy.units as u

u.format.Fits.to_string(None)
```
gives
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/astropy/units/format/fits.py", line 137, in to_string
    return s
UnboundLocalError: local variable 's' referenced before assignment
```
Reason is that `astropy/units/format/fits.py` only assign `s` for certain input types (line 110ff):
```python
    @classmethod
    def to_string(cls, unit):
        # Remove units that aren't known to the format
        unit = utils.decompose_to_known_units(unit, cls._get_unit_name)
        parts = []
        if isinstance(unit, core.CompositeUnit):
            […]
            s = ' '.join(parts)
        elif isinstance(unit, core.NamedUnit):
            s = cls._get_unit_name(unit)
     
        return s
```
IMO `utils.decompose_to_known_units()` should raise an exception (currently, it returns `None` as it has the same `if…elif` logic), or this should be done in `Fits.to_string()`. I would even add in both
```python
        else:
            raise TypeError(f'Illegal type {unit.class.name}')
```
so that one still holds when the other is missed :-)

BTW, the list `[core.CompositeUnit, core.NamedUnit]` is also not complete: `u.format.fits.Fits.to_string(u.ABmag)` shows the same behaviour, although `u.ABmag` is an Astropy unit.

### System Details

That is astropy 4.2, but the code didn't change in the main branch.

title: Unit roundtrips do not always work
description:
### Description

Not sure whether this is an issue, however it would probably nice to have it fixed:

### Expected behavior

I would expect that any roundtrip for `unicode` format works. i.e. for all units `unit`:

```Python
format='unicode'
assert u.Unit(unit.to_string(format=format), format=format) == unit
```

should work. I would expect the same for the other formatters; at least for `generic` and `fits`. 

### Actual behavior

For Angstrom, it works when not giving `unicode` as format in the `u.Unit()` constructor, but not when this is given:

```Python
>>> u.Unit(u.Angstrom.to_string(format='unicode')) == u.Angstrom
True
>>> u.Unit(u.Angstrom.to_string(format='unicode'), format='unicode') == u.Angstrom
[…]
ValueError: 'Å' did not parse as unicode unit: Can not parse Unicode If this […]
```
The second exception comes for any unit; `unicode` seems not be supported as parsing format.

For the solar mass, the first one does not work as well:
```Python
>>>  u.Unit(u.solMass.to_string(format='unicode')) == u.solMass
[…]
ValueError: 'M⊙' did not parse as unit: At col 0, M is not a valid unit. Did you […]
```
I would assume that 

 * the "unicode" parse format is identical to the "generic" format (as we usually use unicode in strings)
 * Unicode output is also parseable, as the generic input

### System Details

The tests were done with Astropy 4.2

title: Unit constructor should not allow formats that are for output only
description: As noticed by @olebole in #11826, `u.Unit('anything', format='unicode')` fails with an error message that is confusing, suggesting that the the unit might be wrong, while really the unicode format, like latex, is meant for output only. The non-parsing output formats should get a different error message.

title: Use sphinx-reredirects for renaming/removed documentation
description:
### Description

The [sphinx-reredirects](https://documatt.gitlab.io/sphinx-reredirects/index.html) Sphinx extension would be useful for declaring redirected pages directly in our `conf.py` when pages get renamed or removed, as opposed to having to set up the redirects manually in RTD (in addition to keeping such redirects under VC which is not currently possible with RTD redirects, it would also work for non-RTD builds of the docs).

### Additional context

We've had a few cases where moving or renaming docs have broken things like search results, or in some cases other packages' documentation that links to the Astropy docs (see e.g. #11754).  Currently, any time we move documentation around we must also take care to set up redirects in RTD, which can only be done by someone with access to the RTD project.  It's easy to miss.

By using a Sphinx extension for this, we can include such redirects in any PR that requires documentation moves.

I've seen some other extensions for this, but this one is quite recent, actively maintained, and seems like one of the simplest to use and quite flexible.

@astrofrog asked

> Could we actually replace the redirects configured on RTD with this? The redirects on RTD currently are ‘top level’ in the sense we can add urls at the level of latest/stable/etc - this would only be useful within a set of docs right?

It's a good question and I'm not 100% sure it could replace *all* use cases for RTD's redirects.  But it would be useful in many caes--for example, I wanted to use this for #11367 which requires an old doc page that I want to remove to be replaced with a redirect to a different doc page.

It also could have been used for the redirect of all developer doc pages to the "latest" docs (which prompted #11754) like:

```python
redirects = {
    'development/*': 'https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/$source.html'
}
```

The redirect could also be made contingent on whether or not the docs are being built for RTD.

title: Allow setting the unit parsing policy when using `Table.read` for FITS
description:
### Description
`astropy.table.fits.connect.read_table_fits` silently ignores units not in FITS format and does not allow either falling back to the more lenient unit parsing (`u.Unit()` without `format="fits"`) or being more strict (warn or raise).

I'd like to add an option to add the warning and be able to fallback to the general parser for units not conforming to the fits standard.

### Additional context

```python
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.table import Table

t = Table({'a': [1, 2, 3]})
t.meta['EXTNAME'] = 'test'
t.write('invalid_unit.fits', overwrite=True)
with fits.open('invalid_unit.fits', mode='update') as hdul:
    hdul['test'].header['TUNIT1'] = '1 / (MeV sr s)'

t = Table.read('invalid_unit.fits')
print(repr(t['a'].unit))  # UnrecognizedUnit('1 / (MeV sr s)')
```

title: Updates/process info for 4.3
description:

- [x] The branching instructions don't mention the fact that github actions should be updated for the newly-created branch (I think? see #11846)
- [ ] The release instructions don't say when the branch of a completed version should be closed [in the pr_consistency script](https://github.com/astropy/astropy-procedures/blob/main/pr_consistency/4.check_consistency.py) (in the past I think it's been when the next version is released, but should write that down.)
- [x] The release instructions call for the gh_issuereport.py script, but it doesn't work anymore.  Need to update it to https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/blob/main/tools/generate_releaserst.xsh (and maybe move that to openastro?)
- [x] Add a note to the instructions to push up the dev tag when branching happens
- [x] Update mentions of astropy-procedures back to astropy-tools
- [ ] Mention what to do about #11689
- [x] Clarify in the release instructions whether/how IERS releases should go in `main` (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/commit/3aaad2220b0c0f85a7c526396b8c63bf154a1f87#commitcomment-53448308)

- [ ] Be more specific about the announcement process (and shouldn't need to coordinate with the CoCo - rather the release team)
- [ ] Be more concrete about the "announcement" part (e.g. 4.2 did not follow the normal process)

title: Labels cleanup
description:
We've had discussions on slack and elsewhere about the state of labels in this repository.  Some feel that there are too many labels--in other cases, some of the labels are underutilized or not useful.  We might want to have a look at the current labels and see if there are any we can pare down or change to make more useful.  This is sort of a meta-triage issue.

One problem with deleting labels, is they are also deleted from the issues they have been used on, which in some cases can make those issues harder fo find.  But I think there are some labels that might not be serving a significant purpose to begin with.

For starters, the question came up as to how to use the "Priority" labels and whether or not they're useful.  So to start with here are some statistics on the "Priority" labels:

* Priority-Low: issues: 27 open / 75 closed / oldest open: August 2012; PRs: 1 open / 27 closed / oldest open: March 2021
* Priority-Medium: 13 open / 16 closed / oldest open: October 2013; PRs: 0 open / 4 closed
* Priority-High: 1 open / 24 closed / oldest open: May 2019; PRs: 0 open / 11 closed

I didn't take exact numbers, but I also found that many "Priority-High" issues actually took several months or even years to resolve.

Another issue I raised about use of "Priority" issues, especially "Priority-Low" is it's very subjective as to how high a priority an issue is to whom.  And marking an issue raised by a user as "Priority-Low" may give the impression that the issue is *unimportant*, or that the report was not valued (it is, even if it's a minor issue that really is not the highest priority to fix!)

"Priority" labels could be useful when labeling issues in a milestone in order to help plan a release.  Like, we might know that we won't get to every issue in a milestone before its release, but we may wish to prioritize them.  However, another approach to that might just be to remove issues from the milestone when close to the release if they are not *high* priority.  Otherwise, unless someone is actively planning to work on some issue, setting a priority for it doesn't seem to have any effect on how likely it is to actually get done.

So I propose we simply remove the "Priority" labels, as they are not being used in a way that provides any value.

One similar label that seems to have more use is the :fire: label, which we've been using the label critical/blocker issues.  From what I can tell these usually get resolved in a timely manner, out of necessity.  And it's useful for release planning to be able to look at a list of these.

Other labels we could consider for removal:

* analytic_functions: this package was removed in Astropy 3.0.  Removing it means more difficulty (but not a ton) finding old issues related to this package, but do we really need that?
* astropy-helpers-removal: this work is mostly finished, do we still need a label for it?  It still has some open issues, but I think most of those issues could use more generic labels (build/installation/etc.)
* astropy-helpers: ditto, should be obsolete
* CASA-installation: not sure why we need a special label for this.  Maybe at one point it was being actively worked on, but it only has 3 issues/4 PRs and was last used in 2018.  New issues related to this can just go in "installation" I think.
* "new benchmark": How is this to be used?
* "potential fix for 2.0.x": I think this had something to do with Sphinx.  It was used twice.  This is obsolete now, right?
* run-asv: I understand what this is for, but does it actually work? I don't know in ASV how to find the benchmarks for a specific PR.
* "Still Needs Manual Backport": What is this for?  It doesn't look like it's been used.  How is it different from just "Manual Backport"
* unusual-merge-dealt-with: This has been used 5 times on some PRs, last in 2017.  Do we need this?

In any case, I think for all labels we want to keep, there should be documentation in the [maintainer docs](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/development/w

title: Add some strategies in the maintainer docs for diagnosing CI failures
description:
Sometimes when a CI run fails on a PR there can be a range of difficulties w.r.t. debugging what went wrong ranging from:

* easy: A new test added to the PR fails on one or more CI jobs
* ...
* hard: Seemingly totally unrelated failure, but that is still unique to the PR.

Additionally it would be good to have an overview of all the CI checks currently performed.  This is sometimes changing, but that's one of the reasons we moved the developer docs to the "latest" docs.  Now, when we modify the CI configuration to add a new job or workflow, it can include a corresponding update to the maintainer docs to mention the check, how to interpret it, and how to interpret failures in the check.

This documentation should also be linked to in the PR checklist for maintainers, as a follow-up to https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11844#discussion_r652974114

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
The `_HeaderCommentaryCards` class is registered as a `Mapping` (via its parent `_CardAccessor`, [here](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/main/astropy/io/fits/header.py#L2143)), but has no method `keys()`. Therefore, when using `isinstance` to check if a commentary card instance is a mapping before using a `Mapping` method such as `keys()` leads to an error. This seems true for `_CardAccessor` and its two subclasses (`_HeaderCommentaryCards` and `_HeaderComments`). I encountered this bug in a code that parses a header and treats each value differently depending on its type (in the [munch](https://github.com/Infinidat/munch) package, but I reproduced a simple example below).

Is this behaviour expected, in which case using `hasattr` or `try/except` instead of `isinstance` in the client code would fix the issue ?

If this is indeed a bug in astropy, I'd be happy to help, although I don't have prior experience with astropy development.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
I think the expected behaviour would be that `_HeaderCommentaryCards` is treated as a Sequence, according to [this section](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/io/fits/usage/headers.html#comment-history-and-blank-keywords) of the documentation. It seems that having keys would be useful in the case of `_HeaderComments`, and for `_CardAccessor` itself I do not know. I am not very experienced with the inner workings of `astropy` so I might be wrong on the expected behaviour. But in any case it seems the object should either be recognized as a mapping and have keys, or be registered as a sequence if it does not have keys. (There is [a TODO comment](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/main/astropy/io/fits/header.py#L2086) about dict/list methods for `CardAccessor` in the source code.)

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
`_HeaderCommentaryCards` (and all `_CardAccessor` instances) are regognized as mappings, but have no `keys()` method. This results in an error: `AttributeError: '_HeaderCommentaryCards' object has no attribute 'keys'`.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

1. Read or create a header with commentary cards.
2. Iterate trough keys (iterating items does not reproduce because it parses commentary card values one at a time).
3. Check if keys are instances of mapping.
4. If true, try to access access their `keys()` method.

```python
from typing import Mapping
from astropy.io import fits

hdr = fits.Header()

hdr['SOMEKEY'] = 'somevalue'  # regular value, no error

# NOTE: Commenting all of the commentary keys removes the issue
hdr['HISTORY'] = 'history1'
hdr['HISTORY'] = 'history2'
hdr[''] = 'blank1'
hdr[''] = 'blank2'
hdr['COMMENT'] = 'A comment'
hdr['COMMENT'] = 'Another comment'


for k in hdr.keys():
    if isinstance(hdr[k], Mapping):
        k.keys()
```

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
I'm currently working with some light curves collected from a ground-based telescope, and I've been using astropy.timeseries.LombScargle() to extract the rotation period. One of the ways I've been assessing the significance of a detection is through the False Alarm Probability (specifically, one that has been calculated by the bootstrap method). What I've found is that the probability I get depends on the normalization I choose for the periodograms. I generally find that the false alarm probability for the 'standard' normalization is 4-5% (absolute) smaller than the 'psd' normalization, even though everything else is identical (e.g. using 'standard' yields a probability of 1%, whereas using 'psd' yields 5%, or using 'standard' yields a probability of 25%, where as using 'psd' yields 30%). The different probabilities holds out to n_bootstraps of 100000, I have not tested larger numbers because of computation times required though.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
I would have expected that the false alarm probability be the same regardless of normalization, especially with all else the same.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
normalization='standard' consistently yields a different false alarm probability than normalization='psd' despite all other things being the same (i.e. same input light curve, same frequency grid, same method used, even the random_seed for the bootstrapping)
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

The code below roughly reproduces the issue, the sampling in time is different for my real data, but even for n_bootstrap of 100000 the printed values are 0.075 vs 0.116

```python
from astropy.timeseries import LombScargle

import numpy as np  

rand = np.random.RandomState(13)
t = 100 * rand.rand(100)
y = 0.6*np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) + rand.randn(100)
lsc1 =  LombScargle(t, y,normalization='standard')
freq, power = lsc1.autopower()
fap1 = lsc1.false_alarm_probability(np.max(power),method='bootstrap',method_kwds={'random_seed': 42, 'n_bootstraps': 10000})
lsc2 =  LombScargle(t, y,normalization='psd')
freq, power = lsc2.autopower()
fap2 = lsc2.false_alarm_probability(np.max(power),method='bootstrap',method_kwds={'random_seed': 42, 'n_bootstraps': 10000})
print(fap1,fap2)
```

title: Consider deprecating and then removing the io.ascii Column.dtype attribute
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md .
Please be sure to check out our code of conduct,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . -->

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

In #11892 there was discussion (and at one point code) to deprecate the `io.ascii.core.Column.dtype` attribute, with a plan to remove it. This issue is created to continue that discussion separately from that PR.

I am not in favor of this because it removes the possibility of user-defined readers specifying the exact `dtype` of columns without writing their own `_convert_vals` method in a custom Outputter. Such readers might already exist in the wild.

Readers like CDS and Rdb currently use `Column.type` to specify generic types such as float, int, str, but that mechanism does not allow fine-grained control like `np.int8`. Before the overhaul of ECSV in v4.3 of astropy, the ECSV reader did use the `Column.dtype` to do exactly that.

`Io.ascii` has been out for about 10 years now and has always been advertised as an extensible reader (though `dtype` came later, probably with ECSV). So we should not take this API change lightly as if it were just an internal change.

As mentioned here https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11892#pullrequestreview-693349877, one reasonable and small-footprint idea for improving the io.ascii.read `converters` API is to allow specifying a numpy dtype directly.

In other words (quoting @mhvk):
```
if not callable(converters): 
    converters = [convert_numpy(converters)]
```
This is syntactic sugar but will make the interface substantially easier to use. I'm very much in favor of this and have had the same thought many times but just never gotten around to doing it. Along with this I would make doc examples all use this formalism and put the original syntax as effectively a technical footnote.

title: Modernize WCS extension test
description:
As noted here: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10581#issue-451434058  In #10581 we updated this test to use `setuptools` instead of `distutils` (since distutils is being deprecated and slated for removal from the stdlib).

However, setuptools still has legacy behavior w.r.t. to how `setup.py install` works.  In fact, in general, we should no longer be using `setup.py install` at all for this test, since it's not how most packages (even test packages!) should be installed anymore, except in very narrow cases (namely packaging for distros, and even that's moving more and more toward pip).

So this is a reminder to redo that test package such that it's packaged in a more "modern" way (this does not require many changes, since writing a `setup.py` is still the most recommended way to build packages containing extension modules).  But it should add a `pyproject.toml` and use pip to install the test package.

title: Order in which units are presented
description:
Hi,

I have a quantity `x` that I would like to be presented in units of `erg/(s Hz)` or `erg s^-1 Hz^-1`, as opposed to `erg/(Hz s)` or `erg Hz^-1 s^-1` because of how it looks when rendered in latex, among other reasons. Another possible solution to my problem is getting the `*` or `\times` symbol to appear when the unit appears in LaTeX, i.e. `erg/(Hz*s)`. Can that be done?

Thank you very much.

title: Questions about API for masked Time
description:
Mostly for @taldcroft, two questions as I'm trying to finish the PR that uses `Masked` inside `Time`:
1. To what extent should we preserve the possibility to get `MaskedArray` as output for `.value`, etc.? (As input, it will be fully preserved.) Options would seem to be
  - Always have `Masked` output.
  - Preserve type of input, i.e., `MaskedArray` in -> `MaskedArray` out (this would not round-trip through disk, though).
  - Have a configuration item, with `MaskedArray`, `Masked`, or 'as_input' or so.
2. Currently, the data underlying any masked input items are replaced with a placeholder - this makes sense in the current implementation, since `jd2` is replaced by `nan` so the original data is corrupted. With `Masked`, this is no longer necessary, and in general the philosophy for `Masked` is that a mask does not indicate data is corrupt but just that data should not be looked at; the class tries to keep data intact (though without trying too hard). So, the question is now what to do. Options:
  - Just keep replacing; masked data is assumed to be crap.
  - Aim to ensure that masked items never lead to warnings or errors, e.g., by replacing only masked non-finite numbers.
  - Do a double trial of time parsing, first with data as they were, and if that does not work, with masked data replaced.
  - Yet another configuration item, perhaps 'replace', 'replace-non-finite', 'nothing'.

p.s. Current implementation at https://github.com/astropy/astropy/compare/main...mhvk:masked-time?expand=1, but that includes the multitude of small bug-fix PRs that I found while implementing it.

title: Edge treatment in convolution when edges are NaN is not consistent
description:
```python
from astropy.convolution import convolve, convolve_fft, Gaussian2DKernel
import numpy as np
x = np.ones([100,100], dtype='float') * np.nan
convolve_fft(x, Gaussian2DKernel(2), fill_value=np.nan, boundary='fill')
convolve(x, Gaussian2DKernel(2), fill_value=np.nan, boundary='fill')
```

The behavior between the above functions is not consistent.  `convolve` returns an image that still includes NaNs even though `interpolate_nan` is specified, while `convolve_fft` does not.

The `convolve_fft` version is naively more intuitive to me, but @adrn showed me a use case where the `convolve` behavior is (probably) what is desired.

We need to make these consistent and document how to achieve the different outcomes.

title: Keyword duplication in compressed image headers
description:
### Description

When creating a compressed image HDU, adding a keyword to `CompImageHDU.header` causes it to be duplicated in the underlying `CompImageHDU._header` if it already existed in the underlying header.

### Steps to Reproduce

This is most easily seen with the `EXTNAME` keyword since all `CompImageHDU` headers start with a default of `EXTNAME = 'COMPRESSED_IMAGE'`, though the same can be reproduced by running something like:

```python
>>> chdu = fits.CompImageHDU()
>>> chdu._header['FOO'] = 'A'
>>> chdu.header['FOO'] = 'A"
>>> chdu.header
XTENSION= 'IMAGE   '           / Image extension                                
BITPIX  =                    8 / array data type                                
NAXIS   =                    0 / number of array dimensions                     
PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of parameters                           
GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups                               
FOO     = 'A       '                                                            
>>> chdu._header
XTENSION= 'BINTABLE'           / binary table extension                         
BITPIX  =                    8 / array data type                                
NAXIS   =                    2 / number of array dimensions                     
NAXIS1  =                    8 / width of table in bytes                        
NAXIS2  =                    0 / number of rows in table                        
PCOUNT  =                    0 / number of group parameters                     
GCOUNT  =                    1 / number of groups                               
TFIELDS =                    1 / number of fields in each row                   
TTYPE1  = 'COMPRESSED_DATA'    / label for field 1                              
TFORM1  = '1PB     '           / data format of field: variable length array    
ZIMAGE  =                    T / extension contains compressed image            
ZTENSION= 'IMAGE   '           / Image extension                                
ZBITPIX =                    8 / data type of original image                    
ZNAXIS  =                    0 / dimension of original image                    
ZPCOUNT =                    0 / number of parameters                           
ZGCOUNT =                    1 / number of groups                               
ZCMPTYPE= 'RICE_1  '           / compression algorithm                          
ZNAME1  = 'BLOCKSIZE'          / compression block size                         
ZVAL1   =                   32 / pixels per block                               
ZNAME2  = 'BYTEPIX '           / bytes per pixel (1, 2, 4, or 8)                
ZVAL2   =                    1 / bytes per pixel (1, 2, 4, or 8)                
EXTNAME = 'COMPRESSED_IMAGE'   / name of this binary table extension            
FOO     = 'A       '                                                            
FOO     = 'A       '
```

In the latter, the `FOO` keyword gets repeated.  This is probably the underlying cause of the bug that #11396 was trying to work around (there never should have been multiple `EXTNAME` keywords in the first place, but it appears to be an artifact of an Astropy bug, which probably existed for some time).

This is another bug caused by the disastrous `CompImageHeader` class.  When assigning a keyword to a header, `Header._update()` gets called, which in turn calls `Header.append()` if the keyword is not already in the header.  But for `CompImageHeader`, that means `CompImageHeader.append()` gets called, which also appends the keyword to the underling `self._table_header` even if it already existed there.

Not sure if there's a quick workaround.

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->
It's great that astropy can calculate the positions of celestial objects to microarcsecond precision, but not everyone needs that level of accuracy all the time. Sometimes, we just need a quick answer, accurate to the nearest arcsecond, and we don't have time to wait for five extra digits of precision that we'll never use. Case in point, I'm doing some stuff with the effects of atmospheric dispersion on solar observations with DKIST, and I don't need five decimals of precision to know how long I can hold a slit at the same position on the solar disk.

Basically, what I'm asking is, would it be possible to add an option for low-precision calculations? I get that a lot of people who use this library need all that precision and can spare the computational time, but if there was an option to say, "Just calculate it to the nearest arcsecond and let me get on with my day," especially with things like geocentric coordinate transformations, I think a lot of users could benefit. After all, as I rather bluntly put it to my advisor today, you wouldn't use a scalpel to butcher a cow.

### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->
If it helps at all, this is the code I'm working with. It's basically a python translation of some old IDL routines my advisor wrote back in '06. The IDL version runs to completion in about 10 seconds. The python version takes 20 minutes. I would be very happy if I could drop a few decimals and get it down to less than a minute.

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

In the fast LS implementation, if `normalization='psd'` and `dy is not None`, the power output gets multiplied by `0.5 * (dy ** -2.0).sum()`.  I'm a bit confused about this, and the output doesn't match what I expected.  Maybe this is converting the units of "power" to be relative to the power in the noise?  I can't find anything in the documentation to describe how to interpret this.  This could be intended behavior, but with opaque intentions.  May also be related to #11891.

title: Setting bounds on model can cause fit to diverge
description:
### Description
When using astropy models to perform astro/photometry, fitting a model to a star image with bounds causes the fit to diverge to the edges of the parameter space. A fit without bounds works fine and converges to a value within the bounds. With the a more complex PSF model, with stronger side-maxima than a plain Airy disc, this happens basically every time. Both with the LevenbergMarquardt and Simplex fitters.

My suspicion without having fully understood the fitting framework is that these lines in  `astropy/modeling/fitting.py` effectively "brickwall" the parameters, throwing off the gradient calculation / simplex direction and cause the fit to "stick" to the edge of the parameter bounds.
```python
# Check bounds constraints
if model.bounds[name] != (None, None):
    _min, _max = model.bounds[name]
    if _min is not None:
        values = np.fmax(values, _min)
    if _max is not None:
        values = np.fmin(values, _max)
```
I found a possible explanation/solution to the issue described here: https://lmfit.github.io/lmfit-py/bounds.html  
More recent versions of `scipy.optimize.least_squares` seem to support bounds on parameters for `trf` directly.


### Expected behavior
Fit with bounds should not perform worse than a unbounded fit that finds the minimum within the bounds.

### Steps to Reproduce
```python
from astropy.modeling.functional_models import AiryDisk2D
from astropy.modeling.fitting import LevMarLSQFitter
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(999999)

fitter = LevMarLSQFitter()
y, x = np.mgrid[-5:5:50j, -5:5:50j]

# Airy Disk mostly works, bigger problems with models that have more sidelobes/wings
input_model = AiryDisk2D(radius=2)

# build noisy image from input model
img = np.random.poisson(1e5*input_model(x, y)) + np.random.normal(0, 20)

fit_model = input_model.copy()

# bad guess for amplitude, decent guesses for position causes fitter to want to explore
# out of bounds, gets stuck there if bounds enabled
fit_model.x_0 = 0.1
fit_model.y_0 = -0.08
fit_model.amplitude = 1e3


fitted = fitter(fit_model, x, y, img)
print(f'without bounds: {fitted.x_0=} {fitted.y_0=} {fitted.amplitude=}')

fit_model.bounds['x_0'] = (-0.2, 0.2)
fit_model.bounds['y_0'] = (-0.2, 0.2)

fitted = fitter(fit_model, x, y, img)
print(f'with bounds: {fitted.x_0=} {fitted.y_0=} {fitted.amplitude=}')
```
prints
```
without bounds: fitted.x_0=Parameter('x_0', value=0.00019776080448936212) fitted.y_0=Parameter('y_0', value=-9.740265185190977e-05) fitted.amplitude=Parameter('amplitude', value=99967.10092998871)
with bounds: fitted.x_0=Parameter('x_0', value=-0.2, bounds=(-0.2, 0.2)) fitted.y_0=Parameter('y_0', value=0.2, bounds=(-0.2, 0.2)) fitted.amplitude=Parameter('amplitude', value=92364.16417303146)
```

title: Table join (left, outer) with missing entries is valid
description:
Joining a table where the left table has a masked array raises an exception:

```python
>>> from astropy import table
>>> tbl = table.Table({'a':[1,2,3], 'b':[4,5,np.ma.masked]})
>>> table.join(tbl, tbl, join_type='left')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<ipython-input-53-617ec8bb45ba>", line 1, in <module>
    table.join(tbl, tbl, join_type='left')
  File "/orange/adamginsburg/repos/astropy/astropy/table/operations.py", line 387, in join
    join_funcs)
  File "/orange/adamginsburg/repos/astropy/astropy/table/operations.py", line 1127, in _join
    .format(arr_label, name))
TableMergeError: Left key column 'b' has missing values
```

but it shouldn't, it's valid to join onto this table - it will just have no match for the third row.

The best workaround I've come up with is:
```python
msk = tbl['b'].mask
tbl['b'].mask = False
tbl['b'][msk] = -999999 # some junk
rslt = table.join(tbl, tbl, join_type='left')
rslt['b'].mask[msk] = True
```

which of course is a bit ugly because of the arbitrary `-9999` entry, but the default masked value appears to be zero.  Is there a better approach to take here?

title: Document towncrier rendering release process
description:
(This is a "sub-issue" of #11847)

In v4.3 I did a very awkward towncrier approach, but we should update the release instructions with a better process.  Here's a proposal @bsipocz , @Cadair, @pllim and I discussed out-of-band in an infrastructure telecon:

1. At the time of an RC, the release manager should look over the rendered changelog and look for issues like things being in the wrong section or changelog entries being too long.  If they see issues, they should ask the maintainer "can you shorten or maybe put this in the what's new? please make the PR to do that into main, and we'll backport to the release branch" But they should *not* run towncrier to clean up the fragments for an RC
2. As a "last before release" (i.e., within 24 hr or so of release) step, the release manager should make a PR into the release branch that runs `towncrier`. It should then be merged just before released.
3. As a post-release step, the commit from step 2 should be forward-ported to main

For bugfix releases, just do 2-3, although the release manager may want to do some of the step 1 items in a PR just before release.


If we agree  with that process, this should get written up into the release procedures docs.

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.

command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

The CDS format unit name string for `mag` and `dB` units is incorrectly rendered.
CDS and MRT format standard designates names of logarithmic units by enclosing it within square brackets. Official standard is defined at http://vizier.u-strasbg.fr/doc/catstd-3.2.htx and https://journals.aas.org/mrt-units/#symbols.

This issue was first encountered in #9946, which was closed by #9971 sometime last year. However, that issue and the accompanying PR don't seem to have addressed all the cases.

Astropy supports three logarithmic units, `Magnitude`, `Decibels` and `Dex`, the later of which is simply the `log_{10}` operation. The previous PR seems to have addressed CDS format name for `Dex` only. So, the following works:

```
In [1]: from astropy import units as u

In [2]: u.K.to_string('cds')
Out[2]: 'K'

In [3]: u.dex('K').to_string('cds')
Out[3]: '[K]'
```

Whereas, while working on a CDS/MRT format writer in #11897, I find that the CDS format name string of Magnitude unit is not properly output. Namely, `mag` is returned instead of `[mag]`. Check out the following code,

```
In [8]: u.mag
Out[8]: Unit("mag")

In [9]: u.mag.to_string('cds')
Out[9]: 'mag'

In [10]: u.dB
Out[10]: Unit("dB")

In [11]: u.dB.to_string('cds')
Out[11]: 'dB'
```

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

It is very handy to use the `quantity_input` decorator to ensure the inputs to a function are Quantities with appropriate units. But this checking makes it impossible to use the function with the python package `uncertainties` or other automatic-differentiation tools that rely on passing things that behave enough like numbers to pass through simple mathematics. In an ideal world one would be able to attach units to such exotic objects, but in practical terms the easiest thing to do is to pass these objects through the raw un-decorated version of the function - if the decorator provided that.

### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

I suggest usage that looks like:
```python
@quantity_input
def f(x: u.m):
    return x**2

f(1*u.m)

f.raw(ufloat(1, 0.1))
```

This should be implementable, if desired, just by storing the function to be wrapped in an attribute of the wrapper object.

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->
In the doc (e.g., [`sigma_clip`](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.stats.sigma_clip.html#astropy.stats.sigma_clip)), it is said that "the minimum and maximum clipping bounds are also returned" if `return_bounds=True`. I just happened to encounter a problem when I want the ``result`` AND the bounds ``low`` and ``upp``.

The simplest example to show this :
```python
import numpy as np
from astropy.stats import sigma_clip

a_allmask = np.ma.array(np.arange(10.), mask=[True]*10)
a = np.ma.array(np.arange(10.), mask=[False]+[True]*9)

for data in [a, a_allmask]:
    res, low, upp = sigma_clip(data, return_bounds=True)
    print(low, upp)
```
This raised ``ValueError``:
```
0.0 0.0
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-18-b2add72739a4> in <module>
      6
      7 for data in [a, a_allmask]:
----> 8     res, low, upp = sigma_clip(data, return_bounds=True)
      9     print(low, upp)

ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 3)
```

So it means lower/upper bounds are not returned at all, even though `return_bounds=True`. Maybe better to let it return NaN for both lower/upper bounds if all data is masked for consistency.

title: Slicing rice compressed image produces file invalid according to cfitsio
description:
When slicing rice compressed file `.fits.fz` using astropy and saving results to a file I am facing an issue, with reading back the resulting file with tools using cftitsio (eg. `funpack`).

Simple reproduction steps:

```python
infile = "input.fits.fz"
outfile = "invalid.fits.fz"
slices = (slice(0, 100), slice(0, 100))
with fits.open(infile, checksum=True) as hdus:
    hdus[1].data = hdus[1].data[slices]
    hdus.writeto(outfile, overwrite=True, checksum=True)

with fits.open(outfile, checksum=True) as hdus:
    pass
```

You can get the example input file from http://dataportal.eso.org/dataPortal/file/ADP.2016-10-06T13:39:47.172 but I was able to reproduce the same behaviour with other `.fits.fz` files as well, so I don't think it's anything special for this particular file.

`funpack` says:

```
funpack invalid.fits.fz
Error processing file: invalid.fits.fz
  in HDU number 1

FITSIO status = 222: second keyword not BITPIX
Second keyword of the extension is not BITPIX: XTENSION
error copying primary keywords from compressed file
```

However the header itself seems fine, so I suspect it's something else, which is just accidentally triggering this particular cfitsio error.
`fv` can open this file, but attempting to plot or display data table crashes.

Not sure if related, but notice also that I save the file with `checksum=True`, yet opening the output with checksum verification shows invalid checksum and datasum keywords (similar to: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/4587 )

I tested this with astropy `4.0` and then on `4.3post1` on Python 3.7 on Windows and Linux environments, and the results are the same.

title: Allow joining of empty tables.
description:
### Description

Astropy raises an error when joining tables that have no rows. This is inconvenient, when tables are not guaranteed to have rows (e.g. when reading from a file). 

If I don't miss anything, joining empty tables is well defined (and for example works in SQL):

* inner join: if any of the two tables is empty, the output is empty
* outer join: no-op if both tables empty, return the non-empty table if only one is empty
* left: no-op if either left or right table is empty → return left
* right: no-op if either left or right table is empty → return right

What was the reason to raise an error on empty tables?

title: config : inconsistent behavior in handling of values of type list
description:
## Problem

When I want to specify a list as value in [configuration](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.config.ConfigItem.html), the behavior seems to be inconsistent and unintuitive.

I will use the existing `css_urls` of `table.jsviewer` as an example. The configuration is:
```
## The URLs to the css file(s) to include.
# css_urls = ['https://cdn.datatables.net/1.10.12/css/jquery.dataTables.css']
```

- The generated config gives the impression that the list should be in the form of a python list, 
- but in practice, using python list will lead to errors. 
- Instead, it expects a kind of comma-separated string.

## Example

For the following code snippets that access the config value, 
```
from astropy.table.jsviewer import conf
print(conf.css_urls)
```

the behavior of reading it: 
- if I uncomment the line in `astropy.cfg`, i.e., specify the value as a list, it results in an error:
```
TypeError: Configuration value not valid:the value "['https://cdn.datatables.net/1.10.12/css/jquery.dataTables.css']" is of the wrong type.
```

- if I specify the value as a comma-separated list, it works. E.g., it works with the following line
```
css_urls = https://cdn.datatables.net/1.10.12/css/jquery.dataTables.css,http://acme.net/foo.css
```

- For a single value, it must end with a comma. E.g., (notice the triling comma at the end. It is neeed)
```
css_urls = https://cdn.datatables.net/1.10.12/css/jquery.dataTables.css,
```

- For a single value, if it does not end with a comma, it also results in an error:
```
TypeError: Configuration value not valid:the value "https://cdn.datatables.net/1.10.12/css/jquery.dataTables.css" is of the wrong type.
```

## Desirable behavior
- If the intent for list-type config item is to accept python list as value, then there are bugs in parsing the config file
- If the intent is to accept a comma-separated string as value, then
  - generated config should not output value as python list
  - requiring an extra trailing comma for single-value case is unintuitive.

## Versions:
- seen in astropy 4.2.1 and 4.1. The issue persists in the current `main`.

---

Reference:
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/f5355161c9df1cb3580a367549501f89f04d80ce/astropy/table/jsviewer.py#L24-L27

title: dynamically removing parameters from an astropy.modeling.Fittable1DModel model
description:
I'm working on an emission-line fitting code and having some speed / timing issues using the `astropy.modeling.Fittable1DModel` Class. I would be grateful for any suggestions or thoughts from the group.

The figure below shows the crux of my problem / question. 

The input optical spectrum is a pure emission-line spectrum of a star-forming galaxy at `z=0.368` (the stellar continuum has been subtracted). From left to right, the three panels are zoomed into the (1) [OII] 3726,29 doublet; (2) the H-beta + [OIII] 4959,5007 lines; and (3) the H-alpha + [NII] 6548,84 doublet. 

The data (and +/-1-sigma uncertainties) are shown as a shaded gray spectrum in every panel; the top row shows the best-fitting model (in orange) using `EMLineModel1` (defined below) and the bottom row (in blue) shows the best-fitting model using `EMLineModel2`.

If inspired, you can reproduce this figure by grabbing the [emlinefit.zip](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/files/7010447/emlinefit.zip) file, which has the data and code, and running it in a dedicated conda environment (and directory). Roughly:
```bash
conda create -y -n emlinefit python=3.9 astropy=4.2 matplotlib pyyaml
conda activate emlinefit
pip install seaborn
python emlinefit.py
```

`EMLineModel1` and `EMLineModel2` both define my [astropy.modeling.Fittable1DModel](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/api/astropy.modeling.Fittable1DModel.html#astropy.modeling.Fittable1DModel), roughly following the instructions [here](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/modeling/new-model.html#a-step-by-step-definition-of-a-1-d-gaussian-model). The only difference between the two is that `EMLineModel1` has 40 emission lines[*] while `EMLineModel2` has 24 emission lines. 

However, the 16 emission lines in `EMLineModel1` but not in `EMLineModel2` are all outside of my observed-frame wavelength range (roughly 3600-9800 A) and therefore not constrained by the data. Nevertheless, **the optimizer** ([astropy.modeling.fitting.LevMarLSQFitter](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.modeling.fitting.LevMarLSQFitter.html)) **using `EMLineModel1` takes nearly a minute longer to reach the same solution as `EMLineModel2`** (see the figure legend, below)!

My sample spans a range of redshift and so I don't know a priori which emission lines will be in the observed-frame wavelength range. (I have tried to *fix* the Parameters of the lines outside the wavelength range so they're not optimized. This change does lead to a significant speed-up using `EMLineModel1`---18 seconds vs 9.4 seconds using `EMLineModel2`---although this is still a factor of two slower.) 

So, my question is: **can I dynamically *remove* Parameters from `EMLineModel1` based on the redshift of a given object so I can minimize the optimization time?** In other words, can I transform `EMLineModel1` (which has all the lines I could ever want to fit) into a lighter-weight `EMLineModel2` (which only has the Parameters constrainable by the data) on the fly? 

Thanks in advance for any ideas or suggestions (or corrections to my code!).

[*] Each emission line has three [Parameters](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/modeling/parameters.html) associated with it, an amplitude, a line-width (in km/s), and a velocity shift (in km/s) with respect to the nominal redshift. However, not all these parameters are independent. For example, the line-widths and velocity shifts of all the Balmer and helium lines are tied together; similarly, all the forbidden transitions are tied together, etc.

![qa-emlinefit](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1431820/129978534-8ecf7e39-5d5c-449c-9667-701b78ec0e09.png)

title: Custom vounit instances are not recognized when defined via `def_unit`
description:
`vounit` has the concept of being able to define an explicit custom unit by using single quotes. We support if one defines a unit via,
```
In [2]: redshift = u.Unit("'redshift'", format='vounit')

In [3]: redshift.to_string()
Out[3]: 'redshift'

In [4]: redshift.to_string('vounit')
Out[4]: "'redshift'"
```
Given this, the failure for the following (found in #11786, hence the example) seems unexpected:
```
In [2]: redshift = u.def_unit(['redshift'], format={'vounit': "'redshift'"})

In [3]: redshift.to_string()
Out[3]: 'redshift'

In [4]: redshift.to_string('vounit')
ValueError: Unit "'redshift'" is not part of the VOUnit standard
```

It would seem to make sense to allow the above to work, either by using `u.format.vounit.VOUnit._def_custom_unit` at definition time, or by letting `_get_unit_name` use a given units `get_format_name` (and check it works as explicit custom unit).

cc @nstarman, @dhomeier

title: Cosmology methods eat units of array-like Quantity
description:
Many cosmology methods start with
```
        if isiterable(z):
            z = np.asarray(z)
```
This eats any units, so is unsafe:
```
In [6]: Planck18.Tcmb([0., 1.]*u.m)
Out[6]: <Quantity [2.7255, 5.451 ] K>
```

Probably should be replaced with `u.Quantity(z, u.dimensionless_unscaled).value` (or just `u.Quantity(z, cu.redshift)` though that will be slower).

p.s. Noticed this while looking at some of the PRs.

title: Follow-up for GSOC 2021: MRT writer in io.ascii
description:
In #11897, @Suyog7130 implemented a MRT writer for io.ascii. That is a very long PR, with >> 100 comments already and it has other PRs depending on it. To get this moving and to avoid excessive rebasing, we decided to split out a few comments about minor functionality, stylistic reworks and code improvements into this new issue.

Below is a list of thinks that we can tick off as they are addresses in follow-up PRs:

- [ ] The rules that decide the write-out precision might drop precision in some cases (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11897#discussion_r693533921)
- [ ] A large block of code could be factored out into a new function, also renaming a variable to be more explicit (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11897#discussion_r693533921)
- [ ] The current implementation does not work with `QTable` (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11897#discussion_r693514532)
- [ ] The default description for columns with no description set can be shortened (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11897#discussion_r693514895)
- [ ] The conversion float/string can be fooled if the float is formatted into something that does not look like a float any longer (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11897#discussion_r693532439)
- [ ] split format into MRT and CDS writers.
- [ ] there was some workaround (but I can't find the line now) for a numpy deprecation warning. That workaround can be removed when support for numpy 1.18 is dropped.

title: Accessing to the raw content of astropy.io.votable.tree.Resource(s)
description:
### Description
In the frame of the VO data modeling efforts, we have been planning to annotate VOTable resources with data model meta-data.

These annotations are XML pieces matching a specific schema independent of the VOTable schema.  An annotated VOTable (work in progress) can be seen [here](https://github.com/ivoa-std/ModelInstanceInVot/blob/votable-schema/schema/validation/snippets/test_rich_instance_1_ok.xml) (branch `votable-schema`)

Annotations are not intended to be consumed by Astropy but rather by some affiliated  package. Anyway,  `astropy.io.votable` must be enabled to provide access to that XML for any end-client. 

In order to avoid to modify the current VOTable schema, these annotations will be enclosed in a Resource of type `meta` with a specific name space:

```xml
 <VOTable>
     <RESOURCE type=result>
         <RESOURCE type=meta>
             <dm-mapping:VODML ... My DM stuff ....>
        </RESOURCE>
       <TABLE/>       
       <TABLE/>
     </RESOURCE>
</VOTABLE>
```
This approach has been validated with regular XML parsers and validators and we need Astropy to support this new VOTable feature.
For this,  the`astropy.io.votable` API must be able to extract the content of such resources. This is apparently not possible yet.

The new endpoint should look like:
```python
votable = parse(votable_path)
   for resource in votable.resources:
       if resource.type == "results":
           for sub_resource in resource.resources:
               if sub_resource.type == "meta":
                   print("Here is my DM stuff")
                   annotation_content = sub_resource.content()
```

The resource content might be delivered as a DOM or/and as a string. The latest  would allow final clients to run their own XML processors.

title: Issue when converting 2D array of coordinates with a 1D WCS
description:
The following example shows an issue that occurs in the corner case where a 2D array of e.g. pixel coordinates is passed to a 1D WCS to convert:

```python
In [1]: import numpy as np
   ...: from astropy.wcs import WCS
   ...: 
   ...: wcs = WCS(naxis=1)
   ...: wcs.wcs.ctype = ['FREQ']
   ...: wcs.wcs.cdelt = [10]
   ...: wcs.wcs.set()

In [2]: wcs.pixel_to_world(1)
   ...: 
Out[2]: <SpectralCoord 20. Hz>

In [3]: wcs.pixel_to_world(np.array([1]))
   ...: 
Out[3]: <SpectralCoord [20.] Hz>

In [4]: wcs.pixel_to_world(np.array([[1,0]]))
   ...: 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-4-96b1ff7c5782> in <module>
----> 1 wcs.pixel_to_world(np.array([[1,0]]))

~/python/dev/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/wcs/wcsapi/high_level_api.py in pixel_to_world(self, *pixel_arrays)
    237 
    238         # Compute the world coordinate values
--> 239         world = self.low_level_wcs.pixel_to_world_values(*pixel_arrays)
    240 
    241         if self.world_n_dim == 1:

~/python/dev/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/wcs/wcsapi/fitswcs.py in pixel_to_world_values(self, *pixel_arrays)
    320 
    321     def pixel_to_world_values(self, *pixel_arrays):
--> 322         world = self.all_pix2world(*pixel_arrays, 0)
    323         return world[0] if self.world_n_dim == 1 else tuple(world)
    324 

~/python/dev/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/wcs/wcs.py in all_pix2world(self, *args, **kwargs)
   1345 
   1346     def all_pix2world(self, *args, **kwargs):
-> 1347         return self._array_converter(
   1348             self._all_pix2world, 'output', *args, **kwargs)
   1349     all_pix2world.__doc__ = """

~/python/dev/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/wcs/wcs.py in _array_converter(self, func, sky, ra_dec_order, *args)
   1322             if xy.shape == () or len(xy.shape) == 1:
   1323                 return _return_list_of_arrays([xy], origin)
-> 1324             return _return_single_array(xy, origin)
   1325 
   1326         elif len(args) == self.naxis + 1:

~/python/dev/lib/python3.8/site-packages/astropy/wcs/wcs.py in _return_single_array(xy, origin)
   1299         def _return_single_array(xy, origin):
   1300             if xy.shape[-1] != self.naxis:
-> 1301                 raise ValueError(
   1302                     "When providing two arguments, the array must be "
   1303                     "of shape (N, {})".format(self.naxis))

ValueError: When providing two arguments, the array must be of shape (N, 1)
```

This runs into issues that the underlying ``pix2world`` function tries to auto-detect whether one is passing N arrays or one array with a dimension of N. While I'm not sure there's anything we can do for that original underlying API, the user's intent is unambiguous when calling the APE 14 API, so we should make sure we handle this case.

There are two options I can see - either we enable a kwarg in ``*_pix2world`` and ``*_world2pix`` to specifically say that we are passing N+1 arguments, and always use this in the APE 14 layer, or alternatively when the underlying WCS is 1D we always ravel and reshape inputs to the ``*_pix2world`` and ``*_world2pix`` methods.

title: np.median drops units if the result is `nan`
description:
As reported by @larrybradley in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/12146#discussion_r707509816:
`np.median` drops the unit on `Quantity` input where the result is `nan`:
```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> data = np.array([1., 2, np.nan, 3, 4]) << u.km
>>> np.median(data)
nan
>>> np.mean(data)
<Quantity nan km>
>>> np.var(data)
<Quantity nan km2>
```

Note that it works fine on multi-dimensional output:
```
In [6]: np.median([[1, 2], [np.nan, 3]] << u.km, axis=1)
Out[6]: <Quantity [1.5, nan] km>
In [8]: np.median([[1, np.nan], [np.nan, 3]] << u.km, axis=1)
Out[8]: <Quantity [nan, nan] km>
```

title: Cosmo : not accept array-like, only array?
description:
### Description

Many of the functions in ``astropy.cosmology`` accept any array-like input and have to perform a check to distinguish between scalars and arrays. While this is faster than just passing everything through ``np.array()`` 
(as discussed in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/12145#discussion_r707597021), the check is still a performance bottleneck.
It seems to me that there is not much added value in Cosmology functions accepting any array-like input rather than actual ndarrays.
I propose limiting the accepted input types to `numbers.Number` (e.g. int, float) and `numpy.ndarray` (includes Quantity) and eliminating array-like inputs, like lists and tuples.

Looking forward, this is part of a longer plan to "vectorize" Cosmology, both the methods (like with #11893), but also have the entire class work with arrays of parameters, not only scalar values. With only Number and ndarray (incl. Quantity) as valid inputs it will eventually be possible to eliminate workaround methods like ``astropy.cosmology.utils.vectorize_if_needed`` which are likewise performance bottlenecks. Also at some point I would like to extend the `c` backend, hopefully with `mypyc` so everything can be written in python and transpiled to performant `c`, and simple type inputs make for much easier / better code.

I would appreciate some second opinions as this is a non-backward compatible change. I think / hope its a painless one, especially since most people just use numpy arrays anyway, but it's still a change. v5.0 seems the right time, if any.

tag: @mhvk @adrn @aconley


https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/23404eeb2caeea315cea89b6cb8b9b2fee4f13be/astropy/cosmology/flrw.py#L417-L419

Checks like the above will not be necessary.

title: Flawed bounding box unit test in modeling
description:
The [`astropy/modeling/tests/test_models.py::TestFittable1DModels::test_bounding_box1D`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/4f54d9eb59f2937f3470869d377c0c357b96e37f/astropy/modeling/tests/test_models.py#L348-L385) unit test is flawed. In particular, it purposely evaluates the model on values outside the bounding box (see [here](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/4f54d9eb59f2937f3470869d377c0c357b96e37f/astropy/modeling/tests/test_models.py#L380-L381)). This is a huge issue because one useful application of explicitly adding a bounding box to a model class would be to purposely restrict the model's inputs to the mathematical domain for the model.

For example if one were to want to create an `arcsin` based model it is completely reasonable to hard code the bounding box so that the arguments made to `arcsin` are in the interval `[-1, 1]` (otherwise you get a warning if you use `numpy.arcsin` or an error if you use `math.asin`).

It is also reasonable to expect user contributed models to `astropy.modeling.models` to be added to [`astropy/modeling/tests/example_models.py`](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/4f54d9eb59f2937f3470869d377c0c357b96e37f/astropy/modeling/tests/example_models.py) so that it can be tested by the "standard" battery of tests, one of which is the one at issue. So adding a model whose bounding box defines the extent of the true domain of the model will have difficulties passing this test.

Moreover, the [latter section](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/4f54d9eb59f2937f3470869d377c0c357b96e37f/astropy/modeling/tests/test_models.py#L366-L385) of this test seems to be making the incorrect assumption that the bounding box defines the majority of the "support" of the model (e.g. `Gaussian1D`) where the values outside are tiny. This is an incorrect assumption in general so the point of this part of the test is questionable at best.

Finally, this test fails to test using the bounding box in a meaningful way because it does not try to evaluate the model using the `with_bounding_box=True` keyword argument. That enforces the bounding box such that the outputs corresponding to inputs outside the bounding box return NaN values (and are not run through the actual model evaluation machinery). I propose that the part of the test at issue be removed and replaced with test code that tests this precise feature.

title: RA/Dec of asteroid SkyCoord from satellite SkyCoord
description:
I'm trying to get the RA/Dec of an asteroid when viewed from a particular satellite.  I have the asteroid's 3D coordinates from astroquery.jplhorizons, and I have the satellite's lat/lon/alt from its datafiles.  I think the right way to do this is with astropy.coordinates.SkyOffsetFrame, but I'm not 100% sure.  I have an example script below:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
from astropy import units
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy.coordinates import SkyOffsetFrame
from astropy.coordinates.builtin_frames import CustomBarycentricEcliptic

# asteroid is from jpl-horizons, this is their custom frame
JPLFrame = CustomBarycentricEcliptic( obliquity=84381.448 * units.arcsec )

# mjd times
t = [57170.0187133196,57170.0190600000,57170.0194072222]
t = Time( t, format='mjd' )

# satellite coordinates
fx  = [-6.070489032e+10,-6.070428525e+10,-6.070368123e+10]
fy  = [-1.386698494e+11,-1.38670121e+11,-1.386703998e+11]
fz  = [-20180790.6,-20112703.04,-20041758.69]
sat = SkyCoord( x=fx, y=fy, z=fz, unit='meter', frame=JPLFrame, representation_type='cartesian' )

# asteroid coordinates
tx  = [-6.070621538e+10,-6.070542194e+10,-6.070462727e+10]
ty  = [-1.393267812e+11,-1.393271418e+11,-1.39327503e+11]
tz  = [996027003.3,996027087.2,996027171.1]
ast = SkyCoord( x=tx, y=ty, z=tz, unit='meter', frame=JPLFrame, representation_type='cartesian' )

origin = SkyOffsetFrame(origin=sat)
coord  = ast.transform_to( origin ).transform_to('fk5')

print('asteroid ra/dec (FK5 J2000.0)') 
print('when viewed from satellite:')
for i in range(len(t)) :
  print('%10.6f'%coord.ra.degree[i], '%10.6f'%coord.dec.degree[i], 'deg')
```

I guess I have a few questions:
1) is this the right way to do this?  The language of the [doc page](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/coordinates/matchsep.html#sky-offset-frames) makes me a little uncertain that this is what SkyOffsetFrame is actually for...
2) I'm creating 3 SkyOffsetFrames.  Is the transform_to(origin) applying the ith origin to the ith asteroid coordinate (and not just using the first origin for all of them)?
3) Is this the instantaneous RA/Dec, or does this account for the speed of light?

The reason this happens is that ``self.name`` is not in the registry because the registry doesn't pick up externally defined units.
