### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
When creating a HDU without specifying any data, the `quantize_level` and `quantize_method` arguments (at least) passed to the HDU class during initialisation are not honoured when data is later set via the HDU's `data` attribute. Initialising the HDU with even `data=np.array([0.])` is enough to (seemingly) solve this issue.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
I would expect the compression settings passed as keyword parameters during initialisation to be remembered in the HDU object and then taken into account when the HDU's data is later updated by the user.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
It seems that if no data is passed during initialisation, the compression settings are assumed to be irrelevant and ignored. I think this should at least be documented (if not already).

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

```python
import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits

tmpfile = 'test_fits.fits'


def diff(hdu):
    # Generate the data to write to the FITS file
    np.random.seed(0)
    data = np.random.rand(50, 30).astype('float32')

    # Set the actual data
    hdu.data = data.copy()

    # Write compressed data to file
    hdul = fits.HDUList([fits.PrimaryHDU(), hdu])
    hdul.writeto(tmpfile, overwrite=True)

    # Print max abs. difference due to compression
    hdul = fits.open(tmpfile)
    print(np.abs(hdul[1].data - data).max())


diff(fits.CompImageHDU(quantize_level=-32))
diff(fits.CompImageHDU(quantize_level=-32, data=np.array([0.])))

kwargs = {'quantize_method': 2, 'dither_seed': 1}
diff(fits.CompImageHDU(**kwargs))
diff(fits.CompImageHDU(**kwargs, data=np.array([0.])))
```

#### Actual Values Returned
```
0.014079988
0.99980855
0.014079988
0.01334089
```

#### Expected Values Returned
```
0.99980855
0.99980855
0.01334089
0.01334089
```
i.e. initialising with `data=None` or `data=np.array([0.])` should ultimately produce identical compressed values.

The "Working with compressed files" section of [this page](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/io/fits/index.html#working-with-compressed-files) notes:

> When writing a file (e.g., with the writeto() function), compression will be determined based on the filename extension given, or the compression used in a pre-existing file that is being written to.

However, this information is not mentioned in the API reference for the [writeto()](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/io/fits/api/files.html#astropy.io.fits.writeto) function. This behaviour is "hidden"; recommend the API reference be updated to reflect this. Ideally, a list of supported compression extensions would be great.

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
The check for a missing SIMPLE card included in astropy v4.3 breaks backwards compatibility in fits.open.  Archival data that contains the SIMPLE keyword, but in an unexpected format, produces an error when opened with default parameters in fits.open.  Prior to v4.3, these files were opened and handled normally.

The associated pull request is: https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10895.

This break in backwards compatibility will require us to change every fits.open command we have that might deal with non-standard archival data.  This is hundreds of lines of code, across many separate packages.  The data cannot easily be changed.


### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
fits.open opens files that can be read as FITS without throwing an error by default.

### Actual behavior

<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
The error "No SIMPLE card found, this file does not appear to be a valid FITS file" is produced and the file is not opened as an HDUList.  The SIMPLE card is present and readable, though, and setting ignore_missing_simple=True allows the file to be opened and handled normally.

title: Unexpected difference of behavior when iterating over FITS header cards
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,

Please be sure to check out our code of conduct,

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
There are several ways of iterating over FITS header cards.  Assuming header is a FITS header, one can do:
```python
for key in header:  # equivalent to header.keys()
   print(header[key])
```
or
```python
for key, value in header.items():
   print(key, value)
```
But it appears that underneath, different accessor methods are used such that `header[key]` is not guaranteed to be identical to `value` in these two examples.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
```python
for key, value in header.items():
   assert header[key] is value  # You should get the same object back!
```

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
In actual practice, the `rawheader[key]` and `value` can be different objects. There are two separate cases where this happens.

1. Value is a string:  *sometimes* `assert rawheader[key] is value` fails, but `assert rawheader[key] == value` succeeds.
2. Value is `None`.  Admittedly this violates the FITS standard, but bear with me:
   * `rawheader[key] is None`
   * However `value` is `astropy.io.fits.card.Undefined`

See examples of both of these below. My personal opinion is that I should not have to modify a test for the particular type of object returned depending on how I iterate over the container object.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

```python
from astropy.io.fits import Header
hdr = Header.fromstring("""SIMPLE  =                    T / conforms to FITS standard
BITPIX  =                    8 / array data type
NAXIS   =                    0 / number of array dimensions
EXTEND  =                    T
FLOAT1  = 3.14159              / Making sure we get all the types
FLOAT2  =              2.71828 / More floating point
STRING1 = 'main    '           / Testing various strings
STRING2 = 'abcdefghijklmnop'   / Testing longer string
STRING3 =                      / Yes this is technically invalid
STRING4 = '        '           / Blank string
""", sep='\n')

for key, value in hdr.items():
    try:
        assert hdr[key] is value
    except AssertionError:
        print("{0}: hdr[key] = {1} is not value = {2}".format(key, repr(hdr[key]), repr(value)))
        try:
            assert hdr[key] == value
        except AssertionError:
            print("{0}: hdr[key] = {1} is not even equal to value = {2}".format(key, repr(hdr[key]), repr(value)))
```

Output:
```
STRING1: hdr[key] = 'main' is not value = 'main'
STRING3: hdr[key] = None is not value = <astropy.io.fits.card.Undefined object at 0x2aaad34c0fa0>
STRING3: hdr[key] = None is not even equal to value = <astropy.io.fits.card.Undefined object at 0x2aaad34c0fa0>
```

title: Height of observer not being properly accounted for in `AltAz` conversions
description:
### Description
The altitude of a star above the horizon is expected to increase as the height of the observer increases. This is the so-called "dip" correction to the altitude referenced in the Nautical Almanac: 

https://thenauticalalmanac.com/Altitude_Correction_Tables.pdf

As visible from the table, the dip correction should be ~5 arcmin at a height of 10m.

### Expected behavior
Altitude of a star observed at a 10m height should be approximately 5 arcmin greater than the same star observed at a height of 0m.

### Actual behavior
The altitude difference is negligible.

### Steps to Reproduce
```
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.coordinates import AltAz, EarthLocation, SkyCoord

t = Time("2021-10-11 00:41:27.463030", scale="utc")
radec = SkyCoord(ra=10 * u.deg, dec=-30 * u.deg, frame="icrs")

location1 = EarthLocation(lat=50 * u.deg, lon=10 * u.deg, height=0 * u.m)
location2 = EarthLocation(lat=50 * u.deg, lon=10 * u.deg, height=10 * u.m)

altaz_frame_1 = AltAz(obstime=t, location=location1)
altaz_frame_2 = AltAz(obstime=t, location=location2)

altaz1 = radec.transform_to(altaz_frame_1)
altaz2 = radec.transform_to(altaz_frame_2)

print(abs(altaz1.alt - altaz2.alt).to_value(u.arcmin))

# prints 2.3586466113556526e-10
```

title: When downsampling a timeseries, what to do with point exactly on the border?
description:
In #11266 support for downsampling with uneven bin sizes for added. In that context, a broader discussion item came up that applies to all downsampling and thus was beyond the scope of that specific PR.
Quoting @dhomeier:

> I had some further thoughts about the overlapping and in particular the "marginally overlapping" bins (i.e. data points exactly on the time_bin_start times). At the time it seemed natural that the desired default behaviour would be to assign a point with
ts.time[i] == time_bin_start[j]
to bin j; but actually if we assume ts.time[i] to represent the mean time of an observation (the perennial issue of sample centre vs. sample borders...), it would be just as natural to assign this with weight 0.5 each to time_bin_start[j-1] and time_bin_start[j]. So I think there is justification for a new option to control how these points are handled, but that could actually be extended to cases where ts.time[i] is not exactly on the boundary (and would be distributed with different weights). So, plenty of tasks for a follow-up on this PR.

CC @aaryapatil @astrofrog

See for more details of the discussion
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11266#issuecomment-865942363

I open this issue to continue the discussion and see if we can reach consensus on what exactly we want to do here.

Personally, I think the current behaviour has a certain simplistic beauty to it. While I see the need for more complex resampling schemes, I'm not sure we would want to stop at what @dhomeier suggested: If half a bin is before and have the bin after the new bon boundary, it seem natural to assign half of the value to the new left and the other half to the new right bin. However, that's only true id the underlying distribution is a constant. If, for example, we look at an exponential decay, more than half of the value should go into the left bin and less into the right bin. Also, any uncertainties will now be correlated between bins.

That's a long way of saying that I think that a reasonable solution is to declare anything that goes beyond the current implementation as "out of scope" for the core package and leave it for more specialized packages with domain knowledge to implement more complex rebinning schemes. Those might be used outside of timeseries, too (e.g. for spectra).

Thus, I label this issue "close?" even though I just opened it, but I'm happy to be convinced otherwise.

One of the most common uses of astropy is to take some input arguments/data and apply a bunch of functions to it.
For a simple example, let's consider taking an input array of of floats Z representing redshifts:
 -  passing it through a cosmology function to get the distance modulus
 - applying some statistical clean-up method, say sigma clipping.
 - fitting a model to it such as a Gaussian1D
 - using visualization or stats to get a meaningful value out of this gaussian fit, or possibly use the output as input into a custom function that produces something of value.
 
 In pseudo-code it looks like this:
```
Z = Table.read('redshifts.ecsv')
dm = Cosmology.distmod(Z)
dm_clipped = SigmaClip(dm, sigma=5)
g1d = Gaussian1D()
results, result_info  = fitter.fit(g1d, Z)
custom_plot_function(results, result_info)
out = custom_report_function(results, result_info)
...
 >>> do something with out
...
```

However, functional composition could be used to pipeline-ify<sup>TM</sup> this process and lose the intermediate variables cluttering up the namespace. While it is possible to custom implement this using functools as an example, packages like scikitlearn ([Pipeline](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html)), pytorch ([Sequential](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Sequential.html#torch.nn.Sequential)), etc. provide inbuilt classes that can take a random set of functions, and apply them sequentially (non-sequential operation using a graph is also possible), and give an output in a clean format. This sort of formalism is useful from a better software design point of view. In addition to not creating intermediate variables, it allows easily reusing the now "pipelined" set of functions without having to copy paste code, with possibly now duplicated variable names, and makes it easier to bug fix, refactor, or maintain code.


<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

In this case the above might be transformed into

```
pipeline = astropy.Pipeline(Table.read, Cosmology.distmod, SigmaClip, fitter.fit, custom_plot_function, custom_report_function)
pipeline('redshift.ecsv')
```

Now, the most common issue would be passing in arguments. There are many ways to handle this. There could be args, kwargs parameters added to Pipeline class. You could use custom decorators, or provide some ready made decorators, that apply their arguments to the functions, etc.

One example using ready made decorators:

```...distmod, kwargs_decorator(SigmaClip, {'sigma':5}), args_decorator(fitter.fit, g1d, set_par_order=(1,0)), ...```

where kwargs_decorator applies keywords arguments to SigmaClip, and args_decorator applies non-keyword args and flips the order. By default, the first returned object would be passed down the chain to each function as the first argument, but not all astropy functions may make sense with that.

So, the proposal is simple, but the implementation may not be. Create a class that can be used to make a pipeline out of a set of functions, thus eliminating the need to save intermediate variables, which is bad practice. The general idea of this is already implemented into base python and afaik is called functional composition. The tools within func

It's possible to decompose a unit, e.g.
```python
import astropy.units as u

What I want is a way to tell if a particular SI base unit is in the decomposed unit, to see what the dimensions of the unit are (e.g. time, 1D spatial, 2D spatial...). title: NumPy Recfunctions and Structured Quantities
description:
### Description

The numpy [`numpy.lib.recfunctions`](https://numpy.org/devdocs/user/basics.rec.html#module-numpy.lib.recfunctions) (numpy v1.16+) module provides functions for working with structured arrays.
Quantity should support these both when there's a single unit and when the unit is structured. For simple units this should be easy. For structured units the behavior should probably depend on whether all the fields have the same unit or not. 

Pulling in @mhvk.


### Examples

```python
>>> m_nu = u.Quantity(
...     np.array([(0, 0, 0.6)], dtype=[("nu1", float, ()), ("nu2", float, ()), ("nu3", float, ())]),
...     u.StructuredUnit(("eV", "eV", "eV")))
>>> m_nu
[(0,0,0.6)](eV,eV,eV)

>>> import numpy.lib.recfunctions as rfn
>>> rfn.structured_to_unstructured(m_nu)
WARNING: function 'structured_to_unstructured' is not known to astropy's Quantity. Will run it anyway, hoping it will treat ndarray subclasses correctly. Please raise an issue at https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues.  [astropy.units.quantity]
[[0, 0, 0.6]](eV,eV,eV)
```

This is right if the structured units were different, but wrong since they are the same. The structured unit should decay into an unstructured unit.

e.g.
```python
>>> rfn.structured_to_unstructured(m_nu.value * u.eV)
WARNING: function 'structured_to_unstructured' is not known to astropy's Quantity. Will run it anyway, hoping it will treat ndarray subclasses correctly. Please raise an issue at https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues.  [astropy.units.quantity]
[[0, 0, 0.6]]eV
```

In any case, ``structured_to_unstructured`` should be known to astropy's Quantity.

Lastly, the following should either not decay the structured unit or error. I was leaning towards the former, but now I'm feeling the latter. This is not something that is unstructurable.
```python
thing = u.Quantity(
    np.array([(0, 0, 0.6)], dtype=[("x", float, ()), ("y", float, ()), ("z", float, ())]),
    u.StructuredUnit(("eV", "km", "s"))
)
rfn.structured_to_unstructured(thing)
```

title: Passing parameters norm and vmin/vmax simultaneously is deprecated since matplotlib 3.3
description:
```
MatplotlibDeprecationWarning: Passing parameters norm and vmin/vmax simultaneously is deprecated since 3.3
and will become an error two minor releases later. Please pass vmin/vmax directly to the norm when creating it.

def displayimage(img):
    minv, maxv = np.percentile(img, [5, 95])
    plt.imshow(img, cmap='gray', vmin=minv, vmax=maxv, norm=simple_norm(img, stretch='asinh'), origin='lower')
    plt.show()
```

On [matplotlib.pyplot.imshow](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.imshow.html?highlight=imshow#matplotlib.pyplot.imshow) it says "It is deprecated to use vmin/vmax when norm is given."

So when using [simple_norm](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.visualization.simple_norm.html?highlight=simple_norm) it will give this warning.

title: Fitting Compound Models containing multiplied units fails
description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

<!-- Please be sure to check out our contributing guidelines,

If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied

If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->

Creating a Compound model that multiplies the underlying output units returns expected units when evaluating, but fails during fitting because its trying to coerce all units to the data units and not accounting for the operators between the internal sub-models.

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->

Fitting should succeed, with consistent behavior between units from calling evaluate and accepted during fitting.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->

Calling evaluate returns the expected units, but those same units as inputs while fitting raises errors.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

Below is a simplified (although non-physical) example:

```
import astropy.units as u
from astropy.modeling import models
from astropy.modeling.fitting import LevMarLSQFitter
import numpy as np

fitter = LevMarLSQFitter()

x = np.linspace(0,1,101) * u.s
y = np.linspace(5,10,101) * u.m * u.kg / u.s

m1 = models.Linear1D(slope=5*u.m/u.s/u.s, intercept=1.0*u.m/u.s
m2 = models.Linear1D(slope=0.0*u.kg/u.s, intercept=10.0*u.kg) 
c = m1 * m2
```

`c(x)` gives the expected units (m * kg / s), but `fitter(c, x, y)` fails.  Under-the-hood, the following is being called:

```
c._parameter_units_for_data_units({'x': x.unit}, {'y': y.unit})
```

which is evaluating to:

```
{'intercept_0': Unit("kg m / s"),
 'slope_0': Unit("kg m / s2"),
 'intercept_1': Unit("kg m / s"),
 'slope_1': Unit("kg m / s2")}
 ```
 
 In other words, `c._parameter_units_for_data_units` is attempting to make sure that each sub-model results in the passed output units, whereas it should make sure that the units _after applying operators_ result in the passed output units.  The following (in this case - obviously the general case is much more complicated) would make sense to be consistent with the forward model:
 
```
m1._parameter_units_for_data_units({'x': x.unit}, {'y': y.unit / m2(x).unit})
m2._parameter_units_for_data_units({'x': x.unit}, {'y': y.unit / m1(x).unit})
```

title: Update the reference for Bayesian Blocks and maybe update the algorithm
description:
A message from Jeff Scargle, the principle author of the Bayesian of this algorithm:

> I just noticed that the reference at
>
> https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.stats.bayesian_blocks.html#
>
> is to my obsolete paper (the greedy algorithm there has been completely
supplanted by the dynamic programming algorithm in wide use) and described in
>
> The Astrophysical Journal, Volume 764, Issue 2, article id. 167, 26 pp. (2013).
https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.5578
> 
> I try to steer people away from the old algorithm as much as possible;
the new one is exact and optimal -- finds the optimal partition of an exponentially
large search space in quadratic time.
>  it would not hurt to reference
> Bellman too .. 
> Bellman, R.E., Dreyfus, S.E., 1962. Applied Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press, Princeton. 
> Bellman, R., Roth, R., 1969. Curve fitting by segmented straight lines. J. Amer. Statist. Assoc. 64, 1079–1084.
>
> the first is general on DP, the second is really the germ of the BB algorithm ..

I don't know for sure which algorithm was implemented in `astropy.stats.bayesian_blocks` though. I.e., I'm not sure if this is the newer algorithm but the older citation, vs the older algorithm and the older citation.  So we should either update the citation if it's the former case, or this issue is to implement the newer algorithm if the implementation is currently the older one.

Maybe @jakevdp  @Gabriel-p or @larrybradley (as people who have touched the meat of this algorithm) want to weigh in?

title: Writing / reading column with u.dex(u.erg/u.s) to FITS Table not supported
description:
### Description

I would like to write out a table with `u.dex(u.erg/u.s)` quantities to FITS using `QTable`.  My understanding of the FITS standard is, that the  unit would have to be written `log(erg/s)` in the column description (`TUNIT..`).  However, astropy throws a warning and just writes `dex(erg/s)` into `TUNIT`.   Reading this table then throws an error.

### Expected behavior

Reading and writing QTable from/to FITS with `u.dex(u.erg/u.s) ` should work?  At least when writing such a table in FITS it is completely opaque that we can't read it with QTable later...

### Actual behavior

Reading a QTable  that was written with columns that have `u.dex(u.erg/u.s)`  does not work and throws an error:
`UnitConversionError: Cannot initialize 'DexUnit' instance with function unit 'dex(erg / s)', as it is not equivalent to default function unit 'dex'.`

Writing such a table just throws a (to me) cryptic warning:
`WARNING: UnitsWarning: 'dex(erg / s)' did not parse as fits unit: Unit 'dex' not supported by the FITS standard.  If this is meant to be a custom unit, define it with 'u.def_unit'. To have it recognized inside a file reader or other code, enable it with 'u.add_enabled_units'. For details, see https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/units/combining_and_defining.html [astropy.units.core]`

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
from astropy.table import QTable
from astropy import units as u
t = QTable()
t['a'] = [1,2,3] * u.dex(u.erg/u.s)
t.write('test.fits', format='fits')  # throws a warning
t1 = QTable.read('test.fits')   # doesn't read in the table (error)
```

title: Determine better way to back out of releasing
description:
In the release docs, we say:

```
In the event there are any issues with the wheel building for the tag (which shouldn’t really happen if it was passing for the release branch), you’ll have to fix whatever the problem is. First you will need to back out the release procedure by dropping the commits you made for release and removing the tag you created:

$ git reset --hard HEAD^^^^ # you could also use the SHA hash of the commit before your first changelog edit
$ git tag -d v<version>
```

However the reset command assumes that no additional commits were added. I think it doesn't necessarily make sense to start from scratch, we can just remove the tag, add more commits (whether backported bug fixes or other) and re-tag?

title: Bug in CompoundModel copy()
description:
`photutils` tests with `astropy` `dev` started failing, and I tracked it down to commit https://github.com/astropy/astropy/commit/afc3f0f7c6fdda53232fd432e3859e882d78b63d (PR https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/11942).

The bug is caused by the newly-added `CompoundModel.copy()` method.  Prior to #11942, this method used to be defined by the parent `Model.copy()`, which simply returns `copy.deepcopy(self)`.  The new `CompoundModel.copy()` method initializes a new `CompoundModel`, meaning that any user-added attributes are lost in the copy.

MWE that worked prior to #11942, but now fails with `AttributeError: Attribute "xname" not found`:

```python
from astropy.modeling.models import Gaussian2D, Identity

model = Gaussian2D(100, 25, 25, 5, 5) | Identity(1)
model.xname = 'x_mean'  # user-defined attribute
model_copy = model.copy()
model_copy.xname
```

title: Support WCS objects as inputs to `SkyCoord`s `frame=` argument
description:
Quite a common pattern in code making use of sunpy is something which looks like this:

```python
wcs = WCS(header)

my_point = SkyCoord(100*u.arcsec, 200*u.arcsec, frame=wcs_to_celestial_frame(wcs))
```
and then going onto transform that SkyCoord or plot it with WCSAxes or similar. This pattern has to be followed almost all the time in solar as our imaging WCSes have many more frame attributes than is common in astro, i.e. observer location, solar radius, obstime.

Coming out of [a long discussion](https://matrix.to/#/!TWSJXVpyflnZOzmSQz:matrix.org/$163603301686657igxFO:matrix.org?via=matrix.org&via=openastronomy.org&via=cadair.com) in the ndcube channel, I think that allowing WCSes as inputs as frames, and then converting them using the wcs machinery would be the cleanest way to support people wanting to do this. Without them having to import a helper function.

This would mean you could do:

```python
wcs = WCS(header)

my_point = SkyCoord(100*u.arcsec, 200*u.arcsec, frame=wcs)
```

and the SkyCoord constructor would go and call the relevant `wcs_to_celestial_frame` function (pending fixes to #12273 etc.).

If this sounds ok to people, I am happy to see if I can figure out the patches needed, but don't really want to dive into the 
`SkyCoord` constructor without an indication it will get merged.

title: Add ability to create `Time` objects with missing values
description:
In the [Missing Values](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/time/index.html#missing-values) section of the docs, there's a nice example of how to flag a `Time` entry as missing or invalid:

```python
from astropy.time import Time
import numpy as np

t = Time(['2001:020', '2001:040', '2001:060', '2001:080'],
         out_subfmt='date')
t[2] = np.ma.masked
```

I would like to **create** a `Time` object with a missing value already present, instead of flagging it after creation. I've tried the following, and none of them seem to work:

```python
Time(['2001-01-02T12:34:56', np.nan, '2001-02-03T00:01:02'])
Time(['2001-01-02T12:34:56', np.ma.masked, '2001-02-03T00:01:02'])
Time(['2001-01-02T12:34:56', '', '2001-02-03T00:01:02'])
Time(['2001-01-02T12:34:56', None, '2001-02-03T00:01:02'])
```

This is either a feature request, to support missing values in the `Time` constructor, or a documentation request if this is already available but not documented in [Missing Values](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/time/index.html#missing-values).

title: `MaskedQuantity` breaking `np.nanmean` etc. methods in `aggregate_downsample`
description:
### Description
A downstream issue lightkurve/lightkurve#1157 appears to have been triggered by the use of `Masked` objects, probably following #11127. The same code that returned a `timeseries` subclass with `Quantity` columns, "masked" with `np.nan` where applicable, with astropy 5.0rc1 is creating columns of `MaskedQuantity`. This is breaking any code using functions like `np.nanmean` that are currently not supported.

### Expected behaviour
`MaskedQuantity` should either fully support required array functions or not be used where still unsupported functions are required.

### Actual behaviour
For a more minimal example that can also be constructed in 4.3 (i.e. the `aggregate_downsample` failure is independently from its updates in 5.0) – note that the array functions do work for `np.ma.array`, but the NaNs don't seem to be correctly caught in the downsampling:
### Steps to Reproduce
```python
import numpy as np
from astropy import units as u
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy.timeseries import Timeseries, aggregate_downsample
from astropy.utils.masked import Masked

ma = np.ma.array([[1, 2, 13, 248, np.nan, np.nan, 303, 12, 21]], mask=np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])).T
np.nanmean(ma)
9.8

np.nanmean(ma.data)
85.71428571428571

mq = Masked(ma) * u.m
np.nanmean(qa)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "<__array_function__ internals>", line 5, in nanmean
TypeError: no implementation found for 'numpy.nanmean' on types that implement __array_function__: [<class 'astropy.utils.masked.core.MaskedQuantity'>]

tsa = TimeSeries(time=Time(np.arange(9)+4e4, format='mjd'), data=ma)
tsq = TimeSeries(time=Time(np.arange(9)+4e4, format='mjd'), data=mq)
aggregate_downsample(tsa, time_bin_size=3*u.d)
<BinnedTimeSeries length=3>
time_bin_start time_bin_size        col0      
                     s                        
    object        float64         float64     
-------------- ------------- -----------------
       40000.0      259200.0 5.333333333333333
40002.99999991      259200.0               nan
40005.99999982      259200.0              16.5

aggregate_downsample(tsq, time_bin_size=3*u.d)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/opt/lib/python3.10/site-packages/astropy/timeseries/downsample.py", line 127, in aggregate_downsample
    data[unique_indices] = u.Quantity(reduceat(values.value, groups, aggregate_func),
  File "/opt/lib/python3.10/site-packages/astropy/timeseries/downsample.py", line 28, in reduceat
    result.append(function(array[indices[i]:indices[i+1]]))

TypeError: no implementation found for 'numpy.nanmean' on types that implement __array_function__: [<class 'astropy.utils.masked.core.MaskedNDArray'>]

I am not sure how exactly the timeseries subclass in the downstream issue is instantiated, but the change to `MaskedQuantity` occurred with 5.0rc1 without any other code changes  (@barentsen may have more background on the read-in details). So the code should probably be more conservative in using Masked objects for now, or functions like `aggregate_downsample` will need to escape those methods applying them either to the `unmasked` instances or their numpy content.

title: the RADECSYS keyword is deprecated, use RADESYSa
description:
```
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.wcs import WCS
f = fits.open("output.fits")
w = WCS(f[0].header)
sky = w.pixel_to_world(30, 40)
print(sky)
```

and it gave me an warning:

```
WARNING: FITSFixedWarning: RADECSYS= 'FK5 ' 
the RADECSYS keyword is deprecated, use RADESYSa. [astropy.wcs.wcs]
```

But my `.fits` image header use `RADECSYS`, I tried: `w = WCS(f[0].header, relax=False)` and:
```
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.wcs import WCS
from astropy.wcs import WCSHDR_AUXIMG
from astropy.wcs import WCSHDR_RADECSYS
f = fits.open("output.fits")
w = WCS(f[0].header,relax=WCSHDR_AUXIMG | WCSHDR_RADECSYS)
sky = w.pixel_to_world(30, 40)
print(sky)
```
but the warning did not disappear.

The only solution is to use `f[0].header.rename_keyword('RADECSYS', 'RADESYSa')` to avoid the warning

Currently there is no way to define a model that is a convolution of a Fittable1DModel and a custom kernel (such as a tabulated line-spread function). Below is an example of desired usage assuming it is possible to modify astropy.convolution.convolve_models to work with numpy.arrays:

```
import numpy as np
from astropy.modeling.models import Gaussian1D
from astropy.convolution import convolve_models, CustomKernel

true_model = Gaussian1D(amplitude=1.0, mean=0.0, stddev=0.5)
kernel = np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 0.5, 0.0])
convolved_model_1 = convolve_models(true_model, CustomKernel(kernel))
convolved_model_2 = convolve_models(true_model, kernel)
```

The newly defined convolved model should be fittable like the input model. Currently attempting either versions of this fail because the kernel is not an astropy Model object.

title: Refactor WCSAxes to avoid calling Axes.contour to draw gridlines inside of drawing
description:
The failure in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/12431 was fixed in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/12437 but the underlying issue was not really fixed and can be reproduced witth the following code which triggers two draws:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from astropy.wcs import WCS
fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 1, 1, projection=WCS())
ax.grid(color='white', grid_type='contours')
fig.savefig('test.png')
fig.savefig('test.png')
```

This crashes with:

```
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'dpi'
```

with Matplotlib 3.5.0rc1 (not previous versions).

I managed to boil this down to the minimal example shown in https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/issues/21569 - as mentioned there by Matplotlib developers, calling ``ax.contour`` during drawing is a bad idea, and even more so removing the existing contour lines.

There are several long-term options I think at this point:

* Find a way to draw contours on-the-fly that doesn't require adding/removing artists from the axes and use that instead of ``ax.contour``. Unfortunately I think the contour-generating code in Matplotlib is private API (``matplotlib._contour``) so I'm not sure how we can do this. We could potentially come up with our own contour-drawing code which seems like a lot of effort.
* See if we can avoid the hack introduced in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/7098 so that we can once again do things like update contour lines etc at the start of ``Axes.draw`` which I *think* would solve the issue. There are two sub-options here to investigate: making it so that all plot elements are regular artists that are added to the axes (I can't remember anymore why this wasn't the case but I feel like there was a good reason at the time!), or better handling the zorder for ticks etc internally in a way that doesn't require the hack.

This is a reasonably urgent issue as users might potentially run into issues when Matplotlib  3.5 is released, so in the mean time I am going to open a PR for a quick fix which is to remove any grid contour lines at the very start of drawing. But I think we do want to think about how to improve/refactor this long-term.

title: Make scipy a required dependency
description:
I would like to suggest making scipy a required dependency of the core package (or some alternative approaches mentioned below).

There are a number of sub-packages in astropy where we use scipy where it's not obvious that would be the case and where users will encounter unexpected ImportErrors if it is not installed. For instance the following code snippets from the docs require scipy:

**astropy.coordinates**

```python
>>> c = SkyCoord(ra=ra1*u.degree, dec=dec1*u.degree, distance=distance1*u.kpc)
>>> catalog = SkyCoord(ra=ra2*u.degree, dec=dec2*u.degree, distance=distance2*u.kpc)
>>> idx, d2d, d3d = c.match_to_catalog_3d(catalog)  # REQUIRES SCIPY
```

**astropy.cosmology**

```python
>>> from astropy.cosmology import WMAP9 as cosmo
>>> cosmo.H(0)
<Quantity 69.32 km / (Mpc s)>
>>> cosmo.kpc_proper_per_arcmin(3)  # REQUIRES SCIPY
<Quantity 472.97709620405266 kpc / arcmin>
```

**astropy.units**
```python
>>> from astropy.cosmology import WMAP9
>>> z = 1100 * cu.redshift
>>> z.to(u.K, cu.with_redshift(WMAP9))
<Quantity 3000.225 K>
>>> z.to(u.Mpc, cu.with_redshift(WMAP9, distance="luminosity"))   # REQUIRES SCIPY
<Quantity 15418438.76317008 Mpc>
```

**astropy.convolution**
```python
>>> gauss_oversample = Gaussian1DKernel(3, mode='oversample', factor=10)
>>> gauss_integrate = Gaussian1DKernel(3, mode='integrate')   # REQUIRES SCIPY
```

**astropy.modeling**

scipy is also used extensively in modeling!

In all of these examples, there is no way the user would know in advance that scipy is required, and they will stumble on these issues and have to install scipy to get them to work. Now that scipy is needed for some of the functionality in at least five sub-packages, I think it is time to consider requiring it. In total, ``from scipy.`` appears 76 times in the astropy core package, and ``doctest-requires:: scipy`` appears 36 times!

As packaging has improved tremendously since the start of the project, and wheels and conda packages are available for scipy for many platforms, I think it would be reasonable to start requiring scipy and would result in fewer surprise errors for users.

The philosophy here is the same as why we added PyYAML as a required dependency - in many cases users couldn't have suspected this dependency.

To give a counter example of something I think doesn't need to be a required dependency, astropy.visualization provides lots of functionality to expand matplotlib, but in many cases matplotlib needs to be installed anyway for the user to want to use the functionality. Take a look at the following example:

```
    from astropy import units as u
    from astropy.visualization import quantity_support
    quantity_support()
    from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
    plt.figure(figsize=(5,3))
    plt.plot([1, 2, 3] * u.m)
```

Here matplotlib is imported explicitly anyway, and a user wouldn't be trying to use ``quantity_support`` without it installed.

Another counter-example would be the table reader/writer for HDF5 - in this case it's ok to error if h5py is not installed with an explicit error that says 'h5py is required to read/write HDF5' files.

Perhaps this requires an APE or a policy document describing some basic rules/tests we can use to determine if a dependency should be required.

**Alternatives**

I suspect there will be resistance to including scipy as a required dependency given that it may not be easy to install on some more exotic platforms. So here are some more options:

1. The option mentioned above, add scipy to ``install_requires``
2. In a lot of cases we might only be using a very limited subset of scipy, eg integration. We could try and replace scipy with another lighter weight dependency in these cases and require that.
3. We could make scipy a required dependency only on the main common platforms where wheels are available (this can be done in the requirements with [environment markers](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0496/)) and make sure that the test suite still passes without 
…（以下省略）

title: Arithmetic operation on dimensionless mag units
description:
### Description

Not sure whether this is a bug or just a misunderstanding: I am wondering how dimensionless units work; especially the conversion to linear.

### Expected behavior

I would expect that `u.mag` works equivalently to f.e. `u.ABmag` when it comes to conversion:

```python
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> m = 12 * u.ABmag
>>> print(m)
12.0 mag(AB)
>>> print(m.to(u.erg/u.s/u.m**2/u.Hz))
5.754399373371543e-21 erg / (Hz m2 s)
>>> flux = 1e-20 * u.erg/u.s/u.m**2/u.Hz
>>> print(flux.to(u.ABmag))
11.399999999999997 mag(AB)
```
i.e. `u.mag` should be convertible to and from a dimensionless unit.

### Actual behavior

```python
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> m = 1 * u.mag
>>> print(m)
1.0 mag
>>> print(m.to(''))
Traceback (most recent call last):

    raise UnitConversionError(
astropy.units.core.UnitConversionError: 'mag' and '' (dimensionless) are not convertible

title: Why looping through hdus at pos=2 in fits files is much slower than looping through hdus at pos=1?

Looping through hdu=2 is much slower (~10 times).

To reproduce you can do

from astropy.table import Table

title: Determine process for fixing changelog
description:
### Summary

During the release process, the release manager checks the changelog generated by towncrier and might find issues - typos, miscategorizations, etc. See https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/12478 for some examples. We need to determine the optimal way of dealing with such fixes.

### When the LTS release branch is the latest release branch

In the first 6 months after a new LTS release, there is only one release branch. At this point, the process is simple - any issues can be fixed directly in the generated changelog and committed to the release branch. This is because the news fragments are deleted and we then forward-port the deletion of the fragments to ``main`` so there are no more news fragments to worry about

### When there are two release branches

Once a non-LTS release is done, there are now two release branches which means that some news fragments will live in both, so we need to be a little more careful. There are several options at this point:

1. Make any changes to the news fragments in ``main`` and backport to both release branches. This will require resolving conflicts when backporting to the LTS branch since some of the news fragments may not exist there. 
2. Make any changes to the news fragments in the release branch, and forward-port that to ``main`` then backport to the other release branch. Then if the current active release being done is non-LTS, we have to then also forward-port the deletion of the news fragments to ``main`` in a separate PR. This is messy because it means several different backports/forward-ports and is just really confusing :exploding_head: 
3. Make any changes to the news fragments in the release branch, then 'side'-port that commit to the other release branch. The idea here is that the news fragments are going to get deleted anyway in ``main`` so why bother going via main when really the fixes just need to be in the release branches. This does still require potential conflict resolution when side-porting because not all news fragments will exist in the other release branch.
4. Follow the same process as when the LTS release is the only release branch, and just make the same changes - manually - in the LTS branch if needed (or if doing the LTS release before the other release, also do the changes manually in the other release branch)

One thing to consider is that once there are two release branches, the number of changes/bug fixes is going to slowly decrease in the LTS branch. In fact out of all the changes for the 5.0 release there were only 6 changes/fixes suggested by @eteq so it might be that no or only a couple of fixes are required to be made in the LTS branch at each release after 6 months. So it may be worth not over-engineering this and seeing if Option 4 is good enough. The other options require manual conflict resolution *anyway* so it might not be much work to do Option 4? If we want to not do it completely manually, then I would advocate Option 3 because it does not delay the release being done, whereas Option 1 does. Option 2 is just... no.

### If issues are caught between releases

If people notice issues with the generated changelog at https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/changelog.html#changelog and it's not release time, I think the correct process is to fix the fragments in ``main`` and mark the PR doing this as needing backporting to the relevant branches.

We have until the 5.1 release to figure this out :smile:

title: Feature Request: Radial Profile tool
description:
This issue is to resuscitate discussion on a radial profile tool in astropy, started here:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6078

Copying my [last comment on that thread](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6078#issuecomment-973208624):

I'd like to reopen discussion on this. We need to use radial profiling in several places in [radio-astro-tools](https://radio-astro-tools.github.io/) for PSF analysis.

The imexam code @pllim posted does not do what is implemented in [this PR](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6078), i.e., compute the azimuthal average over a specified range of radii, with optional binning.

@saimn pointed out that photutils apertures can be used for this, but I don't see any code.

Places this code (i.e., some form of radial profiling / azimuthal averaging) gets used:

<go to the [original post](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/6078#issuecomment-973208624) for a list of links, they didn't copy over>

Could this go in scipy or numpy? Probably not in ndimage; it's only 2D. scipy.signal is 1D. There's not an obvious other home for this, which is probably why it keeps getting reimplemented all over the place.

This belongs in astropy core. Whether [my implementation](https://github.com/keflavich/image_tools/blob/master/image_tools/radialprofile.py) is good enough is a different question.

title: ConfigNamespace is slow
description:
In investigating some performance issues for #12491 I found that a not-insignificant contributor is the performance of looking up values in `ConfigNamespace`.

It is actually quite slow if you look at the code, specifically for `ConfigItem.__get__`, which goes through quite a lot of steps of looking up the correct config object, reading the value from it, checking aliases, validating the value, etc.

This means that if some config option is used in a tight loop or in other common code paths it can be a bit of a drag.

For astropy.io.fits this comes up in particular for header parsing, for which there are a couple of different config options, and these get checked for *every single card* in a header when parsing its value (not a huge problem if you don't read every card in the header, but if you read a few hundred cards of each header it blows up).

I'm still analyzing exactly how much it contributes to the overall time of parsing headers, but it seems to be a significant component.  I have some ideas for fixing this but still experimenting.

title: astropy.cosmology.utils.aszarr does not take Column object
description:
astropy 5.0, `aszarr` in `astropy.cosmology.utils` does not treat Column object correctly. A Column object has the attribute 'unit', but does not have the method `to_value`. Passing a Column object to `aszarr` will get  `AttributeError: 'Column' object has no attribute 'to_value'`.

### Description
I am trying to create a WCSAxes plot that has a huge number of polygon artists on it. I want to set the polygons to be rasterized so that the image loads quickly in PDF viewers. Much to my surprise, I find that adding even a single rasterized polygon to a WCSAxes plot causes the axes frame to be drawn in the wrong place on the figure.

Even more puzzling, adding a grid to the axes causes the frame to be drawn in the correct position!

I notice that as I change the rcparam `figure.dpi`, the position and size of the incorrectly-drawn frame changes.

### Expected behavior
This is what the output looks like when there is a grid present. Observe that the frame is drawn correctly.

![grid-True](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/728407/145086520-79958962-ad72-4bcd-aa0c-c7180819b246.png)

### Actual behavior
This is what the output looks like when there is no grid present. Observe that the frame is drawn with the wrong position and size on the figure, well offset from the axes themselves.

![grid-False](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/728407/145086694-05bc92d6-8e1c-4f2c-88a7-1581c01b8dba.png)

### Steps to Reproduce
Here is a minimal example to reproduce the bug.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from astropy.wcs import WCS
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.utils.data import get_pkg_data_filename

filename = get_pkg_data_filename('galactic_center/gc_msx_e.fits')

hdu = fits.open(filename)[0]
wcs = WCS(hdu.header)

for grid in [False, True]:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw=dict(projection=wcs))

    ax.imshow(hdu.data, vmin=-2.e-5, vmax=2.e-4, origin='lower')
    ax.add_patch(plt.Polygon(
        [[-0.25, -0.25], [0.25, -0.25], [0.25, 0.25], [-0.25, 0.25]],
        transform=ax.get_transform('world'),
        rasterized=True))

    if grid:
        ax.grid(color='white', ls='solid')

    fig.savefig(f'grid-{grid}.pdf')
```

pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
LaTeX exponential notation formatting doesn't handle value of 1 properly and wrongly puts units in the exponent.

### Expected behavior
Not entirely clear how to format value of 1, but just `1` or `10^0` are both decent choices. The first seems more consistent, given that e.g. 1.5 is formatted as `1.5`.
Units should not be in exponent.

### Actual behavior
<!-- What actually happened. -->
1 without units is formatted as an empty string. 1 with units, e.g. 1 cm, is missing power index in the exponent.
Units enter the exponent.
<!-- Was the output confusing or poorly described? -->
This is confusing.

### Steps to Reproduce
<!-- Ideally a code example could be provided so we can run it ourselves. -->
<!-- If you are pasting code, use triple backticks (```) around
your code snippet. -->
<!-- If necessary, sanitize your screen output to be pasted so you do not
reveal secrets like tokens and passwords. -->

```python
import astropy.units as u
print(u.format.Latex.format_exponential_notation(1, ".1e"))
print(u.format.Latex.format_exponential_notation(1*u.cm, ".1e"))
print(u.format.Latex.format_exponential_notation(1.5*u.cm, ".1e"))
print(u.format.Latex.format_exponential_notation(.1*u.cm, ".1e"))
print(u.format.Latex.format_exponential_notation(.15*u.cm, ".1e"))
```
Output:
```

10^{ cm}
1.5 \times 10^{ cm}
10^{-1 cm}
1.5 \times 10^{-1 cm}
```
Expected output:
```
1
1 cm
1.5 cm
10^{-1} cm
1.5 \times 10^{-1} cm
```

import astropy

import numpy as np

from astropy.time import Time

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the bug. -->
Transforming coordinates that include a `radial_velocity` to or from `AltAz` fails with an obscure error. This is related to https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/12593.

This functionality is useful for observation planning and Doppler corrections. For example, if I know that an object has a given radial velocity in the `GalacticLSR` frame, I might want to know what the position is in the `AltAz` frame, so I know where to point the telescope, and what the radial velocity is in the topocentric frame, so that I can set my receiver system to observe the correct frequency.

coord = coord.transform_to(AltAz(location=location, obstime=obstime))

title: Remove extra arguments from `WCSAxes` `draw()` methods
description:
In Matplotlib every `draw()` method has a two arguments, `self` and `renderer`. In WCSAxes this is not the case however, and there are frequently other arguments to `draw()`. This causes at least a couple of issues when interacting with Matplotlib, most recently https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/12568. It also reduces legibility of the code in my opinion - drawing an object should only rely on the state of that object at draw time, not any extra parameters.

I am therefore in the process of refactoring `WCSAxes` to remove extra arguments to the `draw()` methods. This is going to require quite a bit of surgery, so I'm opening this issue to track the progress I make and PRs I open.

`draw()` methods that need fixing:
- [ ] `TickLabels.draw()` (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/14760)

title: Improve updating test images workflow
description:
I'm working on a PR that changes a test image, and the workflow for updating test images is very long:

1. Download each updated test image from circleCI
2. Rename each test image from `result.png` to the name of the test
3. Fork + clone https://github.com/astropy/astropy-data
4. Make a copy of the test image folder (this is as far as I got)
5. Rename the test image folder with the current timestamp
6. Put each test image in the right folder
7. Open a PR on https://github.com/astropy/astropy-data with the changes
8. Wait for this PR to be merged
9. Update the timestamp in `astropy.tests.image_tests` to point to the new images

In contrast, over in sunpy the process is:
1. Download new hashes of changed `.png` files from circleCI
2. Update the hash file in the PR

It would be great to try and improve the astropy experience - currently working through all these steps is a blocker on me working on some stuff. Some immediate thoughts I had:

- Make sure the new images on circleCI have the right filename (instead of `result.png`) would eliminate step 2
- Since the test data repo is version controlled, make use of that to remove the need to have multiple timestamped folders would eliminate steps 4 + 5
- It should be possible to completely automate the process, such that image tests are allowed to fail in PRs, but if a PR is accepted and merged a CI run on the `main` branch automatically uploads (or opens a PR for) the new reference figures to the astropy data repository.

title: Can't create ITRS coordinates from EarthLocations for sources that move along with the Earth
description:
Perhaps this is more of a question or feature request: Given an EarthLocation for some source object (basically, GPS coordinates) fixed relative to Earth, how can I turn this into a coordinate in ITRS (or any other frame), such that I can point my telescope at it by transforming it into the AltAz coordinates of my telescope?

For background: I'm trying to write software to point a telescope at planes and satellites.  For planes, I can get ADS-B data with their GPS coordinates, and I know my telescope's GPS coordinates.  But the discussions here:

https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/coordinates/common_errors.html#altaz-calculations-for-earth-based-objects

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/10983

suggest that it's not as simple as specifying EarthLocations for the plane and telescope, and converting the plane's EarthLocation to ITRS and thence into an AltAz with the telescope's location.  The explanation suggests that if I do that, the plane's ITRS location will be something like "where the plane, not moving with respect to the solar system barycenter, would have to have been, such that it would appear at the given location to an observer at the geocenter".  And that location can be hundreds of meters away from where the plane actually is, so the angles will be very wrong if the plane is close to the telescope.

In other words, the plane's location in ITRS seems to be tweaked to remove stellar aberration based on the Earth's motion around the sun.  But that seems correct only if the plane were not moving relative to the Sun.  Yet I specified the plane's position as an EarthLocation, so I'd expect it to move along with the Earth.  (I also never specified a time, so whatever velocity for Earth it's using in these calculations is arbitrary and surprising.)

The first link above shows a workaround, but that doesn't seem to include computing a coordinate for the plane that is "correct" in the sense that you could use it like any other coordinate to point your telescope at it by transforming it into AltAz.

I actually stumbled upon this while testing my own direct itrs_to_altaz() transform, which I was doing for performance reasons (and to avoid specifying an arbitrary obstime for the AltAz, without which, it crashes when transforming ITRS to AltAz).  And indeed, my result was slightly different from using itrs.transform_to(altaz) for nearby observers, probably in the same way as the issue linked above.

It's possible this is a bug in how AltAz treats the observer location EarthLocations, not doing the same inverse stellar aberration calculation that it does for incoming ITRS coordinates.  Or perhaps EarthLocation.get_itrs() would need to give a coordinate with differentials, so that the stellar aberration calculation could be cancelled out by a light time-of-flight calculation.  Or perhaps there's an easier, more straightforward way?

It's also possible that I'm just confused... any thoughts?

title: Matplotlib documentation base URL has moved
description:
### Description
It seems the base URL of the docs has changed at some point from https://matplotlib.org/ to https://matplotlib.org/stable/.
Intersphinx links to the old addresses are automatically redirected, but apparently stripped of the section references (the `..#matplotlib.widgets.EllipseSelector` part) in the process.
I could not find any cases of references directly into a section down a page in the core docs (the links still being redirected, but not losing relevant information), but a downstream example together with a fix is presented at https://github.com/astropy/regions/pull/392#issuecomment-1008090707.
So I propose to update the link in `docs/conf.py`

### Description
Creating a regularly space set of `Time` objects with `np.linspace` is quite slow:
```python
from astropy.time import Time, TimeDelta
import astropy.units as u
import numpy as np

dt = TimeDelta(1 * u.hour)
t0 = Time('2021-01-01')
t1 = Time('2022-01-01')
```
```python
%timeit Time(np.arange(t0, t1, dt))
3.13 s ± 443 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```
Manually converting to a float and calling arange on that is much faster:
```python
In [10]: %timeit Time(np.arange(t0.jd, t1.jd, dt.to_value(u.day)), format='jd')
360 µs ± 9.66 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000 loops each)
```
It would be nice to improve performance of the first option, so one doesn't have to convert back and forth to floats to get decent performance.

Working in an HPC environment, we routinely follow the guidelines for [using IERS code offline](https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/utils/iers.html#working-offline), including setting `iers.conf.auto_max_age = None`.  Previously, in #10126, we fixed some numerical issues with comparing floating point numbers to `None`.  However, that did not fix some overflow warnings which are distracting, to the point where some colleagues thought that actual time calculations were being corrupted (they are not).

### Expected behavior
<!-- What did you expect to happen. -->
`astropy.utils.iers.iers.LeapSeconds.auto_open()` should be able to handle `iers.conf.auto_max_age = None` gracefully.

In other words, if `iers.conf.auto_max_age = None`, simply pick a value for `good_enough` (in `auto_open()`, see below for link) that doesn't generate an overflow warning.  I actually contributed #10126, but I can't recall why that was not handled at that time.

description:
<!-- This comments are hidden when you submit the issue,
so you do not need to remove them! -->

Please be sure to check out our code of conduct,
https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md . -->

<!-- Please have a search on our GitHub repository to see if a similar
issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->

A significant number of currently open CCDData issues involving metadata (e.g., units, WCS, etc. #11851, #11727, #11325, #10977, #9883, #9397 ) could probably be resolved by adding a from_hdu method to CCDData.  Implementing the from_hdu method would be a trivial: simply pull most of the code from fits_ccddata_reader and make fits_ccddata_reader open the FITS file and call CCDData.from_hdu.

### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->
<!-- This part is optional. -->

Common(?) example: all raw files from the CCD are missing a BUNIT keyword, so in the current system, these files need to be read in with  `CCDData.read(fname, unit=u.adu)`.  Once they are read in, processed, and written to disk, possibly with a different unit (e.g. u.electron/u.s), they cannot be re-read by the code above, since that would clobber the proper units. Some different code would need to be used.  Currently, the only way to trigger different code is to guess based on the file's name or location (external metadata) or open the file with getheader or equivalent to inspect the internal metadata (the better place to look).  But then you need to re-open the file again to get all the machinery of fits_ccddata_reader to ingest all parts of the file.  Why not just work with an open HDU that can have its header(s) checked ahead of time and, if necessary, tweaked before the ingestion process is begun?

title: The problem with the use of finite differences in Astropy transforms.
description:
In radio astronomy, we often are given a set of RA/Dec coordinates along with a VLSR (LSR usually being what Astropy calls LSRK) for each source. From this, we would like to compute the radial velocity of the source in the rest frame of the observer and the sky frequency for a given line in order to tune our receiver. Say we would like to observe the Kleinmann–Low Nebula in Orion. In this case, we would like to set up a `SkyCoord`:
```
orionkln = SkyCoord('5h35m14.16s', '−5d22m21.5s', radial_velocity=9.0*u.km/u.s,
                  location=location, obstime=obstime, frame='lsrk')
```
This can be done, but it is not currently possible to do any transforms with it:
```
orionkln.transform_to(ICRS())
TypeError: Position information stored on coordinate frame is insufficient to do a full-space position transformation (representation class: <class 'astropy.coordinates.representation.UnitSphericalRepresentation'>)
```
This forces one to artificially add a distance and components of proper motion:
```
orionkln = SkyCoord('5h35m14.16s', '−5d22m21.5s', radial_velocity=9.0*u.km/u.s,
                  pm_ra_cosdec=0.0*u.mas/u.yr, pm_dec=0.0*u.mas/u.yr, 
                  distance=1.0*u.Mpc, location=location, obstime=obstime,
                  frame='lsrk')
```
Now the ICRS transform works and gives a reasonable result:
```
<SkyCoord (ICRS): (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    (83.809, -5.37263889, 1.)
 (pm_ra_cosdec, pm_dec, radial_velocity) in (mas / yr, mas / yr, km / s)
    (0.00045478, -0.00176109, 27.04595859)>
```
But if we try to transform this further, the result is ridiculous:
```
orionkln.transform_to(GCRS())
<SkyCoord (GCRS: obstime=2021-12-13T21:10:00.624, obsgeoloc=(0., 0., 0.) m, obsgeovel=(0., 0., 0.) m / s): (ra, dec, distance) in (deg, deg, Mpc)
    (83.81479755, -5.37231745, 1.)
 (pm_ra_cosdec, pm_dec, radial_velocity) in (mas / yr, mas / yr, km / s)
    (5305.56982374, -63394.60062949, -1939.63234404)>
```
I first came across this when I was investigating issue #12594 and much of what I am posting here is cross posted from there. At first, I was quite perplexed, but then I saw this documentation: https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/coordinates/velocities.html#finite-difference-transformations, so it seems that this is a well known problem. I also note that this documentation states:

> Future versions of Astropy will improve on this algorithm to make the results more numerically stable and practical for use in these (not unusual) use cases.

So I am raising this issue in an attempt to get a useful discussion going. I do realize that this has probably been discussed ad infinitum previously, but it's clearly an ongoing problem, so I am hoping that this issue won't be simply ignored. 

It seems to me that the problem here is the way that velocities are computed and intimately coupled to space motion. Using finite differences is rather compute intensive and clearly wildly inaccurate for anything beyond the solar system. Maybe I'm missing something, but it seems that finite differences are only needed for calculating the velocities of solar system objects that don't have an ephemeris such as comets, solar flares, etc. In fact, this is what stymied my ill-fated attempt at getting an astrometric frame implemented. 

Many stars have a known distance along with components of proper motion and radial velocity. For these, position and velocity vectors can be constructed and full 3D space motion can be derived. Parallax can be computed by subtracting the observer's position vector wrt the SSB from that of the target body and redshift can be computed by adding in the component of the observer's velocity wrt the SSB along the line of site to the target body's radial velocity. Please note here that components of the observer's velocity wrt the SSB should *NOT* be added in to the components of proper motion. Proper motion is defined as the *secular* rates of change in right ascension and declination (Explanatory Supplement, 3rd
…（以下省略）

title: Automation of IERS and leap second table updates
description:
This issue is to discuss what we want to do regarding automating updates to the IERS and leap second tables. In https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/10500 @pllim experimented with a proof of concept of updating the tables automatically which worked but @mhvk pointed out that we might not want to pollute the git history with too many updates as at least one of the files has a lot of lines that can change.

I would still advocate for e.g. completely automated monthly updates - that's only 12 pull requests in a year, and would reduce the burden on release managers to have to do the update before/during the release process. The update I did just now for 5.0.1 only had 100 lines change (https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/12756) so I don't think it's going to dominate the git history in any way.

Another question aside from cadence is how to actually completely automate it - in #10500 @pllim used batchpr but that still requires a cron job on a physical machine somewhere. Can we automate this via an actions cron job instead for example?

by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->
In `astropy.io.misc.yaml` there are currently a set of tags/constructors/representers for different astropy objects, including quantities.
These work well, but they are extremely verbose, which makes YAML configuration files that include many astropy quantities quite hard to read. I was wondering whether a syntax like the following might not be desirable:

```
x: !quantity 300.0 | m
```
(as compared to the current):

```
x: !astropy.units.Quantity
  unit: !astropy.units.Unit {unit: m}
  value: 300.0
```

I assume it is considered good practice to namespace YAML tags, which is probably why this is done currently in astropy. However, the tags are then super duper long. It might be possible to have the best of both worlds by including a function in astropy like `register_short_yaml_tags()` which registers the tags/constructors/representers I here describe.

Using the pipe symbol to separate value from unit is kind of arbitrary -- it just needs to be a symbol that won't need to be used in defining either the value or the unit themselves. I think the pipe kinda looks nice. 

The implementation in the constructor would be something like:

```python
def _constructor(loader, node):
    val, unit = node.value.split('|'))
    val = float(val)
    return u.Quantity(val, unit, copy=False)
```

title: Can't open paths beginning with ~
description:
### Plan

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/13107#issuecomment-1104552457

### Description
`astropy.io.fits` can't open files when the path is given with a `~` representing the home directory, e.g. `fits.getdata("~/data/file.fits")`. Instead, the home directory must be spelled out, e.g. `fits.getdata("/home/sam/data/file.fits")`. This can be fixed by passing paths to `os.path.expanduser`, which should do the right thing across operating systems.

There was some discussion about `expanduser` in #10705, and it looks like the function is now in use for finding the Astropy configuration directory.

There is also [precedent in Sunpy](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/blob/main/sunpy/util/io.py#L26), where `expanduser` (as wrapped by `pathlib`) is used for paths passed to Sunpy's `Map` object, so that `sunpy.map.Map("~/data/file.fits")` works. (`Map` is their general object for loading, manipulating and plotting data).

If there's not a reason to avoid adding calls to `os.path.expanduser`, I'm happy to dig into the code and prepare a PR. I'm most interested in the FITS loader, but I might take a look at the rest of `astropy.io`. (The Github search tool doesn't show any uses of `expanduser` there.)

### Expected behavior
`astropy.io.fits.getdata("~/data/file.fits")` loads the file `file.fits` in the `data` directory within the user's home directory.

### Actual behavior
`astropy.io.fits.getdata("~/data/file.fits")` raises `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '~/data/file.fits'`

### Steps to Reproduce

Attempt to load a FITs file in the user's home directory, giving a path beginning with a `~` representing the path to the user's home directory.

### Description
<!-- Provide a general description of the feature you would like. -->
<!-- If you want to, you can suggest a draft design or API. -->
<!-- This way we have a deeper discussion on the feature. -->
I sometimes want to have the option to pass non-quantity objects to a function (because they may come from such a source) that I know have the right physical quantity, but are floats/arrays and not astropy.quantity objects. 

I find it cumbersome to check if they are quantities and convert if they are not, although I now use the shortcut:
``` a = a << u.desired_quantity ```

With this shortcut, if a is convertible, it will be converted, similar to `quantity_input` decorator, BUT ALSO, if a is NOT a quantity object, it will be converted to a quantity object assuming it's in units of u.desired_quantity.

Obviously, there is some danger to this. However, it also allows reusing functions across different codebases, where sometimes you are working with astropy quantity objects, and other times you are not, but you know the unit.

Since the `<<` operator is somewhat cumbersome, for functions with a lot of arguments, it can take many lines to do this on a per function basis. If myfunc has 10 arguments, then it takes 10 lines to accomplish the above. A decorator is a nice way of doing this in a single line, so would be appreciated.

In addition, i think that the usecase I show above should possibly be included in the docs, under https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/units/quantity.html#creating-and-converting-quantities-without-copies , as searching for assigning quantity to non-quantity object returns several results on google, which lead to `quanity_input`, but this decorator doesn't actually do assignment, just conversion of quantity objects and strict quantity checking. 

For implementation details, I can see a few options, but I will leave it up to someone experienced with `quanity_input` decorator.

- Modify `quanity_input` decorator to have `force_convert=False`, which can be changed to `True` to convert args that are marked as a quantity using the above shortcut. This would also nicely skip args not meant to be converted since quantity_input already nicely deals with those as well as annotions. The docts would be changed to (bolded additions): "...If the argument has no unit attribute, i.e. it is not a Quantity object, a ValueError will be raised unless the argument is an annotation **or force_convert=True**. This is to allow non Quantity annotations to pass through"
- Create a new decorator to do forced conversions (the only difference being instead of raising a ValueError, the decorator forces a conversion to equivalent unit.
- Make an optional argument for `Quantity` that forces non-quantity objects to be tried to be converted first. This would be very destructive but the idea: 
```
q = Quantity(10.0, unit=u.unit, force_convert=True)
a = 10.0
print(q + a)
```
would give 20 * u.unit instead of `UnitConversionError`.

My preferred option would be a separate decorator that can extend quantity_input, just to make it really difficult for people to misuse this. I know that the alternative is to force conversions to quantity instances or force all quantities into the "known" unit and take their values. But sometimes mixing is just easy and

title: On a decoder for `JsonCustomEncoder`
Decrease import time of affiliated packages
description:
I've noticed that astropy-affiliated packages take a long time to import. For example, `from astroquery.heasarc import Heasarc` takes 0.9 seconds on my laptop, and `import pyvo` takes 1.1 seconds. That's a little longer than it takes to import ALL of numpy, scipy, matplotlib, astropy, pandas, sklearn, bokeh, and PySide6.

This can be rather frustrating for certain users (e.g., when these packages are embedded into GUIs where the end-user doesn't know that there's a background Python process importing packages which is what's causing the delay to the application startup).

I looked into why this might be, and I found a package named Tuna (https://github.com/nschloe/tuna; see how to use it for examining imports at https://stackoverflow.com/a/51300944). Here are the results for running the two import statements above:
[tuna - astroquery.log.pdf](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/files/7960199/tuna.-.astroquery.log.pdf)
[tuna - pyvo.log.pdf](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/files/7960200/tuna.-.pyvo.log.pdf).

The biggest single-item contributions to the long import time that I see is that 0.3 seconds is spent importing Dask and 0.17 seconds is spent importing Astropy's TestRunner. I suspect that both of these are unnecessary for most astropy-affiliated packages, and removing them from imports might not be too hard.

Regarding TestRunner:
Affiliated packages are required to have the line `from ._astropy_init import *` in their __init__.py file (ex. https://github.com/astropy/astroquery/blob/main/astroquery/__init__.py and https://github.com/astropy/pyvo/blob/main/pyvo/__init__.py). _astropy_init.py has the line `astropy.tests.runner import TestRunner`. If this is only used for developer testing, I don't think this needs to be imported by users.

Regarding Dask:
I'm not so sure what exactly is going on here. Is Dask actually need for all applications? Generally the FITS files that I'm working with are small, so if Dask is just being used to speed up file reads, I'd be much happier sacrificing the <0.01 seconds that I'm expecting Dask is contributing to reading a FITS file to get rid of the 0.3 seconds that it takes for the import. Is there a way to make this import optional?

title: Human readable ecsv table
description:
I find the ecsv extremely useful, I'm a great fan of including units, comments and descriptions in the tables. The only downside of this format is that I can't obtain a ecsv (with a comma as a delimiter, since it guarantees max compatibility) that has all the commas aligned. I realize that it is not in the specs of the format to have all the commas aligned, but researchers that I know,  that are interested in using tables in astropy,  are not adopting it because they can't read the table with their eyes from the ASCII file. So they try to use fixed-size tables, which produce issue with descriptions and units, leading them to abandon any effort to switch to astropy tables. 

I tried to experiment, and a MWE is: 

```import numpy as np
from astropy.table import Table

a = np.array([1.20, 1.21, 2.22])
b = np.array(['u', 'g', 'egr'])
c = np.array([4.20, 1.00, 2.20])

t = Table()
t['a'] = a
t['b'] = b
t['c'] = c

t.write('tmp.txt', format='ascii.ecsv', delimiter=',', strip_whitespace=False,  overwrite=True)
```

resulting in
```# %ECSV 1.0
# ---
# datatype:
# - {name: a, datatype: float64}
# - {name: b, datatype: string}
# - {name: c, datatype: float64}
# delimiter: ','
# schema: astropy-2.0
a,b,c
1.2,u,4.2
1.21,g,1.0
2.22,egr,2.2
```

I modified the file `astropy/astropy/io/ascii/ecsv.py` of the tag v5.0.1, line 383, from `return str(col[idx])` to `return str(col[idx]).rjust(4)` and as an output I get

```
# %ECSV 1.0
# ---
# datatype:
# - {name: a, datatype: float64}
# - {name: b, datatype: string}
# - {name: c, datatype: float64}
# delimiter: ','
# schema: astropy-2.0
a,b,c
 1.2,   u, 4.2
1.21,   g, 1.0
2.22, egr, 2.2
```
which is what I wanted. Of course this is not the way to go, and probably I'm breaking also something somewhere else, but would it be possible to obtain such a feature? My operating system is High Sierra, python 3.9.7 intel, numpy 1.21.2, astropy 5.0.1.

issue has already been posted.
If a similar issue is closed, have a quick look to see if you are satisfied
by the resolution.
If not please go ahead and open an issue! -->

<!-- Please check that the development version still produces the same bug.
You can install development version with
pip install git+https://github.com/astropy/astropy
command. -->

### Description
The 'convolve' function accepts a boundary argument to control how the convolution filter should handle edges. The conservative approach None (values set to zero where the kernel extends beyond the edge of the array) cannot be used because the argument has the default value 'fill' in the function definition.

https://docs.astropy.org/en/stable/api/astropy.convolution.convolve.html#astropy.convolution.convolve

### Expected behavior
`convolve(array, kernel, boundary=None)` should set values to 0 when the kernel extends outside the data.

### Actual behavior
`convolve(array, kernel, boundary=None)` is interpreted as `convolve(array, kernel, boundary='fill')`, so that the documented None value can never be passed to the function.

One way to fix it would be to follow the docstring and use the string 'None'. That requires updating BOUNDARY_OPTIONS = ['None', 'fill', 'wrap', 'extend'] in convolve.py, as well as updating several conditions based on `if boundary is None`.

### Description
