title: Table column related WCS
description:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

I have a number of (FITS) tables that use WCS to describe arrays within table cells, as described in the [WCS paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0207407.pdf) section 3.1. Here basically, each column is associated with a WCS header that has a format slightly differing from the "normal" (global) one. In my case, this is like
```
1CTYP1  = 'AWAV    '           / Grating dispersion function (air)
1CUNI1  = 'Angstrom'           / Wavelength unit
1CRPX1  =                    1 / Pixel zeropoint
1CRVL1  =               3700.0 / Wavelength zeropoint
1CDLT1  =                 0.25 / Wavelength increment
```
where the leftmost "1" is the axis, and the rightmost one is the column index. See table 2 of the paper for a full list of keywords here.

I would like to be able to handle these WCS header within Astropy.

Asking on Slack showed that this is probably not implemented yet.

### Describe the desired outcome

The optimal outcome would be if this could be transparently handled within a table (column). 

Probably the optimal variant would be if the WCS related headers would be bound to the column and renamed into their "usual" variants when a file was read in (i.e. "1CTYP2" --> "CTYPE1"). When writing a FITS file, the column-specific names could be re-generated. This would ensure that the WCS keywords stay correct even when the columns were re-arranged. Also, this would expose familiar keywords to the user, and to the WCS subpackage. Also, exporting table cells as images with a proper WCS would be simple.

The WCS subpackage then could take them as 
```Python
from astropy.wcs import WCS

flux_wcs = WCS(tbl['flux'].meta)
```
or similar without larger changes there. One could even think of a `tbl['flux'].wcs` property (readable and maybe writeable).

title: Discussion of the consistency checks
description:
# Background

Currently, `astropy` maintains three primary branches:

1. The `main` (development) branch.
2. The current bugfix branch (currently `5.3.x`).
3. The LTS branch (currently `5.0.x`); however, the acceptance of [APE21](https://github.com/astropy/astropy-APEs/pull/82) will end this soon.

For the vast majority of changes, they are PRs made against the `main` branch unless they are specific to an issue only present in the other two. We then mark these PRs in the following ways:

- If those changes are determined to be relevant to the other branches, we attempt to use the `meekseeks` bot to "backport" them to those branches (and then manually backport them if the bot fails). Those backports are controlled via setting specific labels on the PR in question, which then tell `meeseeks` if/where to backport the PR. It does this by opening a PR against the backport branches.
- Somewhat separately, we also try (and sometimes fail) to set milestones on the PRs. Those milestones are supposed to correspond to the oldest (lowest) version of `astropy` we expect the change to appear in. For example
	- if it is an LTS bugfix, it would currently get `5.0.7`.
	- if it was only going to the bugfix branch it would currently get `5.3.1`.
	- If it was a new feature and not a bugfixe it would currently get `6.0.0`.

  Essentially, these milestones are used to track where/when a particular change will or has appeared in `astropy`.

Clearly, these to processes are related e.g.

- If something has a `backport-v5.0.x` label, we would currently expect it to have a `5.0.7` milestone and vice versa.
- If something only has a `backport-v5.3.x` label, we would expect it to have a `5.3.1` milestone and vice versa.
- If something does not have a backport label, we would expect it to have a `6.0.0` milestone and vice versa.

However, they are currently two separate unlinked steps we expect (hope) our maintainers to perform sometime before merging a pull request. This tends to introduce human errors, which tend to undermine consistency the checks usefulness (assuming they are working).

# Consistency Checks

It is my understanding that the consistency checks are intended to ensure that all the changes we intend to first appear in a given `astropy` version actually appear in that version. By this I mean:

1. For "backport" versions, all the backport pull requests opened by the bot (or manually created when it fails) are merged.
2. The backport bot has actually run on all PRs intended to be backported to the backport version in question. This is because the bot can sometimes be "down" and not get triggered; meaning, it does not create the backport PR nor does it mark the PR in question for manual backport.
3. For all versions, the PRs marked with a given milestone have been merged. Note that the backport bot will set the milestone on its PR to be the same as the origin PR's.

I understand that the code supporting the consistency checks is both a bit flaky (sometimes it is just broken) and can be tricked by PRs not having the correct labels/milestones set. Both these issues tend to create "problems" for determining if a branch is ready to have its release made.

# Possible PR Level Changes to Alleviate Consistency Check Issues

Most of my ideas revolve around preventing the "human" errors that will make it difficult for any consistency check solution to be completely accurate. That is making sure the backport labels and milestones are in some sort of agreement.

I propose that we add a required CI check to our current PR CI, which does two things:

1. Requires a "backport" related label to be set. For the case that the change will not be backported, I propose a `no-backport` label be created to fill this purpose.
2. Uses the label added by the maintainers to "compute" (determine) what the milestone for the PR should be.
3. If a milestone is already present, check that the computed and listed milestones match (fail if they do not). If no milestone is prese
…（以下省略）

title: Improve consistency of Table sorting
description:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

Currentlly there are at least 3 different implementations of sorting columns and none of them seem quite right.

- `Table.argsort()` makes a numpy structured array using `.as_array()` and calls argsort. So for a `Time` column this will make an object column with each row as a new `Time` object. Bad. And `Table.argsort` exposes a `kind` kwarg which will cause an exception when sorting the table on a `Time` column. https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/aa2c05dc222f36630c4bff7ca2b0c1f676b29561/astropy/table/table.py#L3444-L3445
-  `table/groups.py` uses `represent_mixins_as_columns` to flatten the sorting table. This is one way to do it but for `Time` this gives columns with `jd1` and `jd2` instead of using the `info.get_sortable_arrays()` machinery. https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/aa2c05dc222f36630c4bff7ca2b0c1f676b29561/astropy/table/groups.py#L79
-  `table/index.py` does something different as well, making a list of columns to sort lexically, including a special-case for `Time` that repeates the `get_sortable_arrays` code. https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/aa2c05dc222f36630c4bff7ca2b0c1f676b29561/astropy/table/index.py#L103

It seems like the ideal way to argsort a list of table columns is to call `info.get_sortable_arrays` on each one and assemble all the results into a list of arrays which are then passed to `np.lexsort`. But one problem is that this (once again) would render moot the `kind` argument of `Table.argsort` (and `Table.sort`).


### Describe the desired outcome

More unified and consistent approach to sorting table columns.

### Additional context

Performance and API changes are potential concerns.

title: Switch to squash commits
description:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

We use merge commits, which preserve all the commits in a PR. While this sounds good, in practice the costs outweigh the benefits. In particular, it is a significant hurdle for contributors.

Pros:
- breaking up a large PR into more atomic commits in the git history
- Reverting a change

Cons:
- Experienced contributors constantly squashing commits in their own PRs
- Having to teach new contributors how to squash commits
- Having to review a PR and think about the number of commits in the PR versus the actual content.


Practically though, how often do we revert? And how often do we comb the git history? The answer to both feels like "not too often". Since most of our PRs are small, trying to understand a change by looking at a single commit in the git history versus a whole PR will be minimally impacted. Only the rarer large PR will make git combing / bisecting harder.

OTOH we have this (in my experience) large barrier to entry by asking contributors to master the minutiae of git.
It starts with a maintainer making a seemingly innocuous request like "please squash to a few atomic commits", but if the current set of commits its messy, with half an idea in one commit and the other half in another, then this is a highly non-trivial request. Changing the git history can be very challenging unless one is doing the simplest of operations, like squashing adjacent commits. Rearranging commits, splitting a commit in half and combining it with other commits, etc. are all hard, yet we currently expect this in PRs. Why? Why don't we just squash the commits.

**One PR => one "big" idea in the git history**
**If you want to see all the little ideas, don't look at the git history, look at the PR** which records the discussion and all commits that got squashed.



### Describe the desired outcome

We switch to Squash Commits.
So many projects, big and small, use this simple solution to lower maintainer burden and barrier-to-entry.

Contributors don't need to master git, they can just push as many commits as they want.
Reviewers don't need to think about the commits -- how atomic they are, how many there should be -- only the actual contribution to Astropy.
When a PR is ready we don't need to then wait to squash it down, it's just good to (squash) merge right away.

### Additional context

I have heard from a number of people that they would contribute to Astropy but find it overly burdensome because of how our PR review process is set up. They want a detailed and automated CI and expect their PRs to be merged if they pass the CI, with minimal back and forth with reviewers about style and commits, only about the actual code performance, design, and relevancy.
IMO me hearing this is a large problem. If I'm hearing this from a few people, how many am I not hearing from?
This is one of the many reasons some of us originally championed black and Ruff: to eliminate style discussions in contributions.
While the ruff adoption is ongoing, due to our large technical debt, I think black has been a smashing success.
IMO squashing commits is the next way we lower the barrier to contribution and reduce the time from PR opening to merge.



```[tasklist]
### Tasks
- [ ] Enable squash commits
- [ ] Disable merge commits
- [ ] Live long and prosper
```

Some time ago we added an optional feature to allow users to unshallow their Git repository when cloning them as part of the build process. This feature is going to be removed, as it is now user-configurable.

With the introduction of [build process customization](https://docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/build-customization.html) via `build.jobs` and `build.commands`, this feature is not required anymore and we are deprecating it. title: Table.write(format='ascii.ecsv') ignores formats keyword and column attribute
description:
### Description

When writing a table, the format of the output can be specified with either the `formats` keyword or the `Column.format` attribute. However, when the output file format is `ascii.ecsv` both of these are ignored.

### Expected behavior

That the output file would be formatted as specified (see How to Reproduce for example)

### How to Reproduce

```python
from astropy.table import Table
import numpy as np
x = np.arange(10)/13
tbdata = Table([x], names=['x'])
formats={'x':'%1.2f'}
tbdata.write('test.ecsv', formats=formats)
```


Produces:
```
# %ECSV 1.0
# ---
# datatype:
# - {name: x, datatype: float64}
# schema: astropy-2.0
x
0.0
0.07692307692307693
...
0.6923076923076923
```

while 
```python
tbdata.write('test.asc', format='ascii', formats=formats)
```

Produces:
```
x
0.00
0.08
...
0.69
```

```python
tbdata['x'].format='%1.2f'
```

title: Should astropy move 32bit CI to weekly.
description:
~`numpy` stopped providing wheels for 32-bit systems starting with `numpy 1.22`. Since NEP 29 recently dropped `numpy 1.21` support, per APE 18 `astropy` needs to drop support for it as well.~

~In #15006, we start the process of dropping support for `numpy 1.21` however, it appears that since `numpy` does not provide 32 bit wheels in `1.22+` the [32-bit and parallel CI](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/7c3025269e1ea911019e40a60a9eb85f4e2c3218/.github/workflows/ci_workflows.yml#L110-L141) no longer functions properly without serious work to get `numpy` to build in our 32bit environment.~

`numpy` stopped providing wheels for 32-bit systems starting with `numpy 1.22`. However, NEP 29 indicates that `numpy` recently dropped `numpy 1.21` support, per APE 18 `astropy` needs to drop support for `numpy 1.21` as well.

This leads to an issue with our CI. Namely, PR #15006 starts the process of dropping `numpy 1.21` support, however due to the lack of 32-bit wheels on PyPi for `numpy 1.22+` the [32-bit and parallel CI](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/7c3025269e1ea911019e40a60a9eb85f4e2c3218/.github/workflows/ci_workflows.yml#L110-L141) no longer functions properly because we currently do not have an environment setup to build these wheels.

The current discussion in this Issue indicates that we should not drop 32-bit testing if we can avoid it. This leaves two possibilities:

1. Get `numpy 1.22` to build in the current 32-bit and parallel CI job. This appears to be fairly complex and will require extensive modifications to the existing workflows to get functional.
2. Move the 32-bit CI to the Weekly Cron CI. This is much simpler as we already have CI set up to run the astropy tests on non-standard architectures, and we can add a 32-bit architecture to the list of architectures this job is run on. In this job, we pull a version of `numpy` built and maintained by Debian from the Debian package manager; meaning, we do not have to support figuring out how to build `numpy` on these architectures.

In my opinion option 2 will be better for us to use as 32-bit systems are becoming increasingly "non-standard", and it alleviates our need to figure out how to build `numpy` in this circumstance. The main downside is that errors normally caught by the 32-bit job (though fairly rare) will not be caught at the PR level, but later when the Weekly Cron is run. In the cases where we suspect 32-bit or other architectures may cause issues we have the `Extra CI` label which will run the Daily and Weekly Cron jobs on the PR. One other downside of moving the 32-bit job to the Weekly CI is that it is integrated into our parallel and "double" testing job. In this case the 32-bit portion can be removed from the job and the parallel portion can be moved to one of the other jobs.

title: Incorrect type for columns in GAIA results VOTable
description:
[Edit:] - This issue has been moved up from astroquery, as problem is on the upstream, astropy level. For details see comment https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/15394#issuecomment-1736075742

=======

Original issue text:

I tried downloading a table from GAIA:

```
>>> import astropy.units as u
>>> from astroquery import gaia
>>> tab = gaia.Gaia.query_object_async('Messier 45', 90*u.arcmin)
```

and noticed that some of the columns are object type even though they just contain strings:

```
>>> tab['DESIGNATION'].dtype
dtype('O')
```

This causes all kinds of issues when trying to serialize the table to different file formats.
